The Auditor General said the audit procedures were designed based on assessed risks of material misstatement, including those arising from fraud or error, and included an evaluation of accounting policies, estimates and the overall presentation of the financial statements.

The release of the report comes amid heightened public scrutiny of government spending, revenue collection and financial accountability, making the Legislature’s promised consideration of the GAC’s recommendations a key next step in determining whether the identified issues will result in corrective action.

World.title: CAF CUP: Malagasy side plots Arrows fall
World.content:
Madagascar’s FC Rouge have arrived in Zambia ahead of their CAF Confederation Cup first round preliminary first leg against Red Arrows FC set for this Saturday at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium.

‎

‎A 42-member delegation, comprising a 23-man playing squad plus technical staff and club officials, touched down at Simon Mwansa Kapwepwe International Airport on Wednesday at 15:45 hours aboard an ET flight via Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

‎

‎The visitors were received by officials from the Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) and Red Arrows FC.

‎

‎Speaking upon arrival, FC Rouge head coach Fenososa Maldini said the team was ready for the continental battle and impressed with the reception in Ndola.

‎

‎“We are happy with the way we have been received. From what we have seen so far, we believe our stay here will be good,”_ Maldini said.

‎

‎The Malagasy tactician admitted preparations were tough but said his side did its homework.

‎

‎“We did prepare very well although it is always difficult we will try to persevere,” he said.

‎

‎“We only tried to find out more about Red Arrows through social media. We did our homework and we are here with an ambition to get a positive result. Our objective is to win the first round,” Maldini added.

‎

‎The FC Rouge delegation has checked into Kwetu Lodge in the Dola Hill area of Ndola where they will base and finalize preparations ahead of the match.

‎

‎The encounter on Saturday, 5 September 2026 at 15:00 hours at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium carries significant continental stakes, with both sides seeking a first-leg advantage ahead of the return fixture in Madagascar.

‎

‎Red Arrows will be banking on home support as they kick off their African campaign, with anticipation building for what promises to be a fiercely contested CAF Confederation Cup tie.

President Putin expressed confidence that President Hichilema’s leadership will contribute to further strengthening the friendly relations that exist between Russia and Zambia.

World.title: Nalolo leaders commend President’s call for unity
World.content:
Nalolo District Commissioner Namatama Mupo has described President Hakainde Hichilema’s inauguration speech as a call for unity, hard work and service delivery for all Zambians.

Reacting to the President’s address, Ms Mupo said the Head of State has continued to champion the One Zambia, One Nation motto by urging citizens to reject tribalism, violence and hate speech.

Ms Mupo emphasised that the President’s focus remains on strengthening the economy, lowering the cost of living and positioning Zambia on the global stage.

“The President has walked the talk before and we believe he will deliver even more this time. His leadership is God-fearing, and his vision is to unite the country while ensuring no one is left behind,” Ms Mupo stated.

She noted that the directive for public servants to dedicate themselves beyond stipulated working hours demonstrates the President’s commitment to accelerating development.

“Work is 24/7, as long as there is work to be done. That is the spirit we must embrace if we are to meet the people’s expectations,” she added.

The District Commissioner further stressed the importance of building a strong and dedicated team to implement government policies effectively, adding that it is vital to have a hardworking team in place to deliver the much-needed development to the people of Zambia.

Ms Mupo reaffirmed Nalolo District’s support for the President’s ideologies and policies, saying the community remains confident in his leadership and vision for the nation.

She further underscored that the Grow Zambia Agenda outlined by the President, focusing on economic expansion, opportunity, and prosperity must be embraced at district level to ensure that every household benefits from national progress.

Meanwhile, Nanjucha Ward Councilor-elect Manyando Mushokabanji has echoed the District Commissioner’s sentiments, describing the President’s speech as a love song for every well-meaning Zambian.

Mr Mushokabanji said the message of unity and inclusiveness provides a strong foundation for development at both national and local levels.

“The President has set the tone for servant leadership. As elected representatives, we must dedicate ourselves to working with the people, respecting one another, and ensuring that development reaches every corner of our communities,” he said.

Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to supporting the President’s vision, stressing that teamwork and dedication among public servants will be key to delivering the much-needed development in Nalolo District and across the country.

World.title: Chiengi couple burnt to death
World.content:
An elderly couple has died after their grass-thatched house was allegedly set ablaze by unknown people in Chienge district, Luapula Province.

The deceased have been identified as 70 year old John Kaweme and his 65 year old wife, Chilombo Idah, of Kalembwe Kabobo village in Chief Puta’s area.

Luapula Province Police Commissioner Lucky Munkhondya has confirmed the incident, saying it occurred on August 31, 2026, around 01:00 hours.

Ms Munkhondya said police received a report around 02:00 hours from 35 year old Peter Musonda, a nephew to the deceased, who reported that his uncle and aunt had died after their house was set on fire.

She said police officers rushed to the scene and confirmed the incident, where they found the bodies of the couple burnt beyond recognition.

The bodies were retrieved, while police have since opened a docket and commenced investigations to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and identify those responsible.

World.title: CSDG welcomes Hichilema’s inaugural address
World.content:
Centre for Sustainable Democracy and Governance (CSDG) Executive Director Caroline Katotobwe says President Hakainde Hichilema’s inaugural address, provided hope and confidence that government remains focused on issues affecting ordinary Zambians, particularly the high cost of living.

Dr Katotobwe told the media in an interview today that the President’s declaration that lowering the cost of living is a priority, demonstrates that the government is responsive to the concerns of citizens.

She has called on Zambians to put aside political differences and work collectively towards achieving national development goals.

Dr Katotobwe emphasised that development cannot be achieved when citizens are pulling in different directions, adding that national unity and peace will be essential to delivering tangible benefits at grassroots level.

She has expressed confidence that the second term will focus on implementing programmes whose groundwork was laid during the first five years.

She has also welcomed President Hichilema’s emphasis on unity, peace and inclusivity, saying these are critical foundations for national development.

Dr Katotobwe has since urged Zambians to embrace the President’s call for unity and work towards building a Zambia that benefits both the current and future generations.

World.title: Education sector reacts to President Hichilema’s inauguration speech
World.content:
The National Union of Public and Private Educators of Zambia (NUPPEZ) has welcomed Government’s move to increase investment in education by employing more teachers, constructing additional classrooms and improving teachers’ welfare.

Speaking on the President Hakainde Hichilema’s second-term priorities, NUPPEZ Executive President Charity Kampamba says continued investment in education is essential to producing a skilled population and accelerating national development.

Dr Kampamba stated that the call follows the increase in school enrolment resulting from the introduction of free education, which has placed pressure on existing infrastructure and teaching staff.

She said some classrooms now accommodate between 80 and 90 learners, making it difficult for teachers to effectively manage classes and deliver quality education.

She has called for improved conditions for teachers, particularly those serving in rural areas, saying a motivated workforce is critical to improving the quality of education.

Dr Kampamba further called on the government to ensure that learners have adequate teaching and learning materials, including individual reading materials, instead of sharing books among several pupils.

She commended the UPND administration for its first-term interventions in the education sector, including free education, the recruitment of 30,000 teachers and the expansion of the school feeding programme, adding that the programmes have contributed to increased school enrolment, improved learner retention and greater access to education.

She however, appealed to other stakeholders to complement government efforts in areas such as school construction and the provision of learning materials.

Dr Kampamba has since urged the government to sustain its free education and school feeding programmes while increasing funding towards the construction of classrooms and recruitment of teachers.

Meanwhile, Bridgemark High Schools director Benson Musonda said increased investment will help decongest schools and improve access to quality education, especially in underserved communities.

Mr Musonda congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election and said the sector was encouraged by the renewed focus on education.

He said there is now optimism that the government will scale up infrastructure development, to meet the growing demand for education, following the introduction of free education from Grade One through secondary school.

Mr Musonda has since called for sustained investment in classrooms and other school infrastructure, particularly in rural areas, to ensure learners have access to a conducive learning environment.

World.title: ZANAMACA calls for informal sector focus
World.content:
National Marketers and Traders Association(ZANAMACA) is calling on President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration to place the informal sector at the centre of Zambia’s economic transformation during his second term.

Association President Mupila Kameya said the millions of marketeers, traders, small-scale farmers, bus drivers and taxi operators who sustain livelihoods and facilitate the movement of goods and people deserve greater legal protection, access to finance and meaningful participation in policy-making.

In an exclusive Interview with the media today, Mr Kameya said the government should, as a matter of urgency, fully implement the Markets and Bus Stations Act by establishing and operationalising legal Market and Bus Station Boards across the country.

He said this will help eliminate illegal cadreism, promote transparency in revenue collection and ensure that funds collected from markets are channeled towards improving sanitation, security and infrastructure.

Mr Kameya is further calling for an amendment to the Constituency Development Fund guidelines to ring-fence 2.5 percent of CDF specifically for marketeers, traders and small-scale farmers.

He said such a measure would enable informal economy operators to access affordable micro-capital, equipment and agricultural inputs directly within their communities, without being hindered by bureaucratic processes.

And Mr Kameya has called for deeper collaboration between Government and organisations representing informal sector operators.

He said a structured platform for continuous dialogue and joint decision-making would ensure that policies, urban planning and trade regulations reflect the realities of people operating in markets, farms and bus stations.

Mr Kameya said the informal economy should not be viewed as a burden to be managed, but as an engine of wealth creation capable of contributing significantly to Zambia’s economic development.

He said the success of President Hichilema’s second term should ultimately be measured by whether economic transformation is felt by ordinary Zambians working in markets, farms and bus stations across the country.

World.title: BETUZ Launches Distribution of 90,000 Shirts
World.content:
The Basic Education Teachers Union of Zambia (BETUZ) has launched the distribution of 90,000 shirts to its teacher members ahead of this year’s World Teachers’ Day celebrations slated for October 5, 2026.

BETUZ General Secretary Henry Sinkala said the initiative is aimed at celebrating teachers while reaffirming unity, solidarity, professional pride and the identity of the union.

Dr Sinkala said this in a speech read on his behalf by BETUZ Deputy General Secretary, Christopher Simukonda during the launch at BETUZ Headquarters in Lusaka.

He described the shirts as more than just clothing, stating they symbolised the collective strength and dignity of teachers across the country.

Dr Sinkala said the decision by BETUZ to procure 90,000 shirts also demonstrates how the union values and recognises the contribution of teachers to national development.

He said teachers are not merely employees within the education system, but are architects of the foundation upon which Zambia’s human capital is built.

Dr Sinkala urged teachers to wear the shirts with pride and purpose as a visible declaration of their commitment to the union and the teaching profession.

He announced that distribution of the shirts to provinces would commence immediately following the launch, paving the way for every BETUZ teacher member across the country to receive a shirt.

“A shirt of unity, a symbol of pride, a statement of solidarity,” Dr Sinkala said.

He reaffirmed the Union’s commitment to advocating for issues affecting teachers, including improved remuneration, promotions and upgrades, professional recognition, continuous professional development, better working conditions and improved welfare.

Dr Sinkala said the union will also continue engaging Government and other stakeholders constructively, firmly and consistently to ensure that the welfare, dignity and professional standing of the Zambian teacher remained a national priority.

World.title: Senegal: Senegal and IMF Strike $2.2bn Deal, Two Years After Debt Scandal Froze Funding
World.content:
Senegal and the International Monetary Fund have reached a staff-level agreement on a new $2.2 billion (€1.9 billion) lending programme, nearly two years after an earlier deal was suspended following the discovery of previously unreported public debt.

The 36-month arrangement, announced on Tuesday, is intended to support Senegal's economic and financial reform programme for 2026 to 2029.

However, it still requires approval from the IMF's executive board and depends on Senegal securing financing assurances from international partners.

The deal follows months of negotiations with President Bassirou Diomaye Faye's government, which came to power in 2024 after accusing the administration of former president Macky Sall of concealing the true scale of the country's debt and budget deficit.



Those revelations prompted the IMF to suspend a $1.8 billion (€1.55 billion) programme agreed in 2023 while it sought clarification over Senegal's public finances.

The Fund said the new agreement would require "decisive corrective measures" to address the earlier misreporting.

Finance Minister Cheikh Diba welcomed the breakthrough, saying Senegal and the IMF had reached a technical agreement that "paves the way for financing prospects".

'No blank cheque' for president or government says Senegal's Sonko

Debt burden remains high

Mercedes Vera Martin, a division chief in the IMF's African Department, said the Senegalese authorities had taken steps to improve transparency since the undeclared debt was uncovered.

Those efforts included audits and work to reconcile historical financial data.

Senegal's total public-sector debt was estimated at 132 percent of gross domestic product at the end of 2024, making it one of the most heavily indebted countries in sub-Saharan Africa.

There are, however, signs that the pressure is beginning to ease. The fiscal deficit fell from 13.4 percent of GDP in 2024 to 6.4 percent in 2025, largely as a result of tighter government spending, according to the IMF.

The economy also remained resilient, expanding by 6.7 percent in 2025 as Senegal benefited from its first full year of oil production. Growth outside the hydrocarbon sector was more modest, slowing to 2.2 percent.

Senegal began producing oil from its first offshore field in 2024, providing a new source of growth and revenue as the government works to stabilise the public finances.

The country has meanwhile continued to raise funds on regional markets, although borrowing there is generally more expensive than financing from international institutions and development banks.

Close 

IMF chief outlines plan to resume grants to Senegal

'Debt treatment'

The question of how Senegal should manage its debt has also become politically contentious.

Tensions between Faye and his former prime minister, Ousmane Sonko, intensified earlier this year over several issues, including relations with the IMF.

Faye dismissed Sonko in May, but Sonko later became speaker of the National Assembly, giving him an influential role as reforms linked to the IMF programme move through parliament.

Faye has favoured a more conciliatory approach towards the Fund, while Sonko has rejected conventional debt restructuring.

Asked whether the new programme involved restructuring, Vera Martin said it included "debt treatment", adding that Senegal had developed its own plan.

Diba stressed that the proposal was "not a restructuring in the traditional sense", but an approach designed around Senegal's specific circumstances.

Sonko, however, called for greater transparency in a Facebook post on Tuesday and demanded details of what "debt treatment" would involve.

He also said any commitments would ultimately be debated in the National Assembly, where his Pastef party holds a majority.

The agreement comes after Moody's last week downgraded Senegal's long-term foreign-currency debt rating from Caa1 to Caa2.

World.title: Sudan: Air Attack Destroys Food Aid for Families in South Kordofan
World.content:
A map showing the location of Abyei and Southern Kordofan.

A massive supply of food destined for hungry families in South Kordofan state, Sudan, was destroyed in an aerial attack on two aid trucks over the weekend, the World Food Progamme (WFP) said on Wednesday.

The UN agency strongly condemned the attack which occurred on 30 August outside the city of Dilling.

The trucks carried 50 metric tonnes of WFP food including cereals, yellow split peas, vegetable oil and salt--enough to provide lifesaving assistance to 5,800 people for one month.

They were heading to Kadugli, where WFP is supporting nearly 58,000 people facing emergency levels of food insecurity or worse, and were clearly marked with its banners and flags.

End 'unacceptable' attacks

WFP said the attack was the latest example of the complex operating environment facing it and other humanitarian agencies in Sudan.

The UN has repeatedly called for an end to the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) which erupted in April 2023.

As a result of the conflict, some 30 million people required humanitarian assistance last year.

Since January, WFP has recorded eight aerial attacks that have damaged its premises and disrupted operations.

"Attacks on aid workers and humanitarian operations are unacceptable and must stop," WFP said, urging all sides to uphold international humanitarian law by protecting civilians, aid workers and humanitarian assets.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 2, 2026
World.content:
Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema Sworn In for Second Term

Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second five-year term following an election overshadowed by opposition allegations of irregularities and the arrest of his main rival, Brian Mundubile, on treason charges. Hichilema was declared the winner of the 13 August election with 60% of the vote. Mundubile received 38% and claimed the results had been manipulated. Concerns were also raised after courts were sealed off on the final day available for a legal challenge. European Union observers pointed to weaknesses in the vote tallying and verification process. Despite the political tensions, Hichilema used his inauguration to call for unity and urged the opposition to work with his government. His second term comes after five years focused on stabilising Zambia's economy and restructuring its debt. The president is now pledging to shift his attention towards economic growth and prosperity.

Tunisia Faces Growing Crackdown on Civil Society

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Tunisia is facing growing concern over what activists and human rights organisations describe as an intensifying crackdown on civil society and political dissent under President Kais Saied. Human Rights Watch said that the authorities have increasingly used arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and the suspension of organisations to silence independent voices and restrict the work of civil society groups. Activists have warned that the uncertainty surrounding possible arrests or prosecutions is creating a climate of fear, causing people to think twice before speaking publicly or working on sensitive issues. Saied, who has rejected accusations of authoritarianism, has defended his actions as necessary to tackle corruption and protect Tunisia's national interests. The crackdown comes amid renewed protests over worsening living conditions, water and electricity shortages and democratic backsliding. Surveys suggest a growing divide between younger Tunisians, who remain more sceptical of state institutions, and older citizens who are more supportive of the government.

DR Congo Schools Reopen Amid Ebola, Conflict and Strike Threat

Millions of students across the Democratic Republic of Congo have returned to school for the new academic year amid major challenges posed by an Ebola outbreak, continuing conflict in the east and a dispute between the government and teachers. The Ebola epidemic has affected six provinces, prompting authorities to introduce a three-tier system under which schools in high-risk areas will shift to limited remote learning. Those in lower-risk zones remain open under different health and safety measures. In territories controlled by the AFC/M23 armed group, schools are reopening under the movement's local authority even though teachers continue to receive their salaries from the government in Kinshasa. At the same time, the country's teachers are divided over whether to return to classrooms. One major union is maintaining a strike call and demanding higher salaries, payment for unpaid staff and improvements to pensions and health insurance. The new school year will therefore test the government's ability to keep children learning despite overlapping health, security and labour challenges.

FBI Confirms Tinubu Was Subject of 1990s Drug Probe

The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation has confirmed in a sworn declaration filed in a federal court that Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was the subject of a criminal investigation into drug-trafficking crimes in the early 1990s. The disclosure forms part of an ongoing Freedom of Information Act case seeking the release of FBI records connected to a Chicago heroin-trafficking operation. A court had previously ruled that US agencies could no longer refuse to confirm whether such records existed. However, the FBI's acknowledgement does not establish that Tinubu committed a drug-trafficking offence or was convicted of any crime. Portions of the records remain withheld under exemptions protecting privacy, confidential sources and law-enforcement methods. Tinubu's government has dismissed renewed claims surrounding the records as politically motivated, accusing opposition figures and a Washington-based lobbying firm linked to former vice-president Atiku Abubakar of using decades-old documents to create controversy ahead of Nigeria's 2027 presidential election.

UNICEF Warns 162 Million Children at Risk From Looming El Niño Climate Shocks

UNICEF has warned that more than 162 million children across Eastern and Southern Africa could face severe risks as the strengthening 2026/2027 El Niño brings the threat of droughts, extreme heat and flooding to the region. The UN agency said the climate shocks could worsen food and water insecurity, disrupt healthcare and education. This could leave already vulnerable children exposed to malnutrition, disease, displacement and other dangers across 13 priority countries. Somalia, Ethiopia and South Sudan are among the countries facing particularly serious risks. Existing humanitarian and food crises are likely to be intensified by extreme weather. UNICEF has called for greater investment in anticipatory action, including strengthening nutrition, health and water services, protecting education and expanding social protection before the worst effects are felt. The agency is seeking US$173 million to provide life-saving assistance and warned that acting early could save lives and significantly reduce the costs of responding once a humanitarian crisis has already escalated.

Close 

Nigeria Anti-Corruption Agency Dismisses Over 40 Staff for Financial Misconduct

Nigeria's Economic and Financial Crimes Commission has dismissed more than 40 employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years. Several former staff members are already facing prosecution, and case files are being prepared against others. EFCC chairman Ola Olukoyede said the dismissals were part of efforts to strengthen accountability within an agency tasked with investigating corruption, fraud and money laundering. The commission has also introduced reforms, including renaming its Department of Internal Affairs to the Department of Ethics and Integrity and adopting a policy requiring officers to declare certain gifts and hospitality in an effort to prevent conflicts of interest. Olukoyede said the agency had also recorded significant results since he took office in October 2023, recovering 1.23 trillion naira and securing more than 10,000 convictions. However, the figures also show that the EFCC is increasingly dealing with cybercrime and fraud cases rather than focusing solely on corruption involving high-profile public officials.

World.title: Tunisia: Tunisia's Rights Defenders Decry Civil Society Crackdown
World.content:
Five years into the authoritarian rule of Tunisian President Kais Saied, Human Rights Watch and other activists warn that Tunisia's once vibrant civil society is in danger of being completely stifled.

"Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities."

Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues.

"What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention, the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report, published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely.

"It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights.

"The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW.

He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

Saied was elected president democratically in 2019. But in July 2021, he dissolved parliament and launched a power grab. Since then, he has dismantled most democratic bodies, repressed political dissent and arrested opposition figures.

For Anthony Dworkin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations who focuses on human rights and democracy, Saied's goals remain unchanged. "They have been the same for the last five years, namely to consolidate power and remove potential checks on and critics of his rule," he told DW.

Saied has rejected accusations that he is an authoritarian ruler and argued that his measures are necessary to tackle corruption and uphold democracy. He has accused critics of receiving foreign funding to stir unrest and undermine Tunisia's national interests. DW reached out to the Tunisian presidency for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Growing discontent prompts calls for Saied's resignation

Despite the widespread crackdown on dissent, some people still dare criticize the government. On July 25, the fifth anniversary of the president's power grab, thousands took to the streets of the capital, Tunis, to protest worsening living conditions, democratic backsliding and the government's handling of basic services.

The demonstrations came amid widespread water and electricity outages, which Saied has described as "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumors to sow confusion."

In late August, protesters once again called on the president to step down by chanting "The people want the fall of the regime," a popular slogan from the 2010-2011 Arab Spring uprising.

The demonstration was initiated by Nafas, a new citizen-led umbrella initiative that was launched in May. Mohamed Hawel, a university teacher and member of the Nafas collective, told the news agency AP that Nafas was created to unite people around basic necessities, including water, electricity and food.

Growing gap between older, younger Tunisians

Despite some unity at these protests, according to an Arab Barometer survey, there is an emerging generational divide in Tunisia. A report published in July on the basis of a survey conducted in the fall of 2025 found that older and less educated people had vastly different views on the country's economic and political conditions from younger, better educated people.

The survey showed that the older generation saw the current political and economic situation in the most positive light since the Arab Spring and had more trust in the government than over the past decade.

In comparison, younger Tunisians were more pessimistic about the country's economic and political development. They also remained more skeptical of state institutions while maintaining a high trust in civil society organizations: 49% of people between the ages of 18-39 expressed trust in these, compared with only 32% of those aged 40 and older.

Close 

"What really stands out in Tunisia is that the recent decline in trust in civil society is almost entirely a story about older Tunisians. Two years prior, there was almost no generational gap between citizens," Michael Robbins, the director of Arab Barometer, told DW. "Since then, trust in civil society among Tunisians 40 and older has fallen quite sharply, while it has not changed meaningfully among those who are aged 18-39."

Tunisia has a population of approximately 12 million people. People aged 18–39 account for roughly 30% of the population, while those aged 40 and older account for approximately 43%.

"I think the notion of a divided society is overstated," said Dworkin. "Moreover, the recent demonstrations are not large enough to pose a serious threat to Kais Saied," he added, while admitting that Saied had lost considerable public support over his failure to improve the country's economy. "But there are no attractive political alternatives and people are also tired of political upheaval."

In his view, many Tunisians are just trying to get by with daily life, while many others are looking to emigrate.

DW's Tarek Guizani in Tunis contributed to this report.

World.title: South Africa: Western Cape Braces for Hot Summer - South African News Briefs - September 2, 2026
World.content:
Western Cape Braces for Hotter, Drier Summer

Western Cape residents have been urged to prepare for a potentially hotter and drier summer, reports EWN. Experts are warning of increased wildfire risks and growing pressure on water resources. Local Government, Environmental Affairs and Development Planning MEC Anton Bredell said the province was taking the warnings seriously, particularly because extreme heat could pose greater risks in informal settlements. Authorities are securing firefighting aircraft, investing in equipment and training. They are urging residents and landowners to clear fire hazards and create firebreaks. Dam levels are already lower than last year. The province is also working to repair leaks, upgrade infrastructure and secure alternative water sources.

Ramaphosa's Phala Phala Bid Goes to Court



President Cyril Ramaphosa's application to set aside the Section 89 independent panel report on the Phala Phala saga is set to be heard in the Western Cape High Court, reports SABC News. The report found strong evidence that Ramaphosa may have violated his oath of office by stealing $580,000 in cash from his Limpopo farm. The National Assembly initially voted against the report. The Constitutional Court later invalidated that decision and ordered Parliament to establish an impeachment committee. The committee's proceedings were temporarily halted in July pending the outcome of Ramaphosa's application to review the report.

eThekwini Debt Tops R47 Billion

eThekwini Mayor Cyril Xaba has raised alarm over the municipality's growing debt, which has surpassed R47 billion, reports EWN. Households account for the largest share of the debt at R35 billion, followed by commercial clients owing R10 billion and government departments owing more than R2 billion. Xaba said the municipality could not function effectively with such a large and growing debt burden. He outlined plans to recover some of the money, including through disconnection campaigns and identifying residents who may qualify for indigent support.

World.title: Malawi: Chilima Plane Crash Inquiry Lays Bare Malawi's Aviation Safety Crisis
World.content:
The parliamentary inquiry into the June 10, 2024 plane crash that killed Vice-President Saulos Chilima and eight others has heard troubling testimony suggesting Malawi's aviation infrastructure suffers from long-standing structural deficiencies -- raising uncomfortable questions about institutional readiness that extend well beyond the immediate circumstances of the crash itself.

Fredrick Chisepeya, director of Aerodromes and Air Navigation Standards at the Civil Aviation Authority of Malawi (CAAM), told Parliament's Ad-hoc Committee investigating the disaster that the country risks failing next year's International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) audit unless significant investment is urgently directed towards safety and security infrastructure.

His testimony painted a picture of a system operating with minimal redundancy: Malawi possesses just one secondary flight surveillance radar, situated at Kamuzu International Airport in Lilongwe, whose effective coverage diminishes substantially for aircraft flying at lower altitudes.

It was this gap, Chisepeya confirmed, that meant the Malawi Defence Force aircraft was outside radar coverage entirely when it crashed in Viphya Plantation.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The limitation is the radar coverage. When you are up, the range is wider and when you are down the range is narrower. So that makes the aircraft sometimes not to be seen," he told the committee -- an admission that speaks to a broader question of how a nation manages the tension between resource constraints and the non-negotiable demands of aviation safety.

The inquiry also heard that Mzuzu Airport, the aircraft's intended destination, fell well short of the protection standards required for medium-sized aircraft such as the Malawi Airlines Bombardier involved in the crash.

Using CAAM's own ten-point protection scale, Chisepeya estimated the airport's actual safety level at around three, against a required standard of six. He further noted deficiencies in fire response capacity and runway conditions, describing the surface as bumpy and substandard.

Perhaps most striking was the revelation that Mzuzu Airport was operating without a valid licence at the time of the crash, having only been licensed the following year, in 2025 -- and even then, with conditions attached.

Questions from committee chairperson Walter Nyamilandu drew a candid admission from Chisepeya that enforcement of aviation standards across Malawi's airports remains inconsistent.

The committee's scrutiny extended into the operational detail of the flight itself. Lilongwe Mude MP Mphatso Boti (Malawi Congress Party) probed whether formal aviation codes exist for reporting interference incidents, prompting Chisepeya to acknowledge that communication with aircraft becomes markedly more difficult once outside radar range.

Close 

Mwanza Central MP Felix Njawala (UTM Party) went further still, raising the possibility of frequency interference between the aircraft and ground officials -- noting that the pilot is understood to have made contact with Mzuzu Airport officer-in-charge Joseph Moyo only once throughout the flight.

Taken together, the testimony suggests the Chikangawa crash may prove less an isolated tragedy than a symptom of deeper, systemic underinvestment in the infrastructure meant to keep Malawi's skies safe.

World.title: Namibia: Drought Displaced Angolans Face Human Rights Abuses
World.content:
Angolan women and children displaced by drought into Namibia face serious human rights abuses arising from a lack of safe and legal migration pathways for people forced across borders by natural disasters, Amnesty International said in a new report.

The report, "The Drier it Gets, the Longer You Have to Walk: The Human Rights Impacts of Drought-Induced Displacement on Angolan Women and Children in Namibia, documents the devastating consequences of recurrent drought in southern Angola and the human rights impacts experienced by those displaced into Namibia, including persistent fear of arrest, detention and deportation, which in turn influences their daily decisions about whether to seek healthcare and other services.

"Namibian authorities must establish a rights-based approach to migration, ensuring that people displaced by drought and other natural disasters can access basic rights, including registration and documentation." Said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International's Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.

"The protection of already marginalized Angolans who are forced to move to Namibia in search of livelihoods is not just a humanitarian concern. This is a human rights crisis that demands international solidarity, including legal protection against refoulement," said Tigere Chagutah.



Namibian authorities must establish a rights-based approach to migration,ensuring that people displaced by drought and other natural disasters can access basic rights, including registration and documentation.Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International's Regional Director for East and Southern Africa

Between May 2024 and May 2026, Amnesty International interviewed at least 167 people, including displaced people, community leaders, government officials, representatives of civil society organizations (CSOs), academics, and members of the UN Country Team.

At the time of publication, Nambian government officials had not responded to Amnesty International's request for comment.

"The drier it gets, the longer you have to walk, the deeper you have to dig"

Southern Angola, particularly Cunene, Huíla and Namibe provinces, has been among the hardest hit by recurring droughts, which have been exacerbated by El Niño.

Together with long-standing structural vulnerabilities, these conditions have undermined traditional pastoral and farming systems, eroded people's resilience and forced them to migrate to Namibia in search of safety, food, water, work, and essential services.

The drier it gets, the longer you have to walk, the deeper you have to dig. Angolan Climate Activist

Women and children are disproportionately affected, often taking these journeys under great risk.

A young climate activist told Amnesty International that drought-induced displacement is not a simple story of people "running from drought", but a rational response to collapsing systems. "The drier it gets, the longer you have to walk, the deeper you have to dig," he said.

Namibian response to Angolan displacement

The report notes that Angolans displaced by drought have limited ways to regularize their stay in Namibia, as the current immigration and protection laws do not reflect the realities of climate-driven displacement. This has forced many people into irregular status as they cross the border in search of food, water, grazing land, healthcare, family support, and work following the droughts which destroys crops, livestock, and livelihoods.

In 2026, the Namibian Ministry of Home Affairs immigration control programme announced that more than 1,000 Angolan nationals had been returned to Angola after being found in the country without regular immigration status.

On 4 June 2025, Amnesty International witnessed Namibian authorities round up about 40 Angolan nationals, including women and children, at a community centre in Opuwo, and transport them the same day to the Ruacana border - over 100km away - for handover to Angolan authorities, without individualized screening, information about asylum or protection options, or assessment of the risks upon return. The absence of individual examination raises serious concerns under the prohibition of collective expulsion and the principle of non-refoulement.

The protection of already marginalized Angolans who are forced to move to Namibia in search of livelihoods is not just a humanitarian concern. This is a human rights crisis that demands international solidarity, including legal protection against refoulement.Tigere Chagutah

In other instances, Angolan children have also been subject to government-facilitated forcible returns without sufficient information being made publicly available to establish whether appropriate safeguards were applied.

The report highlights that Namibia's existing immigration framework does not adequately respond to the circumstances of people displaced across the border by drought. Although Angolan passport holders can enter Namibia visa-free through official border posts for limited periods, this does not provide a right to work, longer-term residence or a dedicated protection pathway.

Many people from drought-affected border communities also lack passports or other documentation and use informal crossing points. Once in Namibia without regular status, they have few accessible options to regularize their stay. This has left thousands of Angolans in fear of arrest, detention and deportation, a fear that shapes daily decisions about whether to seek healthcare and other services.

Amnesty International found that for those already living in northern Namibia, housing, water and sanitation conditions fell far short of international law and standards. Many families live in makeshift shelters, built from branches, plastic and cardboard, in severely overcrowded conditions or, in some cases, entirely without shelter.

The report details how undocumented Angolans were charged higher fees in hospitals than Namibian nationals, pushing them to delay treatment until illness became severe, and avoiding clinics altogether for fear that health facilities were linked to immigration enforcement.

"We only go when the pain is too much; otherwise, we just lie down and wait," one woman said.

Amnesty International calls on Namibian authorities to honour its international and regional legal obligations by ensuring that displaced Angolans can access legal protections, including registration and documentation needed to access rights. State authorities must conduct individual assessments before deportations and consider the human risk associated with return.

This reality underscores the need for the international community to recognize the injustice faced by these communities and respond with robust cooperation and support. It cannot wait.Tigere Chagutah

High-income, historically high-emitting states have heightened obligations in relation to climate action, while states that are able to do so must provide international cooperation and assistance, including adequate climate finance, according to their capacity, to support countries such as Angola and Namibia in adaptation, drought preparedness, resilience-building and addressing loss and damage.

"This reality underscores the need for the international community to recognize the injustice faced by these communities and respond with robust cooperation and support. It cannot wait," said Tigere Chagutah.

Angola's failure to invest in adaptation and preparedness

Angola's investment in climate adaptation, drought preparedness, and livelihood protection has remained uneven because of limited finance, weak institutional capacity, inadequate climate-monitoring infrastructure and continued dependence on donor-supported emergency and resilience programmes.

Close 

Angolan authorities must take urgent action to honour their legal obligations by putting in place safeguards to protect the drought affected through drought preparedness and climate adaptation mechanisms and protect communities at risk of displacement.Tigere Chagutah

The report shows how gaps in early warning systems, water infrastructure, veterinary support, and social protection mechanisms have contributed to the progressive erosion of pastoral and subsistence farming systems.

"Drought and the increasing risks posed by climate change cannot absolve the government from its legal obligation to protect people's rights to life, food, water, health, a healthy environment and an adequate standard of living," said Tigere Chagutah

"Angolan authorities must take urgent action to honour their legal obligations by putting in place safeguards to protect the drought affected through drought preparedness and climate adaptation mechanisms and protect communities at risk of displacement."

Background

Between January and July 2021, more than 7,000 Angolans, mainly women, including pregnant and lactating women, children and older persons, crossed into northern Namibia following consecutive years of severe drought and food insecurity in southern Angola. Drought and food insecurity have continued to contribute to cross-border movement in subsequent years, including during renewed severe drought conditions in 2023 and 2024. However, the true scale of drought-related displacement over this period is unknown due to the absence of comprehensive reception, registration, or data collection systems.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe Counts Cost of Wildfires As Communities Urged to Fight Back
World.content:
Local communities have been urged to work with authorities and other stakeholders to prevent veldfires as the country battles an increasing threat from climate change and human activity.

The Environmental Management Agency (EMA) says thousands of hectares of land have already been destroyed by fires with property, infrastructure and livelihoods also at risk.

Speaking at a veldfire management media briefing in Harare, EMA Environmental Education and Publicity Manager Amkela Sidange said preventing wildfires could not be left to one sector.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"If the country wants to fail in preventing wildfires or in fighting them, the duty of discouraging such incidences should not be relegated to one sector," she said.

Ms Sidange said the agency's mandate was to protect the country's natural resources from degradation and pollution while ensuring environmental sustainability.

"That is where our concern is coming from, especially when it comes to the bonfires. Our concern really comes from protecting the ecosystem goods and services, because there are services and goods that we get in our ecosystems, so we are so much keen to look at how best they can be protected," she said.

Wildfires have destroyed lodges, forestry and farming equipment as well as energy infrastructure in recent years.

"It's coming from the energy sector; we lost a lot of energy infrastructure. So these are just some of the things that we consider, not excluding the human livelihoods as it were. It's also our major concern," Ms Sidange said.

EMA said it was strengthening fire monitoring and reporting to identify areas most vulnerable to veldfires and improve preparedness.

The agency uses remote sensing technology as well as reports from communities to track fire incidents.

At least 748 fire incidents were recorded between 31 July and 31 August this year affecting about 276 828 hectares of land.

The country had already recorded 627 fires and lost approximately 186 979 hectares before the official start of the fire season.

One person had also died in Masvingo as a result of wildfires before the season began.

The country's prescribed fire season runs from 31 July to 31 October under Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007.

However, Ms Sidange said climate change was shifting the traditional fire season with fires increasingly being recorded before the official start and after its end.

Close 

In 2025, Zimbabwe recorded 794 fire incidents during the corresponding period.

The 748 incidents recorded this year represent a 5.79% decline but EMA warned that communities should remain vigilant as dry, hot and windy conditions can quickly accelerate the spread of fires.

The agency said preventing veldfires required communities, government departments, farmers and other stakeholders to work together.

World.title: Lady A's Charles Kelley shares before-and-after photos showing how sobriety transformed his life
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Lady A's Charles Kelley is sharing how his life has changed since starting his sobriety journey.

In an Instagram post shared on Monday, the 44-year-old musician shared photos from before and after he began his journey with sobriety, crediting his decision to stop drinking with his healthier appearance.

"My best filter is just…not drinking," he wrote in the caption. "Swipe to see my before 😬 my wife asked me if I ever look at a photo of myself before I was sober and think 'who is that guy?' This is the one 😃."

The before photo shows him looking dazed as he posed for the selfie, while the after picture shows him posing for a photo with his wife while out on the water.

COUNTRY SINGER MARK CHESNUTT SAYS ALCOHOLISM 'ALMOST KILLED' HIM, ADMITS HE DRANK A HANDLE OF VODKA A DAY

He added in the caption that there have been countless "blessings that have come from putting it down" in addition to "looking healthier," noting that the second photo is "a nice reminder of a place I don’t wanna go back to."

Many fans congratulated him in the comments section and shared their experiences with alcoholism and sobriety.

"I’m 1,148 days sober today! So proud of you! I know it’s hard but so worth it! 👏👏👏" one fan wrote. Another added, "Ahhh yes, the puffy drinking face! 4 years sober and I hope I never have to see that puffy face ever again! Proud of you 👏."

Kelley's journey with sobriety first became public knowledge in August 2022, when Lady A shared with their fans that they were postponing their Request Line Tour to support him.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"We are a band, but more importantly we're family," they said in a statement at the time. "⁣⁣We're proud to say that Charles has embarked on a journey to sobriety. So, right now in order to be the healthiest, strongest and most creative band we can be, Lady A will take the time with the support of our families and team of professionals to walk through this together. It's early on this road, but we are determined to do what will best set us up for many more years together."

He later discussed his decision to get sober during an appearance on "CBS Mornings" in May 2023, saying that he would always joke that he was "definitely a functioning alcoholic."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The musician shared that as his drinking continued to become concerning, his bandmates brought their concerns to him, but he pushed them aside. He ultimately decided to seek help after his wife threatened to leave him if he didn't quit drinking, leading him to fly from his vacation in Greece to a treatment center.

"It just makes me feel so grateful at how close I came to losing it all," he said. "And I think the thing that’s hard is to know how much it affected Cassie the most, and my band, and the people around me. And how much it emotionally kinda wrecked them for a while. And that, I can’t really say I’m sorry enough. And it’s just gonna take time to rebuild that."

Kelley shared that he had attempted to quit before but didn't think he needed rehab because he believed that was for people with more serious problems with alcohol.

What he learned, however, is that there are different "degrees of alcoholics" and that "just because you're not living on the street, or you're not waking up in a bush" doesn't mean there isn't a problem.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Ultimately, the musician stayed in rehab for one month and credited group therapy, a case manager and a blood-alcohol detection device that he would blow into twice a day for aiding his recovery.

"I went to treatment for a month in Utah and I really didn't know if I was ever going to be coming back home to my bed," Kelley told People in June 2025. "And that was tough. I'd written a lot of songs about heartbreak, but I don't know if I ever really knew what heartbreak felt like until I was there and had that moment."

World.title: Lincoln Riley dismisses empty seats controversy as a 'false narrative' after low-attendance USC home opener
World.content:
The USC Trojans started their college football season on the right foot, defeating San Jose State University 42-26 in Week 0, as expected given their No. 14 ranking entering the new season.

However, some college football fans were concerned by the turnout at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum after seeing many empty seats for the team’s home opener.

The Trojans are one of the top teams in the country, and though they were five-touchdown favorites entering this matchup against SJSU, pictures of the empty seats caused a stir on social media.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The stir doesn’t matter to Trojans head coach Lincoln Riley, though.

"This is USC, right? People are going to pay attention," Riley said in his latest press conference session. "People are going to have an opinion. It’s part of being a blue-blood school. I don’t buy into the false narrative. I think that comes from a lot of people that don’t follow our program. And most of those who have never set foot in the Coliseum.

DOES USC'S POOR OPENING GAME ATTENDANCE MEAN LINCOLN RILEY'S ON THE HOT SEAT ALREADY?

"The reality is during my years here, attendance has gone up every single year. As has our play in the Coliseum, including running the table last year in front of a lot of epic atmospheres and I expect that to happen again this year."

In Riley’s defense, and USC fans for that matter, it was a 90-plus-degree day out in Los Angeles. Considering USC was a heavy favorite, and the West Coast is known for enjoying its summer days in various capacities, perhaps fans wanted to forego a visit to the Coliseum expecting their Trojans to win.

USC will be right back home on Friday, this time against Fresno State, where the high in Los Angeles is expected to be around 87 degrees. The game will kick off 6 p.m. local time.

The "false narrative" comment from Riley will likely come to fruition for other games this season, especially against ranked opponents.

USC will be taking on No. 2 Oregon at the Coliseum on Sept. 26, while hosting No. 17 Washington the following week. Also, a matchup against the current No. 1-ranked team in the country, Ohio State, will be on Halloween.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The college season has just begun, but there’s already controversy and outside noise. Riley and the Trojans will try to keep that at bay, and perhaps more fans showing up sooner than later will quiet that noise.

World.title: Pabst CEO has blunt message after thieves make off with truckload of PBR in brazen beer heist
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The brazen theft of an entire truckload of Pabst Blue Ribbon (PBR) has taken another wild turn, with the beer giant's CEO personally calling out the thieves and putting a reward on the table to get the stolen haul back.

"Someone had the balls to steal it," Pabst Brewing Company CEO Greig DeBow said in a video posted to TikTok. "I don't know. Kudos to them, perhaps."

But DeBow quickly made clear that he wanted the beer back.

"I'm sure they look cool with a garage full of PBR," he said. "That's actually not cool, though. But we want it back."

THOUSANDS OF BEER CANS SPILL ACROSS CONNECTICUT HIGHWAY AFTER TRACTOR-TRAILER OVERTURNS

DeBow then revealed that Pabst is offering up to $20,000 for new information leading to the recovery of the stolen beer and gave whoever has it until Sept. 9 to return it.

"We want it by September 9th," he said. "If you don't bring it back, well, we have no choice. We're going to offer up to $20,000 for any new information leading to the lost goods."

The public appeal is the latest twist in what Pabst has dubbed the "Great American Beer Heist," which began when 1,602 cases of PBR, roughly 40,000 pounds of beer, disappeared from a warehouse in Montclair, California, on Aug. 17.

"It's that simple," DeBow said of the reward. "There's been a hell of a lot of support thus far, and we really appreciate it."

The $20,000 offer raises the stakes in Pabst's increasingly public effort to track down the massive shipment.

'LET'S BREW IT IN THE UNITED STATES': TEAMSTERS TARGET MODELO AND CORONA IN PUSH FOR MEXICAN BEER TARIFFS

The Texas-based company had previously promised a reward to anyone who helped crack the case, but did not disclose how much it was willing to pay. Pabst also initially gave whoever took the shipment 18 days and 44 minutes to return it with "no questions asked."

The oddly specific countdown appeared to be a nod to 1844, the year Pabst was founded in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Pabst later insisted the bizarre disappearance was not a publicity stunt.

"To clear up the confusion, this story is real," the company wrote on social media while urging anyone with information to come forward.

AMERICA'S FAVORITE BEERS — AND THE JOBS TIED TO THEM — ARE AT THE CENTER OF A BREWING TRADE FIGHT

As the deadline ticked down, Pabst joked that the "beer is getting warmer" while the trail got colder and asked anyone who spotted the truck to take a photo and contact the company.

But behind Pabst’s playful posts is a serious police investigation into what could be a larger cargo theft operation.

Montclair police said in a social media post that investigators were looking into two cargo thefts reported Aug. 17 at an Anheuser-Busch distribution center that could be connected.

In the first case, a shipment worth approximately $45,000 and bound for Tucson, Arizona, was picked up for delivery, but never reached its destination, according to police.

About an hour later, police said a company claiming to be a subcontractor used fraudulent paperwork to arrange the pickup of roughly $25,000 worth of Anheuser-Busch and Pabst Blue Ribbon products.

BEER BANDITS SWIPE PBR TRUCK HAULING 50,000 CANS IN CALIFORNIA, LEAVING BRAND PLEADING FOR HELP

Investigators found discrepancies involving the trucking company information, drivers and vehicles associated with the pickups, leading police to believe the cases could be part of the same fraudulent cargo theft operation.

Pabst is now hoping the promise of up to $20,000 will help break the case.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As many of you might've heard, a great deal of PBR has gone missing," DeBow said. "How much, you ask? Well, 1,602 cases. That's a full truckload of PBR."

Anyone with new information that could help locate the beer is being asked to contact Pabst at hotline@pabst.com.

Montclair police also asked anyone with information about the thefts, vehicles, driver, delivery company or missing cargo to call the department at 909-621-4771.

World.title: ESPN puts 20th ranked Tennessee on upset alert, and you'll never guess who they're playing
World.content:
One of the most exciting parts about college football is the possibility of massive upsets.

On more than one occasion each weekend, a team with a bunch of future NFL Draft picks will line up across from a team of future accountants, and every once in a while, those accountants, through sheer force of will and the power of friendship, will shock the college football world and hand a roster full of five-stars a giant L.

Maybe it's not always that dramatic, but every college football season offers the opportunity to see shocking losses from teams who were supposed to win by four or five touchdowns.

SEC LAWYERS, LANE KIFFIN AND DEATH VALLEY: COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S WEEK 1 IS SET FOR FIREWORKS

Apparently, this coming Saturday is no different, at least if ESPN's Jordan Rodgers is to be believed.

Rodgers was on SportsCenter earlier Wednesday to talk a little college ball, and when pressed to give a big upset pick in the vein of Appalachian State over Michigan in 2007, the former SEC quarterback and Bachelorette contestant gave a shocking answer: Tennessee.

The 20th-ranked Vols are breaking in a lot of new pieces, sure, but they're also playing Furman, an FCS school that went 6-6 last year and got dog-walked by the only FBS team they played in 2025 (45-10 vs. Clemson).

Now, to be fair to Rodgers, he did kind of get put on the spot, and honestly, kudos to him for even being able to give an answer here while keeping a straight face.

This one falls at the feet of the SportsCenter producers for putting him in a position to even have to make a prediction like that.

Tennessee is favored to win this game by nearly seven touchdowns, and frankly, I'd be shocked if Furman even covers.

RANKING THE TEN BEST COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES IN THE COUNTRY AHEAD OF THE 2026 SEASON

The Vols have weapons all over the field, and Josh Heupel's fast-paced, wide-open offense absolutely feasts on lesser-talented teams.

Again, I'm not knocking Rodgers for this answer. It's more of an indictment on the producers for trying to drum up a headline (which I bit on hook, line and sinker, obviously).

However, I did see a few in the comments section mentioning that Rodgers is a former Vanderbilt Commodore, so perhaps this was intentional on his part.

Maybe he didn't want to miss the chance to throw a little shade at the Dores' biggest rivals, and the producers and host just threw him a bone.

WHICH TEAMS ARE OVERRATED OR UNDERRATED IN NEW PRESEASON COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES POLL?

World.title: Mel Gibson reveals ‘The Passion of the Christ’s’ most surprising legacy in new Raymond Arroyo interview
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

More than two decades after becoming a box-office hit, Mel Gibson’s "The Passion of the Christ" is returning to theaters nationwide as the Oscar-winning director prepares to tell the next chapter of the biblical story.

Gibson spoke exclusively with Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo about his upcoming two-part sequel, "The Resurrection of the Christ," reflecting on stories of real-life crime confessions and faith transformations he said were inspired by the original film, as well as the pre-release pushback it faced.

The full interview is featured on the "Arroyo Grande Show with Raymond Arroyo" YouTube channel.

MEL GIBSON'S 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' REVEALS FIRST PHOTOS AFTER LONG-AWAITED PASSION SEQUEL

"I just wanted to make it as real as possible for people to enter into that journey, which is pretty grueling," Gibson told Arroyo about the 2004 film. "And previous depictions of it had been pretty much sanitized, and they made it look easy, and it wasn't. So, I wanted to emphasize that this was not easy. In fact, he didn't want to do it."

"The Passion of the Christ" is a biblical drama depicting the crucifixion of Jesus Christ in excruciating detail. It starred Jim Caviezel as Jesus and focused on the final 12 hours of Jesus’ life, with dialogue mainly in Aramaic, Hebrew and Latin.

HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER BEHIND 'APOLLO 13' REJECTS POLITICS IN HIS MOVIES, SEEKS TO UNITE AUDIENCES

At the time, the film faced significant pushback before its release over its violence, religious themes and concerns that it could fuel antisemitism. Gibson told Arroyo he believes those fears did not materialize and that the film instead brought some people together.

"It didn't do that at all, which I was pleased with," Gibson said. "Because people were like pointing at me and yelling at me, and it didn’t spawn any violence."

GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM

Instead, Gibson said he heard stories of people converting to Christianity or confessing crimes after seeing the film. He recalled one person confessing to bank robberies and another who "confessed to a murder."

Beyond the film’s impact on individuals, it also helped reshape the entertainment landscape by demonstrating an audience for faith-based media. It went on to gross more than $610 million worldwide and has remained popular with Christian audiences.

AMERICA ISN’T DONE WITH JESUS — AND THE BESTSELLER LIST JUST PROVED IT

"Well, because people wanted it," Gibson explained when asked why the film resonated so deeply. "I think there was a hunger for it, and they went to see it in droves. And then I think others realized that there was a place where they could share their visions. And then there was zeal amongst faith-based people and filmmakers to explore it further."

"The Passion of the Christ" returns to theaters Sept. 10 through Sept. 17. Gibson is also returning to the story of Jesus with a two-part sequel about what happened after the crucifixion and the resurrection of Christ.

NEW BOOK ON ARCHAEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE FOR JESUS ROCKETS TO TOP OF BESTSELLER LIST

"The Resurrection of the Christ: Part One" is set for release May 6, 2027, with Part Two scheduled for May 25, 2028. The first film focused on the final hours of Jesus’ life, while Gibson said the sequel requires a larger spectacle to depict his resurrection and the days that followed.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For Gibson, telling the story of the Resurrection is essential because he views the Crucifixion as only part of the larger narrative.

"It's not the climax," Gibson said. "It's a part of it. And it's a big event for sure. But the really astounding part of it is that someone can come back to life under their own strength and power from public death and then be public again after that."

World.title: Far-left writer ripped in viral debate over 'absurd' claim that capitalism is tied to White supremacy
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Liberal Atlantic writer Jemele Hill doubled down after suggesting that capitalism was linked to White supremacy, during a heated clash with another panelist on CNN on Tuesday.

"It's one thing to not think capitalism isn't working ideally. It's another thing entirely to insist that it is oppressive, that it is bound up with White supremacy," Kmele Foster, a podcast host, said.

"How is it not?" Hill pressed.

The panelists were responding to newly unearthed 2020 comments, first reported by CNN, in which Texas Senate candidate James Talarico described capitalism as an "oppressive system" that is linked to White supremacy and climate change and needs to be dismantled.

MODERN CAPITALISM IS TURNING 250, TOO. WE NEED TO REMIND AMERICANS WHY IT’S IMPORTANT

"I've always preferred Adam Smith's description of capitalism as the natural system of liberty, the idea that people can own property, that they can exchange it freely with one another for profit, that they can find ways to put their resources to good use, those private property," Foster continued.

He added, "And profit in a way that is actually beneficial to everyone else, that there can be gains from trade that are mutually beneficial. These are foundational ideas that have created more wealth than any other system in human history. That is what capitalism is, that's not White supremacy."

"Do you think capitalism has always worked that way?" Hill asked Foster.

"I've actually just described the basic facts of economics," Foster responded. "Slavery is an institution that is older than writing. It predates capitalism. The notion that White supremacy and all these other things are bound up with capitalism in an intrinsic and fundamental way is so absurd and laughable, it barely needs to be defended."

Foster asked Hill to substantiate her argument and asked multiple times about the "the White supremacist dynamic of private property."

"But you're talking about capitalism in the purest form of how it was intended to work versus how it's actually working. It's not working," Hill argued.

Hill was called out on social media by other media commentators and hosts.

Political commentor Mary Katharine Ham said, "Kmele: ‘You actually have to articulate what the connection is.' Hill writes for the Atlantic and has years of TV experience, but it didn’t occur to her she would ever need to, and she isn’t prepared to."

Podcast host Stephen Miller noted that Hill worked for the Atlantic and wrote, "She is a staff writer for one of the most prestigious neoliberal publications in the country and she's never been once challenged on any of her ideas like this."

JEMELE HILL FALSELY CLAIMS ELECTORAL COLLEGE IS ENTIRELY 'ROOTED IN SLAVERY' AND IT COST KAMALA THE ELECTION

Liberal commentator Leigh McGowan also made the case that capitalism was not working during the exchange.

"I think that's the problem. I think the problem is it's not working well, today. I think for a long time that is a great way to describe it. Adam Smith capitalism, if we had that, that would be totally different," she said. "We have got to a place where we have deregulated everything so much that only a certain handful of people are actually succeeding in this version of capitalism."

Socialism has gained popularity among younger voters, according to a Fox News Poll from March. The survey found a record 38% believed it would be a good thing for the United States to move away from capitalism and in the direction of socialism — up from 32% in 2022, the last time the question was asked. In 2010, a low of 18% backed socialism.

Hill appeared to double down after the exchange.

"America was built on the institution of slavery. It is how America became a world economic power — the buying and selling of people being tied to the economy. That is effectively white supremacy, since it was a race-based system. Fast-forward to other economic policies that were guided by race — housing, employment, etc. There were rules that prevented Black people from equally participating in the free economy. In fact, one of the most glaring features of American capitalism is racial inequality. The racial wealth gap exists because specific policies were put in place to suppress economic participation. So yes, capitalism is tied to White supremacy," Hill said in a post to X that followed the CNN panel debate.

Hill did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.

Talarico made his 2020 comments at the Austin Sierra Club during a virtual candidate forum while serving his first term as a state representative. His answer came in response to a question about what lawmakers could do to address climate change in communities of color, according to CNN's K-File.

"I am so thankful that you asked this question and also thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country," Talarico said. "And I think only ending the ways that all three of those oppressive systems work together are we gonna be able to begin the process of dismantling them."

During the same event, Talarico said the oil and gas industry was not going to last.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"We all know that Texas has been a leader in oil and gas, but in many ways that’s like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s," Talarico later said, responding to another question. "That industry is not gonna last. And if we wanna ensure we have an economy that’s gonna work for our children and our children’s children, we gotta be ahead of the curve and Texas has to lead instead of follow on this issue."

"James supports the oil and gas industry and believes in an all of the above energy strategy that protects Texas oil and gas jobs. He’s already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, but Ken Paxton is clipping a few old, cringey comments to distract from his career of corruption that includes being impeached by his own party, enriching himself and his billionaire mega-donors, and using his office to protect pedophiles and animal abusers," Talarico campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital in a statement regarding the oil and gas industry remarks.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Ennis' statement also said Talarico is a "proud capitalist," and "agrees with the majority of Texans that racism, natural disasters, and a billionaire-controlled economy are all problems we need to address."

"James has already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, while Ken Paxton has refused to address his comments that the school shooting in Uvalde was ‘God’s plan’ and that Texas’ abortion ban is good for interstate commerce," the statement continued.

The Democratic state representative is facing off against Republican Ken Paxton in the midterm elections for U.S. Senate in November.

World.title: Sheriff suing Maryland says sanctuary laws ignore lessons of 9/11: ‘Stupidity at its best’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Maryland sheriff leading 17 of the Old Line State’s 24 counties in a lawsuit challenging Annapolis’ sanctuary city policy told Congress the lessons of the September 11, 2001, terror attacks are being forgotten as the nation prepares to mark the 25th anniversary.

Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler of Harford County — where local women Rachel Morin and Kayla Hamilton were murdered by illegal immigrants in 2023 and 2022, respectively — is leading the suit and echoed concerns about the consequences of mandated limits on cooperation and communication between local and federal law enforcement.

"There's just many things that [Annapolis’] legislature has done over the past eight years or so, unfortunately, rang into that bell. But when you pass legislation in a world post-9/11 – in 9/11 we learned that we need to communicate with … all federal partners to keep our community safe," Gahler said when questioned by Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, as to why he called Maryland’s sanctuary laws as "pro-criminal."

9/11 TAUGHT US DEADLY LESSONS. 25 YEARS LATER, WE NEED A NEW MODEL TO PREVENT ATTACKS

"Yet, we in our state see fit to pass legislation to say we can't communicate with this law enforcement or that law enforcement," Gahler added. "It's stupidity at its best."

Gahler also told lawmakers that Maryland’s law has changed what his deputies can do when federal immigration authorities want to take custody of someone being released from local detention. He said the restrictions can require deputies to release people they believe could pose a danger rather than hold them for federal authorities.

SANCTUARY COUNTY REFUSED 615 ICE TRANSFER REQUESTS, TURNED OVER JUST 11 ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, RECORDS SHOW

Seated behind Gahler were several of the other plaintiff-sheriffs in the suit against the Moore administration.

Gov. Wes Moore, who is locked in a gubernatorial rematch with former Del. Dan Cox, R-Frederick, signed Maryland’s ban on 287(g) agreements earlier this year while allowing a broader bill to become law without his signature.

State Sen. Clarence Lam, D-Elkridge, authored the bill, called the Community Trust Act, which prohibits "Agents of State," law enforcement and corrections officials from questioning immigration status, detaining suspects to investigate citizenship or immigration status, or detaining them because police believe they committed a civil immigration violation.

The new law also bans law enforcement from notifying federal immigration authorities that a detainee is in their custody unless required by a court order, rather than just an ICE detainer.

Gahler said it is not a burden on his job to honor detainers, contrary to Democrats who have considered whether working with ICE takes away resources from local communities.

DHS UNLOADS ON 'SANCTUARY CALAMITY' VIRGINIA AFTER ILLEGAL ALIEN ACCUSED OF HEINOUS CRIME RELEASED: 'SICKO'

He answered in the affirmative when asked by Gill whether illegal immigrants who become "petty criminals" should be removed rather than limiting enforcement to cases involving more serious crimes.

"That’s 100% what I believe," Gahler said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Moore has said the Community Trust Act advances important goals by keeping law enforcement focused on crime reduction, according to Ocean City’s NPR affiliate, while citing logistical concerns that should be addressed through executive action or during the 2027 legislative session.
