World.title: Chevron to expand in Venezuela, days after the U.S. and Venezuela strike oil deal
World.content:
Chevron to expand in Venezuela, days after the U.S. and Venezuela strike oil deal

toggle caption FEDERICO PARRA/AFP via Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

Chevron is expanding its existing operations in Venezuela, the Houston-based company said Wednesday. This comes in the wake of Friday's announcement that Venezuela will give the U.S. access to 65 billion barrels of oil.

The company will expand its operations in the Orinoco Belt, where much of Venezuela's oil reserves lie.

"Today is a transformative day," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, speaking at a press conference this morning at the Miraflores Palace in Caracas, alongside Chevron CEO Mike Wirth and Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez. "The catalyst for transforming Venezuela is energy. The catalyst for improving the life conditions of Americans, our hemisphere, and everyone in the world, is to massively expand energy production around the world."

Sponsor Message

"Today's agreement is an important milestone for Chevron, our partners, and the Venezuelan people," said Wirth. "It reflects progress toward a more competitive and durable framework for long-term investment. Importantly, it creates the opportunity to unlock growth and development."

Chevron is the largest foreign oil operator in Venezuela. The deal announced today expands its footprint at a time of political and economic uncertainty for Venezuela; the country has been run by an interim unelected president, Rodríguez, who came into office after the U.S. captured former President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Other U.S. oil companies have previously expressed hesitation about re-entering Venezuela after leaving it decades ago, with ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods calling the country " uninvestable " at a White House meeting in January.

In an online statement posted this morning, Chevron says as part of a joint venture, it plans to invest over $7 billion over the next five years. This, the company says, will expand its production to approximately 600,000 barrels of oil per day.

The Chevron deal comes less than a week after the Trump administration announced a new deal to develop 17 Venezuelan oil fields — with an estimated 65 barrels of oil — in a joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners, a private oil company headquartered in Barbados. It also comes as President Trump has encouraged American oil companies to invest in Venezuela's oil operations .

Venezuela's been an oil-producing nation for around a century and was a founding member of OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Chevron first established a presence in Venezuela in the 1920s. It stayed even after the country nationalized its oil industry in 1976, and later tightened control over its oil industry in the 1990s under then-President Hugo Chávez. Rivals ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips left in 2007 after Chavez renegotiated contracts with international companies.

Sponsor Message

While Venezuela is sitting on some of the world's largest oil reserves, they are still underground. It will take some time and effort to refine and extract.

"It's a little bit like sitting on a lottery ticket that's just a little bit out of our reach, and you're always having to try to stretch yourself to get it," says Alejandro Velasco, a New York University historian who specializes in Venezuela and Latin America.

Much of the country's oil infrastructure has been in disrepair for more than a decade. Velasco says corruption and low oil prices in the early 2000s contributed to the dilapidated state of Venezuela's facilities. In refineries today, he says, one would see rusty equipment, leaks, even broken fences where copper thieves came in to steal wire.

World.title: Arrest warrants issued in Mexico for duo accused in alleged condo scam
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Mexican court has issued arrest warrants against the man and woman accused of defrauding a Canadian couple of their retirement savings through an alleged condo-flip scheme, CBC News has learned.

The warrants for Harry Robinson, a British national, and Jacqueline Herrera Herrera, a Mexican national, were issued in late July by a Quintana Roo state court judge.

Both are now before a Mexican federal court seeking to toss those warrants, according to copies of court records.

The criminal case against them, which is being heard at the state level, won’t be impacted by the federal court process around the arrest warrants, however.

Robinson and Herrera are accused by the state prosecutor's office of committing fraud through deception.

The Canadian couple — Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown, of Curve Lake, Ont. — sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by a Robinson and Herrera who promised big returns on a condo flip in Playa del Carmen that never materialized.

"It is not something that leaves your mind because you’re always worried about what’s going to happen, what’s next," said Thompson this week.

Quintana Roo is a popular vacation and investment destination for Canadians, and also home to Cancun and Tulum.

Cindy Thompson, right, and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by Robinson and Herrera — who promised big returns on condos in Playa del Carmen that never materialized. (Courtesy of Cindy Thompson)

Thompson and Brown filed a criminal complaint against Robinson and Herrera earlier this year.

The case stems from late 2024 when Thompson, searching for possible real estate investments in Mexico, came across the web page for XMEX Investments which was run by Robinson.

She eventually met Robinson and Herrera in Playa del Carmen. Herrera pitched her on buying a one-bedroom condo and Thompson sent $170,000 in two installments, but never received the keys.

Robinson then convinced Thompson to move her money, with an additional $110,000 from Brown, into a deal to flip seven condos, saying via WhatApp it was looking "to be 100 per cent profit."

Thompson and Brown’s money then vanished.

A federal court judge granted a stay on Aug. 27 against the warrant seeking Herrera’s arrest, but the process to have it tossed continues, according to court records.

A hearing on Robinson’s application is scheduled for Sept. 8 in Cancun, according to court records.

Herrera has claimed in WhatsApp messages that Robinson took some of the money. Robinson filed a criminal complaint against Herrera in late 2025 alleging she stole all the money.

Neither Robinson, Herrera’s lawyer in Cancun nor the state deputy-prosecutor who is leading the case responded to a request for comment.

Herrera, through another lawyer, offered a cash settlement in early August to Thompson for about $2.3 million pesos, roughly $188,000, according to WhatsApp text and voice messages obtained by CBC News.

She then offered Thompson a commercial property in Cancun which she claimed was worth about $4 million pesos, or roughly $328,000.

Thompson rejected the offers.

"We're not going to get into any deals like that with her, ever again," said Thompson.

She says it’s been frustrating trying to understand the complex workings of the Mexican judicial system and the various moving parts associated with the case.

"I'm a little more hopeful, although today, my anxiety's through the roof," said Thompson. "It's hard not being there and not really knowing firsthand what’s going on."

World.title: Donald Trump mistakes Bank of Canada for retail bank
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday implied the Bank of Canada was a commercial bank with locations south of the border, not a Crown corporation that exists solely up north.

The president made the claim at an Oval Office event with travel executives, repeating his longstanding belief that Canada takes economic advantage of the U.S.

"They basically don't allow banks of America to be in Canada. That's sort of emblematic of the way they treat us," Trump told reporters, having been asked a question about the decline in Canadian tourism.

"They have their banks here, Bank of Canada, all of their big banks, big beautiful banks. I think they have six or seven major banks here. We don't have our banks there. You know why? They don't allow it."

The Bank of Canada is not a commercial bank for everyday citizens looking to open accounts or make transactions and does not operate in the U.S. It is a Crown corporation that oversees banking services on behalf of the federal government.

The bank also sets interest rates. On Wednesday, it held its benchmark interest rate steady at 2.25 per cent as the governor warned inflation was on the rise.

Trump has previously claimed U.S. banks for the public are not allowed to operate in Canada, but the assertion is false.

WATCH | Trump has repeatedly claimed that U.S. banks are barred from operating in Canada: Is Trump lying about U.S. banks not being allowed in Canada? | About That | Duration 9:11

Several U.S. financial institutions have operations in Canada. They fall under the Schedule 2 category (foreign-owned banks with Canadian subsidiaries), and they include JPMorganChase, which has about 600 employees on this side of the border, and Citibank, which has operated in Canada for more than a century.

U.S. banks do face tough competition from Canada's highly concentrated banking industry. The big six domestic banks — Royal Bank, Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, CIBC, TD Bank and National Bank — account for the vast majority of total bank assets.

Canada's Big Six fall under the Schedule 1 category — meaning they must be Canadian-owned institutions that take deposits. Any American bank that wanted to buy a major Canadian bank would face these and other restrictions.

World.title: 2 more B.C. Conservative MLAs quit caucus to sit as Independents
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Conservative Party of B.C. has lost two more MLAs as Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis became the eighth and ninth members to quit caucus in recent weeks, both citing concerns about party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership.

"I never imagined things could go this wrong, this quickly," Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, said in a statement.

Wilson, who was elected in 2024, said she remains a conservative in principle but added that communication within the party had broken down and she has worries about the direction under Findlay, particularly around staffing decisions.

McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, said in a separate statement that he no longer supports "the direction, judgment and decisions of Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership."

"The party has increasingly become an exclusive private club more concerned with ideological bona fides than building the broad coalition required to serve British Columbians and form government," he said.

Wilson and McInnis follow seven other MLAs to step away from the Conservatives, the latest being Á'a:líya Warbus, MLA for Chilliwack-Cultus Lake, who on Monday also said she had lost confidence in Findlay.

The B.C. Conservative caucus said in a statement that it remains focused on its work as the Official Opposition to "[hold] the NDP government accountable and restoring prosperity for the people of this province."

Findlay will run in a byelection triggered by Conservative MLA for Abbotsford-Mission Reann Gasper's decision to step down from her role to allow the Conservative leader to seek a seat.

Findlay said the criticisms by departing members of her caucus are baseless.

"What we are seeing is a co-ordinated political attack designed to sidetrack our campaign at the very moment we are taking our message directly to the people of Abbotsford-Mission," she said.

Findlay said she has spent her career in positions of significant public trust, including as a lawyer, a former Canadian Human Rights Tribunal judge, a King's Counsel, a member of the King's Privy Council for Canada and as a federal cabinet minister.

The B.C. Conservatives' chief of staff Chris Delaney also resigned Wednesday.

Findlay named Gasper as her new chief of staff. Gasper had served as deputy chief of staff after stepping down as MLA.

Findlay was elected as party leader in May. Since then, the party has lost key staffers and faced allegations that she attempted to induce MLAs to step down to open a seat for her in the B.C. Legislature, a claim which she has denied as a political smear.

Two ex-Conservatives, Peter Milobar and Ian Paton, say they intend to form a new party.

World.title: 'I don't feel like a hero,' says Winnipeg woman who saved father, drowning toddler from Red River
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Winnipeg woman says she's still recovering, but glad everyone is safe, days after rescuing both a child who fell into the Red River and the girl's father, who attempted to save the child.

Jayclyn Morrissette, 32, was on a walk with her neighbour at St. John's Park, in Winnipeg's North End, on the evening of Aug. 24.

They stopped at a bench overlooking the Red River, where she "noticed a little girl flailing in the water," Morrissette told CBC on Wednesday.

She went down to the water as her neighbour went to the child's parents, who were frantically searching for the toddler, she said.

"I got down to the edge when the father had jumped in, and it took about 10 seconds before I realized he was not coming back up. So I … emptied my pockets and jumped in."

Trying to rescue the father was difficult, Morrissette said, so her neighbour grabbed her as she held onto him, and they were able to get the man out of the water.

Morrissette then swam back out to get the drowning toddler.

In a Wednesday morning news release detailing the incident, Winnipeg police said the rescuer swam backward toward the riverbank with the unconscious child on her chest.

"When I pulled her out, she was lifeless," Morrissette said. "As I was swimming back, I was also pumping her stomach."

Morrisette says she and her neighbour performed CPR — which she learned over a decade ago —on the child before first responders arrived.

The girl was taken to hospital in critical condition, where she was later stabilized, police said. She is now expected to make a full recovery.

But Morrissette said she suffered nightmares in the days following the incident.

"Her eyes were open and her tongue was purple, so that's all I could see every time I closed my eyes," Morrissette said. "I didn't sleep for a couple of days."

She also says once the adrenaline wore off, she realized she had suffered injuries to her neck and shoulder. She's been taking painkillers and is waiting to get testing, if her injuries do not get better.

Police did not release the child's age nor the names of the people involved, but said in their news release the woman who saved the girl and her father showed "remarkable courage and selflessness" in saving people who were strangers to her, with little regard for her own safety.

"I'm just a mom," Morrissette said. "I don't feel like a hero."

Someone else would have done the same thing in that situation, she said.

"I'm glad I was there. They're lucky I was there. I wish it just never happened," she said.

"Be safe. Watch your kids at all times. It only takes a second."

World.title: Kawhi Leonard avoids suspension in NBA's salary cap probe, clearing major hurdle for Toronto Raptors return
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The NBA has declined to suspend Kawhi Leonard or void his contract after its salary-cap circumvention investigation into the Los Angeles Clippers, clearing a major hurdle for his proposed return to the Toronto Raptors.

The league announced Wednesday it stripped the Clippers of five first-round picks from 2029 through 2033 and fined the team $30 million US after an independent investigation found a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations.

Clippers owner Steve Ballmer and president of business operations Gillian Zucker were suspended for one year, while president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was suspended for six months.

Leonard was ordered to pay the NBA $700,000 after the investigation found he violated circumvention rules by obtaining off-court income opportunities with the Clippers' assistance and failing to reimburse personal expenses paid by the team.

Leonard's uncle and former business manager Dennis Robertson was banned from conducting business with NBA teams and their affiliates for five years.

The Raptors and Clippers put a proposed trade involving Leonard on hold in July pending the outcome of the investigation. The deal would send Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, a 2027 pick swap and two second-round selections to Los Angeles.

WATCH | Raptors put Kawhi Leonard trade on hold: The Raptors put Kawhi Leonard's trade on hold. Why he's being investigated | Duration 6:35 Kawhi Leonard is under investigation by the NBA for a 'no-show' sponsorship deal signed while he was with the Los Angeles Clippers. Savanna Hamilton breaks down what's being investigated and what it means for his future with the Toronto Raptors.

Leonard averaged 27.9 points, 6.3 rebounds, 3.6 assists, 1.9 steals and 0.4 blocks per game last season for the Clippers in 2025-26.

Assuming the Toronto-L.A. deal can now go through, Leonard will join a Raptors lineup that includes Barnes, Canadian swingman RJ Barrett, talented rookie Collin Murray-Boyles, point guard Immanuel Quickley and young rotation pieces Jamal Shead and Ja'Kobe Walter.

Leonard is a seven-time All-Star, seven-time All-NBA selection, a two-time NBA champion (with San Antonio in 2014 and Toronto in 2019) and is generally considered one of the game's top defensive players.

He was the central player in the Raptors' 2019 championship run, including a climactic buzzer beater to win Game 7 of Toronto's Eastern Conference semifinal against the Philadelphia 76ers.

He signed with his hometown Clippers as a free agent that off-season, agreeing to a three-year, $103 million contract.

After opting out of the final year of that contract, Leonard re-signed with the Clippers in August 2021 to a max four-year, $176.3 million contract with the fourth year being a player option. He missed the entire 2021-22 season, however, with a partial ACL tear in his right knee.

That 2021 contract has become embroiled in controversy after allegations emerged in September 2025 that Leonard signed a $28 million "no-show" endorsement deal with Aspiration, an environmental company that entered bankruptcy in March 2025 after co-founder Joe Sanberg was arrested and charged with fraud.

The alleged deal did not require any action on Leonard's part, other than remaining with the Clippers.

World.title: Hilroy says sorry for leaving Newfoundland, Cape Breton off notebooks' Canadian map
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hilroy has apologized for leaving Newfoundland and Cape Breton off the Canadian map on its glossy notebooks, after the mistake led to backlash online.

Hilroy's pastel-coloured paper exercise books are well known across the country for the map of Canada on their covers. But the map on Hilroy's glossy covered notebooks is missing a few parts of the country.

In a post to its Facebook page Tuesday, the company said its team has always been proud of the map, "which is exactly why getting it wrong stings."

The inaccurate map was the result of a production error, the post said. The company has stopped distributing the books and is fixing the cover artwork.

"That's our mistake, and we're sorry," it said. "To everyone who spotted it: you're right and thank you for telling us."

Hilroy's parent company, ACCO Brands, said Wednesday that the faulty books have been on shelves since last year. However, it seems customers only recently noticed the errors. The mishap has generated discussion on social media, prompting posts from Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians expressing their dismay.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham posted a brief but blunt response on Facebook.

"You can leave Newfoundland off an exercise book, but you can't erase us," he wrote Wednesday. "Hilroy will never take away our identity, our history, or our place on the map."

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the incomplete map was "unacceptable."

"I've asked the minister of education to send the makers of Hilroy scribblers a map of Nova Scotia that includes Cape Breton and Newfoundland," Houston said, also in a Facebook post.

The mistaken map also appears to be missing Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the coast of British Columbia. An ACCO Brands spokesperson said the company is aware and addressing the omission is part of its "correction plan."

Sean Cadigan, a history professor at Memorial University in St. John's, said Newfoundland did not join Canada until 1949, and it has been left out of maps and descriptions of the country before. It can be a sensitive issue on the island, he said.

"When there are big tours and people say they're touring Canada, Canada often stops somewhere in Nova Scotia," Cadigan said in an interview Wednesday.

"I think that's just probably an old habit that often predates Newfoundland's joining Confederation," he added. "Obviously, people here want to emphasize, of course, since 1949, we're part of Canada."

Cadigan said the map was an "embarrassing mistake" for Hilroy.

"I wouldn't read it as any intent to slight," he said.

World.title: Liberal MP Idlout violated conflict of interest code, ethics watchdog finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa's ethics commissioner found Liberal MP Lori Idlout violated Parliament's conflict of interest code, but recommended against imposing any penalties against her.

Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein released his findings from an investigation into Idlout's purchases from her own shop that she charged to the House of Commons.

Idlout reimbursed the House, saying she submitted the items in error.

In a statement to CBC News, Idlout thanked the commissioner for the report.

"I acknowledge the commissioner's findings and take this matter seriously," she said.

"At the time, I did not consider that these purchases made for legitimate parliamentary purposes would further private interests, as I receive no income from the businesses in question," Idlout wrote.

In the report, Finckenstein said he believed Idlout's actions "were errors of judgment and made in good faith." He said Idlout did not realize that the purchases would further her own interests, adding the Nunavut MP repaid the House as soon as she learned of the errors.

"In my view, this shows a true desire to fully remedy each instance of non-compliance," Finckenstein wrote in the report. "I therefore recommended that no sanction be imposed.”

Idlout is the sole shareholder and director of Carvings Nunavut , a gallery that sells Inuit-made sculptures and artwork. Idlout claimed 13 purchases as "gifts given as a matter of protocol" since becoming MP, four of which were listed as being from Carvings Nunavut.

The commissioner found Idlout contravened the code of ethics' section prohibiting MPs from acting in any way to further their own private interests.

What did Idlout charge to the House?

The four purchases from Carvings Nunavut amounted to $1,756 and were all made in 2025.

The largest purchase of $1,380 worth of cards, tote bags, hand-crafted keychains and zipper pulls and sculptures was made in August 2025. The commissioner said they were all gifts to First Nations leaders, elders and speakers at the NDP's national caucus meeting in B.C. that September.

She also purchased a wall hanging for $150 in January 2025 that she gifted to a long-term care centre, a $150 lapel pin bought the same month and gifted to Liberal MP Greg Fergus — then speaker of the House of Commons — and a $76 purchase in June 2025, of a fridge magnet, bar of soap and tumbler cup gifted to Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand.

The expenses were made during Idlout's time as an NDP MP, before she crossed the floor to the Liberals in March 2026.

WATCH | Idlout walks into caucus with Carney after crossing the floor: Nunavut MP Lori Idlout walks with Carney to Liberal caucus after crossing the floor from NDP | Duration 1:17 After crossing the floor to the government from the NDP, Nunavut MP Lori Idlout walked into Liberal caucus alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday. When asked what prompted her move, Idlout said there were a 'variety' of things that informed the decision.

The same month, Conservative MP Michael Barrett wrote the ethics commissioner asking for an inquiry into Idlout's conduct under the conflict of interest code.

"Ms. Idlout has — now that she's been caught — admitted to doing what every member of Parliament knows or ought to know they can't do," Barrett said. "This speaks to very poor judgment."

"I regret my error in judgment," Idlout said in her statement to CBC News. "I have since learned from this experience and will work closely with the commissioner's guidance going forward."

World.title: Alanis Morissette sues former tour manager over alleged 'calculated blackmail campaign'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alanis Morissette is suing her former tour manager for what she calls a "calculated blackmail campaign" to frame her for drug trafficking unless the Canadian singer-songwriter agreed to sign her to a lengthy contract.

Morissette filed a lawsuit in California on Tuesday, obtained by CBC News, alleging that Keren Urinov is threatening to report her to British authorities for drug trafficking unless Morissette agreed to employ her as a tour director for 15 years and pay her "massive compensation."

Morissette is suing Urinov for civil extortion, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, writing in the lawsuit that she "will not be coerced into delivering her blackmailer an extraordinary payday" and that she pursued legal action "to expose Urinov's scheme and hold her accountable."

What happened?

Urinov, who previously worked for Live Nation's Israeli operations, was hired in 2025 as a temporary tour manager for Morissette's world tour.

In July 2025, the singer and her team, including Urinov, were allegedly flying from the U.K. to Spain for a concert.

At the airport, the lawsuit claims a British Border Force official flagged a bag, asking who owned it. When Urinov said it was hers, she was arrested and issued a seizure notice alleging that the bag contained marijuana and xylazine — a non-opioid animal tranquilizer.

During questioning, Urinov allegedly admitted that the bag and the drugs were hers, showing the authorities her Israeli medical marijuana licence, the lawsuit says. It was returned to her and she was released.

The next day, Urinov was allegedly detained again at an airport for questioning about the bag they'd taken the previous day.

'A series of increasingly extortionate letters'

The suit claims Urinov told Morissette that — again — she admitted the bag and the drugs belonged to her.

But after the tour wrapped, Urinov and her lawyers allegedly sent "a series of increasingly extortionate letters to Morissette ," threatening to sue her in the U.K. for "unspecified claims" if Morissette refused to tell British law enforcement that the drugs were hers.

According to the lawsuit, the letters said Morissette could "put an end to the matter" by giving Urinov a fixed 15-year contract that included "income equivalent to that of a tour director with annual increases and bonuses."

She also allegedly demanded Morissette arrange for an immigration lawyer to get a work visa that would allow Urinov to work in the United States — and that if the visa couldn't be obtained, she'd demand more pay.

'Reluctant' but 'no choice but to sue'

The lawsuit also details reasons Morissette felt Urinov "was a terrible manager of the 2025 tour."

This includes "unnecessarily" spending nearly $70,000 US after an "inexplicable error with a hotel booking that no competent tour manager would have made," the court filing states.

Morissette also alleges that while on tour, Urinov told the singer's team that she and a friend were arrested in Latin America "years ago" for smuggling drugs in a surfboard and that Urinov illegally fled the country after being released on bail.

"This was an astounding revelation, given that Urinov had told Morissette's team during her interview for the tour manager position that nothing in her past would cause any complications with obtaining visas or travelling, and she never mentioned her arrest or crimes in Latin America," the lawsuit states.

The lawsuit also says Morissette was "reluctant" to file, but that she had "no choice but to sue."

" Morissette will not agree to work with an incompetent blackmailer for the next 15 years or pay her a ransom under the gun," it reads.

Morissette is seeking a trial by jury. CBC News has reached out to Urinov and representatives for Morissette but has not yet heard back.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
