World.title: Meet Ana Valdez, a Forbes ’50 over 50′ illuminating the Latino narrative in the United States
World.content:
At MND, we’re always looking for new perspectives on the United States-Canada-Mexico relationship from leaders and organizations working to improve trilateral relations through fact-based data and reporting.

One of those leaders is Ana Valdez of the Latino Donor Collaborative (LDC), a non-profit organization and think tank she has led as president and CEO since 2014.

Valdez, a Mexico City native, emigrated to the United States in the 1990s and got a volunteer job in the White House when Bill Clinton was president. Fast forward to today, and she is on Forbes’s “50 over 50” list — a selection of women aged over 50 who are doing ambitious, influential and powerful work in the United States.

The LDC, according to the organization’s website, is “dedicated to reshaping the perception of Latinos as part of the American social mainstream.”

This is very important work, Valdez told Mexico News Daily during a recent interview.

“When I [first] came here, I saw a huge disconnect between the perception of who Latinos are in the United States and the reality of who they are,” she said.

“One misconception is that everybody is an immigrant. That matters because about 70% of Latinos in this country have been here for many generations. Some were here even before this [land] was the United States,” Valdez said.

CDMX to LA via Spain and Switzerland

“Since taking the helm of the Latino Donor Collaborative in 2014, Ana Valdez has led an organization that represents the economic interests of all Latinos in the U.S,” states a brief profile of the 64-year-old that Forbes published as part of its “50 over 50” list.

“In 2023 she launched the nonprofit’s Latino Data Collective, which puts economic data and market information about Latinos into the hands of more than 650,000 CEOs, politicians, board directors and media executives.”

Before moving to the United States close to 30 years ago, and joining the Los Angeles-based LDC more than a decade ago, Valdez studied and worked in Europe for a period. Before that, she completed a bachelor’s degree in business and marketing at Mexico’s Tec. de Monterrey university.

“I was born and raised in Mexico City,” she told MND, beginning a highly condensed version of her life story.

Valdez noted later in our interview that she completed a master’s degree in international relations in Spain and subsequently worked with the United Nations in Switzerland.

“After living in Europe for four years, I came to the United States and found the Latino community. I didn’t know about it growing up in Mexico City, and I didn’t know about it in Europe,” she said.

Valdez explained that she traveled to the United States to work on a PhD thesis, but ended up getting a volunteer job at the White House, “and after three months they hired me.”

“I stayed and never finished my PhD,” she said.

In addition to working at the White House in both a volunteer and paid capacity, Valdez held positions at Nielsen and Banamex before her appointment as CEO of LDC.

“My first job was at Nielsen, so I’m a nerd — [I love] using data … to do anything [related] with business,” she told MND.

“I’ve been madly in love with data ever since,” Valdez said before correcting herself to note that her passion for statistics actually dates back to her college days.

The LDC’s mission and vision

The LDC, the organization says on its website, “was founded in 2010 after a group of national business leaders identified a critical gap: the lack of an accurate narrative about Latinos, resulting in the perpetuation of harmful stereotypes.”

“This gap in understanding about U.S. Latinos was particularly troubling, as some states began passing laws that allowed for the arbitrary arrest of individuals based on these stereotypes,” the LDC says.

“In response to these alarming developments, co-founders and national leaders Sol Trujillo and Henry Cisneros [a former U.S. secretary of housing] recognized the urgency of creating a bipartisan non-profit organization and producing reputable data and statistics that accurately reflect the identity of Latinos in America and their contributions to the nation.”

The LDC says it “produces the most reputable data on Latinos in the United States,” much of which is compiled from official U.S. government stats, according to Valdez.

The organization says that the statistics it presents are “critical to the U.S. economy, workforce, business development, entertainment, and several other key aspects of American prosperity” given that members of the U.S. Latino community account for 20% of the entire U.S. population and more than one-quarter of Americans aged 18 and under.

The organization says its mission is to “reframe and advance an accurate perception, portrayal, and understanding of the important contributions that American Latinos make to American society,” while its vision is for “American Latinos to be recognized as valued, patriotic Americans in all facets of American life.”

A central element of the LDC’s strategy to reframe perceptions of Latinos in the United States — including some 40 million people of Mexican origin — is the publication of data-heavy reports focusing on the Latino population’s contributions to the U.S. economy and society. Among the more than 60 reports the organization has published are the “2026 LDC U.S. Latino Economic Impact Report” and “Data Beyond Demographics: U.S. Latinas’ Economic Power, Influence, and Growth.”

Mexico News Daily will soon begin presenting some of the key data in LDC reports in articles with an easy-to-read, visually engaging format.

“For us, collaboration is amplification,” Valdez said, referring to a partnership with MND.

“We believe from the bottom of our hearts and minds that this information helps everybody. It helps Americans in Mexico, too. There are so many Americans living in Mexico right now, and it would be a blind spot not to inform them about people who are doing exactly the opposite,” she said.

Changing Latinos, changing perceptions

Valdez told MND that Latinos made up around 7% of the U.S. population in 1960, whereas they account for 20% today, an increase attributable to both immigration and the birth in the United States of millions of Latino babies.

“People didn’t know Latinos before because they were only 7% [of the U.S. population],” she said.

“The preconceived idea of Latinos was perhaps someone seen as a valet parker, a housekeeper or a gardener.”

Valdez acknowledged that many Latinos worked — and continue to work — such jobs. However, she emphasized that many Latinos are now business owners or work in professional fields. In a 2025 infographic, the LDC highlights that there are “approximately 5.7 million U.S. Latino enterprises in the U.S.”

Valdez noted that many recent — and in some cases undocumented — Latino immigrants to the United States have attempted to maintain a low profile while the Trump administration carries out an aggressive deportation agenda. However, U.S.-born Latino “kids” are “completely different,” she said.

“…[Market research company] Kantar calls these young people ‘200 percenters,'” Valdez said.

“They feel 100% American and 100% Latino too. Contrary to their parents, they are not ashamed or embarrassed. They are unapologetic about being Latino. They’re proud, comfortable and confident. Their friends and peers want to know more [about Latino culture], want to learn Spanish, want to dance to Bad Bunny,” she said, providing one example of how U.S. perceptions of Latinos, and Latino culture, have changed.

“… Every year, thousands or hundreds of thousands of Latinos turn 18. They vote. They go to college. If they don’t go to college, they work in much better environments than the fields where their parents worked. They are assertive [and] speak English perfectly,” Valdez said.

She subsequently noted that her husband is Mexican-American, “from one of the families that came to what is now the United States when it was still Mexico.”

“… The border crossed them when the United States took over New Mexico and many other states,” Valdez said.

“… When my husband was growing up in Colorado, people were bullied for speaking Spanish. He remembers his mother putting burritos in his lunch. He was embarrassed when he opened it and it smelled, so he would put it away, not eat it and throw it out. He was bullied because of it,” she said.

“Fast-forward to our kids in a school on the west side of Los Angeles. We realized that one of them was charging his friends to bring them home for lunch because everyone wanted real Mexican food. His white friends wanted it,” Valdez said.

“So it is a complete change,” she said.

Beyond greater acceptance in the U.S. of Mexican food and the cuisines of other Western Hemisphere countries — and indeed increased desirability and “trendiness” of such food — there is growing recognition of the immense contribution Latinos make to the United States.

Unfortunately, however, there is still discrimination against Latinos in the U.S., while certain stereotypes and misconceptions persist. The LDC, as it has done since its foundation, will continue to work to counteract those enduring problems.

It’s not just Forbes taking notice of Valdez’s work

Forbes is by no means the only prominent media organization that has taken notice of LDC’s work under Valdez’s leadership. Among the others are CBS News, CNBC, Variety and Axios.

Valdez has also come to the attention of the Mexican government, leading to invitations to speak at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conferences.

At Sheinbaum’s May 22 mañanera, the LDC CEO presented a range of data about women of Mexican origin in the United States, including one particularly striking statistic — that those women contribute US $1.1 trillion to U.S. GDP on an annual basis.

When we asked Valdez why she — a Los Angeles-based data expert focused on Latinos in the U.S. — had been invited to speak at the president’s mañanera on numerous occasions, she noted that Sheinbaum is a scientist who “likes numbers.”

“When a scientist realizes that there are almost 40 million nationals or people with Mexican national background living in the United States, and that Mexico was not in touch with them, she wanted to know more about them and begin engaging them,” Valdez said, noting also that Sheinbaum has been a strong supporter of Mexican deportees and the Mexican community in the U.S., including people at risk of deportation.

World.title: Sheinbaum again gripes about the US meddling in her government: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇸 Sheinbaum claims US is seeking to “weaken” and “divide” her government : Sheinbaum said the Trump administration is trying to “create divisions” within her Security Cabinet and cabinet, calling it a longstanding U.S. tactic against “independent governments that defend sovereignty.” She linked the criticism to November’s US midterm elections, saying that US politicians often use Mexico as part of their election campaigns.

: Sheinbaum said the Trump administration is trying to “create divisions” within her Security Cabinet and cabinet, calling it a longstanding U.S. tactic against “independent governments that defend sovereignty.” She linked the criticism to November’s US midterm elections, saying that US politicians often use Mexico as part of their election campaigns. 🚫 Sheinbaum dismisses claims that AMLO is pulling the strings : Responding to talk of “Obradoristas” and “Claudistas” within Morena, Sheinbaum said former President López Obrador has been “extremely respectful” and has never told her what to do. She called the idea that a man is really governing behind her a “sexist” one.

: Responding to talk of “Obradoristas” and “Claudistas” within Morena, Sheinbaum said former President López Obrador has been “extremely respectful” and has never told her what to do. She called the idea that a man is really governing behind her a “sexist” one. 🎢 Sheinbaum reflects on a “complex” year with Washington: Asked about the hardest moment of her second year, Sheinbaum pointed to tensions over U.S. tariffs on steel and vehicles and Washington’s extradition request for 10 officials, including Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. However, she said that friction with the US hasn’t caused a “major problem” overall.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum presided over her Wednesday morning press conference a day after delivering her second annual government report in a lengthy speech at the National Palace.

Sheinbaum largely avoided criticizing the U.S. government during her address on Tuesday, but less than 24 hours later, she reiterated her view that the Trump administration is meddling in Mexican affairs.

Her assertions on Wednesday that the U.S. is seeking to “weaken” and “create divisions” in her government were among the most significant remarks of the press conference.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s dismissal of claims that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador is pulling the strings in her administration. She has previously described such claims as “misogynistic,” and expressed a similar view on Wednesday.

Sheinbaum asserts that the US is seeking to ‘create divisions’ in her government

A reporter noted that DEA Administrator Terry Cole’s has spoken out against Mexico and her government, highlighting that he said last week that there are “high-level officials that are working directly with the cartels.”

The reporter also noted that Cole recently described Security Minister Omar García Harfuch as a “trusted partner” and “good friend of the United States.”

She asked Sheinbaum whether Cole’s remarks about García Harfuch amounted to an endorsement of him as a candidate in upcoming elections. Her suggestion was that the U.S. government — or at least the DEA chief — would like García Harfuch to be the next president of Mexico.

Sheinbaum responded that “they” — i.e., U.S. officials — “seek in one way or another to weaken [foreign] governments, because that’s one of their objectives.”

They “particularly” seek to weaken “independent governments that defend sovereignty,” she said.

They seek to “divide us internally,” Sheinbaum said.

“It’s one of their strategies,” she said, adding that it’s not a new tactic but rather one that U.S. governments have “always” used.

#MañaneraPresidenta | SOBERANÍA ANTE CUALQUIER INTENTO DE INJERENCIA Claudia Sheinbaum afirmó que mantener los principios y la autoridad política y moral es fundamental ante intentos de injerencia extranjera como la red de Fernando Cerimedo y Javier Negre. Reiteró que con EU… pic.twitter.com/JXsmZcKVtQ — Juncal Solano (@juncalssolano) September 2, 2026

Sheinbaum asserted that the current U.S. government is seeking to “create divisions” within the federal Security Cabinet and her cabinet.

“They are tactics of interference that they use,” she said.

“What happens is that they run into a wall because the Security Cabinet of the government of Mexico is highly coordinated and very united,” Sheinbaum said.

“… There are no divisions,” she said.

“… They think that by speaking well about one person and ill of others they’re going to create divisions inside [the Security Cabinet], but they fail,” Sheinbaum said.

She also asserted that recent remarks made by U.S. officials about Mexico are politically motivated given that midterm elections will be held in the United States this November.

“They remember they have elections in November. So they often use Mexico as part of their election [campaigns],” Sheinbaum said.

Pushed as to whether the U.S. government was giving its “vote” to García Harfuch, the president responded:

“No. What they seek, also, is to influence our elections. It’s the same old story.”

Sheinbaum: AMLO has been ‘extremely respectful’ toward our government

Sheinbaum said that opposition politicians and government critics are claiming that there is a “deep division” between her and López Obrador.

“Now [they’re talking about] the Obradoristas and the Claudistas, that’s the way they put it,” she said, referring to broader alleged divisions within the Morena party.

“It’s completely absurd. Firstly, it’s important for everyone to know, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador has been extremely respectful toward our government. Extremely respectful,” Sheinbaum said.

“He hasn’t sent any message saying, ‘Do this’ or ‘Do that’ or ‘I don’t agree with what you did,'” she said.

“… This idea that, behind the president, López Obrador is governing is a very sexist idea,” Sheinbaum said.

“… It has to do with an idea that women can’t govern,” she said.

Sheinbaum acknowledges ‘situations of tension’ with US

A reporter asked the president whether she had identified the most “critical” and “complicated” moment of her second year in office. He also asked Sheinbaum about the most “satisfying” aspect of her presidency.

“Well, I think the relationship with the United States has been complex,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’ve sought a good relationship, but there have been times of difficulty,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the United States’ imposition of tariffs on Mexican products such as steel and vehicles created “times of tension” in the bilateral relationship.

She asserted that the U.S. government also “wanted to provoke a moment of tension” when it sent a request for 10 current and former officials, including Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, to be detained for the purpose of extradition to the U.S. to face drug trafficking charges.

“There were times of tension with the U.S. government, or with some people of the U.S. government,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that friction between her government and the Trump administration hasn’t created a “major problem” for Mexico. But there have been “situations of tension,” Sheinbaum said.

“The truth is that we’ve been able to move on very well,” she added.

Sheinbaum subsequently said that she very much enjoys her “tours” of Mexico on weekends, during which she travels around the country to inspect progress on infrastructure projects and inaugurate completed ones, among other activities. During the tours, she gets up close and personal with Mexicans from all walks of life.

Sheinbaum said that her trips “fill” her with “happiness and energy.”

“… It’s the most beautiful thing,” she added.

World.title: MND Local: Gorillaz, mariachi festival, immersive dining and more in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week, we share details on the 33rd annual International Mariachi and Charrería Encounter, the Gorillaz’s upcoming concert in Zapopan, and an immersive dinner inspired by the indie French film “Amélie.” But first, let’s meet the new U.S. consul general in Guadalajara.

Elizabeth Hoffman Franolich begins new role as US consul general in Guadalajara

Earlier this month, Elizabeth Hoffman Franolich became the new consul general of the United States in Guadalajara. She replaces Amy Scanlon, who finished her term last July.

A career foreign service officer with more than two decades of diplomatic experience, Hoffman Franolich is well-versed in Latin American affairs, with previous postings in El Salvador, Venezuela and Colombia.

Prior to her current post, Hoffman Franolich was director of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement, and deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in El Salvador.

A fluent Spanish speaker, the new consul general arrives in Guadalajara with prior diplomatic experience in Mexico as well, having served as trade and investment counselor at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City.

Originally from Ohio, Hoffman Franolich holds a Bachelor of Science in Public Policy from Vanderbilt University and a Master of Science in Geography from SUNY at Albany.

With reporting from the University of Guadalajara and El Informador.

The 33rd annual International Mariachi and Charrería Encounter is underway

Guadalajara is currently filled with the sound of trumpets, vihuelas and guitarrrones, courtesy of the 33rd edition of the International Mariachi and Charrería Encounter, which runs through Sept. 6.

Over the 11-day event, there will be live concerts, charro contests (Mexican rodeo) and free activities for the whole family, with 95% of the events free and accessible to all.

Mariachi, declared by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, is the soul of this gathering. Year after year it brings together diverse audiences spanning generations.

Performances feature some of Mexico’s most iconic groups and musical collaborators from more than 20 countries, including Croatia, Italy, France, Greece, Canada, Colombia and Australia.

Some of the highlights include:

Mariachi Galas at the Degollado Theater : The best mariachis in the world will join the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra for several unforgettable themed nights on Sept. 2, 3, and 5 at 8 p.m.

A concert with Natalia Jiménez at Telmex Auditorium : Natalia Jiménez is set to perform with the Mariachi Internacional CHG and the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra on Sept. 4.

A closing concert in the Children’s Park in Zapopan: A closing concert featuring a performance by Jalisco’s own Azucena on Sept. 6.

To see the full program, check out this page. Tickets are available at the venue box offices or through Ticketmaster Mexico.

With reporting from Telediario.

Gorillaz to perform at new GNP Seguros Coliseum in December

The legendary British band Gorillaz will bring “The Mountain Tour” to Guadalajara this December. The show is scheduled for the newly revamped GNP Seguros Coliseum on the UAG campus in Zapopan on Dec. 9.

For the uninitiated, Gorillaz’s music spans trip-hop, hip-hop and lo-fi indie rock that really gets a crowd moving. The band burst onto the indie scene more than 25 years ago with their irresistible single “Clint Eastwood,” which blended the hip-hop vocals of Del the Funky Homosapien over electronic music with a heavy bassline.

Gorillaz came into being as British frontman Damon Albarn’s previous indie band, Blur, was dissolving in the late 1990s.

“The Mountain,” the band’s ninth studio LP, is the product of Albarn’s dig through years of Gorillaz recordings, in search of unused material from former collaborators who have now passed. Albarn was able to get approval for all the artists he wished to include on the album — except for one notoriously difficult cat, Lou Reed.

In all, more than two dozen performers, living and dead, appear on “The Mountain,” which took inspiration from Albarn’s visit to India following the death of his father. Live shows on this tour have included a wide cast of characters, including Little Simz, Mos Def and The Smiths’ Johnny Marr.

When : Dec. 9, 2026

Where : Coliseo GNP Seguros, Zapopan, on the UAG campus.

Tickets : Tickets starting from 2,827 pesos are available at Ticketmaster Mexico .

A culinary adventure inspired by the classic French indie film ‘Amélie’

The creative team at Efímero Lab in Colonia Americana is back at it, preparing the latest installment of its “The Taste of Movies” series. This time, the lab is hosting an immersive dinner to celebrate the beloved French film “Amélie,” directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet and starring the adorable Audrey Tautou.

The film tells the story of a Parisian waitress who plays small pranks that improve others’ lives while searching for a romance of her own.

Diners can expect a three-course meal with cocktail pairings that deliver a sensory experience inspired by the film’s characters, plot and unique sensibility.

Created by a collective of architects, artists, designers and mixologists, Efímero Lab is a cozy and sophisticated lounge exploring craft cocktails, gastronomy and immersive experiences.

When : The Amélie immersive dinner is on Sept. 5. The “Taste of Movies” series is a recurring event at Efímero Lab.

Where : Juan Manuel 1575, Colonia Americana, 44600 Guadalajara.

Tickets: Tickets for the dinner are 1,600 pesos per person. To reserve your spot, contact Efímero Lab on Instagram . Seats are limited.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: The MND Sheinbaum Index™ for July 2026: The president sees near 10-point gain since April
World.content:
THE MND SHEINBAUM INDEX™

Measuring Mexico’s president beyond the polls

MND Intelligence · Fifth edition

Welcome to the fifth edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™, an eight-pillar index designed to give our readers balanced, data-driven insight into the current situation in Mexico across a range of areas under the leadership of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

In this edition of the index — which mainly uses data from the month of July — the headline number is 69.3, representing an improvement of 1.8 points compared to the previous score. This is the highest MND Sheinbaum Index™ to date. A detailed summary of the latest results appears below.

The MND Sheinbaum Index™ score has now improved in three consecutive months, increasing by 9.3 points in the period. An analysis of the index trend so far this year also appears below.

The publication of this MND Sheinbaum Index™ score comes just over 23 months into Sheinbaum’s presidency and a day after she delivered her second annual government report. Click here to read MND’s article on that report.

If you need a reminder on how the index works and how each of the eight equally weighted pillars is scored, please read the second edition of the MND Sheinbaum Index™.

Before we look in detail at the latest results and examine the index trend in the first half of 2026, here is a short guide to the significance of a Sheinbaum Index score:

85–100: Exceptional — administration performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— administration performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Excellent — administration performing well across most indicators.

— administration performing well across most indicators. 60–75: Quite good, but room for improvement — meaningful strengths, some areas of concern.

— meaningful strengths, some areas of concern. 50–60: Mixed — passing marks overall.

— passing marks overall. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

The MND Sheinbaum Index™ trend between February and July

We saw the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score fall and rise in the period between February and July, but, as noted above, a consistent upward trend was maintained across the final three months of that interval.

Factors such as inflation of around 4.5% in each of March and April, as well as annual economic growth of 0.5% or lower in those months, caused the index score to deteriorate to 60 from 64.8 in February, when inflation was very close to 4% and economic growth was above 1%.

The 4.8-point month-over-month improvement in the index score in May was mainly due to inflation falling compared to April, homicides declining at a faster annual pace and economic growth improving. We saw all those things happen again in June, compared to May, resulting in an additional 2.7-point month-over-month improvement in the index score.

The additional 1.8-point improvement in July is due to a range of factors, including an additional decline in the inflation rate, an even larger reduction in homicides and stronger economic growth.

MND Sheinbaum Index™ pillars for July 2026

Each pillar is given a stoplight color indicating a strong performance (green: a score above 9.4 out of 12.5), an average performance (yellow: 6.2-9.4) or a poor performance (red: below 6.2).

An upward-pointing arrow ⬆️ indicates that the pillar score improved compared to May. A downward-pointing arrow ⬇️ indicates a deterioration in the pillar score. A pause icon ⏸️ means there was no change in the pillar score compared to the previous month.

As you’ll see below, scores for six of the eight pillars improved in July compared to June. The scores for two other pillars declined.

🟢 ⬆️ INFLATION (12.2 out of 12.5)

In July, the inflation pillar was the top contributor to the overall index score for a third consecutive month.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate declined from 3.37% in June to 3.12% in July, the lowest rate for any month since May 2020 and just 0.12 percentage points above the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target.

The inflation pillar score consequently rose to 12.2 from 11.58 in June — a gain of 0.62 points.

🟢 ⬆️ LABOR POVERTY (10.25 out of 12.5)

The MND Sheinbaum Index™ updates in this edition with second-quarter labor poverty data that was published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Aug. 26. Based on that data, the labor poverty pillar score rose to 10.25 in July from 10.1 in June.

The labor poverty rate decreased 3.2 percentage points annually to 31.9% in the first quarter of 2026. That rate is higher than the 30.7% reading in the first quarter of 2026, but the score for this component of the pillar is unchanged as the year-over-year decline held steady at 3.2%.

The increase in the pillar score is due to an 8% annual increase in real incomes, up from 7.4% in the first quarter of 2026.

For a third consecutive month, this pillar was the second biggest contributor to the overall index score.

🟢 ⬆️ SECURITY (9.84 out of 12.5)

The pace of homicide reduction accelerated in July for a third consecutive month. The year-over-year decline in homicides was 34.8% in July, per data presented at Sheinbaum’s Aug. 11 press conference, up from 32.5% in June

The security pillar score consequently rose from 9.44 in June to 9.84 in July. A perfect score requires a 50% year-over-year decline in homicides.

🟡 ⬆️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (9.25 out of 12.5)

Year-over-year economic growth in July was 2.7%, according to preliminary data from INEGI — a significant improvement on June’s 1.7% reading.

The economic growth pillar score thus rose from 6.75 in June to 9.25 in July, an improvement of 2.5 points.

The improvement allowed the pillar to move to the cusp of green light territory. The July score for the economic growth pillar is easily the highest since we published the first MND Sheinbaum Index™ in April.

One factor that aided the solid economic growth figure in July is that Mexico’s export revenue increased almost 44% annually that month to reach a record high of US $81.4 billion.

🟡 ⬆️ APPROVAL RATING (8.56 out of 12.5)

Sheinbaum’s average approval increased slightly to 68.5% in July from 68% in June. Thus, the approval rating pillar score increased to 8.56 in July from 8.5 in June.

Per El Financiero’s July poll, Sheinbaum’s approval rating was 67%, a decline of one point compared to June. As there was no new Enkoll/El País/W Radio poll on Sheinbaum in July, we used the approval rating detected by the QM Estudios de Opinión/Heraldo Media Group survey. The president has a 70% approval rating, according to that poll, which was conducted between July 29 and Aug. 1.

🟡 ⬆️ EMPLOYMENT (7 out of 12.5)

Mexico’s unemployment rate was 2.9% in July, below the 3% neutral benchmark and unchanged from June.

The informality rate increased by 0.1 percentage points year-over-year in June, an improvement on the 0.2-point rise recorded in May. Mexico’s informality rate in July, at 56.2%, remained very high.

The improvement in the informality component score resulted in a slight increase in the pillar score to 7 in July from 6.88 in June.

🟡 ⬇️ TOURISM (6.91 out of 12.5 — This pillar has a one-month lag)

International arrivals increased 2.1% year-over-year in June, the data period used for July’s index.

That represents a slowdown from the 5.3% rise recorded in May, pulling the tourism pillar score down to 6.91 from 7.91 a month earlier.

The tourism result was disappointing given that Mexico hosted 10 of its 11 FIFA men’s World Cup matches in June. Mexican authorities had anticipated that as many as 5 million additional international tourists would come to Mexico during the quadrennial event.

🟡 ⬇️ BUSINESS CONFIDENCE (5.33 out of 12.5)

Mexico’s business confidence score, as measured by a monthly INEGI survey, was 48.2 in July, unchanged from June. That score is below the neutral benchmark of 50. In late 2024, when Sheinbaum was at the start of her six-year term, the business confidence score was around 52.

In July, the score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar declined significantly as the Economy Ministry reported last week that FDI in Mexico in the first six months of 2026 increased 2.1% annually, a much slower pace of growth compared with the 10.4% year-over-year gain in the first quarter of the year.

The score for this component of the pillar consequently fell by more than 1 point. That decline is the reason why the overall pillar score fell to 5.33 in July from 6.36 in June.

What to watch

The next MND Sheinbaum Index™ will focus on the month of August.

Here are three things to look out for in the August Index:

Inflation: Data for the first half of August indicates that the score for the inflation pillar will decline in the next edition of the index. INEGI reported on Aug. 24 that the annual headline rate was 3.26% in the first 15 days of August, up from 3.12% in July. If the inflation score does fall in August, it will be the first decline in five months.

Data for the first half of August indicates that the score for the inflation pillar will decline in the next edition of the index. INEGI reported on Aug. 24 that the annual headline rate was 3.26% in the first 15 days of August, up from 3.12% in July. If the inflation score does fall in August, it will be the first decline in five months. Economic growth: Mexico’s economy currently has some momentum, growing 1.9% annually in the second quarter of 2026 and 2.7% in July, according to preliminary data. Even higher growth in August would surprise many, but perhaps not President Sheinbaum, who has predicted that economic activity will pick up in the second half of 2026.

Mexico’s economy currently has some momentum, growing 1.9% annually in the second quarter of 2026 and 2.7% in July, according to preliminary data. Even higher growth in August would surprise many, but perhaps not President Sheinbaum, who has predicted that economic activity will pick up in the second half of 2026. Can Sheinbaum break 70? If the MND Sheinbaum Index™ score improves for a fourth consecutive month in August, it is very likely that the 70-point mark will be exceeded for the first time ever. Look out for the next edition of this index to find out whether the mark was surpassed or not.

Mexico News Daily

* MND acknowledges that President Sheinbaum does not directly control outcomes in all eight pillars. For example, global commodity prices and tariff decisions in Washington can affect Mexico’s inflation and growth rates. The MND Sheinbaum Index™ measures what is happening in Mexico on Sheinbaum’s watch.

World.title: In second annual report to the nation, Sheinbaum hails a stronger, safer and more prosperous Mexico
World.content:
Listen to this article

One month shy of completing her second year in office, President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday delivered her second annual report in a 67-minute speech, a wide-ranging and optimistic address that covered government achievements across areas including the economy, security, infrastructure and healthcare.

“I appear before the people of Mexico nearly two years after assuming the presidency of the republic. I do so with the certainty that we are transforming public life in this country,” Sheinbaum said at the beginning of her speech, delivered at the National Palace in the historic center of Mexico City to an audience that included high-ranking federal and state officials as well as Mexican business leaders.

Segundo Informe de Gobierno. Palacio Nacional https://t.co/uCe1PE8VkK — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) September 1, 2026

Early in her address, the president declared she was “convinced” that Mexico is on “the path to shared prosperity, with independence, freedom and a lot of dignity.”

“We have governed with integrity and republican austerity,” Sheinbaum said.

“We are fully aware that public resources belong to the people and must be used for their benefit. … The economic power was separated from the political power and we govern honestly,” she said.

Sheinbaum is approaching the completion of her second year in office with an approval rating of 68%, according to the newspaper El Financiero’s latest national poll, and an MND Sheinbaum Index™ score — to be published this Wednesday — of close to 70 out of 100.

However, her popularity as president doesn’t insulate her from a range of challenges and difficulties she faces as the leader of a nation of some 130 million people that, for better or for worse, neighbors the United States, the world’s largest economy — and the world’s largest consumer market for illicit drugs.

Sheinbaum faces ongoing security challenges — particularly in states such as Guanajuato and Sinaloa — and frequent pressure from the Trump administration to do more to combat Mexico’s notorious drug cartels. She faces economic challenges, such as low productivity and high labor informality, amid uncertainty about the future of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). She faces domestic and external pressure related to drug trafficking accusations against ruling Morena party officials. She faces ongoing claims that she is turning Mexico into a more authoritarian, less democratic nation. Meanwhile, the U.S. tourist visas of more than 50 Morena officials, including that of one of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s sons, have been revoked. The list of challenges and difficulties faced by Mexico’s first female president goes on.

On Tuesday, however, Sheinbaum focused on the positives, and declared at the end of her address that “we” — i.e., Mexico and her administration — are “doing better” now than before, as she said would occur in her inaugural government report a year ago. She also said that Mexico has a clear path forward “set” by the Mexican people.

Below is a recap of Sheinbaum’s second annual report, or “segundo informe de gobierno,” as it is called in Spanish.

The economy

“Even in these difficult conditions, the Mexican economy remains stable and continues to grow.”

Sheinbaum said that in her almost two years in office, Mexico has faced “difficult international circumstances, marked by a change in the tariff policy of the U.S. government.”

“In particular, [U.S] tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminum, and their derivatives, as well as the war in Iran, which drove up international oil prices, have created difficult circumstances for our country and for the entire world,” she said.

“Even in these difficult conditions, the Mexican economy remains stable and continues to grow,” Sheinbaum said.

She subsequently presented various data points to support her statement. They included that:

Sheinbaum also highlighted that the federal government’s revenue reached a record high of more than 6.4 trillion pesos (US $376.76 billion) last year. She said that tax income has continued to increase in 2026.

Sheinbaum also said that Mexico’s monthly minimum wage has increased “154% in real terms” since 2018 to reach 9,582 pesos (US $564) in 2026.

“On the northern border, the minimum wage stands at 13,409 pesos per month. The average wage in the formal economy reached an all-time high of 20,212 pesos per month, the highest on record,” she said.

“As a result, in-work poverty in 2026 is at its lowest level since 2005.”

Plan Mexico

“Twenty-five of the 100 industrial parks we announced are already in operation.”

Sheinbaum noted that early in her six-year term, she presented Plan Mexico, an ambitious economic initiative with 13 goals, including making Mexico the 10th largest economy in the world by 2030, increasing domestic manufacturing production and cutting red tape for investment projects.

“Two decrees with incentives for private investment were published,” the president said before highlighting that 10 of 25 “Economic Development Hubs for Well-Being” for which private investment was sought are now under development.

“Twenty-five of the 100 industrial parks we announced as a goal are now in operation,” Sheinbaum added.

“In addition, we established the Presidential Office for Investment Promotion, which operates a one-stop shop that approves [investment project] applications within a maximum of 60 days. Through this, 19 projects totaling US $3.76 billion have been approved in four months,” she said.

“In addition, 60% of the bureaucratic procedures [for new investments] have been simplified or eliminated, requirements have been reduced by 66%, and the average response time has been cut by 50%,” Sheinbaum said.

Welfare programs

“We have a duty to support those who for a long time were forgotten.”

The Sheinbaum administration has maintained all the welfare, social and employment programs launched by the government led by ex-president López Obrador, and added new ones, including educational scholarship schemes and cash transfers for women aged 60 and over.

The president said on Tuesday that the government’s welfare programs are “an expression of the conviction that nobody builds a nation alone.”

In a jab at pre-2018 governments, she also said that “we have a duty to support those who for a long were forgotten” — i.e., Mexico’s most disadvantaged people.

Mexico’s welfare programs are based on and draw from Mexican humanism, from a simple but powerful idea,” Sheinbaum said.

That idea, she said, is that “the wealth of Mexico must translate into well-being for its people.”

“A pension for a senior, a scholarship for a student or support for those who work the land aren’t concessions from power, but rather a way of recognizing the dignity and effort of millions of Mexicans,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that welfare programs will benefit almost 43 million Mexicans in 2026, “with a historic investment of one trillion pesos (US $58.85 billion).

Healthcare

“We are reversing the damage caused by decades of neglect in the area of health care.”

Sheinbaum said that when a “fourth transformation” (i.e., Morena) government first came to power in Mexico in 2018, a “profound deterioration in Mexico’s public health system” was evident.

She went on to claim that Morena governments are “reversing the damage caused by decades of neglect in the area of health care.”

Sheinbaum said that “in just two years” of her administration, 33 new public hospitals and 47 public healthcare centers have opened. She noted that her government is aiming to add 9,000 beds to the public health system by 2030.

“To ensure the timely supply of medications and medical supplies, we make consolidated purchases directly from suppliers. We also created the ‘Rutas de la Salud’ program for medical facilities and hospitals in the IMSS Bienestar system, through which 2 billion items have been distributed,” Sheinbaum said.

“No hospital that treats cancer lacks medications,” she asserted.

Infrastructure

“We’re recovering the passenger train network, hallmark of the fourth transformation.”

Sheinbaum enumerated infrastructure projects her government has completed, including highways and “70 bridges and interchanges.”

“… We doubled the budget for artisanal [hand-built] roads, and together with Indigenous communities we’ve built 135 roads measuring 368 kilometers,” she said.

Sheinbaum also highlighted that her government completed passenger train lines between Mexico City and Toluca and between Mexico City and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport. She noted that her administration is building various other railroads across Mexico. The president asserted that her government is “recovering the passenger train network” in Mexico, and said that doing so is a “hallmark of the fourth transformation” political movement she leads.

Sheinbaum also said that 2 million tonnes of freight have been transported on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec’s Interoceanic Railroad, on which two derailments — including a fatal one — have occurred during her government.

She said that her government is modernizing “hydro-agricultural infrastructure across more than 250,000 hectares, which will increase productivity on farms and at the same time release water for human consumption.”

Sheinbaum also spoke about various other water projects, including dams, aqueducts and the desalination plant set to be built in Rosarito, Baja California.

In addition, she said the government is “modernizing seven ports” and “11 international airports,” including those in Mexico City, Puerto Escondido and Tepic.

Security

“We’ve achieved a 51% reduction in homicides.”

Sheinbaum said that “the peace and tranquility of families” are a top priority for her government.

“Thousands of National Guard members, soldiers, marines, security agents, and public servants work every day on the four pillars of the National Security Strategy,” she said, highlighting that those pillars are attention to the root causes of crime; consolidation of the National Guard; strengthening of intelligence and investigative practices; and enhanced coordination between federal and state authorities.

“The results speak for themselves,” Sheinbaum asserted before declaring that “we’ve achieved a 51% reduction in homicides since we took office.”

She was referring to the reduction in homicides in July 2026 compared to September 2024, the final month of López Obrador’s presidency. The annual decline in murders in the first seven months of 2026 was a more modest, but still significant, 30.8%.

Sheinbaum also said that the incidence of high-impact crimes — such as murder, violent robbery, kidnapping and extortion — is down 54% so far this year compared to 2018. She highlighted that some 63,000 people were arrested for allegedly committing high-impact crimes between October 2024 and July 2026.

Sheinbaum said that 207 of those people were “priority targets from all the organized crime groups.”

In addition, Mexican security forces have killed high-profile criminal leaders, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel kingpin Rubén Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, who was fatally wounded in a military operation in Jalisco in February.

Sheinbaum noted that authorities have seized 32,824 firearms and 519 tonnes of drugs during her presidency, and dismantled 2,725 clandestine drug laboratories.

Mexico-US relations

“Our relationship with the U.S. government has had its challenges, but we’ve made the decision to always seek understanding.”

Toward the end of her address, Sheinbaum turned her attention to the relationship between Mexico and the United States, a relationship that has been strained by trade and security tensions.

After outlining Mexico’s constitutionally enshrined foreign policy principles, including that of non-intervention in the affairs of other countries, the president said:

“In this context, I would like to highlight our relationship with the U.S. government, which has had its challenges, but we’ve made the decision to always seek understanding.”

Sheinbaum didn’t mention the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in April without the knowledge or authorization of her government. Nor did she refer to U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya and various other current and former officials. Sheinbaum has previously characterized those things as examples of U.S. interference in Mexican affairs. However, on Tuesday, she limited herself to reiterating her commitment to defending Mexican sovereignty.

“Mexico is a sovereign country and sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared,” said Sheinbaum, who has maintained a respectful relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump despite the disparaging remarks he has made about her, including claims that she is “afraid” of Mexican cartels.

She said that “perhaps one of the most painful aspects” of the relationship with the United States “has been the treatment Mexicans have received” while under the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She noted that 17 Mexicans have died in ICE custody or during ICE operations since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

“In response, … we decided to file complaints … and we will follow up on them and demand that the human rights of our compatriots be fully respected,” she said.

Exactly two months after the U.S. government announced that it had declined to renew the USMCA “in its current form” for an additional 16 years, Sheinbaum said that dialogue with the Trump administration on trade issues is ongoing, “and we hope to reach an understanding.”

Despite the U.S. government’s decision to not renew the USMCA, the free trade pact remains in force. In 2026, Mexico has consolidated its position as the top exporter to, and top trade partner of, the United States.

10 more things

During her second government report speech, Sheinbaum also said that:

‘Mexico is strong, it has extraordinary people’

In her closing remarks, Sheinbaum said that “in these 23 months of great changes, we’ve shown that Mexico is strong and has extraordinary people.”

“… We are part of the project of the fourth transformation of public life,” she said.

“Let no one be mistaken — here there are no divisions, there are no ruptures,” Sheinbaum said, dismissing claims that there are rifts within the ruling Morena party.

“The only thing there is is the defense of the people of Mexico and their dignity,” she said.

Sheinbaum asserted that “the eyes of the world are on Mexico because here a great people has decided to write their own history.”

“We are strengthening a project that grew from the grassroots and which places equality, justice and well-being at its center,” she said.

“… Mexico is free and sovereign and is advancing with dignity, with the strength of its people and with our eyes set on a future that stems from our legacy of greatness,” Sheinbaum said.

World.title: An Archery Center of Excellence opens in Tijuana for Mexico’s world class archers
World.content:
Mexico has opened a new specialized archery training center in Tijuana as it builds its Olympic program toward Los Angeles 2028 and prepares to host the archery World Cup Final this month in Saltillo, Coahuila.

The Centro de Excelencia de Tiro con Arco, or Archery Center of Excellence, opened Saturday under the auspices of the federal sports commission Conade, the Baja California government, the state’s sports institute and World Archery Mexico.

The facility is part of a broader project to establish archery facilities in Tijuana and Mérida, Yucatán, at a cost of more than 40 million pesos, then worth about US $2.2 million, Conade said last year. Officials did not specify how much was allocated to each site.

Mexico has emerged as an international archery power, with four athletes currently ranked in the top six of their divisions, plus a bronze medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics and the country’s first World Archery Championships gold in Gwangju, South Korea, in 2025.

The current world rankings show Andrea Maya Becerra No. 1 in women’s compound, Matías Grande No. 3 in men’s recurve, Sebastián García Flores No. 4 in men’s compound and Ana Paula Vázquez Flores No. 6 in women’s recurve. Becerra is from Jalisco, while Grande, García and Vázquez are Coahuila natives.

At the 2026 Pan American Archery Championships held June 22-28 in Santa Úrsula Zimatepec, Tlaxcala, Mexico won seven medals, including two golds.

The new Tijuana center includes rehabilitated synthetic turf, an archery range with 20-22 shooting lanes, lighting, a gym and an equipment room. It is intended for national-team training and talent development.

World Archery Mexico President Gabriel Ramos attended the inauguration and said Mexico is working with 14 archers vying for spots on the national team: eight on Team A and six on Team B.

The approach is designed to deepen domestic competition ahead of the 2028 Olympics. Mexico’s compound-bow athletes recently spent seven weeks training in Switzerland before a camp in Tlaxcala, Ramos added.

The ceremony also drew Baja California Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila Olmeda and Conade Director General Rommel Pacheco.

The next international test for Mexico’s archers will come Sept. 12-13 at the 2026 Hyundai Archery World Cup Final, following qualifying stages in Mexico (Puebla), China, Turkey and Spain.

The two-day competition will bring together 32 elite archers for knockout matches in Saltillo, Coahuila’s capital. The season-ending event is separate from the World Archery Championships.

With reports from Quadratin, ALMA Plus TV, Esto and Infobae

World.title: Pix Is About to Pass Cards at Brazil’s Checkout
World.content:
Brazil · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Card volume Brazilians put 1.19 trillion reais through cards in the second quarter of 2026.

— Share of output That equals 34.7% of quarterly GDP, on Abecs figures using official GDP data.

— Barely moving The ratio is up just 0.2 percentage points on a year earlier.

— Credit carries it Credit card volume grew 11.4% while debit shrank 1.2%.

— What Pix did Pix payments to businesses reached 1.05 trillion reais, growing 25.4%.

— Interest rates The Selic policy rate is 14% after four cuts since March 2026.

Cards still move more money than Pix at the till. On current growth rates that stops being true within a year.

Illustrative photo: a card payment. Brazilians put 1.19 trillion reais through cards in the second quarter of 2026, and 1.05 trillion through Pix at businesses. (Photo: Hloom Templates, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Brazilians put 1.19 trillion reais through payment cards in the second quarter of 2026. The card industry association Abecs says that equals 34.7% of the country’s output for the quarter.

The figure sounds like a milestone and is close to flat. It has moved just 0.2 percentage points in a year, while Pix grew more than three times faster than cards.

What the Number Actually Measures

Abecs compares quarterly card volume with quarterly GDP. The arithmetic holds: 1.19 trillion reais against output of about 3.43 trillion gives 34.7%.

But the two are different kinds of quantity. Card volume counts every time a real changes hands, while GDP counts value added once.

The clearest proof is Pix. By exactly the same method, Pix would come to about 260% of GDP.

That tells you the measure is about payment penetration, not economic share.

Abecs publishes a better number alongside it. Cards accounted for 56.3% of household consumption, which at least compares spending with spending.

Where the Growth Is

Total card volume rose 7.7% on the year. All of that came from credit.

Credit cards moved 846.3 billion reais, up 11.4%. Debit fell 1.2% to 245.6 billion, and prepaid was flat at 96.8 billion.

Interest-free instalments remain enormous. They accounted for 43% of credit card value in the first half, about 798.6 billion reais.

Contactless payments are the strongest line in the data. They reached a trillion reais in the half, up 18.5%, and now make up 76.2% of in-person card transactions.

The Instrument the Numbers Do Not Mention

Abecs does not publish Pix figures, and any account of Brazilian payments that stops at cards is incomplete. Central bank data fills the gap.

Pix moved 8.90 trillion reais in the second quarter across 20.8 billion transactions. That is more than seven times the value of cards.

Most of that is transfers between people and between businesses, which cards never handled. The fair comparison is Pix paid to businesses.

On that measure Pix reached 1.05 trillion reais, against 1.19 trillion on cards. It is 88% of card volume at the till.

Why That Matters More Than the Headline

Pix payments to businesses grew 25.4% in the year. Card volume grew 7.7%.

At those rates Pix passes cards on value at the merchant counter in roughly ten months. Measured as Abecs measures cards, Pix at the till is already 30.7% of GDP against cards’ 34.7%.

The shrinking debit card is the visible edge of that. Pix does the same job without a card and costs individuals nothing.

What cards still own is credit. Pix cannot yet offer the instalment plans that carry almost half of Brazilian card spending.

That is why credit volume grows while debit falls.

The Rate Backdrop

Brazil’s Selic policy rate stands at 14% a year. It has come down from 15% in four consecutive cuts since March 2026, the last on 5 August.

Cheaper funding supports the credit card growth and the lengthening instalment plans. The share of purchases split over more than twelve instalments rose from 1.5% to 2.3% in a year.

A Number Abecs Does Not Lead With

The association’s release highlights that 85% of Brazilians pay their card bill in full. Central bank data points the other way.

Credit card arrears among individuals reached 9.51% in July 2026. That is up from 8.51% a year earlier and the highest in the period.

Household arrears more broadly rose from 4.41% to 5.81% over the same year. Card credit is growing quickly and so is the share of it going bad.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do card payments really equal a third of Brazil’s economy?

The ratio is real but the phrase misleads. Card volume is money changing hands, while GDP measures value added, so the two are not the same kind of number.

How much went through cards?

1.19 trillion reais in the second quarter of 2026, up 7.7%. Credit was 846.3 billion, debit 245.6 billion and prepaid 96.8 billion.

Is Pix bigger than cards?

On the measure that compares like with like, not yet. Pix payments to businesses were 1.05 trillion reais against 1.19 trillion on cards, but Pix grew more than three times faster.

Why is debit card use falling?

Pix does the same job without a card, instantly and free for individuals. Debit volume fell 1.2% in the quarter and the number of debit transactions fell too.

Are Brazilians falling behind on card bills?

More than before. Central bank figures put credit card arrears at 9.51% in July 2026, against 8.51% a year earlier.

Sources: Abecs, Balanço do Setor de Meios de Pagamento for the second quarter of 2026 and Panorama Abecs of 1 September 2026; Banco Central do Brasil, Pix open data and SGS series 432, 4380, 21084 and 21129; IBGE.

World.title: Brazil’s T4F Leaves the Stock Exchange for R$12 Million
World.content:
Brazil · MARKETS

Key Facts — The approval Brazil’s securities regulator cleared T4F’s delisting on 1 September 2026.

— Who bought Co-founder and controlling shareholder Fernando Luiz Alterio, in his own name.

— The price 5.59 reais a share in the valuation, indexed to 6.02 reais by the auction on 20 July.

— What it cost Alterio spent about 11.7 million reais buying 1.95 million shares at the auction.

— Why so small A ten-for-one reverse split in May 2025 left the company with about 6.7 million shares.

— The fall The exit price is about 96% below the 2011 listing price, adjusted for that split.

The company that brings the world’s biggest tours to Brazil left the exchange for about 12 million reais. That is what fifteen years of decline costs.

Illustrative photo: a concert crowd. T4F, which promotes concerts and musicals across Brazil, is leaving the stock exchange. (Photo: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

T4F, the company behind many of the biggest concerts staged in Brazil, is leaving the stock market. Brazil’s securities regulator approved the delisting on 1 September 2026.

Its co-founder and controlling shareholder bought out the minority holders. The whole exercise cost him about 11.7 million reais.

Why the Numbers Look So Small

A buyout of an entire free float for eleven million reais sounds impossible for a listed company. The explanation is a reverse split.

T4F consolidated its shares ten to one in May 2025, leaving about 6.74 million in issue. At the offer price the whole company is worth roughly 40 million reais.

The offer covered 3,353,850 shares, or 49.75% of the company. At the opening price that came to about 18.7 million reais.

Alterio ended up buying 1,946,835 of them at the auction. That is the 11.7 million reais he actually paid.

The Price, and Why It Moved

The tender opened at 5.59 reais a share on 31 March 2026, a premium of 25.9% to the previous close. The figure came from an independent valuation.

By the auction on 20 July it had become 6.02 reais. Nothing was renegotiated.

The tender document provided for the valuation price to be adjusted by Brazil’s policy interest rate between the valuation date and payment. The 43 centavos is that adjustment.

No minority shareholder challenged the price or asked for a second valuation. The Rio Times found no record of any contest.

How the Delisting Cleared

Brazilian rules require holders of more than two thirds of the free float to agree. But the test counts only shares registered for the auction, and that distinction decided this case.

Of the shares registered, 82.18% were tendered, which cleared the bar. Measured against the whole free float the figure was 58.13%, which would not have.

After settlement Alterio and shareholders bound to him held 79.14%. A sell-out window then ran at the same indexed price, extended to 18 September 2026.

The free float is now below 5%. T4F says it will call a meeting to redeem the remaining shares compulsorily.

Why Alterio Wanted Out

He was direct about it. Being a listed company only makes sense, he said, when you have projects that need equity to happen.

That is not what T4F has today, he said. There is no point carrying the costs of a listing without the benefits.

He and partners founded the business around a São Paulo venue in 1983.

The deeper reason is consolidation in live music. Live Nation and AEG take about 80% of the big shows, he said.

Global promoters now operate in thirty or forty countries.

Competing for those tours means paying up and destroying margin. That kind of risk, he said, is not worth taking.

What the Company Will Do Instead

T4F plans to concentrate on niches it controls end to end. That mainly means Broadway musicals, staged in its own theatres in São Paulo and Buenos Aires.

It also owns its ticketing platform, Tickets for Fun. Vertical integration is the strategy for a company no longer chasing stadium tours.

Fifteen Years of Decline

T4F listed on 13 April 2011 at 16.00 reais a share, raising 539.3 million reais. In 2010 it had turned over about 600 million reais with roughly 40 million of profit.

Adjusted for the reverse split, that listing price is equivalent to 160 reais a share today. The exit at 6.02 reais is about 96% below it.

Revenue in 2025 was 180.7 million reais, up 9%, with a net loss of 54.4 million. The first quarter of 2026 narrowed the loss to 4.0 million and turned operating earnings positive.

More than 9,000 individual shareholders held the stock. The largest genuine minority was the fund manager Loyall, with about 7%.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is T4F leaving the stock exchange?

Its controlling shareholder bought out the minorities. He says being listed only makes sense when a company needs equity for projects, and T4F does not.

How much did the buyout cost?

About 11.7 million reais for the shares actually tendered. The whole free float at the offer price would have been about 20 million reais.

How can a listed company be worth so little?

T4F did a ten-for-one reverse split in May 2025, leaving about 6.7 million shares. At the offer price the whole company is valued near 40 million reais.

Did the price go up because minorities objected?

No. The 5.59 reais valuation was simply indexed to Brazil’s policy interest rate, which produced 6.02 reais by the auction date.

What happens to shareholders who did not sell?

A sell-out window ran to 18 September 2026 at the same indexed price. T4F says it will then call a meeting to redeem the remaining shares compulsorily.

Sources: T4F announcement of 1 September 2026; edital of the public tender offer of 29 June 2026; Apsis valuation report; Brazil Journal; InfoMoney; Money Times; Seu Dinheiro; Exame.

World.title: Brazil’s PagBank Guides to a Smaller Dividend, Not a Bigger One
World.content:
Brazil · FINANCE

Key Facts — The guidance PagBank expects at least 2 billion reais of dividends across 2027 and 2028.

— The direction That is 1 billion reais a year, against 1.4 billion planned for 2026.

— Not a promise Payouts stay at the board’s discretion and depend on market conditions.

— Buyback A fourth repurchase programme covers up to US$150 million of Class A shares.

— Also smaller The two previous programmes were US$200 million each, and the first was US$250 million.

— Why now Revenue was flat in the second quarter, up 0.4% on the year.

PagBank has told investors what it plans to pay in 2027 and 2028. It is less each year than what it is paying now.

Avenida Faria Lima, Sao Paulo’s financial district. PagBank plans about 1 billion reais of dividends a year in 2027 and 2028. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

PagBank has set out what it expects to pay shareholders in 2027 and 2028. The figure is at least 2 billion reais over the two years, or about 1 billion a year.

That is a step down. The company is paying about 1.4 billion reais for 2026.

What the Filing Says

PagBank is the banking arm of PagSeguro Digital, which is listed in New York. It disclosed the guidance in a filing dated 1 September 2026, after the American market closed.

The wording is careful. The company expects to distribute at least 2 billion reais during 2027 and 2028, at 1 billion a year.

It is an expectation and not a commitment. Payouts remain subject to market and company conditions and to the board’s discretion.

The Number Is Going Down, Not Up

PagBank announced in September 2025 that it would pay about 1.4 billion reais of dividends across 2026. Three instalments have been declared so far.

The first was US$0.12 a share in February and the second US$0.26 in June. The third is US$0.28 a share, payable on 30 September 2026 to holders on the register on 16 September.

A fourth instalment of roughly 400 million reais is still to come. About 600 million reais of the 1.4 billion had been distributed by mid-year.

So the new guidance is roughly 1 billion a year against 1.4 billion this year. Investors reading it as an increase are reading it wrong.

PagSeguro Digital Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, provides financial and payment solutions for consumers, individual entrepreneurs, micro-merchants, and small and medium-sized companies in Brazil and internationally. The company provides digital banking solutions, including bill payments, deposits, top-ups, debt management, direct deposits, pix, tax collections, tax collections, wire transfer, and ATM withdrawal; cards,…

The Buyback Is Smaller Too

PagBank approved a fourth share repurchase programme in the same filing. It covers up to US$150 million of Class A shares, takes effect immediately and has no expiry date.

The three previous programmes are all complete. The first, from 2018, was US$250 million, and the two that followed were US$200 million each.

So the new authorisation is a quarter smaller than each of the last two. Repurchases follow the standard American safe-harbour rule.

What the Earlier Targets Actually Covered

PagBank has published larger figures before, and they are easy to misread. At an investor day in September 2025 it set out about 3.8 billion reais of shareholder returns across 2025 and 2026.

That figure is not dividends. Roughly half of it is share buybacks, with dividends of about 623 million reais in 2025 and 1.4 billion in 2026.

The same applies to the more than 5.5 billion reais cited for 2021 to 2026. It is the total of dividends and repurchases together.

Over the twelve months to June, PagBank returned about 2 billion reais to shareholders. Half of that was buying back more than 19 million shares.

Why the Company Has Cash and Not Growth

Second-quarter revenue was 5.08 billion reais, up just 0.4% on the year. Net income was 549 million reais, up 1.9%.

Return on equity was 14.9%. The client base reached 34.1 million, growing 3.1%, and payment volume rose 3.0%.

The one fast-growing line is banking. Banking revenue rose 28.9% and now makes up a quarter of the total, with deposits up 15.1%.

Against its peers the picture is awkward. PagBank’s revenue is around 40% larger than StoneCo’s, but its adjusted profit is slightly smaller and its return on equity materially lower.

The Number Worth Watching

PagBank’s credit book grew 30.7% in the year, to 5.1 billion reais. Loans without collateral went from 13.1% of that book to 24.3%.

Arrears beyond ninety days rose to 3.4% of the portfolio, from 2.5% a year earlier. The company says quality remains under control and below the market average.

That is true as far as it goes. It is also a book growing quickly into riskier products while the top line stands still.

How the Shares Took It

The filing landed after the New York close on 1 September, so nothing that day reflects it. The shares had closed at US$9.14.

They rose about 6% during the following session, trading near US$9.69. The stock is roughly flat for 2026 and hit its low for the year in mid-August.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is PagBank paying more or less?

Less, on the guidance. It plans about 1 billion reais a year in 2027 and 2028, against 1.4 billion for 2026.

Is the 2 billion reais a commitment?

No. PagBank calls it an expectation, subject to market and company conditions and to the board’s discretion.

What about the buyback?

A fourth programme allows up to US$150 million of Class A shares, effective immediately with no expiry. The three earlier programmes are complete.

What is the 2026 dividend?

About 1.4 billion reais in four instalments. Three have been declared, most recently US$0.28 a share payable on 30 September 2026.

How is the business doing?

Profit is holding but growth has stalled. Second-quarter revenue rose 0.4% and net income 1.9%, with 34.1 million clients.

Sources: PagSeguro Digital Form 6-K filings of 1 September 2026, 11 August 2026, 13 March 2026 and 19 September 2025; second-quarter 2026 earnings release; StoneCo and Nu Holdings second-quarter 2026 results.

World.title: Brazil’s Vinci Takes Over Navi’s Property Funds
World.content:
Brazil · FINANCE

Key Facts — The deal Vinci Compass agreed on 11 August 2026 to buy Navi’s real estate fund business.

— What it adds About 800 million reais of client money, split roughly 600 million multi-strategy and 200 million residential.

— The funds Five property funds, of which three trade on B3 as NAVT11, APTO11 and NCRI11.

— The price Not disclosed by either side.

— Timing Vinci told the SEC it expected to close in the fourth quarter; Valor reported completion on 1 September.

— Scale Vinci managed 361 billion reais at the end of June 2026, of which about 6.3 billion in property.

The 800 million reais is client money, not a price. And the closing date depends on which document you read.

Illustrative photo: apartment towers in Curitiba. Navi’s platform adds about 800 million reais of client money to Vinci’s property business. (Photo: Mateusmatsuda, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Vinci Compass is taking over the property fund business of the Brazilian manager Navi. The deal adds about 800 million reais of client money to Vinci’s real estate arm.

Vinci agreed the purchase on 11 August 2026 and told American regulators it expected to complete in the fourth quarter. Valor reported on 1 September that it had done so.

When This Actually Happened

Vinci announced the agreement alongside its second-quarter results on 11 August 2026. Its filing describes the signing of an agreement, with closing expected in the fourth quarter.

The same wording appears in the notes to its interim accounts. Vinci has filed nothing since to say the deal completed.

Valor Econômico reported on the evening of 1 September that Vinci had concluded the acquisition. No other outlet carried that, and the company has not confirmed it.

So the honest position is that the agreement is signed and completion is reported but not filed. Anyone treating 1 September as the closing date is relying on one newspaper.

What 800 Million Reais Means

The figure is assets under management, which is the client money Vinci will now run. It is not the purchase price.

Neither Vinci nor Navi disclosed what was paid. The press release, the results presentation and the accounts are all silent on it.

The 800 million splits roughly 600 million reais in multi-strategy funds and 200 million in residential. That matches the funds’ own reported net assets.

How Many Funds, and Which

The platform is five property funds, and their combined net assets at the end of June came to 796 million reais. That is the 800 million figure.

Three of them trade on B3 under the tickers NAVT11, APTO11 and NCRI11. The largest two, Navi Hedge and Navi Residencial Prime Opportunities, are registered on the over-the-counter platform CETIP rather than the exchange.

Vinci describes four of the vehicles as listed on B3 or CETIP. That is its own count across both venues, and it is not the same as four funds trading on the stock exchange.

Why Vinci Is Buying

The rationale is scale in one specific niche. Vinci’s own multi-strategy property funds held about 150 million reais, so Navi’s 600 million transforms that line.

Chief executive Alessandro Horta called the funds highly complementary. He said they strengthen Vinci’s presence in the Brazilian property fund market, particularly in multi-strategy.

He also described Vinci’s role as a consolidator of investment platforms across Latin America. That is not marketing: Vinci bought the forestry manager Lacan in 2024, Verde Asset in 2025 and Argentina’s BACS earlier this year.

Vinci says the funds bring perpetual and long-term locked-up capital. That means fee income that does not walk out of the door at short notice.

Who Navi Is

Navi Capital was formed in 2018 out of the equities team at Kondor Invest. It is primarily an equities and multimarket manager.

It moved into property in 2021 with a fund of funds. Only the real estate arm is being sold; its other businesses remain registered and operating.

Neither company has said why Navi is selling. No Navi executive is quoted anywhere in the announcement.

The Wider Consolidation

Brazilian property fund management is consolidating, and Vinci is not the only buyer. Pátria has been assembling a comparable book and has said it wants to merge funds together.

The logic is the same on both sides. Bigger funds raise money more easily and cost proportionally less to run.

Vinci’s Own Scale

Vinci Compass managed 361 billion reais at the end of June 2026, up 19% on the year. Most of that sits in a global investment products and solutions business.

Its real assets arm held 15.1 billion reais, of which property is about 42%. That puts property at roughly 6.3 billion before Navi, and about 7 billion after.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Vinci buy?

Navi’s real estate fund platform, not the whole of Navi. Navi’s equity and multimarket businesses are unaffected.

How much is it worth?

Neither side disclosed a price. The 800 million reais figure is client money under management, not what Vinci paid.

How many funds are involved?

Five. Three trade on B3 under the tickers NAVT11, APTO11 and NCRI11, and two are registered on the over-the-counter platform CETIP.

Has the deal closed?

Vinci’s own filings said it expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. Valor reported on 1 September that it had completed, and Vinci has filed nothing to confirm that.

Why does Vinci want it?

Scale. Its own multi-strategy property funds held about 150 million reais, so adding Navi’s takes the combined figure to roughly 750 million.

Sources: Vinci Compass Form 6-K of 11 August 2026, including the press release, second-quarter earnings presentation and interim financial statements; CVM monthly reports for property funds; B3 instruments file of 31 August 2026; Valor Econômico.

World.title: Brasilia’s BRB Drops to Auction-Only Trading at B3
World.content:
Brazil · BANKING

Key Facts — The measure B3 moved BRB’s shares to auction-only trading from 31 August 2026.

— The reason BRB has not filed its financial statements, and four filings are now overdue.

— How long Its last statement filed with the regulator covers the second quarter of 2025.

— To undo it Continuous trading resumes once BRB is up to date with all its periodic information.

— The background BRB tried to buy most of Banco Master, was refused, and Master was liquidated in November 2025.

— The cost A central bank supervisor told police the provision could approach 5 billion reais.

The formal reason is paperwork. The paperwork has been missing for a year, and the reason for that is Banco Master.

Brasilia. B3 moved BRB shares to auction-only trading from 31 August 2026, citing undelivered financial statements. (Photo: Senado Federal, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
