He was then left out of matchday squad altogether for the remaining five games of the season as Leicester suffered relegation.

Richards’ lack of minutes ultimately played a role in not being part of the Reggae Boyz squad for the FIFA World Cup Play-offs in March against New Caledonia and DR Congo. He had previously played the final four games in the final round of Concacaf World Cup qualifying.

Despite the challenges during the Leicester loan spell, Richards believes it was a teachable moment.

“I think it was the right thing, it went the right way in my opinion to see where I’m at and to just start focusing on the things that are right,” he said.

He now joins Wimbledon, who finished 19th in League One last season, avoiding relegation by four points. The club are currently have four points from their first three games of the league season.

“I’ve been watching [the team] for the last couple of days. I think after the game against Wigan I was like, they’ve really got a good team that could be successful this season. I’m ready [and] ready to do what it takes to be the fans’ favourite,” Richards said.

He joins former Reggae Boyz Jason Euell and Marcus Gayle as well as 2023 debutant Delano Splatt as Jamaica internationals to play for AFC Wimbledon.

Richards could be involved in today’s contest against Burton Albion at 1:45 pm Jamaica time.

During the announcement by the club, Richards credited his “idol”, fellow Reggae Boy Leon Bailey, for inspiring him.

“When I was growing up it was only him to watch on YouTube back then so he was basically our Messi in Jamaica at the time [and] still is. I’m grateful, he’s basically the person that brought me to the Phoenix Academy so I’m grateful,” he said.

Bailey, meanwhile, was unable to secure a deadline day move from Aston Villa, after being linked with Premier League club Hull City and La Liga side Sevilla.

The 29-year-old was seemingly on the verge of joining newly promoted Hull in July but talks broke down with agent and Phoenix Academy owner Craig Butler telling the Jamaica Observer that he had several options on the table.

Bailey returned to Villa in January after an unsuccessful loan spell at Serie A club AS Roma. Despite making 21 appearances and winning the Europa League, he was told he would not be part of manager Unai Emery’s plans for the season, despite being involved in preseason.

“We were expecting him to leave,” Emery said last Friday “When we left for Asia, he was close to leaving, but he is still with us now. Hopefully, he can get a good opportunity to leave and join another club and continue his career, and this is our objective.”

Reports from England say Bailey, currently training alone at Villa’s facilities, could move to Saudi Arabia with their transfer window open until Sunday. Al-Diriyah are reportedly front-runners who have former Liverpool star Darwin Nunez and former PSG and Everton midfielder Idrissa Gueye in their ranks. Al-Ittihad, former club of French stars Karim Benzema and N’Golo Kante, are also interested.

Bailey joined Villa from Bayer Leverkusen in 2021 and scored 23 goals in 163 appearances in all competitions.

World.title: Amber eyes Jamaica IoT roll-out as Africa device count tops one million
World.content:
Engineers work on electronic components at Amber IoT’s South Africa operation, which designs and develops hardware used in areas including utilities, security, vehicle tracking, and other connected-device applications.

AMBER Group is eyeing an early 2027 start to the roll-out of a network for Internet of Things (IoT) devices in Jamaica, as its South Africa-based Amber IoT business surpasses one million devices manufactured, sold, and deployed across Africa.

Founder and CEO Dushyant Savadia said the Jamaica-headquartered technology group expects the local roll-out to require an investment of about US$750,000.

“Hopefully, from the starting of next year we’ll start putting our own base stations designed by us internally across Jamaica,” Savadia told the Jamaica Observer in an interview from India on Tuesday.

The timetable is not firm. Amber plans to deploy an 0G network, a low-power, low-cost system designed for machines that need to transmit small amounts of information rather than make calls or stream data.

Savadia said Amber IoT has grown from two product lines in 2023 to about 20 today, including vehicle trackers, electricity and water-meter technology, security equipment, and panic buttons.

“What has happened since then, because there’s a diverse amount of products now inside Amber IoT, it also allowed us to scale very, very fast,” he said.

South Africa remains its main market, accounting for an estimated 70 per cent of the devices, with the remaining 30 per cent spread across countries including Ghana, Morocco, Nigeria, and Kenya.

The business now accounts for a sizeable share of Amber Group’s revenue.

“In terms of revenue share, Amber IoT, I would say, is at least eight to 10 per cent of our global revenue now,” Savadia said.

He did not disclose the dollar value, but said most of Amber Group’s income is earned outside Jamaica.

“The majority of our revenue comes from overseas markets, not from Jamaica. Jamaica is perhaps one of the smallest markets for us in the world,” he told the Business Observer.

Amber’s African IoT operation grew out of its 2022 acquisition of South African hardware manufacturer Intelli-Business Solutions, which it bought outright and renamed Amber IoT.

The company had already spent about 13 years developing IoT products, including equipment for the banking, insurance, and security industries, before Amber acquired it.

“We acquired a company with all of these specialisations and then built up even further to add a lot more devices than what they had produced prior to the purchase of 100 per cent of the shares by Amber Group Jamaica,” Savadia said.

He said South Africa was targeted first because businesses there were already more familiar with IoT technology and how it could be used to cut costs and gather information remotely.

The Jamaican roll-out has taken longer than previously envisaged. In September 2024, Savadia told the Financial Gleaner that Amber would “start deploying next year”, pointing at the time to a 2025 start.

Savadia said Amber has since developed its own transponders and radios for the Jamaican network. Potential uses include remote utility-meter readings, vehicle and asset tracking, and security systems that can send alerts when equipment or containers are breached.

“We will have similar impact like in Africa, in the Caribbean too, where we will roll out our own 0G network on which our devices will speak,” he said.

World.title: Moscow likely behind drone-factory arson, says Poland’s Tusk
World.content:
A military operator launches a FlyEye WB Electronics SA, a Polish reconnaissance drone, bought in the frame of program 'The Army of Drones' during test flights in the Kyiv region on August 2, 2022. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

The incident comes amid an intensification of suspected Russian attacks targeting facilities linked to military production supporting Ukraine.

The fire at a Polish drone factory supplying weapons to Ukraine was "deliberate arson," and Russia is likely behind the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at a cabinet meeting Wednesday.

WB Electronics, where the fire broke out on Monday morning, is one of Poland’s largest private defense companies. It produces reconnaissance drones and loitering munitions, including FlyEye and Warmate, used by Ukraine against Russian forces. The fire was soon extinguished, leaving no casualties, Polish radio reported.

“This is a continuation of Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region,” the Polish leader said, adding that "unfortunately, these are not the first cases and, even worse, they certainly won’t be the last."

World.title: China threat bolsters support for EU industrial policy
World.content:
The next wave could be even more destructive, industry officials warned.

Unlike the first shock, the industries now under pressure include sectors that Europe considers central to its economic and technological future, such as electric vehicles and batteries, as well as steel, chemicals, and wind turbines.

The IAA is designed partly to blunt that pressure, limiting Chinese investments in strategic sectors like EVs, raw materials or solar panels. It would also set Made-in-EU requirements for public procurement, potentially excluding Chinese suppliers.

“The level of ambition is justified. If it’s Europe’s main tool to respond to the second China shock, it’s essential to make it count,” Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform think tank, told MEPs. “Do it right or don’t do it at all.”

Beijing has strongly objected to the IAA, but — despite some initial misgivings — it is gaining more support among EU countries and there is broad backing in the Parliament.

“The urgency has increased,” Green MEP Anna Cavazzini, co-lead on the file, said. She called the IAA a “cornerstone” of the EU’s response to China’s aggressive trade policies. “There’s a lot of alignment that we need to strengthen the Commission proposal.”

World.title: Kallas pushes back on Franco-German reform plans for EU diplomatic service
World.content:
Kaja Kallas take part in a joint press conference following an informal meeting of EU Foreign Affairs ministers, at Druids Glen in Wicklow, south of Dublin, Ireland, on September 2, 2026. | Paul Faith/ AFP via Getty Images

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Wednesday poured cold water on plans to overhaul the bloc’s diplomatic branch, arguing that better enforcement of the current rules would make its foreign policy more effective.

France and Germany have floated plans for root-and-branch reforms of Kallas’s European External Action Service, or EEAS, according to a discussion paper seen by POLITICO. The plans include giving her oversight of policy units in the European Commission that deal with external relations.

But after a debate on the proposed reforms among EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, Kallas said that a “majority” of envoys had supported “the current institutional setup” of the EEAS. She added that there was “broad support” from member countries to make it work without big institutional changes.

World.title: No budget deal without new EU taxes, Costa warns
World.content:
Finding an agreement on new EU taxes — so-called own resources — is key to facilitating an overall budget deal in December before national elections in France, Spain and Italy in 2027 threaten the negotiations.

Costa is touring the EU’s 27 capitals to sound out their concerns and assess where there is room for compromise. The Portuguese politician plays a key role in the negotiations as he chairs leaders’ meetings and brokers compromises among different camps.

The issue of EU-wide taxes is among the thorniest in the discussions because national capitals are reluctant to hand more taxing powers to the European Commission and agree to new levies that would hit some countries harder than others.

Last year, the Commission proposed five new levies — targeting carbon imports, emissions, non-collected electronic waste, corporate profits and tobacco products — worth €66 billion per year to finance the budget. But most of the ideas have been met with resistance from governments, who must unanimously approve each new levy.

Tensions were on full display when Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden rejected the proposed EU tobacco tax after a meeting with Costa earlier on Wednesday.

"We won’t accept proposals that impact [Luxembourg] in a disproportionate manner," he told reporters.

World.title: Von der Leyen, Rutte say Russian ‘intimidation will not work’ to stop Ukraine aid
World.content:
EU and NATO chiefs pledge continued support for Ukraine after a thwarted attack on a German airport sending aid to Kyiv was attributed to Russia.

BRUSSELS — The EU and NATO will not back down from supporting Ukraine despite attacks against European countries blamed on Russia, the leaders of the two institutions said Wednesday.

The rare joint statement came after Germany said Russia was behind a foiled attack on an airport used as a key logistics hub for military aid to Ukraine.

“This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil — we will not tolerate it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve; intimidation will not work.”

World.title: Britain’s new finance minister sets date for first big speech on growth
World.content:
Burnham revealed in mid-August that Healey was working on a speech on the government’s economic agenda. The date of next Monday was first reported by Politics at Sam and Anne’s, the morning briefing podcast by POLITICO and Sky News.

The speech will focus heavily on growth, said two of the people quoted above — weeks after Burnham moved responsibility for local economic growth strategy from the Treasury to his new prime ministerial office in Manchester, No. 10 North.

One of the four people cited at the start of this story said the speech is likely to focus less on individual spending policies ahead of the Oct. 28 budget and more on a broader vision and initiatives, including Burnham’s promises to hand more economic levers to regional leaders.

“This isn’t a rushed job — it’s a serious bit of thinking,” they added. Another of the four people said: “It’s the government’s version of their theory of growth.”

A government official, who is not one of the four individuals cited above, said the speech has involved work by multiple government departments contributing potential ideas. “It’s crossed a lot of people’s radar,” they added.

Some in Westminster may see the speech as Healey seeking to emphasize his own role.

World.title: Bardella’s international blitz hints at new role for French far-right leader
World.content:
“Bardella has always been attached to the international credibility of the National Rally,” said the aide, who was granted anonymity to share details of Bardella’s plans. “He will give great attention to the international press during the campaign.”

Since shooting up the National Rally’s ranks in his twenties, Bardella has brought a polished professionalism to a party that long struggled to run a tight ship. He led the party to impressive victories in the 2019 and 2024 European elections and is now the head of the Patriots group in the European Parliament. The party is now more popular than ever, and Le Pen is the front-runner to win next year’s presidential election.

But when it looked like an embezzlement conviction would doom Le Pen’s chances at running for the presidency, Bardella, as the National Rally’s presumptive candidate, tried to woo more fiscally conservative voters — including France’s business elite — by flirting with a more market-friendly platform than his mentor.

But Bardella has been adjusting to a secondary role since an appeals court cleared a path for Le Pen to run as the party’s presidential nominee — and she has made clear that fiscal discipline won’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters. That includes her pledge to lower the retirement age for most workers to 62 at a cost of €9 billion per year.

Bardella is now eyeing a role similar to the one Giorgia Meloni held before she became Italian prime minister in 2022.

Bardella “watched with great interest the campaign of Giorgia Meloni, who flooded the international press to reassure institutions and the financial markets,” the aide said.

World.title: Macron and King Charles hail UK-France ties at Bayeux Tapestry viewing
World.content:
It was the highlight of Emmanuel Macron's two-day visit to the United Kingdom, which began on Wednesday: the French president and the British prime minister joined King Charles III and Queen Camilla for a private viewing of the Bayeux Tapestry.

 

The masterpiece of medieval art, which depicts the Norman conquest of England in 1066, is a centuries-old symbol of Franco-British relations.

Macron personally decided on the one-year loan during his state visit to the UK in July 2025, to "reinvigorate cultural relations" and underline "the trust that now exists" between Paris and London.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed "a major moment in the history" of the two countries.

"As we celebrate our shared heritage, President Macron and I will continue to strengthen the ties between our two nations", he said in a statement.

King Charles III of England, Emmanuel Macron, President of the French Republic, and Queen Camilla arrive at the British Museum in London on 2 September 2026. (AP Photo/Thomas Krych, Pool)

France has loaned the tapestry, insured for €960 million, for a ten-month exhibition opening to the public on 10 September.

It was transported from Bayeux in north-western France to London by road and rail in a high-security convoy in July. It marks the first time the tapestry has been on British soil since the 11th century.

Embroidered in wool on linen, the artwork depicts the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings in October 1066, when William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold's Anglo-Saxon army.

The invasion ended Saxon rule, made William the Conqueror the first Norman king of England and forged a close and complex relationship between Britain and France.

The year 1066 remains one of the best-known dates in British history, and the tapestry's loan is considered a major cultural event.

Burnham's government announced on Wednesday that a digital exhibition will bring the tapestry's story to locations across the UK, while schoolchildren will take part in a live national history lesson on the subject on 14 October.

The loan was announced during Emmanuel Macron's state visit to the United Kingdom in July 2025. In return, the British Museum is lending a number of artefacts, including Viking and Anglo-Saxon treasures, to museums in Normandy.

Ukraine, Middle East and migration on talks agenda

Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, will receive Macron at 10 Downing Street on Thursday for talks.

Burnham's office said efforts to prevent migrants from crossing the English Channel in small boats would top the agenda. The UK government says stronger cooperation between British and French law enforcement agencies has helped reduce the number of crossings by more than 40% this year compared with last year.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine are also expected to be discussed during the talks.

France and the United Kingdom have led efforts to strengthen European support for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion more than four and a half years ago, and Burnham has pledged to maintain British support for Kyiv.

The Prime Minister also wants to forge closer ties with the European Union in an effort to reverse what he has called a "decade of weak growth" following the 2016 Brexit referendum.

World.title: Malta jury clears suspect mastermind businessman in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder case
World.content:
A jury in Malta on Wednesday found Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech not guilty of charges related to the 2017 car bomb killing of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

 

Caruana Galizia's killing shocked Europe, sparked protests that led to the resignation of a prime minister and exposed a culture of impunity in Malta, the European Union's smallest member state.

Fenech, a prominent Maltese businessman, was indicted in 2021 on charges of complicity and criminal conspiracy. He was involved in a consortium that won a controversial contract with the Maltese government to build a power station.

Prosecutors accused Fenech of masterminding the killing and of ordering and paying for it.

Fenech pleaded not guilty, and the jury on Wednesday found him not guilty on both counts. He was the last of a half-dozen people charged over the plot to be prosecuted.

Following the verdicit, he walked out of the Valletta courtroom to a chaotic scene outside, with hecklers yelling as he walked into a waiting car. He made no comment.

Yorgen Fenech leaves court in Valletta, Malta, on 29 November 2019. Martin Agius/AP/str

Targeted over her anti-corruption investigations

Caruana Galizia, 53, was killed on 16 October 2017 when a car bomb exploded as she was driving near her home.

She had reported extensively on suspected corruption involving political and business figures in Malta.

Her investigations included members of then-Prime Minister Joseph Muscat's inner circle, whom she accused of having offshore companies in tax havens revealed by the Panama Papers. Her reporting also scrutinised opposition figures and Maltese business leaders.

At the time of her death, Caruana Galizia was facing more than 40 libel lawsuits.

An independent inquiry into her killing, published in 2021, concluded that the Maltese state “has to bear responsibility” for the assassination due to a culture of impunity that emanated from the highest levels of government.

Protesters in Valletta call for Prime Minister Joseph Muscat's resignation following developments in the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder case, 29 November 2019. Image Rene Rossignaud/AP

Others prosecuted over the killing

In 2022, George Degiorgio and his brother Alfred Degiorgio pleaded guilty to carrying out the killing and were each sentenced to 40 years in prison.

In 2025, Jamie Vella and Robert Agius were sentenced to life in prison, the maximum possible penalty, after being convicted of complicity in the murder. The two men were accused of supplying the bomb that killed Caruana Galizia.

Another man, Vincent Muscat, pleaded guilty in 2021 for his role in the slaying, and was sentenced to 15 years in prison.

Melvin Theuma, a taxi driver who admitted acting as a middleman, was granted a presidential pardon in 2019 in exchange for his testimony.

'Our country failed to protect Daphne'

Caruana Galizia's children were at the forefront in demanding accountability and justice for her death. Her sons were in the courtroom when the verdict was read out but left without commenting.

In a statement later posted to Facebook, the family said the verdict denied Caruana Galizia the “justice she deserves."

“Nine years after Daphne’s brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed. Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again," the statement said. "Our country failed to protect Daphne. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost.”

No cameras were allowed in the courtroom, as is customary in Maltese criminal trials.

World.title: Spain government in disarray as conflicting reports swirl over Morocco’s role in Ceuta
World.content:
The Spanish government was plunged into crisis on Wednesday after a leaked police report suggested Moroccan forces played a role in pushing migrants into Ceuta in an unprecedented border violation, putting Madrid on the defensive.

 

Multiple media outlets, citing a law enforcement document, alleged Moroccan authorities helped push migrants by sea, acted “passively” and concluded that the mass influx of around 80,000 migrants into the Spanish enclave was not accidental.

The allegations have triggered a political frenzy, putting Spain’s Interior Ministry on the back foot.

The Spanish Interior Minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, under fire for his handling of Spain's most serious national security breach in modern history, ordered police to clarify the claims, which directly contradict the government's narrative.

A senior police official later denied that any report directly blaming Morocco exists, but the statement did little to calm tensions as the Sánchez government struggles to contain the crisis, with thousands of migrants still stranded in the city to the frustration of local residents.

Protests in support of Ceuta took place across Spain on Wednesday.

The war of leaks also indicates the Spanish interior ministry, one of the most politically sensitive government departments, seems to have lost control of a part of its police, looking to either embarrass the government or bring to light new information.

It is not uncommon for the Spanish government and opposition to accuse each other of “lawfare”, in reference to courts or police departments seen as politically aligned for partisan gains.

The question of how much the Spanish government knew in the hours prior is central to its political survival as Sánchez faces his most serious crisis to date ahead of an election in 2027.

Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo told reporters that the government “knew it — and covered it up.”

Serious consequences

Spain has not blamed Morocco, even after it described the dramatic events in Ceuta, where more than 150 people died at sea, as a violation of its territorial integrity while calling for solidarity from its European neighbours.

Instead, Madrid has pointed to false social media claims pegged to a court ruling and human traffickers as the principal drivers of the mass influx— a position echoed by the European Commission, which, even as the border collapsed, continued to describe Morocco as a “trusted partner” in tackling irregular migration.

A spokesperson for the European Commission refused to comment on the leaked report, describing it as a national matter.

Earlier this week, Sánchez also suggested that Russia and Israel played a role in amplifying disinformation. Spain and Israel have clashed over the war in Gaza.

Still, questions remain over how Moroccan authorities, who also patrol the border, failed to detect and break up the buildup of migrants along the border.

Juan Fernando López Aguilar, a former socialist justice minister and a member of the European parliament, told Euronews this week "it is only obvious, it couldn't have happened without some overlooking by the Moroccan authorities."

“That’s common sense. But the government has to act based on facts and evidence,” he told Euronews’ flagship show Europe Today.

Spanish ministers have given conflicting accounts of what they knew in the days prior and whether intelligence agencies had passed on critical information.

The issue is politically sensitive: any failure to act on warnings related to national security would amount to serious negligence and could fuel calls for a vote of no confidence in the prime minister and his government.

Ceuta ‘at breaking point’

Beyond the politics, the Spanish government is also facing serious operational difficulties on the ground in Ceuta, where around 5,000 migrants — about half of them understood to be minors — remain in the city. Local authorities put the figure closer to 10,000.

On Wednesday, Ceuta President Juan Jesús Vivas said the city was at breaking point, directly blaming Morocco and accusing Rabat of harassment.

“Morocco has had and continues to have an unwavering objective: to suffocate, harass and bring down our two cities,” he said, referring to Ceuta and its twin city, Melilla, also located in North Africa.

“I think no one doubts that what has happened to us is not a migration crisis. What has happened is that Spain’s territorial integrity has been violated.”

Vivas has demanded that all migrants be returned, describing this as the only way to restore normality in Ceuta. But Spanish authorities face a difficult balancing act.

Strict laws protecting minors prevent immediate returns, even if they crossed illegally, while local authorities have yet to facilitate public spaces for migrant identification, leading to more administrative delays.

Facing scrutiny from its European neighbours, Madrid has also pledged that the situation in Ceuta will not affect the Schengen area, which allows for free movement of people in the EU, but that is limiting its ability to transfer migrants to mainland Spain away from Ceuta to provide relief.

Faced with the complex situation, Spanish authorities have now requested assistance from Frontex, the EU agency responsible for the bloc’s external borders.

Moroccan authorities have argued that Spain’s mass regularisation plan announced earlier this year may have acted as an incentive for migrants to cross.

World.title: The surge of the far-right - who is to blame? MEPs face off in The Ring
World.content:
On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt could become the centre of a political earthquake. The AfD party is polling at more than 40 percent, far ahead of Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats (CDU).

 

Such a strong result could give the far right a path to governing a German state for the first time since World War II. That would shatter one of the most important political taboos in modern Germany — and send a powerful signal to Europe.

A stronger AfD would mean a tougher battle over migration, climate policy and support for Ukraine — and potentially a more difficult Germany for the EU to rely on at a time when Europe is already facing enormous geopolitical pressure.

So, is Saxony-Anhalt simply expressing frustration with the political establishment? Or are we about to witness a turning point for Germany — and potentially for Europe? And who is to blame?

These are the core questions of this edition of The Ring, featuring two members of the European Parliament: Hildegard Bentele, a German MEP from the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) and Jean-Marc Germain, a French MEP from the Socialists & Democrats.

In the European Parliament, Bentele is the Vice-chair of the Committee on Development and a member of the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy. She also chairs the Delegation for relations with Israel.

She says: “As Christian-Democrats, we’re convinced that the only way to counter the rise of the far-right in Saxony-Anhalt, in Germany and across Europe, is listening closely to people, offering realistic solutions and presenting - based on our values - an optimistic vision for the future.”

Germain, an economist, was adviser to former French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and is one of the main figures within the Socialists & Democrats Group (S&D) in the European Parliament, where he serves as the group’s lead on budgetary issues.

Germain says: “As long as Europe fails to build economic sovereignty, the far right will thrive in the regions devastated by globalisation and de-industrialisation."

The Ring is hosted by Stefan Grobe, produced by Luis Albertos Altarejos and Amaia Echevarria, and edited by Vassilis Glynos.

World.title: Swiss rave shooting suspect had 'psychological problems', police say
World.content:
The man suspected of fatally shooting an Italian woman at a rave party in Switzerland is suffering from "psychological problems" and has remained silent while in custody, prosecutors said on Wednesday.

 

According to AFP, the man turned himself in to police and confessed to the shooting, saying he had "been suffering from health problems for some time". He is a 43-year-old Swiss citizen living in the canton of Jura.

The man is in custody and faces charges of intentional homicide, bodily harm and violations of firearms legislation.

Gunfire broke out early on Sunday as an annual rave was coming to an end at a racecourse in Aarau, the capital of Switzerland's northern canton of Aargau, killing 22-year-old Italian woman Maria Spinelli.

According to the latest information provided at a press conference by lead investigator Matthias Schildknecht, six people were injured, rather than the five initially reported.

A search of the suspect's home found no evidence of "ideological or extremist motives", Aargau cantonal police commander Michael Leupold said at the press conference.

The man, who was not previously known to police, "left the army in 2013 and handed back his personal service weapon", Leupold added.

Victim's lawyer calls for full investigation

Maria Spinelli, who had recently moved to Switzerland to look for work, is believed to have been "hit by a bullet" that struck "vital organs in the upper part of her body".

However, the family's lawyer, Bruno Gallo, said in a statement that "the circumstances of the crime have not yet been fully clarified".

"The Swiss investigators," the lawyer said, "say that the man who has been arrested is thought to have suffered from psychiatric problems and, despite this, appears to have been in legal possession of firearms."

"This is a profile that must be fully clarified, establishing how this was possible and examining any potential responsibility, at whatever level, of those whose duty it was to prevent a dangerous situation," Gallo said.

The lawyer has also asked Italian authorities to arrange a state flight to repatriate Spinelli's body.

World.title: Frecciarossa starting tests for new Rome and Milan high-speed rail links to Munich
World.content:
From Rome to Munich on a Frecciarossa train, via Innsbruck. Ferrovie dello Stato (FS) has begun test runs of the Frecciarossa trains operated by Trenitalia in Germany and Austria, as part of the international certification phase.

 

The FS Group has announced that the launch of services between Milan and Munich and between Rome and Munich is scheduled for the summer of 2027 "following the successful completion of the approval process for the new trains".

After France and Spain, and with the goal of reaching the United Kingdom via the Channel Tunnel by 2029, Italy's state railways are now arriving in the heart of Europe as well. The initiative is being carried out in partnership with the German and Austrian national railways, Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB.

The opening of the Brenner Base Tunnel will cut journey times by around an hour and, from December 2028, the full service will consist of ten connections between Italy and Germany, covering the routes between Milan, Rome and Munich and later extended to Naples and Berlin.

Where will the new services stop?

The commercial offer envisages four connections on the Milan - Munich and Rome - Munich routes.

On the Milan - Munich route, with a journey time of about six and a half hours, the main intermediate stops will be Brescia, Verona, Rovereto, Trento, Bolzano and Innsbruck.

On the Rome - Munich route, with a journey time of about eight and a half hours, the main stops will be Florence, Bologna, Verona, Rovereto, Trento, Bolzano and Innsbruck.

Towards the new 'European Metro' network

"The start of test runs in Germany and Austria is a step towards delivering a project that confirms our ambition to make the train the benchmark mode of transport for mobility across Europe," said FS chief executive and general manager Gianpiero Strisciuglio.

"Thanks to our partnership with Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB, we are moving towards creating the High-Speed 'European Metro', offering passengers a service able to bring regions, people and economies closer together," Strisciuglio explained.

The FS chief added that Frecciarossa "is thus continuing its international growth path, taking the FS Group's technological and industrial excellence abroad and helping to develop an increasingly integrated European rail network".

The Minister for Infrastructure and Transport, Matteo Salvini, has also expressed satisfaction with the milestone achieved. Salvini described it as "a further step confirming the growth of the FS Group and its ability to win new markets abroad, while providing better services and infrastructure in Italy. More jobs, more connections, more Italy in Europe".

The agreement between Trenitalia and Deutsche Bahn will also make it possible to share technical expertise so that the trains can adapt to different power-supply and signalling systems, speeding up the required technical process and keeping associated costs under control. At the same time as the prototypes were being built, training programmes for German and Austrian driving staff were also launched.

The Frecciarossa, compliant with European interoperability technical specifications, has been designed and built to run in Italy and on the rail networks of France, Germany, Spain, Austria, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium.

The new connection will also affect rail links with other countries, capturing demand for travel to destinations such as Frankfurt and Krakow.

World.title: Belgium pushes back against new attempt to use Russian assets to support Ukraine
World.content:
Belgium has forcefully pushed back against a new attempt to tap into the Russian Central Bank's immobilised assets to provide additional support to Ukraine.

 

The European Union holds €210 billion in these assets, the bulk of which is kept at Euroclear, a depository in central Brussels.

The hot-button topic was discussed at an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers on Tuesday, with Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland leading the push following their joint letter sent last week. The Baltic countries also voiced support.

But according to Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot, the debate "generated little enthusiasm or appetite among colleagues".

"I made sure to reiterate Belgium's position, which has remained unchanged for a year. The reasons behind our opposition have not magically disappeared in the meantime," Prévot said in comments shared with Euronews at the end of talks in Ireland.

"Using these assets through a process amounting to confiscation would entail very significant risks," he added.

Prévot's remarks mirrored the arguments voiced by the Belgian government last year to oppose a European Commission proposal that sought to channel the €210 billion into a zero-interest credit line for Ukraine.

Belgium demanded a full mutualisation of risks and uncapped guarantees to protect itself against Russia's no-holds-barred retaliation. The country also raised the prospect of financial and reputational disaster for the entire eurozone.

The audacious plan eventually fell apart at a contentious summit in December, when leaders opted instead for joint debt to finance a €90 billion loan.

Around the same time, the Russian Central Bank sued Euroclear.

Belgium continues to argue that the sovereign assets should be kept untouched until the peace negotiations to strengthen the bloc's diplomatic leverage.

"There had previously been broad agreement that it was preferable to keep these amounts immobilised until Russia has compensated Ukraine for all the damage it has caused," Prévot said on Tuesday.

Rising costs, rising doubts

The renewed debate on the assets comes amid growing doubts on whether the €90 billion loan would last until the end of 2027, as originally intended.

In their joint letter, Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland warned the loan "will not be enough" due to Russia's relentless escalation.

"While we should be proud of our achievements, we cannot afford to rest on our laurels," they wrote. "As each day passes, the cost of the war is rising as Russia's relentless attacks continue unabated."

Moscow has launched a new tactic of non-stop drone attacks aimed at disrupting Ukraine's daily economic activity and sowing terror. At the same time, it has ramped up strikes on the Black Sea to prevent Ukraine from trading grain.

With revenues falling and costs mounting, Kyiv has asked allies to plug a €23 billion gap in the Ministry of Defence to cover salaries and weapons purchases.

As a solution, it has suggested the EU front-load a share of the €45 billion earmarked under the loan for next year, which would mean having less funds available in 2027.

The European Commission has not formally received the request.

"Public opinion is growing weary of this support, yet it remains more essential than ever. The security outlook for the European continent is bleak for the years ahead," Prévot said.

"International solidarity with Ukraine is therefore more necessary than ever."

The money crunch has emboldened proponents of using the Russian assets, who never abandoned the idea despite last year's defeat. For them, the assets would equip the bloc with a massive financial firepower while sparing taxpayers and national budgets.

Ukraine has also backed the initiative.

"This is a fair approach to start a serious discussion on how we can use the immobilised assets," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday.

Italy's Antonio Tajani, whose country backed Belgium last year, said the outstanding legal objections needed to be properly addressed before moving forward.

"We're not opposed in principle, but we need to see whether there is a legal basis for doing so," Tajani said.

Officials in the Commission are closely following the trajectory of the discussions but remain hesitant to draft a new proposal without a guarantee of success. Capitals are already ensnared in fraught negotiations over the next EU budget.

World.title: How a quiz show and a dream took Azerbaijan's Sabah to the Champions League
World.content:
"I think this story about the TV quiz is a little overrated," Valdas Dambrauskas told Euronews after he became the first Baltic coach to reach the Champions League main round, leading a club that did not exist nine years ago to fixtures against Arsenal, Manchester United and Barcelona.

 

In 2002, Dambrauskas won the prize money on the Lithuanian television show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" and used it to move to England to fund his UEFA coaching badges.

He had no professional football background.

To pay for the courses, he worked as a babysitter, salesman and newspaper delivery man. He eventually got into the youth academies at Fulham, Brentford and Manchester United. Sabah FC in Baku is his 10th club.

"Sometimes it was difficult. I had to work hard, and sometimes to believe when myself and those around me were doubting," Dambrauskas recalled.

"I take this achievement as a milestone and believe that journey is more important. There are other dreams ahead and I really don't want to stop."

Valdas Dambrauskas, Lithuanian professional football manager, Head Coach of Azerbaijan Premier League club Sabah FC Azertag, August 2026

Sabah beat Hapoel Beer Sheva 5-2 last Tuesday — 6-4 on aggregate — to reach the Champions League main round, guaranteeing eight matches against European football's biggest clubs. Barcelona, Borussia Dortmund, Napoli and Slavia Prague will come to Baku.

Dambrauskas and his squad travel to Arsenal and Manchester United in England, then to Villarreal in Spain and Viking in Norway.

Dambrauskas was equally clear-eyed about what comes next.

"Everyone is speaking about the Champions League, but the Azerbaijan championship is what allows you to play there. It is very important we keep the focus and prepare for every game that we are going to play," he said.

"We have a fantastic international environment where a lot of times we select eleven different nationalities in the starting line-up. In this kind of environment the main word we base our philosophy on is respect."

'It is time to focus'

Sabah Futbol Klubu were founded in Baku in 2017. They won the Azerbaijan Cup in the 2024-25 season and the Azerbaijan Premier League title the following year, ending Qarabağ FK's domestic dominance.

Facing the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal came quickly in a rare footballing dream come true, and for Sabah right-back and right-winger Tellur Mutallimov, the scale of what lies ahead is a matter of focus, not thrills.

"Playing against clubs of this stature gives me a greater sense of responsibility and extra motivation rather than excitement," Mutallimov told Euronews.

"The celebrations are now behind us. It is time to focus all our attention on the important and difficult matches ahead."

Mutallimov paid tribute to supporters who had followed the club through the qualifying rounds.

"Even when we played far away from home in Denmark, England, Finland and Romania, we were not alone. We are grateful to our compatriots living abroad, who came to the stadiums and supported us during those matches."

SABAH FC against Hapoel Beer Sheva FC in Tofiq Bahramov Republican Stadium, Baku, Azerbaijan Azertag, August 2026

Dambrauskas is assisted by Valerio Zuddas, a 37-year-old Italian who has worked across 10 countries and is responsible for the team's defensive organisation and analysis of European opponents.

"The biggest satisfaction for Valdas as head coach and for us as coaching staff is that we can clearly see how the players are into our team principles and how they believe in them," Zuddas told Euronews.

"Sometimes they find solutions by themselves inside our structure, their level of understanding of the game allows us to propose always different strategies and variations that help us to be more and more competitive," he said.

Dreaming differently about football

Club president Magsud Adigozalov said the route to the Champions League was built on analytics rather than spending.

"We could not compete financially with many established European clubs, so we had to find our own competitive advantages," Adigozalov told Euronews.

"We were inspired by the Moneyball philosophy, which demonstrated that intelligent use of data and recruitment can help a club compete far beyond what its financial size might suggest," he explained.

Yet to Adigozalov, the human factor always comes first.

"Footballers are people before they are assets or statistics. We try to provide players with excellent training and living conditions and treat them and their families with respect," Adigozalov said.

Sabah FC's total squad market value is estimated to be around €16.65 million, a far cry from Barcelona's €1.1 billion or Manchester United's €900 million.

Napoli centre-back Benoît Badiashile, who just transferred from Chelsea, is valued at roughly the same as the entire Azerbaijani squad.

Adigozalov remains undeterred and a firm believer in hard work above all.

"The Champions League is the result everyone can see today. What makes us especially proud is the system, the culture and the work behind it that people did not see for nine years."

Qualifying for the main round brings Sabah a base fee of millions of euros in direct UEFA distributions, alongside broadcasting rights income and new sponsorship opportunities.

Adigozalov said the longer-term impact will be on understanding that nothing is out of reach in sports like football.

"A young boy or girl sitting in the stadium and watching Barcelona or Borussia Dortmund play against Sabah may start dreaming differently about football," he said.

"If this achievement brings more children into football, more families into stadiums and creates greater belief in Azerbaijani football, then its impact will be much bigger than Sabah itself."

World.title: Malta: Businessman acquitted of journalist's murder
World.content:
Yorgen Fenech was suspected to have masterminded the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, whose family continue to demand justice for her killing.

A Maltese businessman was acquitted after being accused of being behind the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

Yorgen Fenech, 44, was accused of commissioning the car bomb killing of Caruana Galizia in 2017 in a case that sent waves across Europe.

Caruana Galizia, who was 53 years old at the time of her murder, was driving near her home when the bomb detonated.

Caruana Galizia's journalistic investigations included extensive information about suspected corruption in politics and business in Malta. She faced about 40 libel suits at the time of her murder.

Life in prison avoided

Fenech, who would have faced up to life in prison had he been found guilty, was cleared of both complicity for murder and criminal association to commit murder with a jury margin of 8-1. He denied the allegations that he had wanted the journalist dead due to an investigation about him being about to be published.

A bomb detonated as Daphne Caruana Galizia was driving her car [FILE: October 16, 2017] Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

Fenech did not comment after leaving the courtroom, with a crowd of people waiting outside the court shouting insults in his direction.

Family's demand for justice continues

Caruana Galizia's family responded to the acquittal by saying that the institutional failures that led to the murder "remain unaddressed and unreformed."

"Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne's life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost."

The journalist's murder triggered protests in Malta [FILE: November 29, 2019] Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

Daphne Caruana Galizia's sons were in the courtroom when the verdict was read out.

Five people were convicted in connection to the murder, with three of them being found guilty of carrying it out.

All five are currently in jail.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Berlin's punitive measures unlikely to deter Putin: experts
World.content:
Germany has announced punitive measures after publicly blaming Russia for an attempted airport drone attack. But a former diplomat, political and security analysts warn it will likely do little to deter the Kremlin.

The practical impact of Germany's latest measures against Russia may be limited, according to Russian political scientist Dmitry Oreshkin, who described the response as largely symbolic.

However, Berlin's decision to publicly attribute the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4 to Moscow reflects a growing willingness to respond to Russian President Vladimir Putin and what Berlin sees as hostile actions on its territory.

"It's only a source of joy for Putin. After all, he is restoring this Iron Curtain between Russia and all the other countries. And now he's getting help from the other side as well," Oreshkin told DW. "Putin is someone who cannot be stopped by anything other than escalation and tough restrictions."

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Berlin's decision to close the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn, terminate the contract for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens does not go far enough, according to Boris Bondarev, a former diplomat who worked for the Russian permanent mission to the UN Office at Geneva.

Bondarev, who resigned his post in 2022 over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said reducing staff and restricting diplomatic activities may complicate Russian operations in Germany, but they will not fundamentally alter Moscow's strategic calculus.

"I'm not sure this will be perceived in Russia as something that will make them think twice," he said. "Unless there are other, more coordinated steps at the EU level, they won't stop provocations. At most, they may force them to coordinate a little differently and look for more professional operatives."

Both experts agreed, however, that Germany's measures could have an effect even if they fail to deter Moscow — by setting off another cycle of reciprocal restrictions.

How will Russia respond?

Speaking on Tuesday, President Putin called Germany's response "another mistake, a serious one," with the Kremlin telling the German Press Agency that Russia would respond "in kind."

German security policy expert Wolfgang Richter said the risk of escalation has increased compared with the early years of the Russia-Ukraine war, but said the next phase of confrontation between Berlin and Moscow is likely to remain in the areas of diplomacy and culture.

"They will, for example, close the Goethe-Institut," said Richter, a colonel with Germany's military until his retirement in 2010. "I would not quite exclude that they could also escalate a little bit and do more — for example, limit the number of diplomats in the German embassy in Moscow."

Former diplomat Bondarev, however, said the Kremlin's reaction could be difficult to predict.

"Moscow officials can surprise you. They could say: 'We have all these people under surveillance anyway, so why expel them? Let them work, and we'll continue monitoring them.' It could go either way. But most likely, there will be some high-profile retaliatory steps," he said.

Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The dispute over organizations such as the Goethe-Institut and the Russian House in Berlin reflects a deeper divide in how Moscow and Western governments view their role. The Goethe-Institut, founded in 1951 to promote German language and culture abroad, is seen by Moscow through the lens of its broader suspicion of Western institutions, said Oreshkin. And, he added, the Kremlin tends to assume that such organizations serve intelligence purposes because it projects its own security-service worldview onto Western structures.

"The Russian system of thinking among the security services assumes that all Western institutions are organized in exactly the same way. This symmetrical picture of the world is deeply mistaken," he said.

Oreshkin said it's unlikely the Kremlin will escalate much further than the level of diplomacy and culture.

"Launching a missile strike — that's something Putin doesn't have the guts to do. And all these acts of sabotage and subversion — supporting alternative political movements, like Alternative for Germany — they're already doing that anyway," he said. "So I don't think Putin can escalate much beyond that. He can, in fact, escalate the rhetoric, and that's what he's doing."

Real pressure point: Russia's shadow fleet

Announcing the measures on Monday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks." That included tougher action against Russia's "shadow fleet," though he didn't provide further details.

Russian officials have repeatedly warned that attempts to detain or seize vessels linked to Russia's network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions would be regarded as hostile acts.

NATO listens underwater to guard against Russian sabotage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Oreshkin said if Europe really wants to put pressure on the Kremlin, targeting the financial flows behind the shadow fleet would be more effective. But he pointed to a major obstacle: European governments are constrained by their own legal frameworks, which include maritime law that ensure freedom of navigation.

Security expert Richter, however, sees a broader security risk. Pressure on the shadow fleet could increase the likelihood of incidents at sea, he told DW. "And that would, of course, mean another escalation."

For Richter, the answer lies in making sure both sides understand the risks involved. "The situation has become more tense and it's high time to speak," he said. Without communication between the parties, he warned, any actions could be misinterpreted and might trigger further escalation.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler

World.title: Unity at last: Is Libya's damaging power struggle at an end?
World.content:
For over a decade, Libya has been split between two opposing governments. Elections, meant to end the rivalry and unite the country, are now scheduled within two years.

There have been other attempts made in the past but this time, those involved hope it will finally work out: Thanks to mediation by the United Nations, the two opposing governments in the west and east of Libya have agreed that they will hold parliamentary and presidential elections within the next two years.

"The agreement marks an important step in advancing Libya towards national elections and ending the transitional period," the UN's Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, said in a statement.

Among other things, the country's electoral commission will be restructured and, according to the UN, various points about the legal framework for the elections that had previously led to disagreements have now been resolved.

But whether all this will actually result in free and fair elections in Libya remains to be seen.

Divided for over a decade

After former Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi was overthrown in 2011, Libya ended up divided in two.

Since 2014, the country has been split between opposing governments located in the east and west of the country. A UN-backed administration known as the Government of National Unity is based in Tripoli in the west, and its rival, known as the House of Representatives, is based in the east, in Tobruk.

Former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar, is based in the east while Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah is in charge in the west.

Each is supported by a number of local militias and foreign powers, and each has tried to wrest control from the other. Up until now, attempts to hold an election that would unite the country have failed.

For Andreas Dittmann, a geographic conflict expert and professor at the University of Giessen in Hesse, central Germany, the apparent unity is a positive.

"Things could not continue the way they were," he told DW.

After years of civil war and political division, the desire of many Libyans to end the fighting permanently has only grown. Dittmann believes the attitudes of political actors have also changed in this regard.

Previously foreign actors had supported just one Libyan government, but now that has also changed and the prevailing argument seems to be that Libya can only develop further if both sides are incorporated into one administration.

This is why the UN is trying to go beyond simply arranging a date for elections. It also wants to strengthen the electoral commission and work on electoral laws. The new and united government will be responsible for establishing the conditions for a secure and trusted electoral process.

The UN has also set up what it calls "Structured Dialogues," during which consensus was sought on questions of leadership, security, the economy and reconciliation.

Past agreements didn't work out

Michael Bauer, who heads the Tunisia office of Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, believes the agreement is an important, if limited, step. Its success will depend on how binding any decisions are, he argued.

After all, Bauer said, there have been plenty of political agreements in Libya in the recent past but none were really ever implemented.

Parallel to the UN process, the US is also trying to work on bringing the disparate leadership together. Massad Boulos, the Trump administration's senior adviser on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, has been trying to bring the Dbeibah and Haftar families together.

Libya is potentially a rich country due to its mineral resources and large oil reserves Image: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

In June, Haftar's son Saddam was in Washington where he met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Bauer said the American way of dealing with Libya differentiates from the UN plan. "While the UN mission has basically been very inclusive, in my opinion, the American mission is trying to bring about a kind of deal between the country's elites," he told DW.

He questions how such a deal would fit into free and fair elections in Libya.

"Elections can only be meaningful if the outcome has not already been decided beforehand," Bauer said. The same is true for any pre-election allocation of political positions.

Elites strike a deal?

UK-based think tank Chatham House has already warned that a deal like this, around ministries and resources, will only institutionalize the existing rivalry between Libya's ruling elites. With such an arrangement the rival actors would just divide the state's resources between themselves, and corruption and patronage systems would continue.

The country's division into east and west will be hard to overcome. A new united government would have to deal with preexisting power structures, rather than starting anew.

Dittmann said there is a further problem. Much of the Libyan population lives in the western areas, especially in the Tripoli region. This would see the eastern half of the country lose power if elections are held.

Locals hope for economic growth and stability Image: Islam Alatrash/DW

"If there are elections, and if those elections proceed mostly according to democratic principles, then the east can really only lose," he explained.

Additionally, there are also external actors to consider. Russia has extended its positioning in the east while Turkey supports the government in the west.

Alongside all of that is also the question of what the Libyan people want and what they expect from a united government. Bauer doubts elections alone can resolve Libya's problems.

"The people have a particular interest in seeing the country's dysfunction end," he said.

Libya is rich in raw materials and energy reserves, but also plagued by problems like power outages and inadequate public services. If the state was functioning properly, it would likely curtail the power of those currently benefiting most from the country's resources and, as Bauer argued, "why would they voluntarily give up these opportunities?"

That will be the most difficult question for the next two years. The new agreement between Libya's political rivals must do more than simply establish a path toward elections. It must also create a framework in which those rivals accept the results of an election and in which public institutions function properly.

This story was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany: How to woo voters with an immigrant background
World.content:
The number of voters in Germany with an immigrant background is rising. Yet the established parties barely manage to reach them. Why not?

German voters of immigrant background are distancing themselves from the established parties even more than others, according to a study by the Berlin-based German Center for Integration and Migration Research (DeZIM).

In 2023, 12% of eligible voters in Germany were of immigration background — meaning they or at least one of their parents were born without German citizenship. That amounts to more than seven million people in a population of close to 84 million. But they are drifting away from the traditional centrist parties.

Nevertheless, according to the study, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) continues to have the greatest voter potential among immigrants and their descendants: Two out of three voters with an immigrant background said they considered the SPD a viable option.

The center-right bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) is close behind in second place. Only one in five respondents categorically rejected these parties.

"Older respondents with an immigrant background lean toward the SPD," said Friederike Römer, co-author of the study, at an online press conference this week. "This bond has been relatively strong in the past, but that seems to be breaking down now among younger generations."

Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD targets migrants

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) has the least potential voters of immigrant background. Nearly two-thirds of those surveyed said voting for the far-right was out of the question. People with roots in Turkey, the Middle East and North Africa, in particular, reject the party, though the AfD does enjoy significant support among Germany's Russian community.

Nevertheless, the AfD is working to win over the immigrant voter base.

"For a long time, it was the first party to communicate in immigrants' native languages using images that actually worked," said Martin Gerlach, federal executive director of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), recalling the AfD campaign in Berlin during the 2021 federal election.

"It read: 'Atatürk would vote for the AfD.' Other parties simply don't bother to think about these target groups. That's crazy, because if you win over big segments of voters with a migration background, you win elections."

Safety a priority for immigrants

The TGD was active in 60 German cities ahead of the last federal election in February 2025, encouraging voters of Turkish background to cast their ballots. But Gerlach has noticed that immigrants are not inherently pro-immigration; on the contrary, there is widespread skepticism toward new immigrants or refugees, an issue that the AfD has seized on. This, he argues, is just one of many reasons why other parties are losing support among those voters.

"The political parties don't address safety at all, and that's a huge issue," he said. "Yet people in our community feel extremely threatened in many parts of Germany — they don't even dare go to the Baltic Sea coast," he added, referring to a series of xenophobic attacks in that region.

Gerlach believes that Islamophobia has a significant effect on voters from the Turkish community, but the centrist parties don't pay enough attention to it.

"Anti-discrimination policy is seen in Germany as something progressive and left-wing, yet for the Turkish-origin community, it is about being protected by the constitution in the truest sense of the word," he said. "I believe this is a narrative that could win over a great many people."

Poorly treated? Racism in German medicine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Are the political parties missing a trick on social change?

Political scientist Özgür Özvatan pointed out that by 2030, more than half of Germany's population will have an immigrant background. He has also been critical of the established parties, most recently in his 2025 book "Every Vote Counts — Underestimated by Democrats, Courted by Populists: Migrant Germans as a Political Force."

"They are not reaching out to voters with an immigrant background the way they should — neither to recruit them for their own party, nor as volunteers, nor simply as voters," he said. "Sadly, we're missing the boat with this social change."

Özvatan argues that there is enormous potential to mobilize voters who have moved to Germany from authoritarian countries — people, for example, who have direct experience of trying to defend democracy.

"We can tap into that if we enable them to obtain citizenship with voting rights as quickly as possible," he said.

The AfD, meanwhile, relies on a strategy of addressing the Turkish diaspora while establishing connections to the right-wing authoritarian President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Furthermore, he said, the AfD has become very skilled at pitting people with immigrant backgrounds against one another.

"A great deal of effort is being put into telling older immigrants: 'You are different from the newcomers, this whole debate about migration and deportation won't affect you.' And this tactic works well with those who do not reject the AfD," said Özvatan.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Macron visits Bayeux Tapestry with King Charles, PM Andy Burnham
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron is on a shorter-term visit to the UK than the renowned on-loan 11th century tapestry. He viewed the ancient artwork with the UK monarch and relatively new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

French President Emmanuel Macron began a two-day trip to the UK by visiting another famous new arrival from France, the Bayeux Tapestry, with King Charles III and Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel joined King Charles and Queen Camilla to walk the length of the 70-meter tapestry in the British Museum.

Charles hailed the "unprecedented loan" as a "precious symbol of trust" between the UK and France, while Macron said the two countries were "as close as the threads" in the artwork.

The Bayeux Tapestry depicts the events of 1066, a defining date in the passage of British history and in the creation of the modern French-infused English language Image: Pascal Deloche/Godong/picture alliance

Why is the Bayeux Tapestry in London?

The tapestry, which depicts the momentous events of 1066 culminating in William the Conqueror of Normandy claiming the English throne, is on temporary loan from its usual home in France. It's the first time it's touched British soil since its creation in the 11th century.

The embroidery is on loan for a 10-month exhibiton opening to the public next week, on September 10. The exchange was first announced during Macron's state visit last year.

Though it's thought to have been made in the British Isles, it had been on French soil ever since the 11th century. It's usually on show in Bayeux in Normandy in northern France, hence the name. The effectively priceless artefact was transited across the Channel in secret in July.

Prime Minister Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, called the tapestry's return "a landmark moment" in the history of the two countries.

He also hailed ties with Macron's French government more generally in the House of Commons on Wednesday, alluding to reduced illegal migration crossings of the English Channel — a bid to counter one of Reform UK's favorite summer talking points.

"The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation — the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low," Burnham said.

It's Macron's first UK visit since Burnham took office and their first in-person meeting as leaders.

Moving the artefact from its usual home in Bayeux to Britain was a painstaking process months in the making Image: Lou Benoist/AP Photo/picture alliance

What is the Bayeux Tapestry?

The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.

This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millenium, and turned out to be the last one for a millenium.

The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.

The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.

England's last Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson saw off the Norse viking King Harald Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, but riding south to deal with William the Conqueror soon after proved a battle too far Image: Pascal Deloche/Godong/picture alliance

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
