World.title: BREAKING: Hungary blocks Ukraine’s EU accession again – Here’s what Budapest wants
World.content:
Hungary has blocked Ukraine’s EU accession process for a third time, with the government saying it will only lift its objection if Kyiv makes progress on the rights of the country’s Hungarian minority.

The latest dispute emerged at the European Council’s Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession (COELA), which held its first meeting after the summer recess on Tuesday, 1 September.

According to Ukrainska Pravda citing European Pravda’s sources in Brussels, Hungary refused to approve the screening results for Ukraine’s second and third negotiating clusters. Without unanimous support from all 27 EU member states, the Council cannot move forward with formally opening the clusters.

Budapest links its position to minority rights

The Hungarian government has said that it will not support further progress in Ukraine’s accession talks until Kyiv takes what Budapest considers necessary steps to fulfil its commitments concerning national minority rights.

The issue is particularly sensitive because Ukraine is home to a sizeable ethnic Hungarian community in the Transcarpathia region, near Hungary’s eastern border.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has previously taken a somewhat different approach to Ukraine from his predecessor, Viktor Orbán. In June, Magyar and Ukraine reached what the Hungarian leader described as a “historic agreement” aimed at guaranteeing the educational, cultural, linguistic and political rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia.

Despite that agreement, Budapest has maintained objections to several stages of Ukraine’s EU accession process.

What are the two clusters Hungary is blocking?

The latest Hungarian objection concerns Cluster 2, covering the EU internal market, and Cluster 3, which deals with competitiveness and inclusive growth. Hungary had previously blocked technical preparations for Ukraine’s Clusters 2–6. It subsequently lifted its objection to Cluster 6, which covers foreign and security policy, trade policy and relations with third countries.

In July, Hungary also supported advancing Cluster 3 for Moldova. However, most EU member states, led by Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, opposed separating Moldova’s and Ukraine’s accession tracks. As a result, neither country made progress on the matter at the time.

The next COELA meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, 2 September, although Ukraine and Moldova are reportedly not on the agenda, Kyiv Post writes.

Ukraine’s accession talks remain complicated

Ukraine formally began its EU accession negotiations in 2024, but opening individual negotiating clusters requires the unanimous agreement of the bloc’s member states. That gives Hungary significant leverage over the process.

The latest blockage comes after EU governments formally opened the first negotiating cluster — “Fundamentals” — for Ukraine and Moldova on 15 June.

Under the previous government, Viktor Orbán repeatedly opposed Ukraine’s EU membership and used concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority as one of the reasons for his position. His government had also held up the opening of the first cluster for years.

The change in Budapest’s approach under Magyar has therefore been notable, although it has not removed Hungary’s objections to Ukraine’s accession process.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Budapest says it does not want all clusters opened at once

Magyar has previously argued that Ukraine’s accession negotiations should proceed gradually rather than seeing all six clusters opened simultaneously.

“There are six clusters in total, and we don’t think opening them all at once is a good idea,” he said in June, arguing that the process should also take into account the Western Balkan countries that have spent years working towards EU membership.

For Kyiv, however, every delay is significant as it seeks to advance through the lengthy accession process and bring the country closer to EU membership.

World.title: School canteen employees were stealing food meant for children in Hungary, mayor caught them red-handed — Video
World.content:
Four kitchen employees at a primary school in Gyömrő, Hungary were reportedly caught with large quantities of food intended for pupils, after the town’s mayor stopped them in the school car park. Mayor Szabolcs Kisberk called the police, and an investigation has been launched into the case.

Kisberk, the mayor of Gyömrő, reported the incident on social media and also published video footage of what happened. According to his account, the incident took place on the first day of the new school year, when the four kitchen employees were allegedly preparing to leave the school premises around an hour before the end of their official working hours.

They were reportedly leaving with bags full of food

According to the mayor’s account, he stopped the four employees in the school car park and asked them to show him what they were carrying in their bags. An inspection reportedly revealed significant quantities of food used for school catering.

One particularly striking detail was that, according to the account, the food had been divided equally among the four employees. The mayor said this was not simply leftover food that kitchen staff might normally be allowed to take home, but ingredients intended to be served to pupils, reports 444.hu.

Only 900 grams of six kilograms of grated cheese allegedly left for pupils

One of the largest quantities involved was reportedly grated cheese. According to the account published by the mayor, the kitchen had six kilograms available, of which 5.1 kilograms had allegedly been put into the employees’ bags. That would have left just 900 grams for several hundred pupils.

The same amount of sliced ham was reportedly available. Of the six kilograms, the employees allegedly took 3.5 kilograms, leaving 2.5 kilograms for the children. According to the report, the six kilograms of margarine were also divided equally between the employees and the school kitchen’s supplies for the pupils.

Vegetables, fruit and prepared meals also found

The food allegedly taken was not limited to sandwich ingredients. According to the mayor’s account, nearly three kilograms of green peppers and five kilograms of peaches were also among the items found.

The list also included soup pearls, several prepared sandwiches, portions of cooked food and a diet meal. The mayor further reported that several kilograms of cooked side dishes had been hidden in one of the refrigerators.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Police called to the scene

Following the incident, Kisberk contacted the police. Officers from the Monor Police Department reportedly arrived at the scene and took action. According to the published account, all four employees admitted to the alleged offence during the police intervention. Pest County Police have confirmed that an investigation is indeed under way in connection with the case.

However, as the criminal proceedings are still ongoing, the four people involved cannot legally be considered convicted offenders at this stage. Their criminal responsibility will ultimately be determined through the relevant legal proceedings.

According to the mayor’s statement, the employment of all four kitchen workers was terminated following the incident. He said they were dismissed with immediate effect as part of disciplinary proceedings. The case has attracted particular attention because the food used in school catering is intended specifically to provide meals for pupils, while parents also contribute towards the cost of the school meals.

Parents and residents outraged

The incident has reportedly caused considerable outrage among parents and local residents in Gyömrő. According to the accounts published following the incident, some parents have questioned whether similar losses may have occurred previously and whether such practices could have affected the portions served to children.

However, there is currently no verified evidence in the available sources that similar incidents took place in previous years. The current case alone cannot establish that this was a long-standing practice.

In case you missed it: Police claims five men beaten and kept as modern-day slaves in Hungary for years

Tighter checks planned

Following the incident, the mayor said the local authority would introduce stricter controls in the kitchens of municipal institutions. The planned measures reportedly include closer monitoring of food stocks and stricter accounting for ingredients used in school catering.

The police investigation is ongoing, and the precise legal circumstances and responsibility of those involved will depend on the outcome of the proceedings.

World.title: PM Magyar signals Tisza’s next EU move after meeting with Manfred Weber
World.content:
Péter Magyar says Hungary’s governing Tisza Party will be ready to join the European People’s Party (EPP) once the EU’s Article 7 procedure against Hungary has been closed.

Magyar, who became Hungary’s prime minister after Tisza’s election victory in April, made the announcement after meeting Manfred Weber, the president of the European People’s Party, in Budapest on Wednesday.

The two politicians discussed how Hungary has changed since the election, with Magyar highlighting what he described as the end of publicly funded “hate campaigns” in the country.

According to Magyar, Weber said that supporting Hungary had always been important to him as a Bavarian politician and that he had personally found the previous government’s attacks on him difficult to experience.

Tisza eyes full EPP membership

One of the most politically significant points of the meeting was Magyar’s announcement that Tisza intends to join the European People’s Party itself.

Tisza has already been part of the EPP’s European Parliament political group since 2024, but membership of the wider European party family would represent a further step towards closer cooperation with Europe’s largest centre-right political family.

Magyar said Tisza would “gladly join” the EPP once EU institutions have closed the Article 7 procedure launched against Hungary.

The procedure was initiated by the European Parliament in 2018 over concerns relating to the rule of law and other fundamental EU values. It has remained unresolved for years.

The question of ending the procedure has gained renewed attention since Tisza came to power. Weber said as early as April that the European Parliament should take steps towards ending the process.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Weber offers help over EUR 1 million daily fine

The meeting also focused on Hungary’s long-running dispute with the EU over its asylum and migration policies.

Magyar said Weber had offered to help find a solution that would allow Hungary to stop paying the EUR 1 million daily fine imposed over its failure to comply with EU asylum rules concerning the protection of the bloc’s external borders.

The Hungarian prime minister said he made clear that the country would continue to protect its borders. He also said the new government would seek to have the fines already imposed on Hungary credited during negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget.

The dispute dates back to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which found Hungary had failed to fulfil its obligations under EU asylum law.

If you missed it: Extraditing Hungarian MOL’s head to Croatia? Péter Magyar gives cryptic answer at Bled forum

‘No blank cheque’ for Brussels

Magyar also stressed that closer cooperation with the EU would not mean giving up Hungary’s interests. He said the Tisza government’s priority would remain representing the interests of Hungarian people and businesses, adding that the government would not give anyone a “blank cheque” in EU decision-making.

The comments come as Budapest prepares for negotiations over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, one of the major issues facing the new Hungarian government.

António Costa next on Magyar’s Budapest agenda

Magyar’s meeting with Weber is part of a busy week of high-level European diplomacy. The Hungarian prime minister said he would also meet António Costa, president of the European Council, in Budapest after Wednesday’s government meeting.

According to Magyar, talks with Costa will focus on the EU’s new seven-year budget and the challenges facing Europe.

World.title: Colliers: Construction activity in Romania grew by approximately 12% in H1 2026 on public investment
World.content:
The volume of construction works in Romania increased by approximately 12% in the first five months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, supporting the country’s economic growth, according to Colliers’ report on the real estate market in the first half of 2026.

However, the market continues to be driven largely by public investment, and the second half of the year is set to bring greater risks, ranging from rising costs and increasing pressure on contractors’ cash flows to political uncertainty and concerns over the absorption of European funds, according to the same analysis.

The strongest growth came from the residential sector, where the volume of construction works increased by approximately 16%, and from infrastructure projects, which rose by around 14%. These include works on roads, railways and hospitals and continue to account for more than half of total activity in the sector.

The non-residential segment grew more slowly, by approximately 6%, against a backdrop of persistently expensive financing and greater caution among private investors.

Even so, the construction market is currently operating at almost twice the level seen before the pandemic. The Colliers report stresses that these increases measure the actual volume of works and the intensity of activity on construction sites, rather than the financial value of investments. In other words, the 12% increase shows that significantly more construction work is being carried out, rather than merely reflecting higher project costs.

”More than half of activity comes from state-funded projects, and the key question for the months ahead is whether these investments can continue at the same pace. The stakes are even higher for projects dependent on European funding, where any delays can quickly be felt across the market,” said Alexandru Atanasiu, Partner | Head of Construction Services.

Over the past decade, the volume of construction works in Romania has almost doubled, while the European Union average has increased only marginally. Infrastructure investment explains a significant part of this performance. Romania has gone from approximately 900 kilometres of high-speed roads before the pandemic to more than 1,400 kilometres at the beginning of 2026, while over 1,000 kilometres are in various stages of construction and a further approximately 300 kilometres are in the planning phase.

At the same time, costs are beginning to put renewed pressure on construction companies. Prices for several materials have started rising again, while some raw materials are approaching record levels. Copper, for example, became more than 40% more expensive in 2025, and this year exceeded USD 14,000 per ton, reaching new highs during the summer. The increase reflects both supply constraints and rising demand generated by the energy transition and the development of data centres for artificial intelligence.

Adding to the existing pressure are the new costs generated by the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, which has applied since 2026 to certain materials imported from outside the EU. Initial estimates indicate a cost impact of 10-15%. For Romania, which imports significant volumes of steel, aluminium and other metals, some of these increases will inevitably be passed on into final prices and may reduce both company margins and appetite for new private projects.

Cost pressures are also becoming increasingly visible in construction companies’ cash flows. Long payment terms, particularly for certain public projects, tie up significant liquidity at a time when contractors are also having to absorb high material and labour costs. At the same time, high interest rates make access to the financing needed for working capital more difficult and more expensive.

The stakes are also significant for the economy as a whole, as construction accounts for an increasingly large share of GDP. In 2025, construction represented approximately 8.6% of Romania’s GDP, the highest share in the European Union, where the average is around 5%. At the same time, banks’ exposure to the sector continued to increase, and by the end of the first quarter of 2026, loans to construction companies had exceeded RON 54 billion, approximately 16% above the previous year’s level and almost double that of 2019. This is precisely why any sharp slowdown, particularly in infrastructure projects financed through European funds, could quickly spill over into other sectors.

In the coming months, one of the biggest challenges will be the continuation of projects financed through European funds, with the end of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan having been on August 31.

According to estimates cited by Colliers, road infrastructure alone could face an additional financing requirement of approximately EUR 10-15 billion, which would need to be covered, where possible, from the state budget or other programmes. The pressure is all the greater given that the 2026 budget includes record public investment of more than RON 160 billion, itself largely supported by European funds.

According to Colliers, in the second half of the year, public investment could keep the construction market close to record levels, provided the political situation stabilises and European funds continue to be absorbed. The greatest risk remains a sudden slowdown in state-funded projects, which would also have repercussions across other sectors of the economy.

World.title: Bucharest’s Mezanin Market announces fall season events
World.content:
Mezanin Market, a project meant to support and develop small creative businesses in Bucharest, announced the opening of the fall season on September 5, during which more than 200 local entrepreneurs and creators will participate in seven fairs organized by the end of the year, at Palatul Universul (Beans&Dots, Mezanin Spaces) and in the office buildings of the project’s partners.

Each fair brings together more than 40 creators and different selections of fashion, jewelry, ceramics, illustration, decorations, natural cosmetics, objects, and gourmet products.

The calendar for the Mezanin Market fall-winter season:

September 5-6 - Back to School,

October 3-4 - Pumpkin & Spice,

November 14-15 - Winter Is Coming,

November 28-29 - St. Nick,

December 5-6 - Gift Planning,

December 12-13 - Early Gifting,

December 19-20 - Last Chance.

The calendar is complemented by a series of activations in the office buildings of partners, which bring local brands closer to communities that do not attend weekend fairs.

In November, Mezanin Market also returns to Vienna for its second participation in the international BLICKFANG fair, from November 6 to 8, with a selection of local brands. The participation is meant to create and test opportunities for entrepreneurs in the community outside Romania as well.

Moreover, FactoryLab, the project developed at Bucharest’s Promenada Mall together with Raiffeisen Bank, continues until January 5, 2027, complementing the fair calendar with a daily presence for local brands and maintaining the connection between entrepreneurs and the public throughout the season.

“I believe that we need, perhaps more than ever, creative businesses and entrepreneurs who bring optimism and confidence in the future, regardless of the economic or social context. Behind them are people who continue to create, invest and build, and for this they need the public and constant contexts in which they can test and develop their businesses. For us, the seven fairs this fall mean exactly that: more direct meetings between entrepreneurs and the public and more opportunities for the community we have been building for over 8 years,” says Silvia Floareș, co-founder of Mezanin Market and FactoryLab.

Since its launch in 2018, Mezanin Market has become a landmark for the creative community, bringing together more than 150,000 visitors and more than 400 local entrepreneurs. The project creates contexts for meetings between creators and the public, contributing to the support and development of small creative businesses.

World.title: George Enescu International Competition brings two chamber recitals to Sibiu
World.content:
The George Enescu International Competition will continue its Sibiu program with two chamber music recitals at Thalia Hall on September 8 and 10. The concerts will feature violinist Nemanja Radulović with pianist Laure Favre-Kahn and cellist Enrico Dindo with pianist Monica Cattarossi.

Radulović and Favre-Kahn will perform their violin-and-piano recital on September 8 at 7 p.m. A previous winner of the George Enescu International Competition, Radulović is also serving on the jury of this year’s violin section.

The Serbian-French violinist received an OPUS KLASSIK award in 2024 for Concert Recording of the Year. Favre-Kahn, meanwhile, is a laureate of the International ProPiano Competition in New York and a recipient of the Adami Classical Revelation award.

On September 10 at 7 p.m., Italian musicians Enrico Dindo and Monica Cattarossi will present a cello-and-piano recital.

Dindo is a winner of the Rostropovich International Competition in Paris and a former principal cellist of the Teatro alla Scala Orchestra in Milan. Cattarossi teaches at the Conservatorio della Svizzera Italiana in Lugano and the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory in Milan.

The second concert forms part of the Italy-Romania Cultural Year and is supported by the Italian Cultural Institute in Bucharest.

The Sibiu series will continue with pianist Daria Parkhomenko on September 17, followed by violinist Hyeonjeong Lee and pianist Gabriel Gîțan on September 19. Tickets are available through the IaBilet platform.

World.title: Romanian utilities group Electrica registers 7.7% higher EBITDA in H1 2026
World.content:
The Electrica Group, a major utilities company in Romania, registered a 7.7% increase in EBITDA in H1 2026, reaching RON 1.07 billion, compared to RON 1 billion achieved in the first half of 2025.

The increase in EBITDA mainly comes from the variation in the supply segment, which had a positive evolution in the first six months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, according to the company press release.

As such, the variation in the supply segment recorded an EBITDA improvement of RON 122.8 million, up to RON 181.3 million from RON 58.5 million in the previous period. The increase is due to the improvement in the segment’s operational performance, with a decrease in operating expenses of RON 211.9 million.

Operating revenues recorded an increase in revenues from core activities of RON 948.3 million, as well as a decrease in other operating revenues of RON 1.04 billion, as a result of the elimination of subsidies following the end of the support scheme starting July 1, 2025.

“Electrica has become more than distribution and supply. It has become a group in which we are about to start seeing the results of integrating the entire value chain: generation, storage, supply, distribution and energy services. The second half of the year will see us building new capacities, new services and an increasingly stronger role for Electrica Group in Romania’s energy future,” said Alexandru Chiriță, Electrica CEO.

Operating profit for H1 2026 recorded an increase of RON 66.6 million, reaching RON 773.1 million, compared to RON 706.5 million achieved in H1 2025. This increase is mainly due to the increase in operating revenues by RON 110.3 million, a positive impact diminished by the increase in operating costs by RON 43.7 million.

Revenues from current activities recorded an increase of RON 1.15 billion, a positive impact diminished by the decrease in other operating revenues by RON 1.04 billion, mainly due to the end of the support scheme in the supply segment. Net profit in H1 2026 recorded an increase of 8.6%, or RON 36.1 million, reaching RON 457.5 million.

The volume of electricity distributed by Electrica was 8.9 TWh, slightly down by 0.5% compared to H1 2025. The subsidiary Distribuție Energie Electrică România (DEER) serves approximately 4.011 million users in 18 counties, across an area covering approximately 40.8% of Romania’s territory.

In the generation segment, Electrica Group has renewable energy projects, photovoltaic and wind, with a total capacity of 307.5 MW, either in operation or at various stages of development. Of these, 46.5 MW are already operational. Electrica also has energy storage projects of approximately 949.5 MWh at various stages of development.

World.title: Ipsos survey: Romanians see university education as an opportunity, but doubt return on investment
World.content:
Romanians see education as an opportunity, but have doubts about the return on investment in a university degree, according to the global Ipsos Education Monitor 2026 study, conducted in 31 countries.

According to the study, Romanians are more likely to recommend that young people pursue university studies, but only 47% believe that a university degree is worth the investment.

This result highlights a clear difference between the symbolic value attributed to education and the perception of the concrete benefits it offers in the current labor market context, according to the survey authors.

The results also highlight Romanians’ concern about young people’s prospects. Around 78% of respondents believe that young people in Romania would have better opportunities if they moved abroad, reflecting the perception that access to professional and development opportunities is more favorable outside the country.

Regarding the challenges faced by younger generations, respondents identified economic difficulties as the main problem, followed closely by the mismatch between the education system and labor market requirements, poverty, inequality, the quality of education, and the phenomenon of bullying.

The same study showed that 73% of respondents support banning the use of social media by children under 14, while only 39% believe that artificial intelligence should be banned in schools.

Overall, perception of education in Romania remains predominantly negative. Only 12% of respondents believe that the education system provides quality education. This represents the second-lowest level among the 31 countries analyzed, after Peru.

Romanians’ negative perception of the national education system is longstanding. Its stability indicates that the changes implemented so far have not been sufficiently visible to significantly alter public opinion.

“Last year, we observed that Romanians were losing confidence in the ability of the education system to respond to current needs, while the main concerns were related to outdated curricula, the lack of reforms and young people’s well-being. The results of the Ipsos Education Monitor 2026 show that this lack of trust is now also reflected in the perception of educational outcomes: although university studies continue to be recommended, fewer than half of Romanians believe that a university degree is worth the investment,” said Irina Nicolaescu (Aldesiu), Client Director, Ipsos Romania.

World.title: Romania’s security chief Lucian Pahonțu again under fire over plagiarism allegations
World.content:
Lucian Pahonțu, the longtime director of the Protection and Guard Service (SPP) and alleged backroom power broker, was accused of plagiarizing at least 30% of his 2003 doctoral thesis by independent journalists part of Recorder on Wednesday, September 2.

The doctoral thesis signed by Lucian Pahonțu is entitled “Tactics Used for the Guarding and Protection of Particularly Important Objectives” and was supervised by retired general Prof. Univ. Dr. Valentin Arsenie. It was defended in April 2003 at the Academy of Higher Military Studies, now the “Carol I” National Defence University (UNAP).

The doctoral thesis has a total of 205 pages. Except for the technical pages and appendices, the content of the thesis amounts to 175 pages. Pahonțu allegedly took material from other sources without citation or with citations that do not comply with academic standards, according to the journalists.

Immediately after defending his thesis, Pahonțu was promoted to the rank of general in the Romanian Gendarmerie, and two years later he was appointed by president Traian Băsescu as Director of the Protection and Guard Service.

Pahonțu is also the author of a book entitled “Terrorism and Destabilization,” published in 2003 by Bioterra publishing house. The book contains part of his doctoral thesis, as well as a series of comments on events in the 1990s. In it, the head of the SPP laments the dissolution of the Militia and the Securitate and mocks the victims of the 1991 Mineriad, according to the same source.

The plagiarism accusation comes only a week after Recorder accused Pahonțu of taking part in the repression of the December 1989 Revolution and the June 1990 Mineriad as an officer commanding a unit within the Securitate Troops.

The head of the SPP rejected the accusations and cited official documents showing that he did not take part in the repression.

Snoop, another independent publication, also published an article on the SPP chief on Tuesday, September 1. In it, the journalists showed that Pahonțu earns roughly EUR 9,000 a month from the Romanian state by combining his salary with a special pension of EUR 7,000, in RON equivalent. By comparison, Nicusor Dan, the highest dignitary in the Romanian state and the one Pahonțu is tasked with guarding, among others, earns only RON 16,000 (EUR 3,000) a month.

World.title: Alba Iulia to also host NASA Space Apps Challenge for first time
World.content:
Alba Iulia will host a local edition of the NASA Space Apps Challenge for the first time on November 14-15. Around 100 young people aged between 14 and 35 are expected to take part in the 48-hour hackathon at the Gheorghe Șincai Multicultural Center.

Participants will work in teams and use NASA’s open data to develop solutions to real-world challenges related to Earth and space. This year’s challenges will be announced on September 17.

Each team will receive support from mentors before presenting its project to a jury. The three highest-ranked teams will receive cash prizes and other benefits, while the winners could qualify for the global stage of the competition.

Teams named Global Winners are subsequently invited to visit a NASA center or facility, celebrate their projects, and meet representatives of the US space agency.

“Growing up in Alba Iulia, I felt the absence of programs that show young people how to trust themselves, discover their potential, and put it to use,” said Dare.Gen co-founder Darius Mîndroc, whose organization is coordinating the local event.

The competition will be held under the Alba Iulia Romanian Youth Capital 2026 program.

Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Bistrița and Craiova will also host editions of the NASA Space Apps Challenge this year.

World.title: Romanian Customs Authority launches new X-ray scanner at Constanța Port
World.content:
The Romanian Customs Authority announced that it put a new X-ray scanning system into operation at the Constanța Port. The equipment will allow non-intrusive inspections of freight vehicles and gives both sectors of the Black Sea port access to the same type of scanning technology.

The system produces higher-quality images and will be used to inspect vehicles selected through risk analysis, in accordance with the EU Customs Code.

It was purchased through an EU-funded project to equip border customs offices with scanners for vehicles and containers and establish a National Customs Image Analysis Center. The project forms part of Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) reforms aimed at modernizing the customs system and introducing electronic customs services.

Once integrated into the national analysis center, the scanners will allow customs images to be monitored and analyzed in real time, improving the coordination of inspections.

According to the authority, the technology will help detect illicit shipments and attempted customs fraud while reducing waiting times at border crossings. It is also expected to support more targeted interventions by operational inspection teams.

Constanța is the largest port on the Black Sea and one of the main entry points for goods into the European Union’s customs territory. The authority said equipping the entire port with modern scanners would strengthen controls at the EU’s external border while helping maintain the flow of cross-border traffic.

World.title: Croatia Sentences Bosnian Citizen for Glorifying Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Mural of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade. Photo: EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC

A Croatian court has handed a suspended prison sentence to a Bosnian national found guilty of glorifying the late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

Police from the Korenica Border Police Station announced on Tuesday that they had filed a misdemeanour charge against a 43-year-old over social media posts in which he glorified Mladic. According to police, the man posted photos, symbols, songs and texts on social media that “publicly honoured and expressed gratitude to a person convicted of war crimes”.

Mladic was convicted by the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. He died aged 84 in a UN jail in The Hague on August 26.

In the posts, among other things, the man thanked Mladic for “freedom” and said “he will never be forgotten”. The police stated that such content caused agitation and distress among citizens and so constituted an offence under the Law on Misdemeanours Against Public Order and Peace.

Following an investigation, the 43-year-old was brought before a court, which sentenced him to 15 days in prison but suspended the sentence.

The man had been living in Korenica as a foreign worker with a temporary residence permit.

Such cases are not uncommon in Croatia.

On August 28, police arrested 31-year-old Serbian influencer, Marko Stojkovic, in Split after he displayed tattoos depicting Draza Mihailovic, a Serbian World War II collaborator with the Nazis who is considered a war criminal in Croatia. He was charged with disturbing public order and peace as well as violating the Anti-Discrimination Act.

“By publicly displaying several inappropriate images tattooed on his body, he disturbed public order and peace and, with the aim of causing fear and creating a hostile and humiliating environment, violated human dignity and caused public unrest,” Split police announced, adding that his behaviour also violated the Anti-Discrimination Act.

The court sentenced Stojković to 15 days in prison. Following the conclusion of the proceedings, he will be expelled from Croatia and banned from re-entering the country for the next five years.

World.title: Serbia’s Grief Over Mladic’s Death is Neither Honourable Nor Dignified
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

On August 27, I received a push notification on my phone saying that Ratko Mladic had died.

In Serbia, where denial of war crimes has become part of official policy, and where everyone is now waiting for elections to be announced, I knew we would likely miss this opportunity to deal with the past in a dignified and responsible manner.

If it is true that the past is the story we tell ourselves about ourselves, then our story perfectly explains what is keeping us trapped.

World.title: Serbia NGOs Condemn Push to Allow Construction on Fire-Damaged Land
World.content:
Two non-governmental organisations, Transparency Serbia and the Renewables and Environmental Regulatory Institute, RERI, on Wednesday criticised newly adopted law amendments that may allow construction on sites where forest has been destroyed by wildfires.

The amendments to the Law on Planning and Construction, adopted by parliament on August 31, allow for the construction of public infrastructure facilities, or facilities for which a public interest has been established.

“All of this took place during the horrific and unprecedented wildfires that engulfed Deliblatska Pescara (Debilato Sands), the largest sandy area in Europe, an invaluable reservoir of biodiversity that is a protected area of exceptional (Category I) and national importance, as well as a Special Nature Reserve,” the organisations said in a press release.

The amendments stipulate that “forest land where the forest has been damaged or destroyed by fire” retains the designation assigned to it by the planning document in force prior to the fire.

But they also state that an exception to this rule allows a change of land use where it is necessary to implement a project for which a public interest has been established, or for the construction of public infrastructure facilities.

Transparency Serbia and RERI also noted that the provisions concerning construction on forest land damaged by fire were not included in the original draft law submitted by the government to parliament but were introduced through amendments adopted at a session of the parliamentary committee.

This further reduced the transparency of the legislative process, they said.

“The lack of transparency in the authorities’ handling of these legislative amendments, rather than reassuring an alarmed and concerned public, has instead opened the door to further suspicions regarding the future fate of the land affected by the fires,” their press release added.

More than 3,500 hectares of Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve in northern Serbia were impacted by severe wildfires in August. There have been active wildfires in other parts of Serbia. The wildfires affecting the Deliblato Sands and other areas have burned around 13,920 hectares, according to Copernicus data as of 26 August.

World.title: Kosovo President’s Election Jeopardised by Party’s Inner Divisions
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku at a press conference on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Six MPs from the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, will not follow the decision of the party’s leadership on a joint presidential candidate with the ruling Vetevendosje Movement, potentially jeopardising a possible end to Kosovo’s political crisis and prompting yet another election.

The six have been named as Avdullah Hoti, Hykmete Bajrami, Arben Gashi, Armend Zemaj, Kujtim Shala and Janina Ymeri.

“They are causing irreparable harm to the entire process and – inevitably and unnecessarily – driving the country toward snap elections,” LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku told the media on Tuesday.

“This position is detrimental to Kosovo and to the LDK. Any future elections triggered by this refusal – given that the candidate was excellent – will have electoral consequences that consolidate absolute power and will impact the LDK itself,” he added.

On Monday, following a meeting between Vetevendosje and LDK leaders Albin Kurti and Abdixhiku, the latter announced Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as their joint pick for the presidential post.

But soon after, former PM and LDK MP Avdullah Hoti went on Facebook to warn that he does “not support this candidacy for President of the Republic of Kosovo – not for personal reasons but based on a political and institutional principle”, hinting at the divisions within the LDK.

Acting PM Kurti told the media on Tuesday evening, after Abdixhiku’s announcement, that a fresh election now looked more likely.

“After three rounds of elections [since February 2025], it appears there is a desire, will and an interest to head into a fourth election in less than two years,” he said. He added that a new meeting with Abdixhiku was needed.

In the last elections, in June, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the next-placed Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats – but only 12 of these would now vote for the chosen president.

Vetevendosje has claimed it can call on 62 votes to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

But in the presidential election, Sejdiu must win at least 80 MPs’ votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, he would need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

The announcement of the joint presidential candidate was a move to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since the parliamentary elections in June. Parliament has yet to be inaugurated, as the parties have not agreed on the next president. Without an agreement, new elections seem inevitable.

Amid the institutional logjam, the provisional speaker, Avni Dehari, from Vetevendosje, refused to resume the inaugural session that started on August 6.

Vetevendosje also refused to submit a name for the new speaker, first demanding an agreement with the other parties on the new president.

World.title: ‘This Is How We Lived Here’: Documenting 16 Years in Hungary Under Orban
World.content:
Those who stayed

The vast majority, of course, stayed in Hungary and adopted different survival strategies.

A journalist working for Hungary’s public service broadcaster confessed to Varadi that now he feels he was a coward. He was “only” responsible for cultural content, did not have to do political reporting, but he was one of the hundreds who helped operate what many now refer to as “a factory of lies and propaganda” on state channels.

“I never crossed a professional red line myself,” he justifies in the interview, but goes on to admit that he earned a good salary that afforded him and his family a comfortable life.

While many talk about intimidation, self-censorship and adaption to the system, some stories prove that courage did sometimes pay off. A man who worked on development projects in a provincial town described the mounting pressure he felt from local authorities to award projects – and the public money that came with them – to Fidesz-aligned companies. Yet he did not bow, and decided to maintain strict application criteria. He was prepared to be fired, but to his surprise nothing happened. There were no reprisals.

The conversations often take a turn and raise questions about individual or joint responsibility. “Many people ask the question how could this all happen to us? And above all: why did we let it happen?” Varadi says.

Did Hungarian society simply follow the century-old patterns of making compromises, adapting and succumbing to pressure in order to survive, as was done under the rule of the Turks, the Habsburgs and the Soviets?

“One thing is for sure: there were no guns pointed at people’s heads,” Peter Kreko, director of the Budapest-based Political Capital, tells BIRN.

Kreko, a social psychologist, finds it perhaps most surprising that Orban managed to keep his grip on power for 16 years without resorting to violence, primarily through the manipulation of information. “This was a perfect ‘information autocracy’,” he says.

Kreko believes people always had a choice, and this was especially true for those working for the state media or the public administration. But many followed what historian Timothy Snyder has described as ‘anticipatory obedience’: trying to figure out what is expected of them and behave accordingly.

When it comes to conformism or adaptation, Kreko says, Hungary is not very different from its regional peers, but it is certainly true that Hungarian society has a historical tendency to bow to authoritarian leaders.

“What we see is that many people were afraid, felt intimidated,” is how Varadi explains it. Many feared negative consequences if they spoke up. Many sacrificed their right to free speech for their comfortable lives. And by doing so, many became accomplices of the system.

Stefano Bottoni, an Italian-Hungarian historian researching Central European modern history, points to the general lack of solidarity and mistrust in Hungarian society. “There were no institutions people would have trusted. The most common channel to rebel against the system was to write angry Facebook posts,” Bottoni tells BIRN.

He believes stronger trade unions, something like Solidarity in Poland in the 1980s, would have helped build critical communities, but they are virtually non-existent in Hungary. “We helped weaken the resilience of the system, believing that we don’t need those institutions, we will figure out a survival method all by ourselves,” he says.

Varadi shares this analysis: “Many people felt powerless and left alone. When the teachers went on to strike there was virtually no solidarity from the society.”

World.title: ‘Marine Landfills’: The Garbage Choking Greece’s Seas
World.content:
Last year, on his annual visit to Corfu, Giorgos Kontarinis photographed sun loungers, a pedalo and various other objects on the seabed off Imerolia, a village on the north side of the island.

A keen diver, he took another look this year.

“I went swimming to the spot where I had found the rubbish last summer, wanting to see if anyone had taken the trouble to pick it up,” said 59-year-old Kontarinis, a photojournalist at the leading Greek press photo agency Eurokinissi.

“I was shocked when I saw the same sight again.”

Such a sight is becoming increasingly common in tourist resorts across Greece.

“We’re talking about marine landfills,” said Giorgos Sarelakos, head of the volunteer environmental organisation Aegean Rebreath.

Since 2017, Aegean Rebreath has organised seabed clean-up operations in over 60 areas across the country; it was also the initiator of the Blue Municipalities Network, the first network composed of local municipalities for the protection of the marine environment.

Plastic makes up most of the waste, according to George Papatheodorou, Professor and Director of Oceanus-Lab at the Department of Geology, University of Patras, Peloponnese.

Worse still, large parts of the Greek seabed remain “essentially unexplored”, he warned.

World.title: Demirovski: Macedonian Ammo Maker Untouched by Scandals in Serbia
World.content:
At roughly six o’clock on the morning of July 22, 2024, there was a knock at the door of a 36-year-old weapons engineer in Serbia.

Identified by Serbian authorities by the initials M.O., the man was in bed with his wife, sleeping. His two children were also asleep. His wife got up and opened the door. Police officers in balaclavas stormed inside, accompanied by Serbian security agents, and pinned M.O. to the floor.

The same night, two other weapons engineers, 64-year-old D.L. and 63-year-old D.M., were also arrested.

All three men had previously worked for the state-owned arms manufacturer Krusik. They were suspected of supplying confidential information on Krusik’s production of 120-mm mortar rounds to a company in neighbouring North Macedonia for which they had also done work - ATS Group, owned by Shefshet Demirovski.

It was not the first time Demirovski’s name had surfaced in a case of alleged industrial espionage in Serbia. In 2019, prosecutors accused him of bribing a former employee of Serbian ammunition producer Prvi Partizan to supply him with confidential specifications concerning production machinery.

The 2024 arrests underscored the intensity of competition between defence manufacturers in the Balkans, where Serbia boasts one of the biggest military industries, supplying battlefields across the world.

As global demand for arms and ammunition from the Balkans has increased, so too has the rivalry.

Enter Demirovski, about whom there is scarce publicly available information.

Backed by the state and boasting close ties with Turkey, the 50-year-old businessman has built one of North Macedonia’s most ambitious private defence manufacturers producing small-calibre ammunition.

“God, I wish we had more people like Sheki in this country,” a former government official told BIRN, referring to Demirovski by his nickname.

Demirovski’s alleged activities in Serbia, however, reveal a less savoury side to his success, as well as possible ties to the country’s criminal underworld.

Demirovski did not respond to questions sent to his official email address and via Viber, though the Viber messages were registered as ‘seen’.

World.title: ‘Polish Annexation’ Hoax Campaign Spotlights Czech Disinformation Vulnerability
World.content:
A podcast interview with investigative journalist Lukas Valasek for Seznam Zpravy on Monday laid out a recent well-organised, large-scale disinformation campaign that pushed the notion Poland was preparing to invade and annex a small border area with its southern neighbour around the twin towns of Ciezyn/Tesin.

“It is the first ever operation of this scale,” assessed Valasek. “If we understand this whole thing as a test from a potential Russian actor on how the Czech Republic will respond to a wave of disinformation, then I think that the Czech political scene, and especially the government, did not quite pass.”

The campaign last week relied on paid Facebook ads, AI-generated images, a fake website mimicking Czech Radio’s iRozhlas.cz, as well as fake social media accounts of both ordinary citizens and top officials, including Czechia’s ambassador to Poland.

The apparent goal, most have deduced, was to spark fears of a land grab and property seizures while stirring up historical grievances between the two EU and NATO countries linked to a controversial 1958 border treaty between Poland and then-Czechoslovakia.

According to Czech security expert Bohumil Kartous, the campaign bore all the hallmarks of a Russian-backed hybrid operation, exploiting “a fragment of truth” – the lingering, albeit relatively minor Czech-Polish border dispute – to place it “in a completely different context of fear over losing property”.

“The goal is precisely to trigger a dispute within this pro-Ukrainian coalition,” according to Kartous.

It appears to have mostly missed the mark. Poland was fastest to respond on August 25, with Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski quickly dismissing the claims of imminent annexation as absurd and orchestrated. On August 26, as a symbol of Czech-Polish unity, Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted an image of friendship between the countries’ most famous cartoon characters, the Polish dog Reksio and the Czech mole Krtek, captioning: “Reksio and Krtek have known this for a long time, Poland and Czechia are true friends.”

But over the border the response took longer and was more muddled, with finger-pointing now underway to determine who was to blame for these failings. It took several days for the Czech Foreign Ministry to unequivocally reject “the spread of false information about alleged Polish territorial claims to the Czech Republic”.

Czech President Petr Pavel also weighed in: “This is a targeted provocation. And I’m very glad that people are not listening to this provocation on either side of the border,” going on to assure that “Poland is one of the Czech Republic’s closest and most important partners.”

Czech hesitancy

Yet late last week, Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis lashed out against his intelligence services, saying he had only heard about the ongoing hoax campaign through the media.

On Monday, he again pointed the finger at the Office for Foreign Relations and Information (UZSI) and blamed Czechia’s envoy in Poland, Bretislav Dancak, for the failed response.

Although evidently failing to drive a wedge between Prague and Warsaw, security experts said such a campaign could be used to test both Polish and Czech responses to hybrid threats and influence ops.

Highlighting the decision to entirely scrap the Strategic Communications Department (Stratkom) shortly after taking office, on top of reducing the number of ministerial experts focused on disinformation, many argue the Czech government only has itself to blame.

“If, by chance, there had still been any strategic communication of the state, analysts would have caught [the disinformation campaign] long before and the top representatives of the state could have communicated it,” argued former Stratkom chief Oldrich Bruza. “At least we have our Polish brothers.”

Opposition politicians, too, have accused the government of bringing this upon itself. “We have repeatedly warned about this,” said former foreign minister Jan Lipavsky. “For ideological reasons, the government is liquidating the state’s capacities for combating disinformation and influence operations at the very time when someone is using them against the Czech Republic.”

Hints of Russian involvement abound, but officials have so far refrained from unequivocally accusing Moscow of being behind the operation. Intelligence services in both Poland and Czechia are still investigating the matter.

But in Prague the finger-pointing continues. “We don’t need a Strategic Communications Department,” argued Prime Minister Babis. “We have [intelligence] services here that are supposed to work for the state, for the people and for the interests of the state.”

While failings at the top were evident, the response from the local population did not disappoint, with social media quickly flooded with montages of Reksio and Krtek as long-time chums, nipping in the bud any fears of cross-border animosity.

World.title: Has the Much Anticipated Croatian Robotaxi Failed?
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Has the Croatian robotaxi story ended? It has been revealed that Mate Rimac’s Verne may need to return 89.7 million euros if it is determined that the project has indeed failed.

The company Verne, which has been engaged in developing the much anticipated robotaxi project, is prepared to return 89.7 million euros in advance payments drawn from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan if the evaluation of what has been achieved so far in the project shows that the contracted obligations have not been fully met. “The company is prepared to return all funds,” Verne said in its announcement.

an ongoing procedure

The Verne project, partially financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), officially ended on the 31st of August, but the key part of the procedure is still to come, the final evaluation that will show whether all contracted obligations have been fulfilled. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the company has stated, as touched on above, that it is prepared to return all funds if the competent authorities determine that the objectives have not been fully achieved, according to the announcement. The company has so far drawn 89.7 million euros in advance payments from the NPOO project, while it has raised more than 140 million euros from various private investors.

The Verne robotaxi project has therefore formally ended, but the procedure is not finished. Within one month, Verne must submit a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that documentation, the competent authorities will carry out the final evaluation and determine what of the contracted obligations has actually been fulfilled.

what we know so far

The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, testing has been carried out, and regulations have been adopted. “The project ended on the 31st of August. The company is now submitting, within one month, a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that report, the competent authorities will make the final evaluation of the project, i.e. an assessment of what has been successfully fulfilled in the project,” Verne stated.

According to the company’s claims, some of the objectives have already passed the verification of the competent institutions. The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, appropriate testing has been carried out, and regulations governing autonomous driving have been adopted. However, three remaining objectives still need to receive a final assessment, and the outcome of the project will largely depend on them. These are: the issuance of 50,000 free vouchers for rides in fully autonomous vehicles to persons with disabilities, the production of fully autonomous electric vehicles adapted to the needs of passengers with disabilities, and the establishment and operational readiness of specialised infrastructure.

multiple amendments have already been made

“In the implementation of the project so far, the competent institutions have verified that all verification prototypes of fully autonomous and electric vehicles have been successfully delivered, that appropriate testing has been carried out, and that regulations on autonomous driving have been adopted,” the company stated. They add that the public will be informed after the competent authorities complete the procedure of assessing the success of the project.

The main result of the project, for which Project 3 Mobility was approved 179.5 million euros from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, was supposed to be a fully autonomous electric vehicle of the fifth level of autonomy. That objective did not change even after multiple amendments to the contract and extensions of deadlines. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure particularly emphasised this back in April, when the last annex to the contract was signed.

The fifth level represents the highest level of autonomy. Such a vehicle does not need a driver and is not limited to predefined areas or driving conditions. Neither Verne nor any other company in the world has a vehicle of that level of autonomy today.

there are still many unknowns in the story

As Mate Rimac revealed recently, the fact is that Verne has, in addition to EU funds, also attracted more than 140 million euros in private funds. The robotaxi is already driving the streets of Zagreb. Uber is a strategic partner, and Pony.ai is the technology partner. Verne will be the owner of the fleet and the operator of the service, Pony.ai will provide the autonomous driving solution, while Uber will integrate the service into its global ride-hailing network, which will be an additional option alongside the Verne application. Together, the companies are building a commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb, and over time also in additional European and international markets, with plans to expand to a fleet of thousands of autonomous vehicles in the coming years.

“It’s difficult even to determine precise deadlines for when this will become a profitable business. It’s a kind of adventure, but all partners see potential in it. It will be a great story, but realistically it will take quite a lot of time. It wouldn’t be particularly serious to forecast now when this will be a sustainable business model,” was Rimac’s answer to the question about the profitability of the robotaxi business itself.

World.title: Petition Launched After Removal of Lokrum Nudist Beach
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – A petition has been launched by dissatisfied local people following the removal of a favourite Lokrum nudist beach.

The decision to remove the signs marking out the way to a favourite Lokrum nudist beach has sparked a wave of reactions among residents of Dubrovnik. Morski reports that after the signs were taken down, a group of people decided to take concrete steps and launched a petition calling for a solution that would allow the long-standing practice to continue.

“With this petition, we wish to encourage those responsible to find a legal framework for the lawful continuation of the tradition of naturism on the island of Lokrum. Back during the mid-1960s, with the establishment of the Lokrum Reserve, signs designating a swimming area for nudists were put up by the institution above the cliffs on the eastern side of the island of Lokrum.”

As a reminder, the public first learned about the removal of the signs from a reaction by Professor Igor Legaz, who confirmed on the 26th of August that the signs pointing to the Lokrum nudist beach had been removed, noting that the nudist beach in that area had operated contrary to the applicable regulations.

“This concerns a stretch of coastline about 300 metres long, characterised by a series of large natural stone slabs, which has been under general use since yesterday. For that reason, I thank the Management of the Lokrum Reserve and the director for the step they have taken, because that ‘special-purpose beach’ on the island of Lokrum had in any case been established contrary to the provision of Article 80, paragraph 2, point 2 of the Maritime Domain and Seaports Act,” Legaz said.

While part of the public welcomes the alignment of the situation on the ground with the Maritime Domain Act, the initiators of the petition emphasise the historical and cultural significance of that section of the coast and appeal to the competent institutions to find an appropriate model that would allow the lawful retention of the naturist tradition on the beautiful island of Lokrum.

World.title: September Sea Temperature Records Broken in Split and Komiža
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – The September sea temperature records have been broken in both Split and Komiža, with strong warmth still beating down on the Croatian coast.

The sea was unusually warm along a large part of the Croatian coast on the first day of September. According to DHMZ data, at 14:00 yesterday, the temperature measured in Split was 28.0 degrees, in Komiža 28.2 degrees, and near Dubrovnik it also stood at 28.2 degrees. Index reports that the sea is even warmer on Mljet. In Malo jezero at 2 p.m. as much as 30.2 degrees was measured, in Veliko jezero 29.9 degrees, while on the open sea near Mljet the temperature was 28.8 degrees.

september records have been broken in split and Komiža

Data from both Split and Komiža is particularly interesting. According to the DHMZ bulletin for September 2025, the previous absolute September maximum in Split was measured at 27.3 degrees, measured on the 2nd of September 2015. In Komiža, the record was also 27.3 degrees, set on the 2nd of September 2024. Yesterday afternoon’s 28.0 degrees in Split is therefore 0.7 degrees higher than the previous September record, while Komiža with 28.2 degrees exceeded the old record by as much as 0.9 degrees. These are operational DHMZ data, so the final values will be confirmed after data processing. For comparison, during the whole of September last year the highest measured value in Split was 25.0 degrees, and in Komiža 24.6 degrees. Even in the very warm September of 2024, the maximum recorded in Split was 27.0 degrees. The average sea temperature in Split that September was 24.0 degrees, a full 1.7 degrees above the climatic average for the period 1991–2020.

a mere 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that particular station

Yesterday afternoon’s 28 degrees in Split is only 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that specific station. In Split back on the 15th of July 2024 a temperature of 29.4 degrees was measured. Values from Mljet should not be directly compared with the long-term series from Split and Komiža. Malo and Veliko jezero are measured by automatic sensors and aren’t part of the same long-term series of the four stations – Rab, Split, Hvar and Komiža – that DHMZ uses in monthly analyses of September sea temperatures. Surface sea temperature at the classic stations is measured approximately 30 centimetres below the surface.

World.title: Croatia Records Modest Tourism Growth in First Half of 2026 as EU Nights Rise 1.7%
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Eurostat reports that Croatia has recorded modest tourism growth throughout the entire first half of 2026, as EU overnight stays rise.

Over the first six months of 2026, tourist accommodation establishments across the European Union recorded 1,321 million overnight stays, a 1.7% increase compared with the same period in 2025 (1,299 million nights), according to official data released by Eurostat on 1 September 2026. Eurostat reports that while the EU as a whole continued its recovery and expansion, growth was highly uneven across member states. The strongest increases were recorded in Ireland (+14.6%), Malta (+9.9%) and Slovakia (+5.9%). Nine countries registered declines, with the sharpest falls in Cyprus (–7.7%) and Romania (–6.7%).

Croatia, long one of Europe’s leading tourism destinations, registered only a mild increase of approximately 0.5% in overnight stays during the same period. This placed the country near the bottom of the group of member states that still achieved positive growth, just ahead of Finland and the nine countries that recorded outright declines.

international visitors drive the numbers up

Foreign (non-resident) tourists accounted for 48.9% of all overnight stays in the EU in the first half of 2026. Nights spent by international visitors grew by 2.5%, nearly three times the increase recorded by domestic guests (+0.9%). Dependence on foreign visitors varies dramatically across the bloc. Malta (95.2%), Cyprus (92.6%) and Luxembourg (87.7%) recorded the highest shares of foreign overnight stays, while Germany (18.5%), Poland (19.8%) and Romania (23.0%) remained heavily reliant on domestic tourism.

Croatia’s modest 0.5% growth comes against a backdrop of strong overall EU performance and particularly rapid expansion in several smaller markets. The figures cover the traditionally quieter first half of the year, before the peak summer season. Full-year results will depend heavily on performance in July, August and the shoulder months of September and October. Eurostat’s data underlines that while tourism demand in Europe remains resilient, competition for visitors is intensifying and growth is no longer automatic even for established destinations.

World.title: 35 Million Euro Croatian Football Federation Camp Progressing Well
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – The 35 million euro Croatian Football Federation camp in Velika Gorica not far from Zagreb is progressing well and according to plan.

The construction of the new Croatian Football Federation (HNS) camp in Velika Gorica is progressing according to plan, and the project worth more than 35 million euros is taking its final shape. It will be the new base for Croatia’s national teams and one of the most important football projects in Croatia. Poslovni reports that the camp is being built on land covering 92,206 square metres, which the state donated to the HNS after the administration in Velika Gorica re-designated the area as a sports and recreation zone. The government is investing 15 million euros in the project, while it is also being financed with the help of the HNS, UEFA and FIFA.

The new complex will boast four football pitches. The central one will have a covered stand with around 1,500 seats, while the remaining three are intended for training. Two will have natural grass and one artificial turf. A particularly important part of the project will be the modern HNS business building, into which the Federation’s administration will move. In this way the HNS will for the first time have business and sports facilities combined at one location.

The camp will also have changing rooms for all age categories, restaurants and a kitchen, spaces for coaching staff, analysis and the media. In the second phase the possibility has been left for the construction of a multi-purpose sports hall, gym, wellness centre and medical centre for players’ recovery. The new complex will not be intended only for the senior national team. Younger men’s and women’s national teams as well as futsal selections will also prepare there, and the space will also serve for the education and licensing of coaches and referees. Works should be completed and the camp put into operation by the summer of 2027.

World.title: Split Landlord’s August Worries Point to Deeper Croatian Tourism Issues
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – One Split landlord has shared his August worries about reservations which point to a much deeper problem within Croatian tourism.

A discussion developed on Reddit recently under a post by a resident of Split from Varoš about the bursting of Split’s tourist bubble, prices and “nerve amortisation”.

“Basically, this is the first time it’s happened that I’ve been empty for a longer period in August. I have an apartment in Varoš. So… a week has already passed by without any check-in or reservation made, and my price is low. Is anyone else in a similar situation?” This short post, which an anonymous Split landlord shared on Reddit, instantly laid bare the anxieties that have for some time been creeping among Split’s hospitality workers and property owners. Morski reports that Varoš, a traditional old Split neighbourhood, has experienced unexpected silence right in the very heart the middle of the peak summer season.

stuck between a rock and a hard place – market reality and harsh algorithms…

Many people in the comments immediately pointed out that the problem may not be in Split itself or a general crisis, but in the fact that supply has long exceeded demand. One user vividly explained the situation with the following words: “Supply and demand. In Split there are 15-20% more apartments on the market at any given moment than the city has guests.”

Others located the problem within the digital platforms themselves and suggested the landlord check how the apps treat him at all: “Try searching for your apartment on the site where you rent it out as a guest, preferably in an incognito window… Maybe it’s not even about the price but the algorithm. Most guests don’t scroll past the first 10-15 apartments before booking something.”

A particularly sharp discussion arose around the definition of what exactly a “low price” is, and the mentality of newly minted landlords. Workers from the tourism sector warn that guests have become more cautious and no longer accept just any conditions. “As an employee in a tourist agency, I completely agree with this. All clients who have realistic prices from the start fill up much better, with longer reservations and generally better guests, fewer cancellations, and of course fewer problems.”

Another user described how his family manages to stay competitive, but with enormous effort: “A studio for two 100 euros a night, it’s been full from the May onwards… When Airbnb takes its commission what’s left is quite a bit less than 100, but the occupancy rate is excellent. We clean the place ourselves, greet our guests, wash the bedding… Unfortunately, today everyone would rent out apartments and have a cleaner come, a laundry service… and still make a big profit.”

In contrast to that, landlords from the same neighbourhood appeared on the same post, claiming they have no problems if they position their accommodation well: “I also have an apartment in Varoš… my prices range 150-220 euros and around 400 for Ultra, everything is filled within one day.”

what is the situation with foreign nationals renting purchased properties?

Among the slew of comments, an interesting theory about long-term changes in the structure of guests also stood out. Split and its surroundings are slowly ceasing to be a destination where foreigners exclusively rent accommodation, because many of them have become property owners themselves.

“They count the entry of foreigners into Croatia as visitors, but they don’t count how many of those foreigners already have their own properties located in Croatia. People around Omiš tell me that everything has been bought up by Slovenians, Poles and Austrians. Everyone has sold everything and that’s why the apartments are less filled up. The only ones left are the party crowd that comes to Split every now and then.”

This Reddit post from Varoš actually served as a microcosm of Split’s housing and tourism reality at the moment. While some consider a “week-long hole” in August an anomaly or a bad algorithm, others see it as a fair sobering of a market that has grown for too long on unrealistic foundations. The conclusion of the discussion remains open, but the message is clear: the time when it was enough to “just open the doors” and wait for filling at maximum prices is slowly passing. Split must face the fact that without a sustainable strategy and balancing between the needs of the local population and the real possibilities of supply, empty apartments in August will no longer be a surprise, but the rule.

World.title: Less Heat, Less Crowds, Lower Prices – Croats Travel More in Post-Season
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – Less heat, less crowds and generally fairer prices are leading more and more Croats to opt to travel during the post-season.

With the first days of September arriving, the tourist off-season practically officially begins for Croatia. Booking.com has therefore published its 11th annual research report on consumer attitudes and understanding of the social and environmental impact of travel, with insights from 32,500 travellers across 35 markets worldwide. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that according to that data, the majority of Croatian travellers – 58 percent of them in total, plan to travel during the post-season. Both Croatian and European accommodation providers are trying to make use of this period, while the latter want to monetise the remaining demand and attract bookings in the later part of the season.

less heat, less crowds and (sometimes) better value for money

Speaking further about Croats who decide to travel during the off-season, 80 percent of them stated in the research that they do so in order to avoid destinations with large numbers of visitors, while 55 percent are motivated by the possibility of savings. The results indicate that travelling in the off-season has its advantages: besides smaller crowds, there is also a more price-accessible experience, and 53 percent of Croatian travellers plan to avoid overcrowded tourist destinations, which represents an increase of 11 percent compared to the previous year. This part of the season also reflects a more thoughtful approach to travel, as 65 percent of our travellers state that they want to avoid contributing to mass tourism, while 45 percent of those who travel in the off-season are motivated by the desire to reduce pressure on destinations.

the weather is in charge…

As many as 68 percent of all respondents globally say they actively avoid destinations known for extreme weather conditions. Speaking solely about Europeans, research by the European Travel Commission shows that September stands out as an important month for travel, with 22 percent of residents of the Old Continent planning trips in 2025, compared with 25 percent who do so in July and August.

When it comes to owners of accommodation facilities, attention is focused on more commercial tactics with which they can attract demand. Namely, data from the European Accommodation Barometer for 2026 are based on a survey conducted among 1,240 executives and managers from the European accommodation sector, including representatives of hotels and alternative accommodation facilities, and they state that discounts stand out as the most frequently used tool for attracting guests.

In view of this, 79 percent of Croatian accommodation facilities state that special prices or packages for the off-season bring positive results. Accommodation facilities also rely on broader distribution strategies, with 87 percent of them considering online platforms an effective channel for generating bookings in the off-season. The report states that event-driven tourism is another popular way of attracting alternative demand among accommodation facility owners; 37 percent of them stated that they had benefited from event-motivated travel over the past 12 months.

one third cancelled a planned trip

Nevertheless, the weather is increasingly influencing travel, so Booking notes that extreme weather conditions are actively changing travel choices and travel times. Almost three quarters of all respondents said they take into account the risk of extreme weather conditions when choosing a destination (74 percent) and the time of travel (74 percent), while 68 percent say they actively avoid destinations known for extreme conditions.

Interestingly, 31 percent of travellers stated that they had cancelled or changed their travel plans in the past year due to extreme weather conditions or natural disasters.

World.title: Croatia Introduces Life Imprisonment for 15 Criminal Offences
World.content:
September the 1st, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce life imprisonment for 15 criminal offences as of the 1st of January 2027.

The liability of companies, i.e. legal persons, for criminal offences committed through them by responsible persons will be sanctioned significantly more severely than before. From the 1st of January 2027, life imprisonment in Croatia will be able to be imposed on perpetrators of 15 types of the most serious criminal offences, including those related to irreversible or long-term environmental pollution.

Poslovni reports that the harshest penalty will be able to be imposed on all persons who were 18 or older at the time of committing the offence, which means that younger adults will not be spared either, writes Kristina Turčin for Jutarnji. However, all those sentenced to life imprisonment, regardless of age, will have the right to conditional release after serving 25 years of the sentence.

Specifically, for offences that have caused the most severe environmental pollution, i.e. ecocide, fines will rise to as much as 50 million euros.

Reports (including statements linked to the Ministry of Justice and coverage of the reforms) highlight that life imprisonment will apply to the most serious offences currently punishable by long-term imprisonment. Specific examples repeatedly cited include aggravated/serious murder, femicide, certain forms of genocide, serious forms of human trafficking, sexual abuse and the exploitation of children, terrorist attacks and terrorism-related offences and the aforementioned ecocide.
