Head coach Tim Cone envisions a fast-paced game as the national team parades a rejigged roster for the quadrennial showpiece, a stark contrast to the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers lineup anchored by twin towers Kai Sotto and AJ Edu.

Even June Mar Fajardo, a member of the 2023 championship squad, will not see action in the continental spectacle to be held in Nagoya, Japan, as he retired from national team duty.

Only three players from the Asian Qualifiers team are part of the Asian Games crew, with RJ Abarrientos, Justine Baltazar, and Justin Arana joined by Robert Bolick, Sedrick Barefield, Adrian Nocum, Don Trollano, Zavier Lucero, Brandon Ganuelas-Rosser, Brandon Bates, and Jerrick Ahanmisi in an all-PBA lineup.

“It’s a different system. They’re not playing my system. They’re playing a different system, more of an uptempo, push-the-ball [style], because they’re a little bit smaller. Obviously, they’re smaller because they don’t have Kai and AJ and June Mar playing,” said Cone.

“They’re smaller, so they’re going to use their speed and quickness to get up and down the floor. It will be really interesting to watch.”

Cone and Gilas Pilipinas are ramping up their preparations as they flew to South Korea on Wednesday, September 2, to face its national team in a pair of tuneup games.

Then, from Korea, the Nationals will travel to Japan for the Asian Games, with the men’s basketball tournament running from September 10 to 20, ahead of the official event dates from September 19 to October 4.

Despite the short buildup, Cone likes what he has seen so far from the team, which will go up against China, Bahrain, and Kazakhstan in the group stage.

“The idea of bringing fresher guys, motivated guys, guys who are motivated to come out and play for their country, I think it’s a good idea,” said Cone.

“From what I’ve seen from that team, they’re a lot of fun to watch. I think the fans and the countrymen are going to have a lot of fun watching that team.”

Cone also has his fingers crossed that Justin Brownlee will be healthy enough to join the team, as the coaching staff reserved the 12th roster spot for the naturalized star.

Brownlee, who starred in 2023 as Gilas Pilipinas won its first Asian Games gold medal since 1962, continues to recover from knee and leg injuries that kept him out of the last three games in the Asian Qualifiers.

“We’ve opened up a spot for Justin. We’ll see if he ends up showing up,” said Cone. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tolosa turns up the heat in the courtroom, sparks hot exchanges
World.content:
PROSECUTOR. Atty. Jay Tolosa questions hostile witness, Atty. Michael Poa, during Day 21 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 2, 2026.

The public saw another side of Jay Tolosa in his impeachment court debut. It was a departure from his usual soft-spoken self in media interviews as spokesman of the prosecution.

Lawyer Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr. is known by House reporters as the soft-spoken, mild-mannered legal spokesperson of the prosecution panel.

So it was a rather surprising turn to see the seasoned lawyer raise his voice, confront the witness, and argue with the defense team — and sometimes even with the presiding officer — on the 21st day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial.

Did he come in too hot?

Wednesday’s trial proceeding was not an ordinary day, and even the defense team knew it.

With the prosecution scheduled to call defense lawyer Michael Poa to the stand as a hostile witness, the defense team brought out its lead lawyer Sheila Sison to counter Tolosa’s line of questioning.

Tolosa came in with guns blazing, calling Poa an “abogadong walang alam (lawyer who does not know anything).” Sison took offense at Tolosa’s offer of testimony, and asked him to use a more professional language such as a “witness with no knowledge.” (But… isn’t that just almost the English equivalent of what Tolosa said?)

Escudero sided with Sison and agreed to strike the comments from the records, although it was only the first of many clashes between the two lawyers that day.

Play Video

Later, Tolosa tried to offer stipulations on Poa’s competence to expedite the proceedings, which Sison found unnecessary. Escudero said he found the stipulations irrelevant and asked Tolosa to move on “instead of going through these intramurals.”

Sison also challenged the prosecution’s effort to “read third-party statements” of Poa, and objected to Tolosa’s line of questioning on the basis of non-sequitur.

“This is not an opportunity that should be used by defense to pontificate, argue their position. That’s too much already. Under the rules, if you’re objecting to my question, just state the objection, no need to pontificate your theory of the case,” Tolosa remarked.

“The prosecution has had its fair share of pontificating, I think you are still ahead,” Escudero replied.

Pro-impeachment advocates who are rooting for the prosecution may have been disoriented by Tolosa’s litigation style, which is a stark contrast to how previous prosecutors — lawmakers Jinky Luistro and Joel Chua, as well as private prosecutors Mae Divinagracia, Lorna Kapunan, and Virgil Ligutan — handled past witnesses.

“No two lawyers are alike. Each has its own style. At the end of the day, the question is: did he deliver?” Ligutan said. “It is understandable that Attorney Tolosa’s style (would result) in a heated, tension-filled session.”

“One lawyer can bring tension, what more if two? And take note, the witness is also a lawyer…and a hostile witness,” Ligutan added. “It’s the perfect recipe for tension.”

Play Video

Tolosa had the most dead airs out of all lawyers who have appeared before the court so far (it took him a moment to sort his notes numerous times), and seemed to have the tendency to not move on quickly (he asked Escudero to “reconsider” a ruling he had made, prompting the presiding officer to say there’s no such thing).

But the prosecution’s spokesman also seemed to have found his footing after lunch, and was even able to extract from Poa a confirmation that he prepared DepEd’s defense before the Commission on Audit on the department’s confidential spending despite being unaware that there was a security officer who handled the secret funds.

Tolosa has an impressive portfolio: he lawyered for American soldier Joseph Pemberton, who was convicted of homicide in the killing of Filipino transgender woman Jennifer Laude. His other clients include some of the country’s biggest mining companies, flag carrier Philippine Airlines, and the local affiliate of Fortune 500 company Philip Morris International.

His legal background indicates this is not the first time he participated in — or maybe even caused — a heated courtroom proceeding.

“It’s nothing personal. We’re just doing our jobs,” Tolosa said after Wednesday’s trial. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins First Gold Medals at World Nomad Games in Kyrgyz Republic
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan claimed its first two gold medals at the sixth World Nomad Games in the Kyrgyz Republic, with Nurtalap Kerim and Sailau Mukhamedzhan winning titles in audaryspak, a traditional Kazakh horseback wrestling sport.

In the up to 60-kilogram category, Kerim defeated a Kyrgyz representative in the final to become champion. In the up to 70-kilogram category, Mukhamedzhan also faced a Kyrgyz athlete in the final and won 2-1.

The two victories marked Kazakhstan’s first gold medals at this year’s Games. More than 11,500 people in Kazakhstan regularly practice audaryspak, which combines horseback riding with wrestling and requires strength, agility, speed and courage.

The sixth World Nomad Games officially opened in Bishkek on Aug. 31, bringing together athletes from more than 100 countries. The Games run through Sept. 6, with competitions in Bishkek and the Issyk-Kul region.

The event follows the fifth World Nomad Games, which Kazakhstan hosted in Astana in September 2024. The six-day competition featured 21 sports and athletes from 89 countries, with Kazakhstan sending the largest delegation of 195 athletes. The Kazakh team topped the final medal standings with 112 medals, including 43 gold, 32 silver and 37 bronze.

The World Nomad Games bring together traditional sports and cultural heritage from nomadic civilizations, providing an international platform to preserve and promote these traditions.

World.title: Kazakhstan Positions Itself as Key China-Europe Land Corridor as Ties With Beijing Expand: Key Take-Outs from Tokayev’s Interview with Хinhua
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is positioning itself as a key land corridor between China, Central Asia, the Caucasus and Europe while seeking to deepen cooperation with Beijing in trade, technology and investment, Kazakh political scientist and historian Daniyar Ashimbayev wrote in his Telegram channel, commenting on President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s Sept.1 interview with Xinhua.

Ashimbayev noted that Tokayev’s interview strongly emphasized Xi Jinping’s policy and the development of Kazakhstan-China relations, highlighting trade, Chinese investment, humanitarian cooperation and the importance of ensuring Chinese transit through Kazakhstan.

The analyst also pointed to a broader strategic context. As global competition intensifies and international economic routes evolve, Kazakhstan is seeking to secure its position as a major land bridge between China and European markets.

Middle Corridor strengthens Kazakhstan’s strategic role

Tokayev described Kazakhstan-China relations as being at an “unprecedentedly high level” and reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s readiness to consistently strengthen the two countries’ “eternal comprehensive strategic partnership.”

Trade and investment remain central to the relationship, with China ranking first among Kazakhstan’s external trade partners. At the same time, transport and logistics have become a strategic pillar.

“Together with our Chinese partners, we are transforming this geographical advantage into modern transport and logistics infrastructure of Eurasian scale,” Tokayev said.

Kazakhstan is developing the Middle Corridor, including new railways, dry ports, logistics terminals and border infrastructure. The President stressed the need to make the route more competitive through “smart customs,” digital documentation, synchronized information systems and automated border procedures.

For Kazakhstan, this means turning its geographic position into a long-term economic advantage rather than relying solely on transit potential.

Technology emerges as the next growth area

Ashimbayev highlighted another key point from the interview: Tokayev’s assessment of China as a global leader in artificial intelligence, digital technologies, robotics, new energy and high-tech manufacturing.

This points to a possible new phase in bilateral cooperation as Kazakhstan accelerates its own digital transformation. Tokayev said recent meetings with Chinese technology companies had demonstrated mutual interest in projects covering the digital economy, smart manufacturing, e-commerce, research and workforce training.

“Technological cooperation can become one of the most important areas of the new stage of Kazakh-Chinese cooperation,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s decision to join the 29 founding states of the World Association of International Cooperation on Artificial Intelligence (WAICO) in Shanghai in July also reflects the country’s growing focus on international AI cooperation.

Tokayev stressed that artificial intelligence should serve humanity and that access to technology, knowledge and computing resources should be fair.

Strategic alignment without formal bloc politics

The interview also reaffirmed shared positions on the role of the United Nations, international law, mediation and peaceful settlement of conflicts.

Tokayev reiterated Kazakhstan’s adherence to the One China principle and opposition to violations of territorial integrity. Ashimbayev noted that Beijing values Kazakhstan’s consistency on this issue.

At the same time, he pointed out that Tokayev did not rank Kazakhstan’s strategic partners in the interview, as he sometimes does when speaking in a Western context. In Ashimbayev’s assessment, Beijing does not require such declarations because it already understands the depth of the bilateral relationship.

People-to-people ties add another layer

Economic and strategic cooperation is accompanied by expanding humanitarian ties. Kazakhstan and China are marking the 2026 Cross-Year of Culture, while tens of thousands of Kazakh students study in China and Chinese students study in Kazakhstan.

Chinese university branches, Luban Workshops and academic mobility programs are expanding educational links. The visa-free regime has also boosted tourism: 962,000 Chinese citizens visited Kazakhstan in 2025, up 47% from the previous year.

With diplomatic relations set to reach their 35th anniversary in 2027, the partnership is increasingly extending beyond traditional trade and energy links into transit, technology, education and broader international cooperation.

World.title: Pundit: In Emerging ‘Wolf World,’ Smaller States Need New Flexible Partnerships
World.content:
ASTANA – Smaller states will need flexible, issue-based partnerships to preserve their room for maneuver as the U.S.-led international order gives way to a more fragmented system shaped by power rivalry, German political analyst and writer Marc Saxer said at the launch of his new book in Astana on Aug. 31 titled “Geopolitical Conflict in the Wolf World: Great Power Competition and the Illiberal Revolt against the Liberal Order.”

Saxer coordinates the Asia-Pacific work of the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung (FES) and previously led its offices in India and Thailand. In the book published in June, Saxer examines how countries can navigate what he describes as an increasingly dangerous and asymmetrical multipolar world.

The term “wolf world,” which he derived from the political philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, describes an international system in which institutions are weakening, power increasingly determines outcomes and “the strong prey on the weak,” Saxer said.

“What is the wolf world? The wolf world basically tries to describe the world that is emerging after the collapse of Pax Americana, after the end of the unipolar moment, with the erosion of American hegemony and the erosion and maybe collapse of the world order,” said Saxer.

In 2025, the world saw 65 state-based conflicts across 35 countries, the highest since 1946, according to the Peace Research Institute Oslo.

“We have to understand what the new chessboard really is. How can we navigate as foreign policy makers?” he added, describing this as an “existential question.”

However, Saxer noted the book seeks to move beyond just diagnosing the breakdown of the existing order. Its central questions are about how countries can navigate the emerging system, preserve prosperity and prevent geopolitical competition from producing sustained global instability.

Three theaters of competition

Saxer identified Europe, the Middle East and East Asia as the three principal theaters of contemporary geopolitical competition. In each, U.S. influence is being challenged by a regional power: Russia in Europe, Iran in the Middle East and China in East Asia.

“Even though these theaters are intimately interconnected, there are also trade-offs. There is a zero-sum game. If you are invested in one of them as a great power, you will find it challenging to actually prevail in another,” said Saxer.

He stressed that the U.S. is facing growing military, fiscal and domestic political constraints, prompting a debate in Washington over whether it should concentrate its resources closer to home or continue expanding.

China, meanwhile, views U.S. alliances and military deployments in Asia as a form of strategic encirclement, he said. Beijing’s efforts to expand westward through the Belt and Road Initiative and strengthen its position in the South China Sea can therefore be understood partly as an attempt to protect supply chains and reduce its exposure to maritime chokepoints particularly along the Strait of Malacca, which Saxer describes as the “Strait of Hormuz of Asia.”

“That’s not a theory. That’s a blueprint for action. You saw the intervention in Venezuela. You see the threats to take back the Canal of Panama. You see the threats against Cuba. You see the debate with the Europeans over Greenland,” Saxer said.

This dynamic creates a security dilemma: measures one side considers defensive are interpreted by the other as evidence of aggressive intent.

While Taiwan remains the most dangerous potential flashpoint, Saxer said the costs of a direct U.S.-China conflict could deter both sides from seeking a military confrontation. Their rivalry is therefore likely to be fought primarily through trade, technology, finance and industrial policy.

“Here you basically include the geoeconomic disruption and competition that is so definitive for the dynamics in Asia. Lots of these dynamics we see, of course, already as front line news,” he added.

Economic disruption

The shift from economic integration to strategic competition is already transforming the global economy, Saxer said. Supply chains are being reorganized as governments seek to reduce dependencies that could be exploited by geopolitical rivals.

The principle of globalization has shifted from efficiency and “just in time” production to resilience and “just in case,” he said. Reshoring, nearshoring and friendshoring are accelerating, while access to technology, markets, payment systems and critical resources is increasingly treated as a matter of national security.

These changes pose a particular challenge for developing economies. Saxer stressed that the development model used by several successful Asian economies combining low-cost labor, export-led growth and technological catch-up is becoming less viable.

“Cheap labor is no longer your comparative advantage if you compete against AI robots and algorithms. Export-led growth is not possible if in a protectionist world, your export markets are freezing up,” he said.

Industrialization is also constrained when technology transfers and access to supply chains become geopolitical tools, he added.

For Central Asia, these shifts could create opportunities as companies and governments search for new trade routes, production sites and supply partners. They also increase the risk that countries will face pressure to align with one economic or technological bloc.

Finding room between powers

In terms of navigating foreign policy in such a world, Saxer suggested a few strategies. Major powers can use economic, technological and military leverage to build asymmetric dependencies and pressure other states to choose sides.

“You can build asymmetrical dependencies, especially through geotech and geoeconomics, and try to coerce others to extract advantages. At the end of the day, it is all about forcing others to choose sides,” said Saxer.

Smaller countries, by contrast, are more likely to rely on hedging and balancing, a strategy familiar across Central and Southeast Asia.

“The question here is what is the room of maneuver? How much space do you actually have to hedge and balance when you end up in the sharp end of great powers coercing power?” he posed.

Saxer sees more value in “partnerships in the middle,” which refers to flexible arrangements in which states cooperate on specific issues without forming a rigid geopolitical bloc. Such partnerships could include smaller countries as well as established middle powers, allowing them to pool resources, diversify their relationships and exercise greater influence over the rules of the emerging system.

“Issue-based, flexible partnerships in the middle could be one of the ways to navigate the wolf world,” Saxer said.

“How to stabilize this wolf world very much depends on what kind of world is actually emerging. What we have seen is the end of the unicorner moment, and therefore the end of an order will be at rest upon its dominance,” he added.

Emerging order

“I think what we are seeing emerging is an asymmetrical multipolar world,” Saxer said.

The U.S. and China remain in a “league of their own,” but neither has the dominance Washington and Moscow exercised during the Cold War. Regional powers, including in the Global South, are gaining influence, while Russia, India and the European Union retain the potential to become independent global poles but also face significant internal constraints.

“The takeaway from this is that I believe in an asymmetrical multipolar world it is unlikely that a single power will emerge as a victor,” he said.

“I believe that for the first time in 600 years, we are in a situation where the next world order either doesn’t emerge or has to be negotiated between western and non-western powers,” he added.

Reforming global order

Addressing the gathering, Saxer outlined three possible forms the next order could take: an imperial system based on great-power spheres of influence; a Westphalian system centered on sovereignty and noninterference or a reformed multilateral order.

He also noted he believed more in preserving and adapting the rules-based system, emphasizing that global challenges such as climate change, pandemics, migration and conflict cannot be addressed without international cooperation.

“Smaller countries obviously prefer the reemergence or strengthening of a Westphalian order, where sovereignty, non-interference and territorial integrity rule,” Saxer said.

“I believe that the best course of action would be to save whatever can be saved from the rule-based multilateral order by reforming it,” he added.

The existing system, however, cannot simply remain in its form that was established in 1945, he said. Many countries in the Global South question who created its rules, whose interests they serve and why non-Western states were given so little influence over their design.

“Rules, yes, but whose rules? Who made these rules? We were not on the table,” he added.

Western countries will have to relinquish some of their influence in international institutions if they want those institutions to retain legitimacy, the expert said. They must also confront criticism over the inconsistent application of international law, what Saxer referred to as “double standards,” and universal principles.

Saxer proposed a “Helsinki 2.0” compromise modeled on the 1975 Helsinki Final Act: continued recognition of universal human rights combined with a stronger commitment to sovereignty and noninterference.

“Universality without intervention, universalism without interference,” he said, describing the approach as a possible foundation for a more inclusive international order.

Central Asia navigates this world much longer

Philipp Jahn, head of the FES Office Central Asia, said the region may need less convincing than most audiences about the book’s central premise because it has long navigated a world in which no single power can dictate the rules.

“When Marc [Saxer] set out to describe what he called the wolf world, a system in which single superpowers’ rules have quietly stopped applying, and no one has yet agreed on what could replace them, he was effectively describing something Central Asia has lived and managed for three decades or, more likely, for much longer,” said Jahn.

“The region did not discover multivector diplomacy (…) last week, because of some new geopolitical fashion. It built that doctrine out of necessity, long before multipolarity became the term Western capitals reached for to describe a world that makes them uncomfortable,” he explained.

He said Saxer’s framework should be treated as “a set of hypotheses, not a finished verdict,” with Central Asia offering an important test of where those arguments hold and where the region’s experience suggests otherwise.

Ullrich Kinne, deputy head of mission and economic counsellor at the German Embassy in Kazakhstan, said Kazakhstan was a fitting venue for the launch because of its position among the major powers and regions examined in the book.

“It seems to me very fitting that it is presented here in Kazakhstan, as we are at the crossroads of the various forces described herein: China, Russia, the U.S., and Europe. But Central Asia is increasingly becoming a global player in its own right. Deepening regional integration has allowed Kazakhstan to pursue multivector foreign policy,” said Kinne.

Kinne noted Europe and Central Asia were both seeking to diversify their political and economic relationships, reduce strategic dependencies and strengthen ties with each other. This approach could help mitigate some of the pressures described by Saxer.

World.title: Two Amur Tiger Cubs Planned for Release in Kazakhstan in May 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Two young Amur tigers brought from Russia as part of Kazakhstan’s tiger reintroduction program are planned to be released into the wild in May 2027, marking the next stage of efforts to restore the species in the Ili-Balkhash ecosystem.

“Two tiger cubs are planned to be released in spring 2027, in May. They will be released differently, through a temporary enclosure. In this way, we will be able to try all possible release methods in Kazakhstan. The decision will be made in 2027,” Director General of the Amur Tiger Center Sergey Aramilev told TASS at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Sept. 1.

Four Amur tigers were brought from Russia for the program: two adults, a male and female aged three to four years, and two cubs that were six to seven months old at the time of transfer.

The first adult female, Umit, was released into the wild in August. Specialists are monitoring her adaptation to the new territory, and the results will help determine when the male can join her.

Restoring the tiger to Kazakhstan

The program aims to establish a self-sustaining tiger population in the Ili River delta and southern Lake Balkhash region, the historical habitat of the extinct Turan, or Caspian, tiger.

Kazakhstan began preparations for tiger restoration in 2010. The reintroduction program was subsequently developed in cooperation with the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), while the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve was established in 2018 as a key part of the project.

Amur tigers were selected because of their close genetic relationship to the extinct Turan tiger, making them suitable for the reintroduction program.

Preparing the ecosystem

The project involves not only bringing tigers to Kazakhstan but also restoring the habitat and prey base needed to support them. Kazakhstan has reintroduced kulans and Bukhara deer and is monitoring other potential prey species.

The four tigers from Russia were joined by two animals transferred from the Netherlands in 2024. Specialists use satellite collars, camera traps and field observations to track the animals and assess their adaptation.

Umit’s release marked the first return of a tiger to the wild in Kazakhstan in more than 70 years. The planned release of the two cubs through a temporary enclosure will allow specialists to test another approach as the reintroduction program develops.

The ultimate goal is to establish a stable wild tiger population in the Ili-Balkhash region through successful adaptation and reproduction.

World.title: From Commodities to Production Chains: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan Deepen Economic Ties
World.content:
ALMATY – Trade between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan reached $2.8 billion in the first half of 2026, making Kazakhstan Uzbekistan’s third-largest trading partner and highlighting a relationship that is moving beyond traditional commodity exchanges toward manufacturing, agricultural trade and integrated production chains.

According to Uzbekistan’s National Statistics Committee, Kazakhstan accounted for the third-largest share of Uzbekistan’s foreign trade in January-June, behind China with $9.5 billion and Russia with $7 billion. Türkiye ranked fourth with $1.4 billion.

The latest figures come as businesses and governments on both sides seek to turn rapidly expanding trade into longer-term investment and production cooperation. In 2025, bilateral trade reached $4.8 billion, up 16.2% year on year. The first months of 2026 suggest that momentum has continued.

According to data presented by the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs on Aug. 6, trade between the two countries reached $2.3 billion in January-May, 37.2% higher than in the same period of 2025. Kazakhstan’s exports increased particularly rapidly, while imports from Uzbekistan also continued to grow, reported the Chamber of International Commerce of Kazakhstan.

The figures point to a relationship that is becoming important for both countries as they seek to strengthen regional value chains and reduce dependence on distant markets.

From trade growth to deeper economic integration

The headline increase in trade is significant, but its composition may be more important than the total value itself. Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with Uzbekistan grew by 34.7% year on year to $2.8 billion in January-June. Uzbekistan has moved from eighth to sixth place among Kazakhstan’s trading partners over the past year, while its share of Kazakhstan’s total trade increased from 3.1% to 3.9%.

The strongest growth has come from Kazakhstan’s exports, which rose 39.5% to nearly $2.1 billion. Wheat accounted for almost 27% of Kazakhstan’s exports to Uzbekistan, reaching $571.6 million. Wheat exports nearly doubled over the year. Other significant increases were recorded in sunflower oil, beef, lamb and metal products.

The trend is notable because Kazakhstan has traditionally been associated with commodity exports. Yet the structure of its exports to Uzbekistan has been changing.

In 2017, raw materials and products classified as “near-raw materials” accounted for 65.3% of Kazakhstan’s exports to Uzbekistan. By 2025, their share had fallen to 35.5%, while semi-finished products increased from 29% to 40.2% and finished goods, excluding re-exports, rose from 3.4% to 20.5%. The first half of 2026, however, shows that this transition is not yet linear. Raw materials accounted for 39.9% of exports, semi-finished products for 38.2% and finished goods for 17.9%.

This longer-term shift reflects a broader challenge for Kazakhstan: increasing the value generated from its existing resource base rather than relying primarily on higher volumes of commodity exports.

“Metal products, for example, can be different. You can simply export ore or some initial products of processing, or you can already export rolled metal and metal products. They may fall under approximately the same export category, but each time this actually implies an increasingly higher level of processing of the same raw material,” said Farkhad Kassenov, head of the A+ Analytics research center, political scientist and international relations expert.

He said diversification has become increasingly important because Kazakhstan cannot rely indefinitely on expanding raw-material exports.

“Diversification is extremely important, and recent efforts have been aimed exclusively at this, because it is impossible to increase GDP only through a mechanical increase in raw material exports,” he said.

The data on trade with Uzbekistan show both progress and limitations. The share of finished goods in Kazakhstan’s exports to the Uzbek market has increased significantly since 2017, but the first half of 2026 also saw the share of raw materials rise again. In other words, the transition toward higher-value exports is visible over the longer term, but it is not yet firmly established.

Uzbekistan becomes part of Kazakhstan’s production chains

Around $162 million, or 24% of Kazakhstan’s imports from Uzbekistan, consisted of vehicles, parts and components. Among the largest individual categories were passenger-car bodies, worth $81.6 million, and engines, worth $51.8 million.

Kazakhstan’s broader push toward higher-value production could make such cross-border industrial links increasingly important. Kassen highlights that the country’s next stage of economic development should involve bringing foreign partners into domestic technological and production chains rather than relying on a simple exchange of raw materials for investment.

This is particularly relevant to Kazakhstan’s automotive industry, where Uzbek-made components could become inputs into domestic production.

Investment cooperation is already beginning to develop alongside trade. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are currently implementing 80 joint projects worth approximately $1.8 billion. At a recent Uzbekistan-Kazakhstan Business Council meeting in Tashkent, representatives of the two countries discussed moving from trade growth toward joint production, localization and the development of shared value chains.

The next challenge: turning trade into production

At the seventh meeting of the Uzbekistan-Kazakhstan Business Council, participants also proposed creating a unified list of joint projects with designated responsible parties and implementation timelines. The objective is to track whether agreements actually progress into investment and production.

They also identified customs procedures, technical regulation, phytosanitary controls, access to raw materials, logistics, cross-border payments and mutual recognition of permits as barriers that businesses continue to face. The proposed response is a more permanent mechanism for collecting business requests and bringing the most significant problems to the level of the intergovernmental commission.

The $2.8 billion trade figure therefore represents more than another annual increase in bilateral commerce. It points to an economic relationship that is becoming broader and more interconnected. For Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, the opportunity is to move from trading across a border to producing across it.

World.title: Manufacturing Overtakes Mining in Kazakhstan: Experts Assess Whether Shift Signals Structural Change
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s manufacturing sector has overtaken mining in its share of industrial output for the first time, marking a potentially important shift in the country’s economic structure. But economists say the headline figure should be viewed alongside a second trend: rising demand for imported machinery, equipment and technology as Kazakhstan enters a major investment cycle.

Manufacturing accounted for 46.7% of industrial production in January-July 2026, compared with 45.8% for mining, according to the Prime Minister’s press service. Manufacturing output reached 18.8 trillion tenge (US$40.7 billion), increasing 9% compared with the same period last year.

The shift comes as the government seeks to reduce the economy’s dependence on the export of raw materials by encouraging deeper processing, domestic production and higher-value industries. The policy is supported by investment incentives, special economic zones, preferential access to domestic raw materials, offtake agreements and measures designed to increase the participation of Kazakh manufacturers in regulated procurement.

From raw materials to higher-value production

The government’s figures show strong growth across several manufacturing industries. Machine building increased 22% in the first seven months of the year, reaching 3.2 trillion tenge (US$6.92 billion). Metallurgy generated 8.1 trillion tenge (US$17.52 billion), while chemical production increased 26.9% to 1 trillion tenge (US$2.16 billion).

Automotive manufacturing illustrates the direction of the policy particularly clearly. More than 96,000 vehicles were produced during the period, while the share of small-scale assembly reached 28.3%. New production facilities are also creating demand for locally produced tyres, batteries, seats and multimedia systems.

State support creates demand, but competitiveness remains the test

One of the government’s main instruments is an offtake contract, which gives manufacturers a guaranteed buyer for products that are yet to be produced. In the first half of 2026, long-term agreements and offtake contracts involving subsoil users and the quasi-public sector amounted to 466 billion tenge (US$1.01 billion). Samruk Kazyna’s purchases from domestic manufacturers more than doubled and exceeded 2.1 trillion tenge (US$4.54 billion).

Special economic zones provide another layer of support. According to government figures, 577 projects in 18 zones have attracted 11.1 trillion tenge (US$24 billion) in investment and created more than 39,000 jobs. Residents have generated 865.4 billion tenge (US$1.87 billion) in tax revenues, compared with 507.4 billion tenge (US$1.1 billion) in state spending on infrastructure.

However, leading Kazakh financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov cautioned that the latest figures should not yet be interpreted as evidence of a completed structural transformation.

“First of all, just as an introduction, I would say that we do not yet have a structural shift, but it is beginning. We will probably only be able to speak about a genuine structural shift in several years, after we have sustainably and consistently earned not from oil and not from the extractive sector, but from processing and manufacturing,” he said.

Rysmambetov also highlighted that industrial policy should reach beyond the country’s largest companies and create opportunities for medium-sized businesses.

“Large business is good, but in my view it is better to support 10 medium-sized companies than one large one, because this is classic portfolio management: supporting 10 companies at a medium level is more important than supporting one large company,” he said.

“Can such a model create competitive production in the long term? Well, I think yes, if we manage this portfolio of companies correctly,” Rysmambetov added.

Regional economies are moving at different speeds

The transformation is also uneven across Kazakhstan. Manufacturing growth was particularly strong in the Aktobe Region, where output increased 10.7%, and the Karagandy Region, where it rose 10.6%. These are traditionally industrial regions, meaning that part of the current expansion is taking place on an existing industrial base rather than being built entirely from scratch.

Influential Kazakh economist Ruslan Sultanov points to a contrast between regions whose growth remains strongly tied to commodity exports and those beginning to develop a broader industrial and investment base.

In the Abai Region, for example, exports remain heavily concentrated in raw materials. Copper ore exports to China increased from $24 million to $2 billion over the year, while copper cathodes and molybdenum ore also remain among the region’s main export products, he wrote on his Telegram channel.

At the same time, the Aktobe Region is combining its traditional industrial base with new investment, including imports of Chinese equipment for wind-energy projects.

“One region increases its revenues through commodity exports, while another is simultaneously restructuring its industrial and investment agenda,” he wrote.

This divergence illustrates an important point about Kazakhstan’s industrial transition: the country is not moving away from commodities at the same pace everywhere. Some regions are using their resource base as the foundation for deeper processing, while others remain dependent on the export of relatively unprocessed materials.

The import paradox of industrial growth

There is another side to Kazakhstan’s investment-driven industrial expansion.

According to the government’s approved economic forecast, imports are expected to reach $90.7 billion in 2028, up from an earlier forecast of $87.7 billion. By 2029, imports are projected at $88.4 billion, while exports are expected to reach $88.5 billion, leaving only a marginal trade surplus. The figures are significant because imports are rising at the same time that Kazakhstan is investing heavily in domestic production.

That is not necessarily a negative development. New factories require machinery, industrial equipment, electrical systems, transport equipment, technologies and other goods that Kazakhstan does not yet produce in sufficient quantities.

But it creates an important policy challenge: investment should eventually expand domestic productive capacity rather than permanently increase dependence on imported inputs.

The 46.7% manufacturing share may ultimately prove to be less important than what happens behind the number. Over the next five to 10 years, several indicators will show whether Kazakhstan’s industrial policy has produced a structural transformation: the share of manufactured goods in exports, the depth of local processing, domestic value added, productivity growth, private investment, the development of local suppliers and the ability of new industries to compete without permanent state support.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Population Reaches 20.6 Million As Astana Records Fastest Growth
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s population increased by 14,230 people in July, reaching 20.6 million as of Aug. 1, according to data from the Bureau of National Statistics.

The country’s population stood at 20,590,000 as of July 1. By Aug. 1, it had increased to 20,604,800. Since the beginning of the year, Kazakhstan’s population has grown by 104,997 people, compared with 90,767 people as of July 1. The population growth rate increased from 0.44% to 0.51%.

Meanwhile, the migration balance remained almost unchanged. The positive migration balance stood at 5,703 people as of July 1 and 5,578 people as of Aug. 1.

Urban population continues to grow

The number of people living in urban areas increased from 13.19 million on July 1 to 13.21 million on Aug. 1. Urban areas gained 21,174 residents during the month. In the first half of the year, urban population grew by 105,475 people.

Migration accounted for a significant share of urban population growth. The positive migration balance in cities reached 65,914 people in January-July, compared with 53,539 people as of July 1. Natural population growth in urban areas also increased to 60,735 people, up from 51,936 as of July 1.

The rural population declined during July. The rural population decreased from 7.4 million people on July 1 to 7.393 million on Aug. 1, a decline of nearly 6,900 people. At the same time, natural population growth in rural areas remained positive, reaching 38,684 people since the beginning of the year, compared with 33,128 people as of July 1.

Migration outflows drove the decline. The negative migration balance increased from 47,836 people in the first half of the year to 60,336 people as of Aug. 1.

Astana leads among major cities

Astana recorded the largest population increase among Kazakhstan’s cities of national significance. The capital’s population grew from 1.683 million people on July 1 to nearly 1.69 million on Aug. 1, an increase of nearly 7,900 people. Since the beginning of the year, Astana’s population has increased by 51,429 people, or 3.14%.

Almaty’s population rose from 2.374 million to 2.38 million during July, adding nearly 5,900 residents. In Shymkent, the number of residents increased by approximately 2,700, from 1.31 million to 1.313 million.

World.title: Kazakhstan Remembers Akzhan Mashanov, Scientist Who Helped Bring Al-Farabi’s Legacy Home
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is marking the legacy of Akzhan Mashanov (1906–1997) on the 120th anniversary of his birth on Sept. 2, one of the country’s prominent scientists and an important figure in the development of Kazakh scientific thought.

A geologist, engineer, educator, translator and researcher, Mashanov made significant contributions to the development of geomechanics and technical education in Kazakhstan. His name is perhaps most closely associated with a decades-long effort to research the life and legacy of Abu Nasr Al-Farabi and establish his connection with the ancient city of Farab, now Otrar in South Kazakhstan.

His work ultimately helped bring international attention to Al-Farabi’s roots and contributed to the organization of an international conference in Almaty marking the 1,100th anniversary of the medieval scholar.

From geology to the history of science

Born in 1906 in the Karkaraly district of the Karagandy Region, Mashanov came from a family with deep roots in Kazakh history. His grandfather was the prominent bi Mashan, whose reputation was reflected in Kazakh oral tradition and who is considered one of the prototypes for the character Masanbi in Ilyas Yessenberlin’s historical novel “The Nomads.”

Mashanov received his early education at the Karkaraly technical school before entering the mining institute in Almaty, which later became the Kazakh Polytechnic Institute.

He began his scientific career at a time when technical literature in the Kazakh language was scarce. While still a student, he translated geological works into Kazakh. Translation remained an important part of his work throughout his life. He later translated works by such figures as Al-Farabi, Mikhail Lomonosov and Vladimir Obruchev and contributed to the development of technical terminology in Kazakh.

His textbook “Crystallography, Mineralogy and Petrography” became an important contribution to scientific education in the Kazakh language. At the same time, Mashani was developing his own scientific approach to geology and mining.

In 1940, while pursuing postgraduate studies, he used his methodology to identify the Akbastau-Kosmury­n and Zhartas deposits. His approaches were subsequently applied by other researchers, including in studies of the Zhezkazgan deposit.

His subsequent works helped establish geomechanics as an important field of scientific research in Kazakhstan. His work attracted attention abroad, with several of his studies translated into German.

The question that changed his life

Mashanov’s scientific career took an unexpected turn in the 1940s. In 1943, while in Almaty, he learned from Czech scientist Ernest Kolman about Al-Farabi, a medieval philosopher and polymath whose name had long been known throughout the Islamic world. The connection between Al-Farabi and Farab immediately caught Mashanov’s attention.

As a geologist familiar with the historical geography of Central Asia, he began examining the evidence linking the ancient city of Farab with Otrar and searching for information about the scholar who took his name from the city.

His research gradually expanded into an international investigation. Mashanov sent inquiries to major libraries and research institutions in Berlin, Lisbon, Paris, Cairo, Madrid and other cities. In Ufa, he discovered three works by Al-Farabi in the library of the Galiya Madrasah. Other materials were obtained from Istanbul, Canada and European research centres.

Some of Al-Farabi’s works that had long been considered lost were eventually traced to libraries in different countries. Mashanov also recognized that studying Al-Farabi required access to his original texts. He therefore began learning Arabic and Persian himself. By the age of more than 50, he had acquired the languages necessary to study the philosopher’s works in their original form.

His research increasingly became a personal intellectual mission: to demonstrate that Kazakhstan’s scientific and cultural history was connected to a much older intellectual tradition that flourished across Central Asia.

A difficult search in the Soviet era

Mashanov pursued his research into Islamic intellectual history during the Soviet era, when religion and religious scholarship were officially discouraged. Biographical accounts indicate that he nevertheless began practicing Islam, performing daily prayers and studying Arabic and the Islamic intellectual tradition.

His religious convictions became closely intertwined with his scholarly work. He sought to understand Al-Farabi not simply as a philosopher of the medieval world, but as a representative of a sophisticated scientific civilization that had developed across Central Asia.

His research took him beyond libraries and archives. In 1968, Mashanov travelled to Damascus, Syria, where he located Al-Farabi’s grave at the Bab Al-Saghir cemetery. The journey symbolized the personal nature of his decades-long research.

Defending Al-Farabi’s connection to Kazakhstan

Mashanov’s research also became part of a wider scholarly discussion in Central Asia about the heritage of medieval scientists whose lives predated modern national borders. Once, during a visit to Tashkent, he met Muzafar Khayrullayev, deputy director of the Institute of Oriental Studies named after Abu Rayhan Al-Biruni. Mashanov introduced him to his findings on Al-Farabi.

The two scholars discussed whether Al-Farabi could be regarded as a shared heritage of the peoples of Central Asia. Mashanov agreed that the medieval scholar’s legacy belonged to the broader region, but argued that if Al-Farabi was to be considered a shared figure, the same principle should apply to other major scholars such as Al-Biruni, Ibn Sina and Al-Khwarizmi.

The debate reflected a larger historical reality: the intellectual networks of medieval Central Asia existed long before the modern borders of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and other states. For Mashanov, however, historical evidence remained central. He continued searching for sources that could establish Farab and Otrar’s place in Al-Farabi’s biography. His efforts eventually reached the international scientific community.

The 1,100th anniversary of Al-Farabi

In 1971, discussions at a UNESCO congress in Moscow considered plans to commemorate the 1100th anniversary of Al-Farabi. There were competing proposals over where the international conference should be held. Mashanov advocated for Almaty and presented his arguments. The conference was ultimately held in Almaty in 1975 with UNESCO support, bringing international scholars together to examine the legacy of Al-Farabi.

For Mashanov, it was the culmination of decades of research. His work had helped ensure that Kazakhstan became a major venue for international discussion of Al-Farabi’s intellectual heritage. Arab scholars began referring to him as “Al-Mashani” in recognition of his research into Al-Farabi. He later adopted the name and used it in his own scientific works.

A scholar who refused to stay within one discipline

Al-Mashani’s intellectual interests extended far beyond geology and the history of Al-Farabi. He studied the history of science in the Islamic world, Turkic cultural heritage, astronomy, philosophy and the relationship between scientific knowledge and religion.

He also explored the intellectual links between Al-Farabi and the Kazakh poet and philosopher Abai, arguing that the intellectual foundations of Abai’s worldview could be traced through the broader philosophical tradition of the East.

His approach was unusually interdisciplinary for his time. He combined geology, archaeology, astronomy, history, folklore, philosophy and religious scholarship in his attempts to understand the development of knowledge in Central Asia.

He authored more than 350 scientific works, which his students later compiled into 16 volumes. Alongside Kanysh Satpayev, Mashani helped lay the foundations of the Academy of Sciences of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic and became its first corresponding member.

Despite his contribution to the country’s scientific institutions, he never became an academician. His independence was reflected in his approach to both science and personal convictions.

Why his legacy remains relevant

Al-Mashani’s contribution is difficult to define through a single discipline. He was a geologist who helped establish geomechanics in Kazakhstan, an educator who expanded technical literature in the Kazakh language, a translator, a researcher of Islamic science and a historian of Central Asian intellectual traditions. He was also among the pioneers of Kazakh science fiction.

But his most distinctive contribution may have been the bridge he built between Kazakhstan’s modern scientific institutions and the region’s medieval intellectual heritage. Al-Mashani believed that the history of science should be studied as an interconnected process rather than divided into isolated national traditions.

His own life reflected that philosophy. He moved between geology and philosophy, mathematics and astronomy, Arabic manuscripts and Kazakh folklore, modern scientific methods and the history of Islamic scholarship.

“The measure of humanity is comprehensive education, therefore it is necessary to know and study the history of all sciences,” Al-Mashani wrote.

Recognition and remembrance

Al-Mashani’s contribution was recognized both in Kazakhstan and internationally. UNESCO marked his centenary, and in 2006, Kazpost issued a commemorative stamp dedicated to the scientist. His name has been given to a street in Almaty and an educational institution at the Satpayev Kazakh National Technical University.

At a ceremony unveiling a bust of Al-Mashani in 2020, former state secretary of Kazakhstan Krymbek Kusherbayev highlighted his role in promoting Al-Farabi’s heritage.

“Thanks to him, the return of Al-Farabi to Kazakh soil took place,” Kusherbayev said.

Mashani died in 1997, but the questions he devoted his life to continue to shape discussions about Kazakhstan’s scientific and cultural heritage.

World.title: Georgian businessman, animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili begins prison hunger strike
World.content:
Activist Elizbarashvili on hunger strike

Georgian businessman, animal rights activist and outspoken critic of the Georgian Dream government Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who was detained earlier, has gone on hunger strike.

Tamaz Elizbarashvili was detained at his home after law enforcement officers searched his car and flat. The Interior Ministry said the search of Elizbarashvili’s car was carried out as part of an investigation into alleged threats and the illegal acquisition and possession of weapons.

According to his lawyer, Elizbarashvili is currently being held in administrative detention.

What is known so far?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Iako Siranashvili, her client was detained by law enforcement officers as he was attempting to jump from a balcony and take his own life.

Siranashvili said Elizbarashvili attempted to take his own life after seeing law enforcement officers use force against his lawyer and witnessing his children in distress.

“Tamaz Elizbarashvili was going to take his own life when he saw me being pushed into the building and beaten. When he saw his children crying and in distress, he tried to jump from the balcony. Tamaz was detained over this and charged with disobeying police orders,” Siranashvili said.

According to the lawyer, law enforcement officers tried to take her phone away when she began filming the search. She alleges that around 20 officers then used physical force against her.

“They tried to take my phone away to stop me filming the search. Anyone is allowed to film, especially a lawyer. They probably wanted to plant a weapon or some other prohibited item, but I prevented them from doing so because I was filming. Around 20 people then attacked me: they grabbed me and snatched the phone from my hands. When I resisted their attempts to take it, they twisted my arms, threw me to the ground and began kicking me,” Siranashvili said.

The lawyer said she had sustained injuries to various parts of her body and was having difficulty walking. Siranashvili said she had left the clinic of her own accord.

“My injuries are such that I can barely walk. I have difficulty moving around. My left arm is in severe pain. My hearing has also deteriorated and I have swelling around my facial bone. I left the clinic of my own accord because I did not think it was necessary to remain there,” she said.

According to Siranashvili, an investigation has been launched under Article 333 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers abuse of official powers. She said, however, that investigators should also examine whether offences had been committed under Articles 364 and 365, which concern obstruction of a lawyer’s professional activities.

“What angers me most is not the fact that I was beaten, but that I was prevented from carrying out my professional duties. That is what makes me most angry, as does the fact that violence was used against a lawyer. Other articles must also be applied; the investigation cannot be limited to Article 333 alone,” the lawyer said.

She said her health had so far prevented her from attending the investigative authorities for a medical examination.

“I feel very unwell and have not yet been physically able to get to the relevant authorities. Investigators have ordered a medical examination, and I hope it will be carried out,” Siranashvili said.

World.title: Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee arrested after appearing in court on stretcher
World.content:
Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

In Armenia, the arrest of former State Revenue Committee chairman Gagik Khachatryan has sparked widespread debate. He faces charges of accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. The Anti-Corruption Court is also considering cases seeking to confiscate allegedly illicitly acquired property from Khachatryan and people linked to him, including his sons.

However, the video that his lawyers shared on social media, rather than the charges against Khachatryan, has caused the biggest public outcry. The footage shows National Security Service officers carrying the 71-year-old Khachatryan, who is groaning in pain, from a bed onto a stretcher during his arrest. His lawyers said they consider the law enforcement officers’ actions equivalent to torture.

Human rights defenders and civil society representatives have also condemned the actions. They said authorities handled the transport of a person with serious health problems “improperly”, causing him physical suffering.

“No legal procedure or procedural necessity can justify violating human dignity,” experts from the NGO Disability Rights Agenda said.

What is Khachatryan accused of: all known details

The Investigative Committee said the previous day that investigators had carried out searches at the homes of the former head of the State Revenue Committee and his son as part of a case involving particularly large-scale bribery and money laundering. They also searched the offices and branches of more than 20 companies linked to them. Shortly afterwards, reports emerged that authorities had arrested Gagik Khachatryan for two months.

According to the case file, Khachatryan faces charges of:

accepting a particularly large bribe from the directors of Progress Armenia and Local Developers,

misappropriating 174 million 581 thousand drams ($482,000) in state funds during the reconstruction of the Dilijan training centre,

illegally transferring property belonging to a local university, worth 208 million 908 thousand drams ($577,000),

and laundering particularly large sums of money. The charge concerns concealing 151 million 126 thousand drams ($417,000) of illegally obtained funds.

Meanwhile, the Anti-Corruption Court is hearing a case seeking the confiscation of allegedly illicitly acquired property. The Prosecutor General’s Office is seeking to confiscate from Khachatryan and people linked to him:

193 properties, including properties in Yerevan’s most expensive central district,

89 properties in Kotayk Province,

stakes in 29 legal entities,

14 movable assets,

bonds worth $1,451,074,

a bank deposit of $147,210,

claims arising from loans worth approximately $23.1 million, 409.8 million drams (more than $1 million) and €9,800, and

7 billion 761 million drams ($49 million).

Defence lawyers and prosecutors disagree over the defendant’s health

The Prosecutor General’s Office says it conducted a forensic medical examination.

“Khachatryan has no health problems that could prevent him from taking part in any procedural actions as part of the criminal proceedings,” the experts concluded.

However, his defence team takes the opposite view.

Lawyer Yerevan Sargsyan told reporters that in June, authorities also took Khachatryan to the investigative body and then to court on a stretcher. At the time, however, the court found that his detention could pose health risks.

“They waited so long until they got the [forensic medical] conclusion they wanted. How they did it is known to them. And now they have organised the arrest in the same way again,” Sargsyan stressed.

Ombudsman’s office examines the case

On 2 September, a day after the lawyers published the video, the Human Rights Defender’s Office issued a statement. It said that the ombudsman had initiated an urgent examination of the case. A team of experts has already gone to the penitentiary to speak with Khachatryan and monitor respect for his rights.

The ombudsman’s office has also asked the relevant authorities for explanations to establish all the circumstances. After it completes the investigation and reviews its findings, the Human Rights Defender will present its position.

Comments

Human rights defender Zaruhi Hovhannisyan believes that the published photograph of the defendant on a stretcher in the courtroom is “not simply a sad scene”. In her view, the situation raises questions about the state’s attitude towards human rights:

“The photograph shows a 71-year-old man with serious health problems lying on a stretcher, completely covered, in the middle of a courtroom. People involved in the proceedings, tables, microphones and documents surround him. On one side stands the entire institutional machinery of criminal justice, organised by the state. On the other stands a person whom the system completely ignores.

The issue is not to make people feel sorry for the man lying on that stretcher, or to discuss why he ended up in court, what case he faces or how many charges he faces. The issue is that this is an extremely dangerous picture. When the state becomes accustomed to subordinating human dignity to a judicial process, it puts not only one person’s rights at risk but also the boundary that should prevent the state from gaining unlimited power over an individual. Human dignity and the prohibition of torture limit the state’s power over a person.”

Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee in court on a stretcher

The NGO Disability Rights Agenda also issued a statement about the videos that Gagik Khachatryan’s lawyers circulated:

“According to the defence, doctors diagnosed Gagik Khachatryan with spinal stenosis in 2015 and implanted special devices in his cervical spine. The footage also shows him in a semi-conscious state while people were moving him.”

The organisation’s experts believe the authorities should structure the court proceedings in a way that prevents harm to a person’s health or humiliating conditions. Appropriate specialists should accompany people with limited mobility at all times. Medical professionals should supervise their movement and authorities should provide the necessary technical equipment.

“Regardless of the nature of the charges or his former position, humanitarian principles and safeguards for physical integrity must remain unchanged,” the statement says.

The organisation called on law enforcement agencies to take the following steps during further procedural actions:

rely only on impartial professional assessments,

provide the necessary medical care,

prevent any actions that cause a person unnecessary physical pain.

Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

World.title: Amnesty International: Georgia must not deport Denis Kulanin to Russia
World.content:
Denis Kulanin’s case

Amnesty International is calling on the Georgian authorities to prevent the deportation of Russian citizen Denis Kulanin to Russia, where the organisation says he faces a real risk of imprisonment and torture.

The organisation says Georgia should protect Kulanin from being forcibly returned to Russia because he has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for opposition leader Alexei Navalny. According to Amnesty International, both positions could lead to criminal prosecution in Russia.

“Denis Kulanin has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for Alexei Navalny — both actions constitute criminal offences in Russia and can lead to imprisonment. The Georgian authorities must ensure that he is not deported to Russia. Amid the harsh repression of people who oppose the war, he faces a real risk of arbitrary criminal prosecution, imprisonment, torture or other ill-treatment,” said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

He said Georgia must uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning a person to a country where they face a real risk of serious human rights violations.

“The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin has an effective opportunity to seek international protection, including by allowing him to leave voluntarily for a safe third country,” Krivosheev added.

Who is Denis Kulanin?

Denis Kulanin is a Russian citizen who lived in Georgia and took part in pro-European protests. Police arrested him on 28 March 2025 during a demonstration outside parliament. The authorities accused him of smashing a police car window and sentenced him to two years in prison.

On the Orthodox Christian feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned Kulanin. However, because Kulanin is not a Georgian citizen, the authorities did not release him. Instead, they transferred him to the migration department.

According to his lawyer, deporting Kulanin to Russia would be both unacceptable and dangerous. While in detention, Kulanin sent a letter in which he wished Ukraine glory and peace. His lawyer says that in Russia, authorities can interpret almost any statement about the war in a way that could lead to criminal charges.

Denis Kulanin. Photo: Publica

On 30 August 2026, the Tbilisi City Court ordered Denis Kulanin to be held at the temporary detention centre run by the Georgian Interior Ministry’s Migration Department. He will remain at the centre until the grounds for his detention cease to apply or the authorities enforce the decision to deport him from Georgia, but for no longer than three months.

On 31 August, Kulanin’s lawyer was told that he would not be allowed to leave Georgia voluntarily until the Tbilisi City Court considers his deportation case.

On 1 September, Kulanin’s lawyer said the Migration Department had asked the Tbilisi City Court to deport him to his country of citizenship, the Russian Federation.

Denis Kulanin’s case

World.title: Opinion: ‘An attempt to make Abkhazia’s residents feel part of single political space with Russia’
World.content:
Abkhazia is actively preparing for Russia’s State Duma elections, which will take place on 20 September 2026. Most Abkhazia residents hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, which gives them the right to vote in the elections.

Russia will open 319 polling stations in 152 countries for citizens voting abroad. 35 of them — more than 10% — will open in Abkhazia.

Many people think this is excessive for a small republic with a population of 250,000.

One of those who objects is Akhra Bzhania, a prominent Abkhaz blogger and public figure. He believes that the “excessive” number of polling stations and the active election campaign aim to create a sense among Abkhazia’s residents that they somehow “belong” to Russia.

Akhra Bzhania: “There is a standard procedure for people with dual citizenship who vote abroad.

Usually, two or three polling stations open, plus a polling station at the consulate or embassy. That’s it.

Abkhazia cannot use its budget to cover the costs of holding a constitutional event of a foreign state. That makes no sense.

If someone argues that the Russian side is paying for the campaign, that is even worse!

Let me explain why. Fifty or 60,000 votes from Abkhazia will have no impact on the overall balance of parties in the State Duma.

This means the election campaign here must serve a different, ideological purpose — to create a sense among Abkhazia’s citizens that they share a single political and administrative space with Russia. And from there, a common state is not far away.”

I have no doubt that some Abkhaz citizens with dual citizenship care deeply about the differences between the programmes of Russian political parties. For them, State Duma elections are therefore not only a civic but also a political act.

But in that case, they can plan ahead and vote in Sochi, Krasnodar or Moscow, as Russians living in Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere do.

Yet our entire republic is covered with banners urging people to vote for a government body of another country! We plan to open 35 polling stations, just as we do for our own presidential elections!

It seems strange to me — and not only to me — and out of line with the status of our state and the level of Abkhaz-Russian relations.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia prepares for Russia’s State Duma elections

World.title: What Pashinyan and Putin agreed in Bishkek amid peak tensions in relations
World.content:
Pashinyan-Putin meeting in Bishkek

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Bishkek, where an SCO+ meeting was held as part of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. Their talks took place late in the evening.

There was no shortage of issues to discuss as bilateral relations have recently become increasingly strained. The previous meeting between Pashinyan and Putin took place on 1 April. Since then, Armenia held parliamentary elections in June, in which Pashinyan’s party won a majority and formed a government. However, the Russian president has yet to congratulate Pashinyan on his victory.

Judging by statements from Moscow, the main issue concerning the Russian authorities is Armenia’s ambition to join the European Union.

In the opening minutes of the Bishkek meeting, Putin said Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU was the country’s legitimate right. However, he said this “creates difficulties” for Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

“The sooner Armenia decides on the issue of joining the EU, the better. Moscow needs to understand how to develop relations further. The adoption of a law launching the process of Armenia joining another organisation amounts to a declaration of withdrawal from ours,” Putin said.

Pashinyan responded by reiterating that Armenia had no intention of leaving the EAEU.

The Armenian prime minister also recalled that, under the EAEU’s charter, there was no procedure for expelling a member state unless the country itself decided to leave.

“We greatly value our relations with the Russian Federation. We hope these relations are important to Russia as well. I think that Armenia and Russia, and we personally, should treat these relations with great care. I want to confirm that I personally and our government treat them with great care. I am sure that you also treat these relations with great care, and I want to thank you for that,” Pashinyan said.

He stressed that the issue of EU membership had not yet reached the stage at which a referendum could be held. He explained that Armenia did not currently have the alternative of actual EU membership to put before the public. In other words, the issue would be decided once the Armenian authorities had a concrete alternative to offer voters.

Putin, however, stood his ground: “The people should indeed always have a choice. So give them one, and we will close the matter. That’s all. The simplest thing is to ask people: what do you want — this or that?”

After the meeting, the Armenian prime minister posted a video on social media summarising the outcome of the talks.

Pashinyan described the meeting as “very good” and said he and Putin had agreed to continue their “sincere and constructive dialogue” during his visit to Moscow, which is apparently expected to take place in the near future.

“It should be noted that bilateral relations between Armenia and Russia are extremely important for both countries. […]However, it should also be noted that, in the new environment and under the new circumstances, there is a need to rethink these relations. I am convinced that, as a result of this reassessment, relations will become better, more constructive, more mutually beneficial and warmer,” he said.

Context: other issues on agenda

In Armenia, the meeting had been expected to involve difficult discussions on several critical issues. Armenian analysts had also warned that the meeting was unlikely to produce any positive developments on any of them.

In Armenia, there were expectations that the two leaders would discuss holding a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Russia and other EAEU member states have recently been pressing for such a referendum. The Armenian authorities have responded that there is little point in holding one at this stage, as the country has not yet formally applied for EU membership.

The EAEU comprises Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, there has already been talk within the EAEU of discussing Armenia’s status in the bloc. However, under the union’s charter, only Armenia itself can decide to withdraw. As Pashinyan has repeatedly pointed out, there is no other procedure for ending its membership.

At the same time, on 24 August, the Armenian prime minister raised the possibility of submitting a formal application for EU membership. This prompted a fresh wave of criticism and an even sharper reaction in Russia. Commentators there said that “EU membership is a marathon lasting decades”, while Yerevan would feel “the costs of breaking with Russia and the EAEU here and now”.

Russian experts even predicted a “fatal outcome” for Armenia. According to them, the country faces a choice between “Turkification” and a “Ukrainian scenario”.

The two leaders had also been expected to discuss Russian restrictions on imports of Armenian food and other goods, which were introduced in May and remain in place.

Russia has traditionally been a key export market for Armenia. However, since the restrictions were introduced — which Russia has attributed to concerns over product quality — Armenian goods have increasingly been exported to EU countries, where higher standards apply.

Armenian analysts had also expected the two leaders to discuss Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led CSTO military alliance.

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation comprises Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Armenia.

Armenia has effectively frozen its participation in the organisation for the past two years in response to what Yerevan sees as inaction by its allies.

When Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2021-22, its CSTO allies neither intervened nor condemned Baku’s actions. They argued that the Armenian-Azerbaijani border had not been delimited. Pashinyan responded:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to say that the CSTO has no defined area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

While Pashinyan had previously said he was not concerned about the possibility of Armenia being expelled from the military bloc, just a week before his meeting with Putin he went further, saying he would welcome such a move:

“At least it would relieve us of the dilemma of whether or not to leave [the CSTO].”

In addition, ahead of the leaders’ meeting, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

He was referring, among others, to the arrest of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan. Kocharyan is accused of abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered him to be held for two months. It is the former president’s fourth arrest.

In Armenia, there was speculation that Putin, who has close ties with Kocharyan, might once again ask for his release.

During his previous meeting with Pashinyan in April, Putin expressed hope that Russia’s “friends” and pro-Russian political forces would be able to take part in Armenia’s elections.

He was believed to have been referring to the party of Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, who is currently under house arrest on charges of making calls to seize power, as well as a bloc led by former President Robert Kocharyan. Both contested the elections but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Representatives of Armenia’s ruling party believe that these pro-Russian forces are encouraging the Russian authorities to take steps that could fuel public discontent. Pashinyan’s team believes the opposition hopes to use such discontent as a means of coming to power.

World.title: Ex Georgian PM Gharibashvili: Unanswered questions over deaths under current leadership
World.content:
Ex-Georgian PM Gharibashvili accuses authorities

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili has published another letter from prison, calling on the authorities to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a human rights defender who had criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Gharibashvili writes that Jorbenadze died by suicide shortly after journalist Dito Chubinidze published an article for which Jorbenadze had given an interview.

The newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, which published the interview, questioned the theory that Jorbenadze died by suicide. Gharibashvili stresses that the public should receive an answer about the real cause of Jorbenadze’s death.

The former prime minister says he decided to speak publicly on the issue after comparing the contents of a letter he received from government representatives in February this year with other circumstances surrounding the case.

According to Garibashvili, on February 12, he was sent, on the instructions of Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze, an article published in Asaval-Dasavali on February 2, 2026.

The article featured an interview by journalist Dito Chubinidze with Lazare Jorbenadze. Gharibashvili says the article focused mainly on criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.

The former prime minister says the message he received expressed suspicion that he himself was behind the article.

“I was sent a message expressing the suspicion — based on a completely false assumption — that I was behind the article,” Gharibashvili writes.

Gharibashvili says he categorically rejected the allegations and told the government representatives that publishing “commissioned articles” was not something he did.

In his letter, Gharibashvili also mentions journalist Dito Chubinidze and former Alliance of Patriots leader Irma Inashvili, stressing that he had no involvement in their political or journalistic activities.
