The former prime minister believes these events shed more light on one of the points in the letter he received, which referred to “supporters” such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili.

“Now the picture is clear to me, and I have received answers to all my questions: why did the first point of the letter say that ‘such supporters as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili’ raise serious doubts and cause significant damage to the interests of the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze team” Gharibashvili writes.

In another part of the letter, the former prime minister criticises Mamuka Mdinaradze, saying that his mistakes led not only to his removal from office but also to his departure from politics.

Gharibashvili stresses, however, that in his view, Mdinaradze’s departure from politics will not make up for the damage he believes Mdinaradze and Irakli Kobakhidze caused to the country, its people and the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Gharibashvili also writes that questions remain in society about the deaths of other people during the period when Irakli Kobakhidze and Mamuka Mdinaradze were leading the country.

Context

The first corruption charge against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was brought in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. A second charge – accepting a bribe on a particularly large scale – was brought on August 24, 2026.

Gharibashvili made his first statement from prison on August 17. In a Facebook post, he wrote that a letter had been sent to him on the orders of Bidzina Ivanishvili [oligarch, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party] and that it “left him no choice” but to confront the “evil that insults his dignity”.

Gharibashvili published his second letter from prison on August 19. In it, the former prime minister claimed that the aim of his arrest was his political destruction and said he had initially decided against legal action to avoid confrontation with the authorities.

According to Gharibashvili, he was forced to fight back.

Gharibashvili also said he received a letter from Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. He said that on the same day he explained his position to Mdinaradze and again confirmed that he had no intention of returning to politics.

News from Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan versus Western media: Why were different reports labelled a single ‘information campaign’?
World.content:
Azerbaijan and foreign media

Four separate reports about Azerbaijan have appeared in international media: a TVP World programme by Poland’s public broadcaster on political repression, an Independent report on the conditions in which Ali Karimli is being held, a BBC analysis of political prisoners, and a Guardian review of a documentary about Karabakh.

Baku responded with two official statements. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Poland’s ambassador over the TVP World programme and handed him a protest note. In a separate statement, the Media Development Agency described the other three publications as possible elements of a single “targeted information campaign”.

However, when examined individually, the reports clearly differ in their subject matter, format and main sources.

TVP: international success and domestic repression

The central question of the TVP World programme “Peace in Azerbaijan comes with repression”, broadcast on 26 August, is why Azerbaijan’s political space continues to shrink despite Baku’s growing international influence.

The programme discusses the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia, Meydan TV and Toplum TV, as well as criminal cases against opposition figures, activists and researchers. Presenter Benjamin Lee and İPEK Centre deputy director Türkan Bozkurt discuss oil revenues, the transfer of power within one family, the legitimacy Ilham Aliyev gained from victory in Karabakh, relations with the West and the position of national minorities.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the programme as biased and the presenter’s conduct as provocative. Since TVP receives state funding from Poland’s budget, the Azerbaijani side linked the programme’s content to the Polish government’s position and described its broadcast as an “unfriendly act”.

The Independent: conditions of Ali Karimli’s detention

The British newspaper’s 30 August report focuses on a narrower issue. The family and lawyers of Ali Karimli, the detained chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, say he has no access to safe drinking water, ventilation, adequate sleep, outdoor exercise or reading materials. A Human Rights Watch representative says the authorities have not presented convincing evidence to the public in his case. The UK Foreign Office confirms that it has raised the issue with Azerbaijani authorities.

The article’s emotive headline highlights the family’s claim that authorities are trying to “break” Karimli. The report also describes the charge against him as “treason”. Officially, however, prosecutors have charged him under an article concerning actions aimed at the violent seizure of power and the forcible alteration of the constitutional order. This is a specific point on which Baku could request a correction.

The newspaper also says it contacted Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry for comment but received no response.

BBC: figures and the case of Igbal Abilov

The Russian Service of the BBC’s article “Why is Ilham Aliyev stepping up repression?”, published on 31 August, focuses not on Ali Karimli but on Talysh researcher Igbal Abilov, who received an 18-year prison sentence.

The BBC analysed lists compiled by the Institute for Peace and Democracy from 2021 to May 2026. It concluded that the number of political prisoners had more than tripled, while the average prison sentence in politically motivated cases reached about 12 years in 2026. The article also examines the cases involving AbzasMedia, Radio Azadliq and Toplum TV, as well as the trials of researchers Bahruz Samadov and Igbal Abilov.

The fact that the calculations rely on lists compiled by a single human rights organisation may be open to debate. However, the BBC explains its methodology in detail, includes Ilham Aliyev’s position that he denies political persecution, and says it contacted the Penitentiary Service for comment but received no response.

Who is restricting access to the official position?

The MEDİA Agency accuses foreign news organisations of failing to seek Azerbaijan’s official position. However, in February 2025, the BBC closed its Baku bureau on the Foreign Ministry’s instructions. The bureau had operated in the country since 1994.

The Foreign Ministry cited the principle of reciprocity and the lack of a legal basis for the bureau’s operation. When authorities restrict the work of local bureaus and government agencies leave journalists’ requests unanswered, foreign news organisations have to rely more heavily on lawyers, relatives and experts based outside the country.

The information landscape that Baku describes as one-sided may therefore partly result from the authorities’ own media policies.

The Guardian: a review of a film about Karabakh

The Guardian article is not a political investigation. It is a short review of The Black Garden, a documentary by director Alexis Pazoumian. The film explores the wartime experience of Karabakh Armenians through the stories of two children and a young soldier who lost a leg.

The review’s introduction says Karabakh Armenians fought against “countless military campaigns” by the Azerbaijani army. However, it does not mention the First Karabakh War, the occupation of Azerbaijani territories, Azerbaijani internally displaced people or other aspects of the conflict. The reviewer also acknowledges that the film lacks a broader political and historical context.

Baku can reasonably criticise this one-sided presentation. However, expecting a film critic to seek comment from the Azerbaijani government would mean applying standards associated with news journalism to a piece about culture.

What do the different reports have in common?

What the four publications have in common is not any proven coordination between them, but the fact that the picture of Azerbaijan they present differs from the government’s official narratives.

TVP and the BBC question the authorities’ arguments about domestic stability and the legitimacy of criminal prosecutions. The Independent raises concerns about the conditions in which a particular detainee is being held. The Guardian, meanwhile, presents the Karabakh war primarily through the experience of the Armenian side.

The reports therefore cover different subjects, but within a single week they touch on three sensitive areas for the Azerbaijani state: domestic political control, relations with international partners and the historical narrative surrounding Karabakh. Baku sees them as part of a single attack not because their content is similar, but because all four diverge from the international image that the Azerbaijani authorities seek to project.

Is the “information campaign” proven?

The MEDİA Agency statement does not specify which facts in the reports are incorrect, nor does it provide evidence that could indicate coordination between the news organisations. At the same time, it claims that the authors did not attempt to establish Azerbaijan’s official position.

However, The Independent says it sent a request for comment to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry. The BBC quotes the president’s position and says it also sought comment from the Penitentiary Service.

A separate response to each report would have been more convincing. In the case of the Guardian, the authorities could have pointed out factual inaccuracies in its account of the historical context. For The Independent, they could have provided a documented response to the claims about the charges against Karimli and his conditions of detention. The BBC could have received alternative data on the criteria for including people on political prisoner lists and on sentencing statistics. TVP could also have been asked to give the Azerbaijani side a right of reply on air.

Grouping all the reports together in a single statement and presenting them as a politically motivated campaign erases the differences between them. Moreover, the absence of specific rebuttals does not end the debate. Instead, it creates the conditions for further reporting.

The confrontation here is not simply a conflict between “Baku and Western media”. The main problem is that the state places verifiable factual errors, editorial assessments, statements by human rights groups and even a film review in the same political category. This approach does not weaken the criticism. On the contrary, it creates the impression that different news organisations really are acting as a united front.

Although the agency said it intended to take “necessary measures”, it did not specify whether this meant seeking corrections and a right of reply, filing an official complaint or taking other steps.

Azerbaijan and foreign media

World.title: Georgia’s central bank explains how new transfer restrictions for people over 60 will work
World.content:
Georgia’s central bank on new rules for older customers

Georgia‘s central bank has clarified that new restrictions on electronic transfers for people over 60 will not apply to regular payments and transactions.

The new rule applies only when a bank or other payment service provider suspects that a customer may be the victim of fraud.

Under the National Bank’s new regulation, if a person over 60 makes an electronic transfer of more than 500 lari and the bank suspects that the transaction may be linked to fraud, it will suspend the transfer for 48 hours.

When does the rule apply?

According to the National Bank, all four conditions must be met for a transaction to be suspended:

The user must be over 60;

The transfer must exceed 500 lari;

The bank or payment organisation must detect unusual spending or behaviour by the customer;

The payment must involve activity that carries a high risk of fraud.

In other words, being over 60 and making a transfer of more than 500 lari are not, by themselves, enough to trigger a suspension.

For example, if a 65-year-old regularly pays 700 lari in utility bills each month or transfers money to a family member, the transaction will not be automatically suspended.

The situation changes if, for example, the same person is suddenly asked to transfer a large sum to an unknown account and their behaviour within the banking system appears suspicious. In that case, the new protection mechanism may be triggered.

What can the bank do?

If all four of the above conditions are met, the bank or relevant payment service provider will suspend the electronic transaction for 48 hours.

During this period, the bank must contact the customer and explain in simple terms why it considers the transaction suspicious and what risks it may involve.

The final decision then rests with the customer.

If the customer decides they still want to transfer the funds, they must confirm this to the bank, and the transaction will go through.

Why did the central bank introduce the rule?

The National Bank of Georgia says the measure aims to protect vulnerable customers, particularly older people, from fraud.

The idea is simple: if a fraudster convinces someone to make an urgent transfer, the 48-hour pause gives them additional time to consider whether they really want to go ahead with the transaction.

According to the National Bank, a similar approach is used in other countries, including the US, Canada, Brazil, the UK and EU member states.

The new rule therefore does not ban people over 60 from making bank transfers. Instead, it temporarily suspends transactions that appear suspicious based on a number of indicators. This gives customers another opportunity to reconsider their decision before falling victim to fraud or losing their money.

Georgia’s central bank on new rules for older customers

World.title: Why it may get harder for tourists to find favourite local spots
World.content:
Now that maps are digital, bookings are online and artificial intelligence can plan a holiday in seconds, fewer road trippers are stopping at visitor information centres in search of brochures.

Yet, as some information centres close their doors, many travellers maintain the services offer what social media and the internet never will.

Alex Murrie and his partner are five months into driving around Australia in their van named The Loaf.

Alex Murrie is driving around Australia in his van, trying to visit places many others miss. (Supplied: Adam Hoteit)

"Pretty early on, one of the grey nomads told us, 'Every town you go to, get to that information centre and you'll get a good idea of what's around,'" Mr Murrie said.

Since then, the couple look for the distinct yellow 'i' in most towns they visit.

"It's good, especially if we see someone who's been around the town a while — a true local — that's really helpful," Mr Murrie said.

"You can let them know what you're looking for, and they'll straight away say, 'Check out these four places, you'll really like them.'

"Sometimes it's provided us with places to visit that we had no idea about and no intention of going to whatsoever."

Alex Murrie says he spent a few extra days in Nooga Nooga National Park after visiting the visitor information centre. (Supplied: Adam Hoteit)

He said in a world of social media, visitor information centres provided something different.

"It can be a bit overwhelming — just the amount of information online," he said.

"You'll just see hundreds and hundreds of places and ideas and photos and I don't necessarily want to get to the same place that 300 people have just posted their Instagram video of. It can be a bit crowded."

But as the couple head north from Townsville in North Queensland, they will drive past the recently closed visitor information centre in Tully.

Some visitor information centres have their own stamps, which Alex Murrie has collected in his homemade passport. (Supplied: Adam Hoteit)

'Not commercially viable'

Cassowary Coast Tourism executive officer Patrick Bluett said his company would no longer be operating the Tully service as an accredited visitor information centre from August.

Mr Bluett said only 6 per cent of visitors to the region used the information centre and that foot traffic had been steadily declining for the past decade — particularly after COVID.

He said there would still be a visitor information centre down the road at Mission Beach.

Patrick Bluett says visitor information centres are not commercially sustainable unless funded by the council. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Mr Bluett said even with volunteer labour, it cost about $240,000 annually in insurance, maintenance and rates to keep the centre open.

"They are not commercially viable unless backed by a local council," Mr Bluett said, adding that he did not think the decision would affect tourism.

Patrick Bluett says visitor information centres have pamphlets advertising activities all around the region and further afield, so travellers can plan their trips in advance. (Supplied: Adam Hoteit)

"People don't come to an area for the information centre.

"When they're in the area, they may seek out the centre, but even that isn't really reflected in the people coming through the door."

Five years on, closure a 'good decision'

A 28-hour drive south from Tully on the NSW south coast, Eurobodalla Shire Council closed Batemans Bay Visitor Information Centre in 2021, saying fewer than one in 10 travellers was visiting the centre.

Tourism is the second-biggest industry in the region, but two-thirds of council's investment in tourism was supporting just 5 per cent of visitors, a review for the council found.

Councillors were told at the time the new tourism strategy was "fish where the fish are feeding".

Mathew Hatcher was Batemans Bay Business and Tourism Chamber president at the time and lobbied the council to keep the centre.

Mat Hatcher says closing the Batemans Bay visitors information centre has been a good decision. (Supplied: Eurobodalla Coast Tourism)

Now he is the mayor and says his opinions have changed.

"It's proved a good decision. We're getting a lot more value for money now," he said.

He said the money the council saved had been invested in more advertising for the region and supporting more events that brought in tourists during the off-season.

A dollar value on their worth

Wayne Clift, program manager for the accredited visitor information centre network across Queensland, said it was difficult to track the impact visitor information centres had on visitation and tourism spending.

"It's easy to think visitor information centres don't have an impact, but they really do," he said.

"Nobody knows that the reason the tourists stayed an extra day was because the visitor information centre had a really passionate staff member who convinced them to stay and explore the area."

Mr Clift says visitor information centres hold tourists in the region for longer, spending more tourist dollars. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

A 2023 review conducted by Painted Dog Research for Tourism WA found people who visited a visitor information centre in regional Western Australia spent $150 more in the region.

It found visitor centres led to $261 million more being spent by tourists in WA in 2023.

Hybrid path forward

New Kangaroo Island visitor centre opens A new tourist centre at Flinders Chase National Park has opened on Kangaroo Island.

Mr Clift said about 15 centres had closed in Queensland over the past decade.

Yet Dalby, 200km west of Brisbane, is currently working towards a new visitor information centre combined with a cultural centre.

Mr Clift said the future of visitor information centres was strong if they were able to adapt and engage online audiences using strategies like their own social media or online chatbots.

Wayne Clift says the future of visitor information centres needs to be a hybrid model. (Supplied: Visit the Tweed)

"Whilst everybody thinks the digital has all the answers, clearly it doesn't, but also visitor information centres — if they don't start to change and insert themselves into the digital world, will be irrelevant," he said.

Mr Clift said ultimately visitor information centres offered something the internet and social media could never match. And he said that was what kept tourists in the region for longer and spending more.

Wayne Clift is confident visitor information centres will be able to adapt to what tourists need in the future. (Supplied: Visit Victoria)

"If you go into a centre, you will find things that aren't easy to find online — the secret whispers — the sorts of things people didn't even know existed," he said.

"Some people believe in 10 years they won't be here. But those people have been saying that for the last 10 years."

World.title: Coalition promises to slash tobacco tax, legalise and regulate vapes
World.content:
A future Coalition government would slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent, legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches and bolster law enforcement to shut down the illicit trade.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor on Thursday pledged to reduce the excise on a standard packet of 20 cigarettes from about $30 to just $6 if elected, declaring the dramatic price reduction would smash the thriving black market.

More than half of the tobacco consumed in Australia last year was bought illegally, with the illicit market share jumping to 80 per cent when vapes and nicotine pouches are included.

Public health authorities have long used tobacco excise to reduce smoking by making cigarettes more expensive and have consistently warned dropping the tax risked reversing this.

Australia's tobacco tax crushed smoking. Has it gone too far? The Liberals and One Nation have a simple solution to end Australia's tobacco black market. But Labor says there's no easy fix.

The Coalition has also vowed to legalise, regulate and tax vapes and nicotine pouches for adults.

Australians aged over 18 can purchase legal vapes through pharmacies, while pouches are banned.

Under the Coalition's plan, vapes would have a "low rate" of excise of 50c per millilitre of e-liquid, while pouches would be taxed at 2.5 cents per milligram of nicotine.

A $60 million three-year national public awareness and education campaign would "expose the organised crime" behind illegal tobacco and vapes and warn people of the dangers of smoking.

A further $200 million would be spent on a nationwide law enforcement "surge" to support more raids, arrests, border seizures and the closure of illegal tobacco shops.

The surge in illegal sales has cost the federal budget tens of billions of dollars in lost excise revenue, with the Coalition's policy assuming this trend would reverse if legal cigarette prices were lowered to attract customers away from illicit alternatives.

Modelling of the Coalition's policy package by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) found it would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over the first four years — about double current forecasts.

Last month, One Nation unveiled a plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent, while Labor has argued there is no evidence a dramatic cut would end the illicit trade.

The Coalition policy assumes lower cigarette prices would draw customers away from illicit alternatives. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Taylor says excise cut will shut down black market

Mr Taylor argued the Coalition's policy would attack the source of the black market by taking away the profits enjoyed by organised criminals selling illicit tobacco and vapes.

"Organised crime is waging a campaign of economic terrorism on Australians," he said.

" Labor has allowed a criminal industry to thrive on our streets. We will shut it down. "

Mr Taylor said Australians were getting the "worst of all worlds" with higher tobacco consumption, crime and the loss of billions of dollars in revenue.

"Tobacco consumption has gone up around 30 per cent since the end of 2021, while taxes have kept rising, clearly showing that the government's current approach has failed," he said.

Smoking data differs from Coalition claims

In June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) estimated nicotine consumption had risen by about 30 per cent in the last four years, but this increase included growing use of vapes and other nicotine products.

The ABS cautioned the estimates as experimental, and while its analysis suggested higher legal cigarette prices enabled the illicit market, it does not establish the excise caused overall tobacco consumption to increase.

Shadow health minister Anne Ruston said there could be "no doubt" the Coalition wanted to see smoking and vaping rates decrease.

"Under Labor's current policy settings that simply isn't happening," she said.

But the latest National Drug Strategy Health Survey found daily smoking among Australians aged 14 and over fell from 8.3 per cent in 2022-23 to a record low 5.6 per cent in 2025.

The survey, conducted by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) found daily vaping was broadly unchanged at 3.6 per cent.

The AIHW specifically asked people about their smoking behaviour, while the ABS consumption estimates tried to capture the quantity of all nicotine consumed.

Question remains over black market prices

A legal packet of 20 cigarettes costs between $40 and $50, of which the excise makes up as much as $30.

Illicit cigarettes retail for between $15 and $20.

The Coalition said the PBO had estimated an 80 per cent excise cut was "sufficient" to bring the prices of legal and illegal cigarettes into "alignment", making it harder for the black market to compete.

It is not clear whether that calculation assumed black market prices would remain the same or drop to continue to undercut legal sales.

Nationals Leader Matt Canavan said the current excise rate had created a "massive profit margin for organised crime".

"Cutting the excise will take billions of dollars out of the hands of criminal gangs, bring the market back under Australian law and give our police a fighting chance to shut down those who remain," he said.

The Coalition's excise cut would be reviewed after two years.

World.title: Prime-time era Magbegor leads Opals' World Cup charge
World.content:
The Opals have produced a consistent pipeline of global superstars throughout their silverware-packed history, an impressive feat in one of the world's most competitive sports.

In the 2026 incarnation of the Opals, Ezi Magbegor, 27, carries that tag.

After bursting onto the international stage as a highly promising 18-year-old, she is now a defensive linchpin, a leader, and the type of player whose influence will likely dictate how far the Opals go at the Women's Basketball World Cup.

And she is in her prime-time era.

Magbegor was part of the team that won bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

Throwing a fit

Magbegor entered this WNBA season as a hot commodity — becoming the equal highest paid Australian player in the league, and one of the richest female Australian athletes overall.

But an Achilles injury, then broken nose, wiped her out for most of the season, delivering a harsh reality check for the Seattle Storm forward-centre.

Magbegor has been wearing a mask for the Seattle Storm, since returning from a broken nose. (Getty Images: Olivia Vanni)

"I've been so blessed to not have many injuries at all in my first seven years of my W season," she told ABC Sport.

"You just realise injuries are a part of sport and it's about how you reset your mind and bounce back and prepare for the next thing.

"And so, yes, I was injured, but I just used it as a great opportunity to work on my body and put myself in the best position to be ready."

It also gave her a chance to spend some time on her 'tunnel fits', aka the casual outfits that players wear when arriving at arenas, which have become a core part of the WNBA.

"This year I really wanted to lean into my Nigerian culture and heritage, and my mum's been begging me to wear traditional clothing," she said.

"My favourite was definitely my traditional attire. My parents had bought the material from Nigeria and then one of our friends had sewn it together in Melbourne.

Loading Instagram content

"I worry about being too dressed up sometimes, but my mum's like, yeah, it's not enough, nothing's too dressed up. So, it was really fun to be able to share that with her."

She traded high fashion for a protective face mask when she returned to the court for the Storm in late July, adding to her already intimidating aura as one of the league's best shot blockers.

And while her domestic season has been stunted, she is coming back to full fitness and form just in time for the World Cup, tipping-off in Berlin this weekend.

Opals going big

Magbegor was part of the team that won World Cup silver in 2018, bronze at home in Sydney in 2022, and bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

Magbegor is known as an elite rim defender and shot blocker. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

There has been substantial turnover since Paris with the emotional core of the team including Tess Madgen, Lauren Jackson, Cayla George, and Marianna Tolo, all missing.

And with captain and point guard Sami Whitcomb belatedly ruled out of this World Cup, the side's star power now largely shines around Magbegor and Alanna Smith.

"It's expected for me to pass on the cultural values and expectations onto the next group coming up," Magbegor said.

"But for me it's just about leading by example, touching base with my teammates, making sure that I'm being the best professional, best teammate, best person I can be come tournament play, and in the lead up as well.

"I've been in the Opals team and squad for a while now and I want to have an impact for the team in any way I can, whether that's on the floor, off the floor.

"But definitely looking to play my best basketball for the group and hopefully come away with the medal."

Smith, who was last year named WNBA defensive player of the year, had her own injury interrupted start to the season.

Alongside Magbegor, Dallas Wings player Alanna Smith is regarded as one of the Opals' best players. (Getty Images: Stacy Revere)

Coach Sandy Brondello is confident Magbegor and Smith are recovered and ready to lead Australia's charge in Berlin.

"They can hold themselves with any of the best post players in the world here. And that's what we're going to need from them without putting pressure," Brondello told ABC Sport.

"I've coached [Ezi] since she was 18. And this is her time, back healthy.

"The best is to come to her, but I'm just excited for her to get out, her athleticism, her rim protection. But now she's a three-level scorer, so that's a great asset.

"And Alanna was our best player in Paris, most consistent player over the whole tournament.

"And it's good to see her getting some rhythm now and getting that confidence back because we need them. We have to lean into them. They're our two best bigs."

Chasing the elusive gold

The Opals enter the World Cup ranked third. The Olympic bronze was followed by a breakthrough Asia Cup win last year, without any WNBA players, and they had a limited preparation for this tournament.

Coach Sandy Brondello says the team's culture is key to its continued success over many years. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

"The results that we've had, it shows that the continuity that we've developed over many years, not just one year, is showing because our chemistry is strong, our culture is strong," Brondello said.

"Everyone's accepting their roles and coming in and playing at a high level. And that's the beauty of Australian teams that we have."

Culture is always the constant with the Opals and what they attribute their sustained performance over decades to.

"It really just comes down our sisterhood and how gritty and tough we are and how we play together and we'll play whatever role to help us to have great success," Brondello said.

"These players, they've become family.

"Playing at the highest level just means everyone has to buy into the values for the success of the program. And there's no one player bigger than the program."

While the Opals are perennial podium finishers at major tournaments, gold has eluded them since their one and only world title in 2006.

Players from the 2006 World Champion Opals met with the current squad during a series in Melbourne in July. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"It's just something that comes with being an Opal, that legacy piece and recognising and acknowledging who put us in this position and who started that legacy," Magbegor said.

"Medals is quite synonymous with Opals, and we've won in the past and want to continue to win."

As had been the case for decades, the world number one USA is a seemingly immovable object from the top step of the podium, although was pushed all the way by France in the gold medal match at the Paris Olympics.

"[The USA are] the best of the best and they're great, but they've got the best talent," Brondello said.

"But we've got a talented group, we've built some more chemistry over the years, and that's what we have to lean into."

Growing the game

Half the Opals squad plays in the WNBA, the rest are in the local WNBL, and both leagues have experienced significant changes in the past year.

Zitina Aokuso is one of the local WNBL players in this World Cup squad. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

After drawn out, often bitter negotiations, the WNBA and players' association finally signed a new collective bargaining agreement which saw player salaries skyrocket.

Magbegor went from earning $US186,000 ($260,000) a year to $US1.25 million, a figure matched by Smith at the Dallas Wings, and significantly larger than the base salaries of other leading Australian female athletes in team sports, including the top Matildas and cricketers.

"I think that's just a testament to people that came before us and really pushing for the growth of women's basketball in particular, but just women's sports in general," Magbegor said.

"And I think now is a greater time than ever to push forward, invest in women's sports and just advocate for ourselves, but each other as well."

The WNBL has been making its own moves on a much smaller scale, including a new ownership group taking over last year.

And after starting her career there, Magbegor hopes it too can thrive.

"That's what is probably lacking right now, exposure, and knowing that it's going to pay off in the long run," she said.

"People need to see the product and see the game and realise that women's basketball, basketball is incredible.

"We have great athletes, especially coming up, and I think it's just a matter of investing, a matter of showing up and a matter of supporting."

World.title: More Australians tumble as rain causes schedule chaos at US Open
World.content:
Taylah Preston's US Open adventure has ended abruptly in the second round.

The first Australian through to round two was the first to exit following a 6-1, 6-1 loss to big-hitting American Taylor Townsend.

The 20-year-old wildcard was eliminated in just 48 minutes.

Preston was one of five Australians scheduled for day-four action at Flushing Meadows.

Australian women's number one Daria Kasatkina was also removed from the draw, but not before offering more considerable resistance against Spaniard Paula Badosa.

The pair resumed their stop-start affair that was halted on Tuesday morning (AEST) in sensational fashion.

After first being forced off court because of rain early in the second set while trailing Badosa 6-1, 1-2, Kasatkina was delighted when officials called it a night immediately after she saved a third match point.

Badosa was furious and had to return 15 hours later trying to serve out the contest at 5-4 and deuce in the second set.

Kasatkina saved her first two match points in an epic 22-point game serving at 3-5 in the second set, before fighting off another six more.

Kasatkina also conjured two break point chances to level up at 5-5 before Badosa, a one-time world number two, finally closed out the contest to book a second-round date with 2023 champion Coco Gauff.

Maya Joint is scheduled to take on ninth seed Elina Svitolina this morning, hoping to reach the third round in New York for a third straight year.

Meanwhile Kim Birrell is up against Russian Ekaterina Alexandrova believing she can also topple the Russian 18th seed after taking down world number five and 2024 US Open finalist Jessica Pegula at the French Open.

De Minaur delayed again

New York's lousy weather has dealt Alex de Minaur's US Open title hopes another setback with the top-ranked Australian's first-round clash delayed further by rain for at least an hour.

Former champion Daniil Medvedev and American home hope Alex Michelsen were already safely through to round three before de Minaur even made it on court for his tournament opener.

When he finally opened his campaign on day four, de Minaur looked intent on making up for lost time, racing to a 6-2, 4-2 lead over Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri in just 49 minutes.

Then the heavens opened again, forcing de Minaur scampering back to the locker room.

The scheduling backlog has left Australia's big hope needing to win seven best-of-five-set matches in 12 days to lift the trophy.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Fierce division over highly flammable grass pastoralists rely on
World.content:
Parts of South Australia are facing a heightened bushfire risk this spring after the boom of one of the nation's most invasive and flammable weeds.

But there is division about what to do about it.

SA has begun a parliamentary inquiry into the management of buffel grass, which has exploded in growth this year due to significant rain in the state's remote north-west.

It comes as the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services' national bushfire outlook for spring predicts a heightened risk of fire in that district.

The Country Fire Service says high fuel loads fed by an explosion of buffel grass growth are a "particular concern" heading into warmer months.

Buffel grass has been linked to fuelling significant fires in Australia and overseas. (Supplied: Bushfires NT)

CFS director of community risk, resilience and planning Alison May said vegetation would continue growing into spring, but was already drying out.

"Buffel grass … has been on the agenda amongst fire response agencies for quite some time now and continues to be … and we'll be working together to see what the way forward is on that," Ms May said.

Inquiry underway

Native to parts of Africa and Asia, buffel grass was brought to Australia in the 19th century to improve pasture and soil, but its spread can overcome native species and fuel bushfires.

MP Erin Thompson is chairing a parliamentary inquiry into the spread and management of buffel grass in SA — the first state to officially declare it a weed.

Erin Thompson is looking for opportunities to improve the way buffel grass is managed. (Supplied: NRC)

"We know it is doing significant damage across our state and … with the recent rainfall we've had over 2026, it's becoming more of an issue for SA," Ms Thompson said.

"We're keen to have a look at how it's already being managed and for opportunities to improve that, so that we can reduce the spread of buffel grass across South Australia."

Fire risk grows

Invasive Species Council senior advocate James Johnston said it was imperative to halt the spread of buffel grass further south.

"We need to know [what] resources we need to deal with this at scale and essentially prioritise where those resources need to go, so we can best protect our communities," Mr Johnston said.

"Buffel grass burns at 300 degrees, a significant amount more than our native grasses, so we're just not adapted in our local environment to deal with such pressures in an already bushfire prone region.

James Johnston says further spread of buffel grass would be catastrophic for SA. (Supplied: James Johnston)

"Earlier this year we had a shocker season, where it's gone to seed early because of the rainfall patterns that we've been receiving.

" We're now going into spring where there's going to be a lot more growth of buffel grass, and the real risk is that, going into summer, bushfire risk will escalate. "

But not everyone views buffel grass as a negative.

Feed for livestock

Livestock SA chair Gillian Fennell said buffel grass had been a "very valuable feed source" for pastoralists running livestock in arid areas.

"It does provide significant environmental benefits in the sense that it does hold creek beds together, it does hold soil together in areas where there's been erosion and degradation," Ms Fennell said.

Debate continues over whether buffel grass should be declared a weed of national significance. (ABC News: Else Kennedy)

"Buffel grass is always the first thing to re-sprout after a drought, which means it's also the first thing to be eaten, giving native grasses the opportunity to grow and set seed because there's another fodder source available.

Gillian Fennell says balance must be achieved in managing buffel grass. (Supplied)

"It is quite easy to control buffel grass with livestock. You just eat it.

"I can also appreciate that moving further south into higher rainfall areas, into mixed farming and cropping systems, it has the potential to become quite costly to manage and control."

She said SA already had a "generally good framework" for addressing buffel grass, supported by good land management by producers.

"I think anything to do with the buffel discussion needs to be approached with a bit of common sense," Ms Fennell said.

"It does have its upsides, but it also has its downsides. There's definitely a way to balance it."

World.title: Inside the $2 billion thrift store expanding in Australia
World.content:
The buzz was palpable at the latest Savers store opening in Geelong.

Some people had driven hours to line up on August 27 outside the retailer's newest big red box, with one heavily pregnant woman right at the front of the 100-metre queue.

"I have two babies in here, so I need a lot of clothes," she laughed.

The regional Victorian site is the company's 19th store in Australia.

But what is not commonly known is that Savers Australia is the subsidiary of a much larger US company.

The parent company, Savers Value Village (SVV), is worth $2.2 billion, has shares which trade on the New York Stock Exhange and is majority owned by American private equity firm Ares Management.

Customers queue for the new Savers store. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

SVV is also North America's largest for-profit second-hand retailer with 185 stores in the US and 172 in Canada.

Its 50 per cent gross profit margin is well above the industry average and the company earned more than $300 million last year, according to Refinitiv data.

"Larger retailers like Cash Converters, Savers and Vinnies have consistently outperformed their smaller, non-employing counterparts," analytics firm IBISWorld noted recently of its place in the Australian second-hand retail market.

"Primarily owing to their capacity to harness economies of scale."

Why is Savers controversial?

In Australia, its for-profit mission makes Savers an outlier.

It competes directly with non-profit, second-hand retailers Vinnies and Salvos, and smaller charity op shops that rely on selling donated goods to fund community programs.

Esther Koning-Oakes is worried about what the arrival of Savers means. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Some of them are not happy about Savers' expansion.

"We should be keeping as much as what we can in Australia," Esther Koning-Oakes, the boss of one charity near Savers' new store in Geelong, told ABC News.

Ms Koning-Oakes's charity, Norlane Community House, operates an op shop in Geelong called Treasures, which helps fund its drop-in centre.

Unlike Savers, it is small, manned by volunteers and relies heavily on direct community donations.

She is worried Treasures will get fewer customers and donations with its new competitor on the scene.

"I think a lot of people, when they donate things, they want to donate it for a good cause," she said.

"Having it for a for-profit company means that that is going into shareholders or upper management, and it doesn't actually go back into community."

Volunteers keep Norlane Community Op Shop running. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

How does Savers' charity partnership work?

Responding to the concerns from local charities, Savers' American head office told ABC News it gave its Australian non-profit partners $5.6 million last year, which works out to about $310,000 per local store.

"I'm sorry to hear those concerns because [at] Savers, it's important to us to make sure that we grow in the circular economy," local boss Michael Fisher said.

"In Australia and globally, we partner with not-for-profit organisations.

"They go and solicit donations from the general public, they bring them to the stores, and we pay them for those donations.

Savers Australia boss Michael Fisher (left) with CEO Mark Walsh (right). (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"So if you donate to us at the store, you're actually donating to the not-for-profit, and we pay them for that."

Diabetes Victoria boss Glen Noonan was at Savers' recent Geelong launch, where big green bins with his non-profit's logo were on proud display for people to donate into.

Mr Noonan would not disclose what Diabetes Victoria was paid to collect goods for Savers, describing it as confidential.

Yet he said the millions it received last year from Savers was beneficial, and allowed Diabetes Victoria to revenue raise from second-hand donations without the grunt work of running shops themselves.

"From the revenue that we generate, we provide much-needed services to Victorians," he said.

Savers is clearly aware of the space it is operating in and the public perceptions around second-hand retailing.

Savers is the biggest for-profit thrift retailer in the US and is expanding across Australia. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

At its latest Geelong launch, one woman who was excitedly waiting in line to buy Savers goods had some reservations about donating her own belongings to the organisation.

"I will not be donating my clothes here," she said.

"I would rather give back to the Salvation Army or the Geelong Animal Welfare Society."

Those who decide to donate, however, get a 20 per cent off voucher for their next shop at Savers.

Where does the unsold merchandise go?

Savers' financial filings do not break down its overheads in great detail.

Michael Lasser, a retail analyst from investment bank UBS, which has done work for Savers, said its biggest overheads would be staff wages, store overheads, and the undisclosed cost of buying used items.

Clothes and goods are donated to Diabetes Victoria which has a contract with for-profit thrift store chain Savers. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"This is a business that is aimed at more effectively monetising the donated goods for charities," he said.

Like op shops and non-profit second-hand retailers, Savers also needs to deal with all of the donations from charity partners that it cannot sell in Australian stores.

It does not disclose how much stock ends up in landfill, gets sent overseas to the rag trade, or is recycled.

Savers, however, emphasises that it offers a solution to waste, with Australia among the largest per-capita consumers of clothing.

Pricing decisions with help of AI

In North America, the company has been using a program backed by artificial intelligence, ThriftIQ, that helps speed up its decision-making on how much to charge for goods.

"It's just in the process of rolling out," Mr Lasser said.

The company known to Australians as Savers started in the United States in the 1950s. (Supplied: Savers)

"But it leads to better pricing of products, more productive use of labour, and faster sell-through of the goods."

Savers would not reveal whether it would expand the use of ThriftIQ to its Australian stores.

On a recent analyst call for its quarterly financials, its top executives talked up the technology, as well as the growth the company was experiencing.

The global resale of fashion alone is projected to be worth $444 billion ($US317b) by 2027, according to research by consulting firm McKinsey & Company.

"Younger and more affluent consumer cohorts are still our fastest-growing demographics, which speaks to the power of our model and its ability to resonate with all shoppers," attendees of the Savers' analyst call were told.

"For 2026, our plan remains to open around 25 new stores, more than 20 of which will be in the US in 11 states."

Savers opened its first Australian store on Melbourne's Sydney Rd in Brunswick in 1997. (Supplied: Savers)

The company is more tight-lipped on its plans for Australia, where it employs 1,250 staff across its stores in NSW, Victoria and South Australia.

However, its local boss Michael Fisher was evidently preparing for more openings with long lines and gigantic ribbon cuttings.

"It's fair to say that we'll open another store next year," he said.

"We're really excited with the growth of second-hand across Australia and we're happy to participate in that."

World.title: The gruesome tactic locals have resorted to as influencers flock to scenic hilltop lookout
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictoria The gruesome tactic locals have resorted to as influencers flock to scenic hilltop lookout Eleanor Campbell Updated September 3, 2026 — 7:02am ,first published 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A scenic lookout north of Melbourne has gone so viral that locals have resorted to dumping roadkill to deter influencers from littering and trespassing on private land. The Milky Way Point lookout, which sits on top of a hill that overlooks rolling slopes and green valleys stretching across central Victoria about 100 kilometres north of Melbourne, has long been recognised for its panoramic beauty but is suffering from an influx of visitors after going viral on social media. Visitors at the lookout near Strath Creek on Wednesday. Joe Armao Influencers sharing photos and videos of two picturesque spots located along the same, narrow one-way dirt road have lured hundreds of visitors to Strath Creek, a small rural farming town that borders the southern edge of the Tallarook State Forest. The main attraction is Hangs Tree, a large dead stringybark on an organic farm overlooking the valley, about one hundred metres before the main lookout.



One tour operator is charging tourists more than $500 a day for “viral magic tree” photography tours near the property. Some residents say they witnessed people defecating on private driveways, while other visitors left piles of garbage and toilet paper on cattle grazing land and outside people’s homes. Alex Whitford, who grew up 15 minutes away in Broadford, has started organising local clean-ups two to three times a week with other concerned community members. Last Tuesday, the group filled 13 bags with nappies, coffee cups, toilet paper and other rubbish left behind by visitors that day.



“People are coming here and having lunch, and they’re having a couple of wines, and then leaving, you know, smashed wine bottles everywhere and beer bottles. I’ve never seen so many Red Bull cans in my life,” Alex said. Alex said people were getting hurt because the steep hillside was not meant to accommodate heavy traffic. Alex Whitford and two young residents during a cleanup last week. “It’s a very, very narrow road, and it’s very under cared for. It’s a dirt road that’s full of potholes. There are trees down on the way through and people don’t know how to drive to the conditions up here,” she says. “There was a car that went off the edge maybe three weeks ago, and three people got hospitalised because it’s so busy and people don’t understand that this is not actually a publicly accessible space – it’s peoples homes and people’s backyards.”



Locals have starting placing dead kangaroos and wombats along the road to stop people from setting up bush camps and picnics on their properties. They have also erected signs asking people to take their rubbish home when leaving the spot. Melbourne resident Akhil Bollikonda and his wife, Sravani, made the day trip on Wednesday after discovering the location on YouTube. “It’s even more beautiful in person,” Akhil said.



Related Article Climate crisis Melbourne records its warmest winter on record, as bushfire season looms The pair also noticed the dumped roadkill and rubbish left by other visitors. “I think it’s really sad to see animals like that,” Akhil said. “As far as what I have seen, I saw some people littering and throwing some stuff – I don’t think that’s acceptable.” David Francis Palmer, who helps install garden beds and water beds in nearby farming properties, thinks the government should hire a security presence to monitor the area.



“I can’t honestly see the police going and knocking on people’s doors because they might have seen them taking a poo on the side of the road,” he said. “But if they know that it’s monitored, it may well restrict their bad behaviour.” Even more concerning than littering and trespassing was the issue of public safety. During the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires, the area was engulfed by flames that swept through townships in regional Victoria. Devastation in nearby Flowerdale during the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires. Pat Scala Local photographer Sara, who lives nearby and has photographed the lookout for years, says the situation could become “catastrophic” heading into the warmer summer months. “It’s not a patrolled area, the grass isn’t mown. If people are lighting little barbecue fires up there, and something like a fire did break out, and all these people are just parked across this one-way road, you wouldn’t even be able to get out of there,” she said. “It’d just be a disaster.”



A Country Fire Authority spokesperson said the local commander had reported “no issue” with the crowds or emergency access at the site. Police said they have increased their presence in the area after receiving complaints about littering, traffic congestion, illegal parking and trespassing. While Alex ultimately welcomes visitors, the ongoing damage and lack of respect shown by tourists to the place she calls home has taken a toll. “This is a place that I’ve come to every time that I’m in love, out of love, every major crossroads in my life,” she said. “Every time that I just need to think and be somewhere beautiful, this is where I come. To have that then ruined consistently – it’s devastating.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Meta released its most powerful artificial intelligence model yet, with its chief AI officer saying its capabilities are edging closer to top competitors.

Developers will be able to access and pay for Muse Spark 1.3, an updated version of its most advanced model, the company said. It will soon roll out the update to users of Meta’s social media platforms, like Instagram and Facebook, as well as Meta AI.

Alexandr Wang, chief AI officer of Meta. Bloomberg

“This is our biggest jump so far on model performance,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said in an interview, pointing to advancements in the model’s coding and agentic capabilities, or ability to complete tasks on behalf of human users. Wang said the update put Meta on par with recently released AI models from its rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.

Wang said Muse Spark 1.3 is “competitive” with Anthropic’s model, Claude Fable 5.1, and “better than” OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, particularly when it comes to coding, though OpenAI will soon be releasing a new, even more advanced model known as Astra. In his opinion, Meta’s model outperforms “any of the current Chinese models out there.”

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street climbs; Meta releases new AI model
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street climbs; Meta releases new AI model Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated September 3, 2026 — 6:23am ,first published 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks rose on Wall Street as gains by big technology companies and relatively steady oil prices and bond yields helped boost the market after a downbeat start to the week. Nvidia rallied more than 3 per cent, lifting the Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.6 per cent. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq composite both gained 0.5 per cent. Wall Street climbed as oil prices and bond yields steadied. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Brent crude settled up 1 per cent at $US95.63 as the Iran conflict continued. Chevron edged 0.3 per cent higher after confirming it will expand operations in Venezuela. The Australian sharemarket is set for gains, with futures at 5.57am AEST pointing to a rise of 38 points, or 0.4 per cent at the open. The ASX lost 1 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.71¢



Related Article Energy One Nation wants this coal plant kept open. Its owner warns that will spell trouble Wall Street has been under pressure this week from rising oil prices and a bond-market sell-off. The rocky start to September follows a mostly positive August during which every major index notched a gain for the month. However, Wall Street remains gripped by anxiety over rising prices, government debt and the impact of global conflicts on the US and the global economy. Technology and communication services stocks accounted for some of the strongest gains Wednesday. Chipmaker Nvidia, whose big market value tend to give it more influence over the broader market’s direction, rose 3.2 per cent, while computer memory seller Micron Technology gained 2.4 per cent. Meta added 2.5 per cent as it released its most powerful artificial intelligence model yet, with its chief AI officer saying its capabilities are edging closer to top competitors. Developers on Wednesday will be able to access and pay for Muse Spark 1.3, an updated version of its most advanced model, the company said. It will soon roll out the update to users of Meta’s social media platforms, like Instagram and Facebook, as well as Meta AI.



“This is our biggest jump so far on model performance,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said in an interview on Wednesday, pointing to advancements in the model’s coding and agentic capabilities, or ability to complete tasks on behalf of human users. Wang said the update put Meta on par with recently released AI models from its rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. Dell Technologies jumped 15.8 per cent for the biggest gain among S&P 500 stocks after delivering strong second-quarter profits amid accelerating demand for artificial intelligence computing. The company also raised its fiscal year revenue outlook. Palo Alto Networks also reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street’s expectations, citing a strong market for AI cybersecurity, but its shares fell 9.3 per cent. Meanwhile, banks and credit card issuers also helped boost the market. Capital One Financial rose 2.5 per cent and American Express added 1.8 per cent. Markets in Europe fell after markets in Asia closed lower.



Oil prices held relatively steady despite the intensification in the six-month long US war with Iran. The US attacked sites in Iran over the weekend, ending a lull in major hostilities and Iran has since retaliated against sites around the Gulf region. Prices for Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.7 per cent to $US95.33 a barrel. Energy stocks were mixed. Chevron edged 0.4 per cent higher after confirming it will expand operations in Venezuela. A surge in oil prices following the start of the US war with Iran fuelled a jump in gasoline prices and global shipping costs. The conflict shut down the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 per cent of the world’s oil is typically shipped. Higher energy costs worsened inflation that was already stubbornly high amid a volatile US tariff war with much of the world. Inflation has been squeezing businesses and households at the same time that the mostly resilient jobs market shows signs of weakening. Payrolls processing firm ADP reported that private-sector employment slipped in August, according to its monthly survey. It is just a small snapshot, though, of the broader labour market and follows a government report on Tuesday that showed US job openings rose in July.



The big focus this week will be the government’s broader employment report for August, which will be released on Friday. The previous report for July showed that the jobs market stalled, with employers cutting positions. Related Article Opinion

Oil Trump kidnapped Venezuela’s president. Now he’s hijacking its future Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Both inflation and the jobs market have been key focuses for Wall Street and the Federal Reserve. “Friday’s employment report, and perhaps even more importantly next week’s inflation data, will play a significant role in determining whether policymakers decide to raise rates in September,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist, investment strategy at Edward Jones, in a research note. The Fed is trying to balance its task of supporting employment and taming inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation, which remains well above 3 per cent. The Fed has a stated goal of cooling inflation to a target of 2 per cent.



The bond market has been selling off, which is a signal that it expects borrowing costs to rise. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which tends to impact mortgage rates, rose to 4.80 per cent from 4.79 per cent late Tuesday. It has been rising steadily throughout the year and was as low as 4.20 per cent at the beginning of 2026. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for Federal Reserve moves on interest rates, held steady at 4.39 per cent. It is significantly higher for the year, though, and was as low as 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. Investors are also betting on a 64 per cent chance that the Fed will raise rates at its upcoming meeting in September, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed’s position is growing more complicated. Raising the benchmark interest rate would help cool inflation by making borrowing costs higher and slowing the economy. Doing so, though, could also hurt the employment market at a time when it is seemingly already weakening.

World.title: ‘Not a fan’: Trump ‘happy’ Harry and Meghan left the US
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaPrince Harry ‘Not a fan’: Trump ‘happy’ Harry and Meghan left the US Bo Erickson September 3, 2026 — 6:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US President Donald Trump says he’s “happy” Prince Harry and his family left the United States and relocated back to Britain. “I am happy about it. I was not a fan,” Trump said in the Oval Office when asked about the recent decision by Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, to leave California after six years. US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday (US time). AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The family arrived back in Britain at the end of August. The couple stepped down from official royal duties in 2020 when they moved to the US. “I thought they treated the royal family with great disrespect. I didn’t like it,” Trump said, mentioning his “good relationship” with the late Queen Elizabeth and her successor King Charles, who is undergoing treatment for cancer.



The president specifically criticised Meghan. “I didn’t like the way she acted. I thought she was terribly disrespectful,” he said. It’s not the first time Trump has taken aim at the pair. In April, Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine and called on Trump and the US to end the war with Russia. ”This is a moment for American leadership. A moment for America to show that it can honour its international treaty obligations,” he said. Harry and Meghan in Sydney in April. Getty Trump dismissed the call and made a passing remark about the prince’s wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex. “Prince Harry? How’s his wife? Please give her my regards,” he said. “Prince Harry is not speaking for the UK, that’s for sure,” Trump said. “I think I’m speaking for the UK more than Prince Harry.”



In February, Trump ruled out deporting Harry from the US over his immigration status. The president insisted he had “no interest” in removing Harry from the country and said he had “enough problems” with Meghan, who he said was “terrible”. After the couple’s move to the US, Harry in an Oprah interview accused the royal family of neglect. Meghan, whose mother is Black and father is white, said that when she was pregnant with her son there were “concerns and conversations about how dark his skin might be when he’s born” within the royal family. Loading Prince William, Harry’s older brother, defended the family after the accusation and said “we’re not racist”. Harry also cited press scrutiny and the government’s failure to provide security for his family as reasons for moving to California.



Now back in Britain, Harry and Meghan are expected to remain non-working royals. A person close to the couple said last month the family planned to move somewhere outside London for an extended period ‌with their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, who will go to school in Britain. Loading It is unclear what changed for the couple, but Harry has said he wants his children to spend time in Britain. “If I were the royal family, I would not have taken them back,” Trump added on Wednesday.

World.title: Rain briefly halted Demon’s US Open charge. He still breezed into the second round
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Rain briefly halted Demon’s US Open charge. He still breezed into the second round Marc McGowan September 3, 2026 — 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur had to wait until the fourth day of the US Open to play his first match. Fifty minutes later, he was off court again. New York’s wet weather continues to wreak havoc with the tournament’s first week as Australia’s world No.7, who was supposed to start his campaign on Wednesday (AEST), endured another rain delay before returning to blitz Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri, 6-2, 6-2, 6-4. Alex de Minaur, pictured during a drier practice session last week, has endured a frustrating start to the US Open. Getty Images De Minaur broke Guerrieri – playing his first-ever grand slam main draw match at age 27 – in the first game of each of the first two sets and appeared poised for a quick passage to the second round until weather intervened. He led 6-2, 4-2 when the chair umpire suspended play, with the delay lasting about two hours before he joined fellow Australians Dane Sweeny, Tristan Schoolkate, Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth as a first-round winner.



De Minaur needed only 99 minutes either side of the latest rain disruption to demolish his left-handed rival, looking sharp with his ball-striking and movement from the outset, albeit with a slight detour in the third set. With the finish line in sight, the three-time US Open quarter-finalist threw in a sloppy service game that he lost to love when trying to push 4-2 ahead. He also slipped 0-30 behind his next time with the Wilson balls before getting back on track to complete his victory. Australia’s Taylah Preston has been knocked out in the second round. Getty Images But 20-year-old wildcard Preston’s US Open is over, trounced 6-1, 6-1 in a mere 48 minutes by American Taylor Townsend in her second-round match, hitting only two winners compared to 28 unforced errors. Daria Kasatkina is also out, losing her rain-interrupted first-round clash with Spain’s former world No.2 Paula Badosa that was carried over from the previous day.



Badosa was only two points from victory when the match was paused, and had to stave off two break-back points before clinching a 6-1, 5-4 win on her ninth match point to lock in a showdown with 2024 champion Coco Gauff. Pushed out to Flushing Meadows’ back blocks on court 11, after originally being scheduled on the bigger Grandstand stadium a day earlier, de Minaur did not have the fortune of playing on one of the event’s two courts with a retractable roof. It has been a wet and wild week for tennis fans in New York. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth The challenges for de Minaur rise steeply from here – beginning in the second round with dangerous Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp, who also advanced in straight sets against outmatched Brit Jan Choinski. De Minaur’s projected rivals beyond that are 31st seed Zizou Bergs (third round) and top seed Alexander Zverev (quarter-finals), who needed almost five hours to battle past Italy’s Lorenzo Sonego in the first round.



Related Article Updated

US Open From GoFundMe to making big bank: Australian’s US Open breakthrough However, his potential path was made somewhat easier when possible fourth-round opponent, in-form No.12 seed Rafael Jodar, suffered a shock 6-2, 6-1, 6-1 loss to lucky loser Bu Yunchaokete, who entered the draw when Australia’s Thanasi Kokkinakis withdrew with an ankle issue. Joint (against No.9 seed Elina Svitolina), Duckworth (Wu Yibing) and Birrell (18th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova) are due to play their second-round matches on Thursday (AEST).
