World.title: Jonathan LaPaglia has one word for fans boycotting Australian Survivor: ‘Good’
World.content:
Jonathan LaPaglia returns to reality TV in the new Binge series Apocalypse – but he still has a few things to say about Australian Survivor.

A year on from his controversial sacking, the reality host is returning with a new show – and new appreciation for his loyal audience.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last time I spoke with Jonathan LaPaglia, we were on set in Samoa for what neither of us knew would be his final season of Australian Survivor. It was a brief and sometimes tight-lipped interview, snuck between filming commitments on a sweaty day which followed a tricky late-night tribal council. Had I known what was coming, I tell him at the start of this new interview two years later, this time over the phone, I would have asked different questions. “Well, had I known, I probably would have given you different answers,” he says, laughing. Related Article Reality TV Australian Survivor scored a world-first TV event. Then it sacked the host... LaPaglia certainly didn’t hold back this time. A year on from his controversial sacking, the longtime host is returning to reality TV with a new show and a new appreciation for his surprisingly loyal audience. “I really had no idea how much [fans] appreciated what I was doing,” he says, reflecting on the outrage that many Survivor fans and past players have expressed over the past 12 months at his “blindside” from the network. “I was just head down, grinding away – and I wasn’t doing it to get praise or approval … [The response] has been heartwarming and humbling. And it still continues now.” His discontent with former employer Network 10 continues, too. When I ask for his response to the many Australian Survivor fans who say they’re boycotting the show without him as host, he had a cheeky one-word reply: “Good.”



The network, he says, “told me ratings were declining, and they were looking for a way to boost that. But that hasn’t worked out, has it? They’ve lost 40 per cent of their audience. Honestly, I can’t believe they’re going again with ratings like that. Those ratings are really catastrophic. And if it continues like this, I don’t see how they can sustain it.” Former Australian Survivor host Jonathan LaPaglia, who was replaced by David Genat. Night Wright/Ten That 40 per cent drop refers to the overnight ratings for this year’s finale. It’s slightly less than that, but he’s not far off. Related Article Australian TV ‘I can’t touch Jonathan’s legacy’: David Genat on hosting Survivor – and LaPaglia’s sacking On free-to-air and 10Play that night, 462,000 people tuned in to see new host David Genat crown Caleb Beeby in April; that’s compared to a total of 764,000 the year before when Myles Kuah triumphed. Notably, this year’s final episode clashed with the finale of Australian Idol (which pulled 1.08 million viewers) but that doesn’t wholly explain the smaller audience. JLP’s last season, a shorter international special called Australia v The World, pulled 653,000 viewers for its final instalment at the end of 2025 despite being up against The Block with a mammoth audience of 1.62 million. In response, Network 10 said that much of the show’s audience comes from catch-up after those figures are collected. And if you look at the whole season, livestream numbers were up 6 per cent from the season Myles Kuah won in 2025. The latest season premiere, for instance, grew its audience 58 per cent in the seven days after it aired. But a drop of 300,000 viewers between the 2025 and 2026 finale is undeniably significant either way – especially considering the latter was triumphantly billed as a live finale and reunion.



“It makes me sad in a way because we all worked really hard on that show,” LaPaglia says. “For 10 years, we worked hard trying to build success … It’s kind of sad to see it crumble like that. It’s not what it was. And there’s a whole bunch of reasons for that.” “Honestly, I can’t believe they’re going again with ratings like that. Those ratings are really catastrophic.” Former Australian Survivor host Jonathan LaPaglia Speaking over the phone from his home in Los Angeles, LaPaglia seems unfazed by the prospect of appearing impolite or ungracious. He feels Network 10 and the production company Endemol Shine Australia have made “terrible decisions” for Australian Survivor – from this year’s “clunky” theme to what he perceives as heavy-handed production and, of course, the decision to let him go. Though he admits to not watching the full 2026 season, not having access to it in the US, LaPaglia is also happy to comment on his successor’s performance: “The stuff with David felt weird, you know?” LaPaglia theorises Genat is being “fed everything in his earpiece … it disconnects you from the players – and I think that’s what the audience is sensing”. Loading Wearing an earpiece to communicate with producers is standard practice in TV production, and in Australian Survivor scripts are often used as jumping off points for broader conversations – especially in unpredictable situations such as challenges or tribal councils. But LaPaglia, a trained actor, says he prided himself on memorising as much as possible before filming to make things feel organic.



“If the producer is trying to control every word that comes out of your mouth, you’re not in the moment any more,” LaPaglia says. He specifically praises Jeff Probst, the host and executive producer of Survivor in the US, who famously operates without an earpiece at all – occasionally to the show’s detriment. A spokesperson for Endemol Shine Australia, however, defended Genat saying, “Australian Survivor is produced today exactly as it always has been, including how the host communicates with the cast. Nothing about that process has changed between hosts. Any suggestion otherwise is untrue.” David Genat, the new host of Australian Survivor. Network 10 It’s tempting to read LaPaglia’s comments as sour grapes – and that might be partly true – but he’s also clearly motivated by a genuine passion for the show. Two of the three interviews LaPaglia has done in the past year have been with respected fan podcasts, diving deep into the mechanics of the game and how it could be improved. And that’s a passion the show’s former executive producer also appreciated. Shortly after LaPaglia’s shock exit, former EP David Forster (who had left the show around the same time and was not speaking on behalf of Network 10 or Endemol Shine) told me the pair had “epic fights” and “creative differences” over the years but “Jonathan was a brilliant host. And he was super, super, super dedicated to making the show the best it could be.” Forster does not share the former host’s criticisms of the network or production company. LaPaglia is also liberated, of course, by the fact he has a new gig to focus on. The presenter is returning to reality TV as the narrator of Apocalypse, a new series co-commissioned by Binge and Channel 4 in the UK, which drops five Australians and nine Brits into an abandoned town for 28 days with no food, running water or power – and no rules. It’s Survivor-adjacent. But a closer comparison would be Alone. The series is actually produced by some of the team behind Alone Australia, as well as the much flashier Netflix sensation Squid Game: The Challenge.



Some of the contestants on new series Apocalypse who must survive with no food, no power and no running water. Binge “This show doesn’t have [Survivor’s] game element,” LaPaglia says. “It’s more an experiment about survival and society.” It has a far spookier aesthetic, too, at least partially informed by its unique setting. The eight-part series is filmed in Muscatatuck, Indiana, a once fully functional town the size of Sydney’s CBD that was created in the 1920s for psychiatric patients but has since been abandoned. The site has been used for the past two decades to train civilian first responders and military personnel in urban warfare. As it’s depicted in the show, it could just as easily be a set for The Last of Us or The Walking Dead. “When I first saw the trailer, it really reminded me of The Blair Witch Project,” LaPaglia says. “It forced me to ask more questions than I was getting answers, and to me, that’s good, right? That’s good TV.” Loading There are a few surprises, but LaPaglia confirms there are no zombie jump scares. All the same, the show reveals reasons for contestants to be nervous around each other. Unlike Alone, these people are not survivalists. They’re everyday people with everyday jobs – from taxi drivers to cattle farmers to content creators – who occasionally have very different ideas on how to get things done. Before the first episode is over, one contestant has already unilaterally decided to start rationing food and threatened to burn everyone’s shelter to the ground if they disagree.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on SBS On Demand right now
World.content:
Rachel McAdams (left) as Esti and Rachel Weisz as Ronit in Disobedience.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great movies that span genres, filmmakers and languages. This week: SBS on Demand. For 150 other movie choices, check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+. Aftersun (2022) What we remember and what we will never know underpins this intimately audacious debut drama from Scottish filmmaker Charlotte Wells, with a young British father (Paul Mescal) taking his 11-year-old daughter (Frankie Corio) on a holiday to Turkey. Frankie Corio (left) with Paul Mescal in Aftersun. A Matter of Life and Death (1946) A romantic fantasy intended as a balm for World War II’s losses, this wonderfully constructed tale follows a British airman (David Niven) who dodges the hereafter. His second-chance appreciation of life becomes joyful. Anatomy of a Fall (2023)



A legal thriller – in a rarely experienced Swiss setting – rendered as an investigation of how malleable truth and family have to be, this riveting drama delivers a powerhouse performance from a pre-Project Hail Mary Sandra Hüller. Sandra Hüller plays Sandra Voyter, who is accused of murdering her husband Samuel (Samuel Theis) in Anatomy of a Fall. The Big Lebowski (1998) With an all-time performance from Jeff Bridges as Los Angeles slacker “The Dude”, this noir-ringed black comedy from the Coen brothers remains a winningly idiosyncratic affair, complete with a scene-stealing John Turturro. The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957) David Lean’s first epic is a sober examination of duty and heroism during World War II, as imprisoned American and British officers (William Holden and Sir Alec Guinness) clash over a bridge they built for their brutal Japanese captors. Cemetery of Splendour (2015)



Thai director Apichatpong Weerasethakul is a revered figure in world cinema and this is a signature work – a gracefully fluid exploration of national trauma and private memory that turns a military hospital into a spiritual way-station. The Conformist (1970) All too relevant, Bernardo Bertolucci’s drama of warped political belonging follows a 1930s Italian civil servant (Jean-Louis Trintignant) who takes part in a fascist murder plot against his former professor. A film of cruel beauty and erotic malaise. Zoe Carides and Sam Neill in the Australian cult comedy Death in Brunswick. Alamy Stock Photo Death in Brunswick (1990) The great Sam Neill was at ease in any genre, and this mordant Australian farce, where he plays a Melbourne chef in over his head with his girlfriend and associated gangsters, is a showcase of his comedic skills. Disobedience (2017)



When an exiled photographer (Rachel Weisz) returns to her insular Orthodox Jewish community and the best friend (Rachel McAdams) she left behind, the roiling emotions between them become overwhelming. The leads are sublime together. Rachel McAdams (left) as Esti and Rachel Weisz as Ronit in Disobedience. Ghost Dog: Way of the Samurai (1999) Anchored by a graceful Forest Whitaker as the titular hitman, Jim Jarmusch’s take on the wronged gangster flick intertwines hip-hop beats and Japanese philosophy. Sometimes violent, often wry, always unique. Gone Girl (2014) With David Fincher directing, this portrait of marital discord has a forensic fierceness as a cheating husband (Ben Affleck) becomes embroiled in suspicion when his wife (Rosamund Pike) disappears. The storytelling delivers brutal implications. Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl.



La Grande Illusion (1937) An enduring masterpiece of French cinema, Jean Renoir’s humanist classic explores the bond during World War I between two captured French aviators and their German overseer. Individual connection can’t trump duty’s tragic demands. The Handmaiden (2016) The South Korean master Park Chan-wook delivers a stinging mix of erotic thriller and period crime drama in this twisty, immaculately staged tale of obsessive 1930s love between a trapped heiress and her knowing servant. Hell or High Water (2016) Taylor Sheridan’s best writing, this modern-day western from director David Mackenzie is a withering attack on inequality couched as a thriller pitting bank-robbing siblings (Chris Pine and Ben Foster) against a wily lawman (Jeff Bridges). Chris Pine and Ben Foster in Hell or High Water.

Cooking shows are boring, and supermarket shopping is too easy. So says Mario Kalpou, a Sydney chef who ditched restaurants to hunt his own food in the wild. His debut TV series, Man Eats Wild, saw him travel from the Amazon jungle to the ice floes of Greenland. Editor's pick Reality TV ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified Still firmly of the belief that food “tastes way better, and the reward is much sweeter, once you’ve almost killed yourself catching it”, he’s back with a new action-adventure foodie travelogue, Deadliest Dinners Australia. Over eight episodes, Kalpou dodges sharks and crocodiles, hunts wild buffalo, abseils down cliffs to fish off rocks lashed by waves, and maroons himself for a week on a raft on the Great Barrier Reef. And when he’s dodged death and caught his prize, he pops on a singlet and cooks it right then and there, with a fancy French sauce. “The whole point is me showing these elements in an exciting and adrenaline-fuelled manner, because I find food shows very boring,” says Kalpou, on the phone from the Greek island of Tinos. He’s there attending a family wedding with his Australian wife, Danielle, with whom he lives in Florida. “I’m a chef, and even I can’t watch a cooking segment on TV for 20 minutes. You lose interest! But if you’ve got some crazy guy abseiling down a 600-foot cliff to catch a fish and then he cooks for you, well, that’s a bit more interesting.” Mario Kalpou finds food shows “very boring”, so he made his own version... Binge Having grown up between his mother’s home near Sydney’s Wentworth Hotel, where she worked as a waitress, and his grandparents’ pig farm in rural western Sydney, Kalpou’s appreciation for both ends of the food industry is ingrained. He went on to open the Zagat-awarded Old Library restaurant in Cronulla, before deciding he was done with commercial kitchens.



“I don’t miss drunk patrons and staying up ’til three in the morning every night. But I have a lot of respect for hospitality. For me, now, it’s all about reconnecting people to the outdoors, getting them to eat clean food, respecting nature and getting healthy. I think that’s a really big missing part of today’s culture. I’m hoping this show can get people to start thinking more adventurously.” After a stint in New Zealand operating an extreme adventure lodge, he left for the US nine years ago, where he now divides his time between Miami and his Montana ranch. “It’s a perfect mix for me – I’m out on the ocean, and then I’ve got the mountains.” Kalpou hopes his show will help audiences “start thinking more about where your food comes from”. Binge Kalpou says learning from local Indigenous communities was one of the highlights of this series. Binge In the new series, Kalpou also garners knowledge from traditional owners. “Everywhere I go in the world, I meet local indigenous people. They are the original harvesters of the land. They have knowledge that is far beyond anything that I can bring to the table … The Aboriginal community in Tiwi was no different. They taught me a lot and I had a great time with them. Understanding how they’ve been doing it for thousands of years was one of my highlights of making the show.” He’s disappointed that some of the most dangerous aspects of the shoot weren’t caught on camera, though. Specifically, when he was charged by a wild buffalo in the outback, and the camera operator stopped filming and ran. Another time, he narrowly missed being stung by a box jellyfish.



Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in September “Thankfully, my spear caught the tip of the tentacles before my shin did,” he says. “That would’ve killed me. I had sharks attacking my raft at one point. I was caught in a storm out at sea. Once, when I went spearing for stingrays, I said, ‘Why don’t we just throw the drone up, just in case?’ And sure enough, there was a massive crocodile right where we were going to go in. So there were a few close calls.” Unsurprisingly, the late Steve Irwin was an early influence. “For me, it’s very important that there’s an abundance of game out there,” Kalpou explains. “We only take what we need for the plate. I had a lot of respect for that guy, and it was definitely a very, very sad moment for everyone when we lost Steve … Obviously, you have to be as careful as you can. We are dealing with a lot of uncertainty and with wild animals, nothing’s guaranteed.” Mario Kalpou (right) cites the late Steve Irwin as an early influence. Binge Kalpou is often stopped by celebrity fans in America, from UFC mixed martial arts fighters Luke Rockhold and Chuck Liddell to (once) Matt Damon. And that success suggests the trope of the rugged and fearless outback Aussie still holds appeal. “It doesn’t matter where we are in the world, anyone will tell you, ‘Those Australians are crazy!’ So we’ve got to keep that reputation going,” he says. “A lot of Americans have that idea of Australia being deadly, which it is. We have some of the most dangerous animals on the planet. But among those dangerous animals also live some of the freshest ingredients in the world. Our oceans have got some of the tastiest protein, and we have an abundance of it, so I think this show is going to be really well received.”



He’s not suggesting that everyone risk their lives for their evening meal. Rather, that Deadliest Dinners Australia encourages a closer look at what’s on our plates. Editor's pick Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now “I understand that not everyone can jump on a raft and catch their own fish, or go out and hunt … And no one should be doing anything that’s not within their parameters,” he says. “I’m a professional. I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and I don’t have a death wish. If anything, I’m telling people, ‘Hey, this is a beautiful line-caught fish. If you can access it in the supermarket, this is what you should be buying.’ “We’re getting a lot of processed foods, and there’s a lot of nasty stuff coming out of the food industry on a mass scale. So watch me do the crazy stuff, but you, at home, should be able to start thinking more about where your food comes from.” Deadliest Dinners Australia is streaming from September 9 on Binge. World.title: The gruesome tactic locals have resorted to as influencers flock to scenic hilltop lookout
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictoria The gruesome tactic locals have resorted to as influencers flock to scenic hilltop lookout Eleanor Campbell Updated September 3, 2026 — 7:02am ,first published 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A scenic lookout north of Melbourne has gone so viral that locals have resorted to dumping roadkill to deter influencers from littering and trespassing on private land. The Milky Way Point lookout, which sits on top of a hill that overlooks rolling slopes and green valleys stretching across central Victoria about 100 kilometres north of Melbourne, has long been recognised for its panoramic beauty but is suffering from an influx of visitors after going viral on social media. Visitors at the lookout near Strath Creek on Wednesday. Joe Armao Influencers sharing photos and videos of two picturesque spots located along the same, narrow one-way dirt road have lured hundreds of visitors to Strath Creek, a small rural farming town that borders the southern edge of the Tallarook State Forest. The main attraction is Hangs Tree, a large dead stringybark on an organic farm overlooking the valley, about one hundred metres before the main lookout.



One tour operator is charging tourists more than $500 a day for “viral magic tree” photography tours near the property. Some residents say they witnessed people defecating on private driveways, while other visitors left piles of garbage and toilet paper on cattle grazing land and outside people’s homes. Alex Whitford, who grew up 15 minutes away in Broadford, has started organising local clean-ups two to three times a week with other concerned community members. Last Tuesday, the group filled 13 bags with nappies, coffee cups, toilet paper and other rubbish left behind by visitors that day.



“People are coming here and having lunch, and they’re having a couple of wines, and then leaving, you know, smashed wine bottles everywhere and beer bottles. I’ve never seen so many Red Bull cans in my life,” Alex said. Alex said people were getting hurt because the steep hillside was not meant to accommodate heavy traffic. Alex Whitford and two young residents during a cleanup last week. “It’s a very, very narrow road, and it’s very under cared for. It’s a dirt road that’s full of potholes. There are trees down on the way through and people don’t know how to drive to the conditions up here,” she says. “There was a car that went off the edge maybe three weeks ago, and three people got hospitalised because it’s so busy and people don’t understand that this is not actually a publicly accessible space – it’s peoples homes and people’s backyards.”



Locals have starting placing dead kangaroos and wombats along the road to stop people from setting up bush camps and picnics on their properties. They have also erected signs asking people to take their rubbish home when leaving the spot. Melbourne resident Akhil Bollikonda and his wife, Sravani, made the day trip on Wednesday after discovering the location on YouTube. “It’s even more beautiful in person,” Akhil said.



Related Article Climate crisis Melbourne records its warmest winter on record, as bushfire season looms The pair also noticed the dumped roadkill and rubbish left by other visitors. “I think it’s really sad to see animals like that,” Akhil said. “As far as what I have seen, I saw some people littering and throwing some stuff – I don’t think that’s acceptable.” David Francis Palmer, who helps install garden beds and water beds in nearby farming properties, thinks the government should hire a security presence to monitor the area.



“I can’t honestly see the police going and knocking on people’s doors because they might have seen them taking a poo on the side of the road,” he said. “But if they know that it’s monitored, it may well restrict their bad behaviour.” Even more concerning than littering and trespassing was the issue of public safety. During the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires, the area was engulfed by flames that swept through townships in regional Victoria. Devastation in nearby Flowerdale during the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires. Pat Scala Local photographer Sara, who lives nearby and has photographed the lookout for years, says the situation could become “catastrophic” heading into the warmer summer months. “It’s not a patrolled area, the grass isn’t mown. If people are lighting little barbecue fires up there, and something like a fire did break out, and all these people are just parked across this one-way road, you wouldn’t even be able to get out of there,” she said. “It’d just be a disaster.”



A Country Fire Authority spokesperson said the local commander had reported “no issue” with the crowds or emergency access at the site. Police said they have increased their presence in the area after receiving complaints about littering, traffic congestion, illegal parking and trespassing. While Alex ultimately welcomes visitors, the ongoing damage and lack of respect shown by tourists to the place she calls home has taken a toll. “This is a place that I’ve come to every time that I’m in love, out of love, every major crossroads in my life,” she said. “Every time that I just need to think and be somewhere beautiful, this is where I come. To have that then ruined consistently – it’s devastating.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Meta released its most powerful artificial intelligence model yet, with its chief AI officer saying its capabilities are edging closer to top competitors.

Developers will be able to access and pay for Muse Spark 1.3, an updated version of its most advanced model, the company said. It will soon roll out the update to users of Meta’s social media platforms, like Instagram and Facebook, as well as Meta AI.

Alexandr Wang, chief AI officer of Meta. Bloomberg

“This is our biggest jump so far on model performance,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said in an interview, pointing to advancements in the model’s coding and agentic capabilities, or ability to complete tasks on behalf of human users. Wang said the update put Meta on par with recently released AI models from its rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.

Wang said Muse Spark 1.3 is “competitive” with Anthropic’s model, Claude Fable 5.1, and “better than” OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, particularly when it comes to coding, though OpenAI will soon be releasing a new, even more advanced model known as Astra. In his opinion, Meta’s model outperforms “any of the current Chinese models out there.”

World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street climbs; Meta releases new AI model
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street climbs; Meta releases new AI model Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated September 3, 2026 — 6:23am ,first published 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks rose on Wall Street as gains by big technology companies and relatively steady oil prices and bond yields helped boost the market after a downbeat start to the week. Nvidia rallied more than 3 per cent, lifting the Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.6 per cent. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq composite both gained 0.5 per cent. Wall Street climbed as oil prices and bond yields steadied. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Brent crude settled up 1 per cent at $US95.63 as the Iran conflict continued. Chevron edged 0.3 per cent higher after confirming it will expand operations in Venezuela. The Australian sharemarket is set for gains, with futures at 5.57am AEST pointing to a rise of 38 points, or 0.4 per cent at the open. The ASX lost 1 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.71¢



Related Article Energy One Nation wants this coal plant kept open. Its owner warns that will spell trouble Wall Street has been under pressure this week from rising oil prices and a bond-market sell-off. The rocky start to September follows a mostly positive August during which every major index notched a gain for the month. However, Wall Street remains gripped by anxiety over rising prices, government debt and the impact of global conflicts on the US and the global economy. Technology and communication services stocks accounted for some of the strongest gains Wednesday. Chipmaker Nvidia, whose big market value tend to give it more influence over the broader market’s direction, rose 3.2 per cent, while computer memory seller Micron Technology gained 2.4 per cent. Meta added 2.5 per cent as it released its most powerful artificial intelligence model yet, with its chief AI officer saying its capabilities are edging closer to top competitors. Developers on Wednesday will be able to access and pay for Muse Spark 1.3, an updated version of its most advanced model, the company said. It will soon roll out the update to users of Meta’s social media platforms, like Instagram and Facebook, as well as Meta AI.



“This is our biggest jump so far on model performance,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said in an interview on Wednesday, pointing to advancements in the model’s coding and agentic capabilities, or ability to complete tasks on behalf of human users. Wang said the update put Meta on par with recently released AI models from its rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. Dell Technologies jumped 15.8 per cent for the biggest gain among S&P 500 stocks after delivering strong second-quarter profits amid accelerating demand for artificial intelligence computing. The company also raised its fiscal year revenue outlook. Palo Alto Networks also reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street’s expectations, citing a strong market for AI cybersecurity, but its shares fell 9.3 per cent. Meanwhile, banks and credit card issuers also helped boost the market. Capital One Financial rose 2.5 per cent and American Express added 1.8 per cent. Markets in Europe fell after markets in Asia closed lower.



Oil prices held relatively steady despite the intensification in the six-month long US war with Iran. The US attacked sites in Iran over the weekend, ending a lull in major hostilities and Iran has since retaliated against sites around the Gulf region. Prices for Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.7 per cent to $US95.33 a barrel. Energy stocks were mixed. Chevron edged 0.4 per cent higher after confirming it will expand operations in Venezuela. A surge in oil prices following the start of the US war with Iran fuelled a jump in gasoline prices and global shipping costs. The conflict shut down the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 per cent of the world’s oil is typically shipped. Higher energy costs worsened inflation that was already stubbornly high amid a volatile US tariff war with much of the world. Inflation has been squeezing businesses and households at the same time that the mostly resilient jobs market shows signs of weakening. Payrolls processing firm ADP reported that private-sector employment slipped in August, according to its monthly survey. It is just a small snapshot, though, of the broader labour market and follows a government report on Tuesday that showed US job openings rose in July.



The big focus this week will be the government’s broader employment report for August, which will be released on Friday. The previous report for July showed that the jobs market stalled, with employers cutting positions. Related Article Opinion

Oil Trump kidnapped Venezuela’s president. Now he’s hijacking its future Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Both inflation and the jobs market have been key focuses for Wall Street and the Federal Reserve. “Friday’s employment report, and perhaps even more importantly next week’s inflation data, will play a significant role in determining whether policymakers decide to raise rates in September,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist, investment strategy at Edward Jones, in a research note. The Fed is trying to balance its task of supporting employment and taming inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation, which remains well above 3 per cent. The Fed has a stated goal of cooling inflation to a target of 2 per cent.



The bond market has been selling off, which is a signal that it expects borrowing costs to rise. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which tends to impact mortgage rates, rose to 4.80 per cent from 4.79 per cent late Tuesday. It has been rising steadily throughout the year and was as low as 4.20 per cent at the beginning of 2026. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for Federal Reserve moves on interest rates, held steady at 4.39 per cent. It is significantly higher for the year, though, and was as low as 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. Investors are also betting on a 64 per cent chance that the Fed will raise rates at its upcoming meeting in September, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed’s position is growing more complicated. Raising the benchmark interest rate would help cool inflation by making borrowing costs higher and slowing the economy. Doing so, though, could also hurt the employment market at a time when it is seemingly already weakening.

World.title: ‘Not a fan’: Trump ‘happy’ Harry and Meghan left the US
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaPrince Harry ‘Not a fan’: Trump ‘happy’ Harry and Meghan left the US Bo Erickson September 3, 2026 — 6:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US President Donald Trump says he’s “happy” Prince Harry and his family left the United States and relocated back to Britain. “I am happy about it. I was not a fan,” Trump said in the Oval Office when asked about the recent decision by Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, to leave California after six years. US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday (US time). AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The family arrived back in Britain at the end of August. The couple stepped down from official royal duties in 2020 when they moved to the US. “I thought they treated the royal family with great disrespect. I didn’t like it,” Trump said, mentioning his “good relationship” with the late Queen Elizabeth and her successor King Charles, who is undergoing treatment for cancer.



The president specifically criticised Meghan. “I didn’t like the way she acted. I thought she was terribly disrespectful,” he said. It’s not the first time Trump has taken aim at the pair. In April, Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine and called on Trump and the US to end the war with Russia. ”This is a moment for American leadership. A moment for America to show that it can honour its international treaty obligations,” he said. Harry and Meghan in Sydney in April. Getty Trump dismissed the call and made a passing remark about the prince’s wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex. “Prince Harry? How’s his wife? Please give her my regards,” he said. “Prince Harry is not speaking for the UK, that’s for sure,” Trump said. “I think I’m speaking for the UK more than Prince Harry.”



In February, Trump ruled out deporting Harry from the US over his immigration status. The president insisted he had “no interest” in removing Harry from the country and said he had “enough problems” with Meghan, who he said was “terrible”. After the couple’s move to the US, Harry in an Oprah interview accused the royal family of neglect. Meghan, whose mother is Black and father is white, said that when she was pregnant with her son there were “concerns and conversations about how dark his skin might be when he’s born” within the royal family. Loading Prince William, Harry’s older brother, defended the family after the accusation and said “we’re not racist”. Harry also cited press scrutiny and the government’s failure to provide security for his family as reasons for moving to California.



Now back in Britain, Harry and Meghan are expected to remain non-working royals. A person close to the couple said last month the family planned to move somewhere outside London for an extended period ‌with their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, who will go to school in Britain. Loading It is unclear what changed for the couple, but Harry has said he wants his children to spend time in Britain. “If I were the royal family, I would not have taken them back,” Trump added on Wednesday.

World.title: Rain briefly halted Demon’s US Open charge. He still breezed into the second round
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Rain briefly halted Demon’s US Open charge. He still breezed into the second round Marc McGowan September 3, 2026 — 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur had to wait until the fourth day of the US Open to play his first match. Fifty minutes later, he was off court again. New York’s wet weather continues to wreak havoc with the tournament’s first week as Australia’s world No.7, who was supposed to start his campaign on Wednesday (AEST), endured another rain delay before returning to blitz Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri, 6-2, 6-2, 6-4. Alex de Minaur, pictured during a drier practice session last week, has endured a frustrating start to the US Open. Getty Images De Minaur broke Guerrieri – playing his first-ever grand slam main draw match at age 27 – in the first game of each of the first two sets and appeared poised for a quick passage to the second round until weather intervened. He led 6-2, 4-2 when the chair umpire suspended play, with the delay lasting about two hours before he joined fellow Australians Dane Sweeny, Tristan Schoolkate, Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth as a first-round winner.



De Minaur needed only 99 minutes either side of the latest rain disruption to demolish his left-handed rival, looking sharp with his ball-striking and movement from the outset, albeit with a slight detour in the third set. With the finish line in sight, the three-time US Open quarter-finalist threw in a sloppy service game that he lost to love when trying to push 4-2 ahead. He also slipped 0-30 behind his next time with the Wilson balls before getting back on track to complete his victory. Australia’s Taylah Preston has been knocked out in the second round. Getty Images But 20-year-old wildcard Preston’s US Open is over, trounced 6-1, 6-1 in a mere 48 minutes by American Taylor Townsend in her second-round match, hitting only two winners compared to 28 unforced errors. Daria Kasatkina is also out, losing her rain-interrupted first-round clash with Spain’s former world No.2 Paula Badosa that was carried over from the previous day.



Badosa was only two points from victory when the match was paused, and had to stave off two break-back points before clinching a 6-1, 5-4 win on her ninth match point to lock in a showdown with 2024 champion Coco Gauff. Pushed out to Flushing Meadows’ back blocks on court 11, after originally being scheduled on the bigger Grandstand stadium a day earlier, de Minaur did not have the fortune of playing on one of the event’s two courts with a retractable roof. It has been a wet and wild week for tennis fans in New York. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth The challenges for de Minaur rise steeply from here – beginning in the second round with dangerous Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp, who also advanced in straight sets against outmatched Brit Jan Choinski. De Minaur’s projected rivals beyond that are 31st seed Zizou Bergs (third round) and top seed Alexander Zverev (quarter-finals), who needed almost five hours to battle past Italy’s Lorenzo Sonego in the first round.



Related Article Updated

US Open From GoFundMe to making big bank: Australian’s US Open breakthrough However, his potential path was made somewhat easier when possible fourth-round opponent, in-form No.12 seed Rafael Jodar, suffered a shock 6-2, 6-1, 6-1 loss to lucky loser Bu Yunchaokete, who entered the draw when Australia’s Thanasi Kokkinakis withdrew with an ankle issue. Joint (against No.9 seed Elina Svitolina), Duckworth (Wu Yibing) and Birrell (18th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova) are due to play their second-round matches on Thursday (AEST). World.title: Jonathan LaPaglia has one word for fans boycotting Australian Survivor: ‘Good’
World.content:
Jonathan LaPaglia returns to reality TV in the new Binge series Apocalypse – but he still has a few things to say about Australian Survivor.

A year on from his controversial sacking, the reality host is returning with a new show – and new appreciation for his loyal audience.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last time I spoke with Jonathan LaPaglia, we were on set in Samoa for what neither of us knew would be his final season of Australian Survivor. It was a brief and sometimes tight-lipped interview, snuck between filming commitments on a sweaty day which followed a tricky late-night tribal council. Had I known what was coming, I tell him at the start of this new interview two years later, this time over the phone, I would have asked different questions. “Well, had I known, I probably would have given you different answers,” he says, laughing. Related Article Reality TV Australian Survivor scored a world-first TV event. Then it sacked the host... LaPaglia certainly didn’t hold back this time. A year on from his controversial sacking, the longtime host is returning to reality TV with a new show and a new appreciation for his surprisingly loyal audience. “I really had no idea how much [fans] appreciated what I was doing,” he says, reflecting on the outrage that many Survivor fans and past players have expressed over the past 12 months at his “blindside” from the network. “I was just head down, grinding away – and I wasn’t doing it to get praise or approval … [The response] has been heartwarming and humbling. And it still continues now.” His discontent with former employer Network 10 continues, too. When I ask for his response to the many Australian Survivor fans who say they’re boycotting the show without him as host, he had a cheeky one-word reply: “Good.”



The network, he says, “told me ratings were declining, and they were looking for a way to boost that. But that hasn’t worked out, has it? They’ve lost 40 per cent of their audience. Honestly, I can’t believe they’re going again with ratings like that. Those ratings are really catastrophic. And if it continues like this, I don’t see how they can sustain it.” Former Australian Survivor host Jonathan LaPaglia, who was replaced by David Genat. Night Wright/Ten That 40 per cent drop refers to the overnight ratings for this year’s finale. It’s slightly less than that, but he’s not far off. Related Article Australian TV ‘I can’t touch Jonathan’s legacy’: David Genat on hosting Survivor – and LaPaglia’s sacking On free-to-air and 10Play that night, 462,000 people tuned in to see new host David Genat crown Caleb Beeby in April; that’s compared to a total of 764,000 the year before when Myles Kuah triumphed. Notably, this year’s final episode clashed with the finale of Australian Idol (which pulled 1.08 million viewers) but that doesn’t wholly explain the smaller audience. JLP’s last season, a shorter international special called Australia v The World, pulled 653,000 viewers for its final instalment at the end of 2025 despite being up against The Block with a mammoth audience of 1.62 million. In response, Network 10 said that much of the show’s audience comes from catch-up after those figures are collected. And if you look at the whole season, livestream numbers were up 6 per cent from the season Myles Kuah won in 2025. The latest season premiere, for instance, grew its audience 58 per cent in the seven days after it aired. But a drop of 300,000 viewers between the 2025 and 2026 finale is undeniably significant either way – especially considering the latter was triumphantly billed as a live finale and reunion.



“It makes me sad in a way because we all worked really hard on that show,” LaPaglia says. “For 10 years, we worked hard trying to build success … It’s kind of sad to see it crumble like that. It’s not what it was. And there’s a whole bunch of reasons for that.” “Honestly, I can’t believe they’re going again with ratings like that. Those ratings are really catastrophic.” Former Australian Survivor host Jonathan LaPaglia Speaking over the phone from his home in Los Angeles, LaPaglia seems unfazed by the prospect of appearing impolite or ungracious. He feels Network 10 and the production company Endemol Shine Australia have made “terrible decisions” for Australian Survivor – from this year’s “clunky” theme to what he perceives as heavy-handed production and, of course, the decision to let him go. Though he admits to not watching the full 2026 season, not having access to it in the US, LaPaglia is also happy to comment on his successor’s performance: “The stuff with David felt weird, you know?” LaPaglia theorises Genat is being “fed everything in his earpiece … it disconnects you from the players – and I think that’s what the audience is sensing”. Loading Wearing an earpiece to communicate with producers is standard practice in TV production, and in Australian Survivor scripts are often used as jumping off points for broader conversations – especially in unpredictable situations such as challenges or tribal councils. But LaPaglia, a trained actor, says he prided himself on memorising as much as possible before filming to make things feel organic.



“If the producer is trying to control every word that comes out of your mouth, you’re not in the moment any more,” LaPaglia says. He specifically praises Jeff Probst, the host and executive producer of Survivor in the US, who famously operates without an earpiece at all – occasionally to the show’s detriment. A spokesperson for Endemol Shine Australia, however, defended Genat saying, “Australian Survivor is produced today exactly as it always has been, including how the host communicates with the cast. Nothing about that process has changed between hosts. Any suggestion otherwise is untrue.” David Genat, the new host of Australian Survivor. Network 10 It’s tempting to read LaPaglia’s comments as sour grapes – and that might be partly true – but he’s also clearly motivated by a genuine passion for the show. Two of the three interviews LaPaglia has done in the past year have been with respected fan podcasts, diving deep into the mechanics of the game and how it could be improved. And that’s a passion the show’s former executive producer also appreciated. Shortly after LaPaglia’s shock exit, former EP David Forster (who had left the show around the same time and was not speaking on behalf of Network 10 or Endemol Shine) told me the pair had “epic fights” and “creative differences” over the years but “Jonathan was a brilliant host. And he was super, super, super dedicated to making the show the best it could be.” Forster does not share the former host’s criticisms of the network or production company. LaPaglia is also liberated, of course, by the fact he has a new gig to focus on. The presenter is returning to reality TV as the narrator of Apocalypse, a new series co-commissioned by Binge and Channel 4 in the UK, which drops five Australians and nine Brits into an abandoned town for 28 days with no food, running water or power – and no rules. It’s Survivor-adjacent. But a closer comparison would be Alone. The series is actually produced by some of the team behind Alone Australia, as well as the much flashier Netflix sensation Squid Game: The Challenge.



Some of the contestants on new series Apocalypse who must survive with no food, no power and no running water. Binge “This show doesn’t have [Survivor’s] game element,” LaPaglia says. “It’s more an experiment about survival and society.” It has a far spookier aesthetic, too, at least partially informed by its unique setting. The eight-part series is filmed in Muscatatuck, Indiana, a once fully functional town the size of Sydney’s CBD that was created in the 1920s for psychiatric patients but has since been abandoned. The site has been used for the past two decades to train civilian first responders and military personnel in urban warfare. As it’s depicted in the show, it could just as easily be a set for The Last of Us or The Walking Dead. “When I first saw the trailer, it really reminded me of The Blair Witch Project,” LaPaglia says. “It forced me to ask more questions than I was getting answers, and to me, that’s good, right? That’s good TV.” Loading There are a few surprises, but LaPaglia confirms there are no zombie jump scares. All the same, the show reveals reasons for contestants to be nervous around each other. Unlike Alone, these people are not survivalists. They’re everyday people with everyday jobs – from taxi drivers to cattle farmers to content creators – who occasionally have very different ideas on how to get things done. Before the first episode is over, one contestant has already unilaterally decided to start rationing food and threatened to burn everyone’s shelter to the ground if they disagree.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on SBS On Demand right now
World.content:
Rachel McAdams (left) as Esti and Rachel Weisz as Ronit in Disobedience.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great movies that span genres, filmmakers and languages. This week: SBS on Demand. For 150 other movie choices, check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+. Aftersun (2022) What we remember and what we will never know underpins this intimately audacious debut drama from Scottish filmmaker Charlotte Wells, with a young British father (Paul Mescal) taking his 11-year-old daughter (Frankie Corio) on a holiday to Turkey. Frankie Corio (left) with Paul Mescal in Aftersun. A Matter of Life and Death (1946) A romantic fantasy intended as a balm for World War II’s losses, this wonderfully constructed tale follows a British airman (David Niven) who dodges the hereafter. His second-chance appreciation of life becomes joyful. Anatomy of a Fall (2023)



A legal thriller – in a rarely experienced Swiss setting – rendered as an investigation of how malleable truth and family have to be, this riveting drama delivers a powerhouse performance from a pre-Project Hail Mary Sandra Hüller. Sandra Hüller plays Sandra Voyter, who is accused of murdering her husband Samuel (Samuel Theis) in Anatomy of a Fall. The Big Lebowski (1998) With an all-time performance from Jeff Bridges as Los Angeles slacker “The Dude”, this noir-ringed black comedy from the Coen brothers remains a winningly idiosyncratic affair, complete with a scene-stealing John Turturro. The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957) David Lean’s first epic is a sober examination of duty and heroism during World War II, as imprisoned American and British officers (William Holden and Sir Alec Guinness) clash over a bridge they built for their brutal Japanese captors. Cemetery of Splendour (2015)



Thai director Apichatpong Weerasethakul is a revered figure in world cinema and this is a signature work – a gracefully fluid exploration of national trauma and private memory that turns a military hospital into a spiritual way-station. The Conformist (1970) All too relevant, Bernardo Bertolucci’s drama of warped political belonging follows a 1930s Italian civil servant (Jean-Louis Trintignant) who takes part in a fascist murder plot against his former professor. A film of cruel beauty and erotic malaise. Zoe Carides and Sam Neill in the Australian cult comedy Death in Brunswick. Alamy Stock Photo Death in Brunswick (1990) The great Sam Neill was at ease in any genre, and this mordant Australian farce, where he plays a Melbourne chef in over his head with his girlfriend and associated gangsters, is a showcase of his comedic skills. Disobedience (2017)



When an exiled photographer (Rachel Weisz) returns to her insular Orthodox Jewish community and the best friend (Rachel McAdams) she left behind, the roiling emotions between them become overwhelming. The leads are sublime together. Rachel McAdams (left) as Esti and Rachel Weisz as Ronit in Disobedience. Ghost Dog: Way of the Samurai (1999) Anchored by a graceful Forest Whitaker as the titular hitman, Jim Jarmusch’s take on the wronged gangster flick intertwines hip-hop beats and Japanese philosophy. Sometimes violent, often wry, always unique. Gone Girl (2014) With David Fincher directing, this portrait of marital discord has a forensic fierceness as a cheating husband (Ben Affleck) becomes embroiled in suspicion when his wife (Rosamund Pike) disappears. The storytelling delivers brutal implications. Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl.



La Grande Illusion (1937) An enduring masterpiece of French cinema, Jean Renoir’s humanist classic explores the bond during World War I between two captured French aviators and their German overseer. Individual connection can’t trump duty’s tragic demands. The Handmaiden (2016) The South Korean master Park Chan-wook delivers a stinging mix of erotic thriller and period crime drama in this twisty, immaculately staged tale of obsessive 1930s love between a trapped heiress and her knowing servant. Hell or High Water (2016) Taylor Sheridan’s best writing, this modern-day western from director David Mackenzie is a withering attack on inequality couched as a thriller pitting bank-robbing siblings (Chris Pine and Ben Foster) against a wily lawman (Jeff Bridges). Chris Pine and Ben Foster in Hell or High Water.

World.title: ‘I don’t have a death wish’: Meet the Aussie chef who swapped restaurants for the wild
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cooking shows are boring, and supermarket shopping is too easy. So says Mario Kalpou, a Sydney chef who ditched restaurants to hunt his own food in the wild. His debut TV series, Man Eats Wild, saw him travel from the Amazon jungle to the ice floes of Greenland. Editor's pick Reality TV ‘There was no precedent’: The moment that had Alone producers terrified Still firmly of the belief that food “tastes way better, and the reward is much sweeter, once you’ve almost killed yourself catching it”, he’s back with a new action-adventure foodie travelogue, Deadliest Dinners Australia. Over eight episodes, Kalpou dodges sharks and crocodiles, hunts wild buffalo, abseils down cliffs to fish off rocks lashed by waves, and maroons himself for a week on a raft on the Great Barrier Reef. And when he’s dodged death and caught his prize, he pops on a singlet and cooks it right then and there, with a fancy French sauce. “The whole point is me showing these elements in an exciting and adrenaline-fuelled manner, because I find food shows very boring,” says Kalpou, on the phone from the Greek island of Tinos. He’s there attending a family wedding with his Australian wife, Danielle, with whom he lives in Florida. “I’m a chef, and even I can’t watch a cooking segment on TV for 20 minutes. You lose interest! But if you’ve got some crazy guy abseiling down a 600-foot cliff to catch a fish and then he cooks for you, well, that’s a bit more interesting.” Mario Kalpou finds food shows “very boring”, so he made his own version... Binge Having grown up between his mother’s home near Sydney’s Wentworth Hotel, where she worked as a waitress, and his grandparents’ pig farm in rural western Sydney, Kalpou’s appreciation for both ends of the food industry is ingrained. He went on to open the Zagat-awarded Old Library restaurant in Cronulla, before deciding he was done with commercial kitchens.



“I don’t miss drunk patrons and staying up ’til three in the morning every night. But I have a lot of respect for hospitality. For me, now, it’s all about reconnecting people to the outdoors, getting them to eat clean food, respecting nature and getting healthy. I think that’s a really big missing part of today’s culture. I’m hoping this show can get people to start thinking more adventurously.” After a stint in New Zealand operating an extreme adventure lodge, he left for the US nine years ago, where he now divides his time between Miami and his Montana ranch. “It’s a perfect mix for me – I’m out on the ocean, and then I’ve got the mountains.” Kalpou hopes his show will help audiences “start thinking more about where your food comes from”. Binge Kalpou says learning from local Indigenous communities was one of the highlights of this series. Binge In the new series, Kalpou also garners knowledge from traditional owners. “Everywhere I go in the world, I meet local indigenous people. They are the original harvesters of the land. They have knowledge that is far beyond anything that I can bring to the table … The Aboriginal community in Tiwi was no different. They taught me a lot and I had a great time with them. Understanding how they’ve been doing it for thousands of years was one of my highlights of making the show.” He’s disappointed that some of the most dangerous aspects of the shoot weren’t caught on camera, though. Specifically, when he was charged by a wild buffalo in the outback, and the camera operator stopped filming and ran. Another time, he narrowly missed being stung by a box jellyfish.



Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in September “Thankfully, my spear caught the tip of the tentacles before my shin did,” he says. “That would’ve killed me. I had sharks attacking my raft at one point. I was caught in a storm out at sea. Once, when I went spearing for stingrays, I said, ‘Why don’t we just throw the drone up, just in case?’ And sure enough, there was a massive crocodile right where we were going to go in. So there were a few close calls.” Unsurprisingly, the late Steve Irwin was an early influence. “For me, it’s very important that there’s an abundance of game out there,” Kalpou explains. “We only take what we need for the plate. I had a lot of respect for that guy, and it was definitely a very, very sad moment for everyone when we lost Steve … Obviously, you have to be as careful as you can. We are dealing with a lot of uncertainty and with wild animals, nothing’s guaranteed.” Mario Kalpou (right) cites the late Steve Irwin as an early influence. Binge Kalpou is often stopped by celebrity fans in America, from UFC mixed martial arts fighters Luke Rockhold and Chuck Liddell to (once) Matt Damon. And that success suggests the trope of the rugged and fearless outback Aussie still holds appeal. “It doesn’t matter where we are in the world, anyone will tell you, ‘Those Australians are crazy!’ So we’ve got to keep that reputation going,” he says. “A lot of Americans have that idea of Australia being deadly, which it is. We have some of the most dangerous animals on the planet. But among those dangerous animals also live some of the freshest ingredients in the world. Our oceans have got some of the tastiest protein, and we have an abundance of it, so I think this show is going to be really well received.”



He’s not suggesting that everyone risk their lives for their evening meal. Rather, that Deadliest Dinners Australia encourages a closer look at what’s on our plates. Editor's pick Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now “I understand that not everyone can jump on a raft and catch their own fish, or go out and hunt … And no one should be doing anything that’s not within their parameters,” he says. “I’m a professional. I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and I don’t have a death wish. If anything, I’m telling people, ‘Hey, this is a beautiful line-caught fish. If you can access it in the supermarket, this is what you should be buying.’ “We’re getting a lot of processed foods, and there’s a lot of nasty stuff coming out of the food industry on a mass scale. So watch me do the crazy stuff, but you, at home, should be able to start thinking more about where your food comes from.” Deadliest Dinners Australia is streaming from September 9 on Binge. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: Explainer: Why you need to enrol to vote by 25 October
World.content:
Explainer - If you plan on casting a vote in November's general election, the clock is ticking - unlike past elections, you have to enrol well before Election Day this year to get your say at the ballot box.

You must enrol by no later than 25 October to vote in the 7 November election.

The decision has been promoted by the government as boosting efficiency and quicker results, but the opposition and some other groups have criticised it as making it harder to vote.

The nonpartisan Electoral Commission has launched a campaign to make sure all eligible voters know about the changes.

"We are working hard to make sure voters are aware of the changes to this year's enrolment deadline," said Anusha Guler, the commission's deputy chief executive of operations.

The goal now is to get the message out to as many as possible before the window closes.

"We have seen a lot of enrolment activity in the past few months and our engagement teams report high interest in enrolling for the election when they are at community events," Guler said.

But there's still concern the new changes won't get across to everyone.

"The majority of New Zealanders - young and old - don't fully understand the changes to election rules," said Kassie Hartendorp, director of the progressive campaign organisation ActionStation Aotearoa.

"Even long-term voters we are talking to are unaware of the changes."

As of 31 August, the commission reports that 89.75 percent of eligible voters are now enrolled, and the rate for youth aged 18 to 24 - which has been falling fast - has risen some to 57.45 percent at the end of August, from 53.89 percent at the end of July.

"There are now 3,636,524 people enrolled to vote, up from 3,609,435 on 31 July," Guler said.

Of course, there could be even more.

Here's what you need to know about getting sorted to vote this year.

VNP / Daniela Maoate-Cox

You must enrol to vote by midnight Sunday, 25 October

In the past few elections, you could enrol at any time during early voting right up to Election Day.

Not any more. Enrolment ends before the early voting period begins 26 October.

How to enrol to vote:

Online: Visit the Electoral Commission website and put in your details.

Phone: Call 0800 36 76 56 to get an enrolment form sent to you in the mail.

Text: Text your name and address to 3676 to get a form sent to you in the mail. Calls and texts are free.

If you need additional help to enrol, the Electoral Commission has details on that too.

But actually, enrolling by 4 October is even better

If you enrol by 4 October, which is Writ Day, you can get your EasyVote card - which isn't mandatory, but helps staff find your name and details on the electoral roll on Election Day.

Many people this year may get their EasyVote card by email instead of the post - read here for more details on why that is.

You'll also be on the printed roll, which closes 4 October - if you enrol after that date and before 25 October, your vote will be a "special vote."

Special votes are by anyone who isn't on the electoral roll or unpublished roll, lives overseas or votes away from a polling place because they can't get to one.

I think I'm already enrolled - how do I check?

More than 3.6 million enrolment packs were sent out to enrolled voters between 17 to 22 August so they could confirm their details were up to date.

If you didn't receive an enrolment pack in the mail, you definitely want to check your status.

Once again, you'll go online to check that. You'll need to have a New Zealand driver licence, passport or RealMe verified identity.

"We're getting a lot of packs returned to us because people have moved. If you didn't receive a pack, it means you are not enrolled or need to update your address," said the Electoral Commission's director of strategic engagement and partnerships Shane Whitfield.

The commission will also send 2 million followup email reminders to voters, and eight community hubs will be set up at shopping malls and other locations in major cities to sign up voters.

Some electorate boundaries and names have also changed since the last general election, so make sure you know where you vote from.

If you need additional help, contact the commission at the freephone number 0800 36 76 56.

Voter enrolment packs returned to the Electoral Commission this year because the intended recipient has moved. Supplied

Will earlier enrolment deadlines actually affect many people?

Going by the last election, it sure could. The Electoral Commission said that in 2023 there were about 450,000 new enrolments or updates during the early voting period, including 110,000 on Election Day.

Guler said the commission is using a "multi-channel approach to reach people on the channels they use every day and in person, so that we reach all voters, including younger voters and new New Zealanders".

"We are using a wide range of advertising channels including TV, radio, print, digital advertising and social media."

That work may be paying off.

"We are seeing higher enrolment numbers than in the previous two elections," Guler said.

The number of main roll electors signed up as of 31 August is up 5.9 percent from the same time in 2023 and 10.4 percent from 2020, the commission said.

The Electoral Commission has previously estimated about 55,000 party votes and 73,000 electorate votes could be disallowed this year due to a lack of enrolment.

The Electoral Commission has said it won't be keeping track of how many voters are turned away on Election Day if they're not enrolled, Newsroom reported.

Groups such as the Citizens Advice Bureau, ActionStation and local ratepayers associations are among many leading the drive to enrol voters.

"ActionStation is working alongside thousands of community leaders, local groups, and organisations in the biggest community-led 'get out the vote' effort Aotearoa has ever seen," Hartendorp said.

"In 12 years, we've never seen such passion and energy from local people to get involved in an election. We're seeing communities in every single electorate work hard to make sure their friends and whānau are enrolled before October 25."

Christopher Luxon casts his vote in 2023. RNZ / Tim Collins

What's the reason for these changes, anyway?

The coalition government eliminated same-day enrolment as part of a suite of changes in the Electoral Amendment Bill which was passed last December.

In announcing the changes last year, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said that "allowing late enrolments, however well intentioned, has placed too much strain on the system".

Special votes have to undergo checks before they're finalised, and the number of special votes has been growing in recent elections - in 2023, nearly 21 percent, or 603,257 of all votes cast, were special votes. Only 78,030 of those were from overseas voters.

In 2023 it took three weeks for special votes to be counted to confirm the election results.

This year the Electoral Commission is expecting to process about 700,000 special votes.

"I just think three weeks is way too long to count special votes, I think that needs to be sped up," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said in 2023.

Special votes have tended to tilt election results to the left in past elections - in 2023 they gave Te Pāti Māori two more electorates and the Greens an extra list seat. National lost two MPs and needed New Zealand First to form a government.

RNZ / Russell Palmer

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins has promised if elected his government would reverse the changes to electoral enrolments.

Senior Labour MP Damien O'Connor said the coalition was trying to "cut out and eliminate" the votes of poorer, more transient people, while Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty has said the electoral law changes could have a "massive" impact on the election.

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown has said there is "plenty of time" for people to sort their enrolment.

"People know that they need to enrol to vote," he said. "There'll be an advertising campaign run by the Electoral Commission. There's plenty of opportunity for people to enrol. Plenty of time."

But ActionStation's director said the change will make it harder for people to vote.

"These changes are dangerous to democracy. Any expert in how voter turnout works will tell you these changes will likely disenfranchise voters," Hartendorp said.

"For the last 100 years, we've had a history of making it easier to access our right to vote. The current government has quietly flipped that proud tradition, knowing this change would make it harder for people to have their say."

Goldsmith said there was enough time before the next election for people to enrol in time: "I absolutely reject any idea that people will not be able to vote, they just need to be enrolled."

Despite a delay in results being one of the main reason the government pushed to change enrolment dates, the Electoral Commission has said it won't dramatically speed up the official results.

World.title: Confused ASB customers report $0 balance in KiwiSaver
World.content:
ASB customers have reported widespread issues with KiwiSaver, with balances showing up at zero.

One told RNZ he checked his KiwiSaver last night, only to find no money there.

"I check my KiwiSaver everyday, and last night the balance was at zero," Peter said.

He said he called the ASB fraud line, and was met with a pre-recorded message saying the bank was working to resolve the issue.

ASB said its KiwiSaver and Investment Fund Balances were now displaying correctly after a "technical issue" last night.

"Customers' funds were not affected by last night's display issue. ASB apologises to customers for any concern or confusion this issue may have caused."

World.title: Solomons Islands reopens debate over dialogue partners at Pacific Islands Forum
World.content:
RNZ's Teuila Fuatai in Koror, Palau

The Solomon Islands is asking its fellow Pacific Island Forum (PIF) members to reconsider the presence of dialogue partners at the regional body's annual leaders meeting, RNZ Pacific understands.

The issue was raised at a closed meeting of the PIF on Wednesday morning in Palau, with the Solomon Islands asking members to consider whether the leaders meeting should be separate from the dialogue partners' process, RNZ Pacific understands.

The presence of partners at the annual leaders' meeting has been a contentious issue over the past few years.

Each year, a partners dialogue meeting is held as part of the leaders' meeting week. In total, 21 countries are PIF dialogue partners, with key regional players like the United States, China, Japan and France among them. Taiwan, which also has a delegation in Koror, is a development partner.

However, last year, then-host Solomon Islands banned partners from attending and deferred the dialogue partner meeting to Palau. It was held on Tuesday in Koror.

As interest in the region has grown, the presence of partner delegations, as well as NGOs and observers has increased substantially. The current leaders' meeting was expected to bring 2000 people to Palau.

While interest and investment in the region are welcomed by members, the sheer number of people, countries and organisations now attending the leaders' week has resulted in an extensive list of bilateral meetings and sideline events that sit outside the official PIFs agenda.

Christopher Landau United States Deputy Secretary of State at the opening ceremony of 55 PIFLM in Koror, Palau. 31 August 2026. TMC Palau/Ohanna Rabo Galo

RNZ Pacific understands several delegations from Pacific nations have struggled to keep up with the demands of the week. It is understood that a separate partner process could offer more time for members to speak directly with one another and focus on the PIF agenda.

Despite that, support for the Solomon Islands proposal among the membership is unlikely to be clearcut. The Solomons' decision to stop partners' attending last year divided members.

New Zealand foreign minister Winston Peters made it clear at the time he believed partners needed to be at the leaders' meeting because of the investment role they played in the region - a sentiment he repeated this year. While Sāmoa, represented by previous prime minister Fiame Naomi Mata'afa, and Palau president Surangel Whipps Jnr supported the decision from then-Solomons Prime Minister Jeremiah Manele.

The Solomons proposal also comes as the 18 PIF members have been deliberating on a new partnership structure. The proposed structure would divide partners into two tiers, with the top tier having greater access to member states.

With large delegations from China, the US and Taiwan present, geopolitical competition around the PIF has dominated headlines.

The absences of five leaders, including Solomons Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, has also been reported extensively. Wale had to return home after landing in Koror due to a motion of no confidence in his leadership.

World.title: 'I don't need to carry her anymore': Family relieved by newly installed lift
World.content:
Queenstown farmer funds wheelchair lift for Wellington family Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A dad who has been lifting his teenage daughter from her wheelchair up the stairs to their front door is relieved a lift has been installed with the help of a generous benefactor.

The Thomas family live on a steep section in Wellington and work to put in a lift was on hold for more than a year because the funding would not cover the cost.

After hearing the story on Morning Report in April, a farmer got in contact with RNZ to offer help and the lift is now complete.

Dinson Thomas said his 13-year-old daughter Ann was already using the lift herself.

"She's very happy because before when I carried her, she was scared. Now she's very happy because she's operating the lift and she's happy with it."

He said he is relieved to have a lift and thanks the farmer, who wishes to remain anonymous.

"Now it's really easy I don't need to carry her anymore," Thomas said.

"She's very safe now and I am also safe I don't need to carry her, it's also [good for] my health."

The Thomas family have seven steps to their front door in Newlands, which became a hazard as Ann grew older.

They bought the house when Ann was three and carrying her was much easier.

She weighs close to 40 kilograms and has cerebral palsy and complex needs.

Thomas said they received the maximum funding to have a platform lift installed, just over $15,000. The work started last February but a month later he was advised the quote came in $4000 over the funding - so he put the project on hold because he could not afford it.

The farmer earlier said that sounded like a hard situation to be in, and he wanted to help.

World.title: Apprenticeship numbers hit 15-year low
World.content:
The number of people learning on the job has nose dived Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The number of people in apprenticeships and workplace training hit a 15-year low last year and continued falling in the first quarter of the year.

Education Ministry figures showed there were 108,315 people in workplace-based learning last year, fewer than in any year since 2011 and down 32 percent from a 15-year high of 158,570 reached in 2022.

A briefing to Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds in July showed enrolments had fallen further in the first three months of the year - 11 percent lower than in the same period of 2025.

Industry insiders said the drop was caused by factors including a struggling economy, the expiry of various government subsidies for apprentices, and several years of change in vocational education and training policy.

The annual figures showed workplace learning in Agriculture and Environmental Studies was worst hit, halving since 2022 to 9390 learners.

Engineering and related technologies dropped by a third to 29,870 enrolments and Architecture and Building by 29 percent to 28,650.

Energy and Infrastructure Industry Skills Board chief executive, Philip Aldridge, said the drop in numbers was a worry.

"We have certainly noticed it and we are concerned," he said.

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge RNZ/John Gerritsen

He said business was likely to improve, but the current downturn would have a lasting effect.

"We're going to struggle for labour and that means we're going to have difficulty resourcing up for key initiatives, whether its roading, water, extractive projects and we'll be over-reliant on immigration to fill those gaps," he said.

"Water for example, there's a $48 billion investment plan over the next 10 years with the new water entities and that requires 6000 new people and so we're worried about where we're going to find those people because the training pipeline is nowhere near 6000 people."

Primary Industry Training Organisation (ITO) chief executive Ginny Vincent said the primary sector's big drop in trainees and apprentices was partly a comedown from abnormally high enrolments post-Covid and partly a response to the economy.

Primary Industry Training Organisation chief executive Ginny Vincent. Supplied / Primary ITO

"If I talk about primary sector businesses they're probably operating cautiously because of cost pressures and some uncertainty, probably not recruiting as much as they would so employers are deferring starting any new apprenticeships or trainees," she said.

Vincent said there was also confusion after six years of constant change in vocational training.

"From an industry perspective, six years-plus of structural change has meant considerable disruption and a little bit of uncertainty around how the workplace training is funded ... and how things are being arranged and delivered."

Vincent said another factor was that many farm employees were immigrants on work visas and they were not eligible for government-subsidised training.

Vincent said the Primary ITO's numbers were still down but she was confident they would pick up.

Building and Construction ITO (BCITO) chief executive Jason Hungerford said there was no shortage of people wanting an apprenticeship but the industry was in tough times.

"At BCITO for the trades we cover we've got around 600 people ready and willing to start an apprenticeship right now. What we don't have is perhaps the confidence of some of those employers that are willing to take that next step and take them on," he said.

Building and Construction ITO chief executive Jason Hungerford. Supplied / Building and Construction ITO

Hungerford said 75,000 people had left the sector in the past year or two and while many had been replaced, that churn was itself a problem in terms of the industry's skill base.

"I think a bigger issue than growing our apprentices is how do we retain them. How do we retain them in the sector, both from an industry point of view but also from a completing-a-qualification [point of view]," he said.

Hungerford said the boom-bust cycle in industry training was a problem and the government could help by investing in infrastructure projects when the economy was lagging.
