Tech.title: Pangram Has Emerged as the Gold Standard of AI Detection. Should You Trust It?
Tech.content:
Pangram is an AI startup with 24 employees, headquartered above a Popeyes in Brooklyn. It has raised $13 million to date—about 0.0072 percent of what OpenAI has—and was virtually unknown until earlier this year. But if Pangram is to be believed, it’s the one force standing in the way of a full machine takeover of the written word.

Pangram promises to detect how much AI was involved in the generation of any given text, and it does so as a best-guess percentage (using AI, of course). In January, speculation swirled on Reddit and YouTube that the author Mia Ballard may have used AI to write Shy Girl, a self-published novel picked up for traditional publication by Hachette. Although Ballard denied it, Pangram’s CEO posted on X that the book was 78 percent AI-generated. Hachette later canceled the release.

A barrage of similar accusations followed. The New York Times was called out for running an AI-generated installment of its Modern Love column. Pangram score: 100 percent. Then came a winner of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize (100 percent), the novel Daggermouth (60 percent), and a thriller titled Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body that had sold for $2.4 million (97 percent). In late July, Substack announced it was integrating Pangram into its platform so readers could quickly determine possible AI use.

Not all writers see this as a good thing. “There is such distaste and anger at the AI detection software,” says Jane Friedman, an author and publishing expert. “There’s this feeling like they are just as evil, if not more evil, than the AI companies themselves.” Outside of publishing and higher education, Pangram isn’t a household name, but I suspect it’s about to be; the demand to distinguish LLM churn from human writing grows with each passing day. The question to ask now is: How much can the company be trusted?

Max Spero, Pangram’s 30-year-old cofounder and CEO, dials into our Google Meet from his phone, takeout box in one hand and skyscrapers in the background. He’s wearing a beige T-shirt and has short dark hair, a boyish expression, and a wide smile. He says he’s rushing home with lunch and will call back. Ten minutes later, Spero reappears inside his Brooklyn apartment. He’s been on hiring calls all morning, he says. In July, Pangram raised $9 million and announced the launch of its newest model, Pangram 4. The company’s website lists six new job openings, which would increase headcount by 25 percent.

I ask Spero about growing up in California, a softball question that makes him visibly uncomfortable. Discussing the nuances of Pangram’s tech comes more naturally to him than answering personal queries—or speaking to the company’s involvement in literary scandals. Spero takes a bite of his meal and says he was raised in the Los Angeles suburb of La Crescenta. He loved programming and joined his school’s robotics team. As an undergrad at Stanford, he met Bradley Emi, his eventual Pangram cofounder. (My several emailed requests to interview Emi were ignored by the company’s comms team.) After school, Spero went to Google, where he worked on FLoC, a technology designed to replace third-party cookies by grouping Chrome users by interests. (Google killed off FLoC in 2022 after the product was met with privacy concerns.) Spero later worked for the autonomous car company Nuro, while Emi made his way through Tesla and AI biotech company Absci. After ChatGPT launched in 2022, the duo saw a business opportunity to confront a future filled with AI content. In 2023, they founded Checkfor.ai, then renamed the company Pangram a year later. By then, at least a dozen other companies were crowding the detection space, including Originality.ai, GPTZero, and Turnitin; Pangram performed well in some early, independent testing and emerged as a front-runner.

Tech.title: The New York Times Just Dropped a Brand-New Wordle Spinoff
Tech.content:
Wordle fans, start marking your calendars for hump day.

On Wednesday, the New York Times introduced a weekly drop of five to six new puzzles created by the newspaper’s puzzle constructors and editors. The new puzzles aren’t daily but will be released every Wednesday in a group and will include twists on current puzzles. They’re only available to people who pay for a New York Times Games or All Access subscription.

The types of bonus puzzles offered may vary from week to week. Other puzzles, including Wordle, Connections, Strands, Pips, and Connections: Sports Edition, remain free, while some others are behind a paywall.

CNET offers daily hints and answers for Wordle, Connections, Strands, Connections: Sports Edition and the Mini Crossword.

Wordle in 1

I played the new batch of games, and I think the most popular game will be Wordle in 1. Regular Wordle gives you six tries to guess a five-letter word, uses specific colors to indicate if you’ve guessed a letter that’s included, and also notes if you put it in the right spot. Wordle in 1 sets up five five-letter grids, each with a different word, and fills them in with some correct and some incorrect letters. You use the letters provided to figure out the answers.

Wordle in 1 provides you with some correct and some incorrect letters, and you take it from there. NYT/Screenshot by CNET

In the example above, the colored letters indicate that the U and T are in the right spaces, that there’s no N at all, and the S and the other T needs to be relocated. (Answer at the bottom of this post if you want a spoiler.)

More games: Connections 3×3, Colorful Strands

Other games in the weekly drop also play off the current New York Times puzzles.

Connections 3×3 is a smaller version of the regular Connections puzzle, offering just nine words or phrases that you have to separate into three groups.

Colorful Strands is exactly the same as regular Strands, but the answers show up in color, which is something the regular puzzle does from time to time.

Mystery Mini is another Mini Crossword, with a creative twist. The first one, for example, uses two answers twice, with different clues, and other answers are also related.

Easy Mode Crossword simply takes the standard Friday crossword and just makes the clues easier. There’s also a monthly Special Crossword, which might be written in collaboration with a famous person or feature a theme. Comedian Rachel Dratch, a former Saturday Night Live cast member, co-constructed a puzzle released Tuesday.

That promised spoiler

Spoiler for the pictured Wordle in 1 puzzle above: The answer is TRUST.

Tech.title: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe’s Surprise Switch 2 Update Brings Multiplayer Mayhem
Tech.content:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is seemingly the game that Nintendo refuses to move on from. The racing game, originally released on the Wii U back in 2014 and then updated for the Nintendo Switch in 2017, received what could be the greatest update for the game that could get players back on the track.

Nintendo surprise dropped the Version 4.0.0 update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe on Tuesday, which adds a new eight-player, split-screen option when playing the game on the Nintendo Switch 2, as well as CameraPlay support and support for higher-resolution TVs. It’s the new multiplayer option that has gone viral on social media as gamers are trying to wrap their heads around playing an eight-player race on the Switch 2’s 7.9-inch screen.

While this split-screen mode can work on the Switch 2 in handheld mode, it’s clear that the new multiplayer option is designed for gamers to play the game with friends on a TV. This update also expands Mario Kart 8 Deluxe’s multiplayer beyond the four-player limit it had since launch. Instead, up to eight racers can play together, with each racer able to have their own individual Joy-Con, Switch Pro Controller or Switch 2 Pro Controller. Those who paid the $25 for the Mario Kart 8 Deluxe – Booster Course Pass will also have access to all 96 courses in the VS Race multiplayer mode.

CameraPlay support was also added on Tuesday. This feature, which made its debut on the Switch 2, lets players connect a USB camera to their console during multiplayer and online matches so other players can see their faces while playing. Nintendo sells an official USB camera for the console, but there are many alternatives that work just as well.

Another welcome change in the update is shortened loading times when playing on the Switch 2. Players should notice it takes less time to start races and battles when playing.

This update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is part of Nintendo’s current initiative to update its Switch games and optimize them for the Switch 2. On Monday, Pikmin 3 Deluxe received a similar update to match the resolution of the newer handheld console. Tuesday’s update also marks the date of the new Switch 2 price tag of $500.

Nintendo announced the price jump of its newest console back in May, citing “changes in market conditions.” Gaming hardware companies such as Nintendo, Sony, Microsoft and Valve have had to deal with the rising costs of components, mainly memory and storage, in what’s been dubbed RAMaggeddon. So far, there’s no sign that the memory shortage driving these price increases will end anytime soon.

Tech.title: At G20, Big Tech and Global Leaders Can’t Escape AI’s Data Center Problem
Tech.content:
At the G20 Innovation Ministerial summit on Wednesday, US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, on stage with Anthropic Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown, made a controversial argument: If the world wants to grow AI, we need data centers.

On the surface, this is logical. Data centers are a crucial piece of infrastructure that tech companies need to power their training of new AI models. But the first part of that “if-then” statement is questionable. These massive AI server farms are wildly unpopular, in large part because of serious environmental concerns, energy costs and resource guzzling.

Over the past few years, data center construction projects have been sprouting across the US, with about 3,400 sites already operational and another 2,000 planned, according to Cleanview’s data center tracker tool. The facilities are notorious for demanding massive amounts of electricity to power AI compute, clean water to cool the computer chips and acreage to build on.

Tech companies are quick to claim that data centers create jobs and give back to the tax base. But local residents are footing the bill and have pushed back, saying they bring noise and air pollution and higher utility bills. And the growing opposition is bipartisan: Both Democrats and Republicans (as well as independents) are against new data centers in their area.

That’s why the US government is launching a campaign to persuade other global leaders to promote AI data centers. Will it work?

Rising anti-Big Tech protests

The backlash against AI and Big Tech came right to the G20’s doorstep on Wednesday, as the summit is being held at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. About 100 students and local residents participated in a protest against the in-person and virtual appearances by Lutnick, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk.

UNC-Chapel Hill students and local residents gathered outside The Carolina Inn, where the G20 forum is being held. Katelyn Chedraoui/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

“We as students and community members are showing up because we do not think that tech billionaires should feel comfortable and have a place on our campus,” said Amy, a student and member of UNC’s Sunrise organization, which advocates for social and economic justice.

Amy, who did not provide her last name, told me that students have been protesting the addition of over 20 Flock surveillance cameras across campus. Protestors chanted, “Hey ho, hey ho, Sam Altman has got to go.” Some signs called out Lutnick’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein, while others advocated for tech companies to put people over profits.

Government response: No more doomerism

Pro-AI tactics often use a common message: Anyone who doesn’t get on board will be left behind. President Donald Trump doubled down on this claim with a post on Truth Social this week, saying that communities that don’t allow data centers to move in will end up “backwards and poor.” Beyond the inflammatory rhetoric, there’s no proof this is true.

The administration’s approach during this week’s summit has been to focus on growth, unburdened by new regulation. Lutnick and other officials are adamant that existing laws and statutes are sufficient to address any issues posed by AI and that additional rules would be burdensome. But we’ve already seen how AI can perpetrate harm under current US laws.

“This is an opportunity to democratize intelligence,” Lutnick said on Wednesday, adding that he “doesn’t buy the AI doomerism at all.” AI doomers tend to believe AI poses a serious, existential risk to humanity.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) and US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick on stage at the G20 forum. Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

In an effort to assuage concerns that data centers raise people’s electric bills, the Trump administration got the biggest tech companies to sign a ratepayer protection pledge, which says tech companies, not individuals, will absorb any rising energy costs. But as CNET reported, the pledge is voluntary, and there’s no way to enforce it.

Energy constraints on the US’s already overtaxed electrical grid, combined with community opposition to data centers, could create a new incentive for tech companies to optimize their operating systems and software to run on less energy. And tech companies say that once they have sufficient energy, the excess will be returned to communities. But that’s speaking optimistically.

Tech response: Focus on curing cancer

There’s no one better suited (or less objective) to speak about data centers than Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

“Every single country that we’ve worked with, the moment we created [AI] infrastructure locally, all of a sudden, the startups and researchers just really get activated,” Huang told G20 ministers on Wednesday.

Huang said the US’s regulatory environment allows for substantial build-out of AI infrastructure. Though tech companies often boast that data centers create jobs, many studies say that job growth is overstated. After construction is complete, employment opportunities tend to be minimal once the site is built and running.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (left) on stage with Lutnick discussing AI at the G20 Innovation Ministerial. Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

In an effort to combat data centers’ growing reputation problem, tech companies have pivoted their focus to the potential scientific advances AI could help cultivate in the future. The marketing pitch goes: If AI cures cancer, isn’t the cost worth it?

“The economic scientific impacts [of AI] that we’ll see five years from now will be immense. I think that we will make a major impact in things like curing cancer,” Anthropic’s Brown said on Wednesday.

But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei seems to discern that AI hype isn’t entirely effective. In August, he said that tech companies need to win back people’s trust, writing on X: “At this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*.”

That at least appears to read the room, even if it doesn’t prevent the harm data centers cause to communities in the meantime.

Tech.title: Trump Administration Sides With OpenAI in Publishers’ Copyright Lawsuits
Tech.content:
The Trump administration has weighed in on a series of copyright disputes between news organizations and OpenAI, supporting the ChatGPT-maker’s position that its use of publishers’ content to train AI models constituted fair use.

The statement of interest of the United States (PDF) was filed Tuesday in a series of cases in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, including one initiated by The New York Times and another by Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company. Ziff Davis filed the suit in 2025, alleging OpenAI infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.

In its filing, the federal government said a ruling in publishers’ favor could hinder AI development, limit competition among AI firms and hurt the country’s competitiveness with foreign developers.

“Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States … threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” the filing states.

Graham James, a spokesperson for The New York Times, told CNET in a statement that the administration is “siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies” instead of American creators and that doing so undermines both creators and AI developers.

“Both AI and creators can thrive – AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires,” James said. “The Administration’s proposal to let companies take that content without permission or compensation would undermine the sustainability of the human-created content that a healthy society depends on, and which AI needs to function.”

CNET has reached out to representatives for OpenAI and Ziff Davis for comment.

The Times initiated the lawsuit at the end of 2023, a year after ChatGPT’s debut. In its initial complaint (PDF), the news organization said large language models, such as those that power ChatGPT, were built using content that included millions of its articles. That training constituted an effort to “free-ride” on the Times’ investment in journalism and create products that compete.

The government said it sees LLMs’ ability to help others compete with large media corporations as a positive development. It cited independent authors using AI models to generate images that might otherwise require a photographer or license, and LLMs directing users to “dissenting sources that offer contrary information or perspectives.”

“It is not in the public’s interest for the largest technology companies to have an oligopoly on LLM training due to licensing entry barriers that function primarily as large subsidies for old mainstream media companies,” the government stated.

Major media companies aren’t the only ones who’ve sued OpenAI over copyright infringement. Authors, including big names like George R.R. Martin, have also accused the company of using their works in model training. OpenAI rival Anthropic, which makes Claude, settled piracy claims with authors for $1.5 billion, although a judge ruled the company’s use of copyrighted material was fair use.

Earlier this summer, publishers accused OpenAI of withholding evidence about how it trains its models, claims the company has denied.

Tech.title: Acer Shows Off a Transformer-ish Concept for a Windows Gaming Handheld
Tech.content:
Project DualPlay Mini Acer/CNET

While we tend to think of Windows gaming handhelds as primarily gaming devices, they really have more in common with ultralight laptops: They run Windows, have a built-in screen and perform like them thanks to mobile processors with integrated graphics. And though some people have always used them as a primary computer, today’s high prices for both handhelds and traditional computers make handhelds seem like an even more attractive general-purpose option for gamers.

But if you want to play a game with a keyboard and mouse, much less nongaming uses, you frequently experience the cumbersome process of connecting to the input devices or being restricted to wherever you’ve got a dock set up.

Project DualPlay Mini Tara Brown/CNET

Acer’s Project DualPlay Mini concept takes a Transformers-like approach to making a handheld more suitable for general computing and KBM gaming: It’s a clamshell laptop design with the speakers on either side of the display, but the 8-inch screen flips up, and the grips are on the back of the speakers, so it turns into a traditional handheld when closed.

You’d still have to connect a mouse, but the built-in keyboard remedies the most awkward design issue. As with any of these devices, you can connect to an external monitor as well as other peripherals as well.

The closest I’ve seen to a multipurpose design in a Windows gaming handheld is Lenovo’s Legion Go series (not the Legion Go Fold, though). But “close” in this case just comes down to a built-in kickstand that makes it a little easier to use on a desktop.

Predator Atlas 7

There aren’t any specs for it — it’s not a real product, at least at the moment — but Acer says it will use the same Intel G3 chips as in its Predator Atlas 8, announced at Computex 2026 in May and slated to ship later this month for an as-yet-unannounced price. The company has followed that with another launch this week for the Predator Atlas 7, a slightly smaller, lighter — and presumably cheaper — 7-inch model. It’s expected to ship around October or later in 2026.

Tech.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Color Leak Claims Black Model Will Replace Silver This Year
Tech.content:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to be unveiled at the company’s Sept. 9 launch event, and a new rumor appears to be firming up the three-color lineup for these phones.

According to leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Weibo (h/t MacRumors), the iPhone 18 Pro is now in full production and is set to come in sky blue, pure black and burgundy models. Prior iPhone 18 rumors have pointed to these colors, although the names have varied (dark cherry instead of burgundy, for instance).

For anyone hoping for a silver or gray shade, this report suggests Apple may skip that color this year, instead bringing back black after abandoning it on the iPhone 17 Pro series. Last year, black was available on other iPhone models, such as the iPhone Air, the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17E.

With just about a week to go until Apple’s official event, it’s likely that reports on the iPhone 17 Pro’s looks will continue to leak.

Even more prescient than the color of the iPhone 18 Pro will be its cost. The tech giant has hiked prices across other Apple products amid the ongoing memory shortage that’s making consumer electronics more expensive.

The new Mac Mini with an M6 processor, for instance, starts at $899, which is quite a bit higher than the $599 Mac Mini with an M4 processor it replaced. It’s entirely possible that the iPhone 18 Pro line could have a higher starting price than the $1,099 iPhone 17 Pro, should Apple follow this trend. We’ll find out more on Sept. 9.

Tech.title: Is The Calorie Counter on Your Smartwatch Accurate? Not Really, Study Finds
Tech.content:
If you use your smartwatch for activity and sleep tracking, that’s great, but if your main goal is to track calories burned during those activities, you may want to find a new method. According to a new Florida International University study, smartwatches overestimate how many calories people are actually burning, with some watches making more mistakes than others.

The study focused on four smartwatches: the Apple Watch Series 8, Fitbit Sense 2, Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 and Garmin Forerunner 955, and had a total of 58 participants.

Each participant in the study wore the smartwatches along with a Cosmed K5, a device that measures energy burn, and an electrocardiogram chest strap to track heart rate. Participants’ age, sex, height and weight were entered into all of the devices. They then completed a workout on a stationary exercise machine in a controlled setting and the results from each device were compared.

The study found that the watches averaged a 15 to 25% margin of error and overestimated calories burned across the board. That means that if you take a brisk evening walk and your watch says you burned 200 calories, your actual burn would likely be somewhere between 160 and 174 calories.

However, accuracy also varies by brand. The study found that the Apple Watch had the smallest margin of error, while Samsung and Garmin struggled more with overestimation. It was also noted that Fitbit had numerous glitches during testing, so researchers excluded some data due to its tracking issues.

From left, FIU student Gabriel Cabeda Ramirez, Ph.D student Daimien Campos and FIU researcher Jason Kostrna participate in a demonstration of the study protocol Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, at Florida International University in Miami. Taimy Alvarez/Florida International University

The researchers also found that accuracy worsened when body fat increased, but have not discovered why that is.

In a press release about the study, Jason Kostrna, the study’s lead author and associate professor of kinesiology and exercise science in FIU’s College of Arts, Sciences & Education, cautioned against relying too heavily on your smartwatch’s calorie readings day in and day out.

“You could be hundreds of calories off each week and easily end up in a calorie surplus when you think you’re in a calorie deficit,” he said.

Instead, smartwatch wearers should take those calorie numbers with a grain of salt and pay close attention to how their bodies and energy levels feel.

Tech.title: Circular’s New Smart Ring Brings Mobile Payments to Your Finger
Tech.content:
Circular is putting mobile payments at your fingertips with its new Circular Ring 3 series. Announced at IFA, the consumer tech show in Berlin, the Circular Ring 3 Pro and Circular Ring 3 Slim are bringing more smartwatch-like capability to the ring category.

Both models add contactless payments to Circular’s existing health tracking and bring back the haptic vibration feature from the original Circular Ring. That means the rings can buzz your finger for app notifications, medication reminders and health alerts without a screen or phone as the middle man.

The screen-free wearable category is having its moment in the spotlight with an explosion of new rings and wrist-based trackers from Oura, Ultrahuman, Google and Garmin promising to track long-term health trends round the clock without the battery limitations and distractions that come along with tiny smartwatch screens. But that same lack of a screen has limited how much these devices can do beyond collecting health data.

Circular, based in Paris, is carving out its own lane by pushing more functionality onto the finger. Its FDA-cleared ECG feature and AFib detection, and NFC payments and haptic alerts push the Ring 3 series closer to smartwatch territory, without giving up the low-profile design that draws people to rings in the first place.

The trade-off is that Circular’s platform still isn’t as established as competitors such as Oura, Whoop and Google, which have had more time to build out their health insights, coaching and ecosystems.

The Ring 3 lineup also expands Circular’s health tracking with blood pressure trends, glucose trend estimates and advanced sleep metrics. But without FDA clearance, these remain wellness features designed for spotting trends and more conversation starters with a doctor rather than diagnostic tools.

Circular/CNET

Circular Ring 3 Slim vs. Circular Ring 3 Pro

Both rings share Circular’s core health tracking, NFC payments and the returning haptic vibration motor, but there are some important hardware differences.

Dimensions: As the name suggests, the Ring 3 Slim is a lot smaller, in both height and width, than the Pro and the previous generation, putting it closer to the ultra-slim Oura Ring 5, which was the smallest ring I’d tested at the time. The Ring 3 Pro, by contrast, is also slightly shorter than its predecessor, but it’s gained thickness and weighs exactly the same as the Gen 2 ring.

Circular Ring 3 Slim Circular Ring 3 Pro Oura Ring 5 Width 5.9mm 6.8mm 6.09mm Thickness 2.35mm 2.78mm 2.28mm Weight 1.9–3g, depending on size 3–4g, depending on size From 2g, depending on size

Materials: The Pro uses titanium, while the Slim is made from a biocompatible resin with a titanium coating.

Battery: The Pro will outlast the Slim by about two days. Circular claims up to 12 days for the Ring 3 Pro, versus 10 days for the Slim.

Health tracking: Only the Pro has the ECG feature and blood pressure tracking.

Circular

Circular Ring platform and AI coach

Circular has built its following on a subscription-free model, giving ring owners full access to core health tracking metrics along with its Kira AI health companion, a feature most competitors charge for even when they offer a free tier.

However, the company isn’t fully closing the door on charging for advanced medical features, with some of these showing as “limited time” in the app.

Price and availability

Circular hasn’t announced pricing or a firm release date for either Ring 3 model yet. The company says those details, along with preorder timing, will arrive in the coming months. We’ll update this article when the company announces more details.
